ORDERS OF THE DAY.
Unemployment Insurance (Amendment) Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.
Motion made and Question proposed:
"That the Bill be now read a Second
time."
The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.
Andrews): I desire to explain to the
House, at the very beginning of the remarks which I feel it is necessary that I
should make on this occasion, that this
House could not have been called together
sooner, because the British Bill, of which
this is a counterpart, did not receive the
Royal Assent until about a fortnight ago.
Since then our Measure had to be drafted
and modified in certain instances so as to
make it applicable to Northern Ireland
A White Paper of an explanatory nature
--which no doubt hon. Members have received-had to be prepared.
I was
anxious that hon. Members on both sides
2057 Unemployment Insurance Bill- 18 FEBRUARY 1930

Second Reading
of the House should have the Bill and
this explanatory statement in their possession for approximately a week before
being called upon to consider the Measure here to-day.
In the first place, I would like to point
out that I do not intend to say one word
of a party character to-day, because I
have always felt that Unemployment Insurance, and in fact the unemployment
problem generally, should be lifted above
ordinary party politics and placed upon
a higher level. It may be said that the
Measure, which was considered "Red"
at Westminster, has turned "Blue"
owing to the fact that it has crossed
the Channel. That does not worry me
to the smallest extent, because what
really counts is what the Measure contains. Unemployment Insurance dates.
back a very long time. The State first
felt it its duty to deal with the matter in
1911, but as far back as 1905 we find that
122 friendly societies and 80 trade unions
were paying unemployment allowance to
their members during periods of trade depression which brought unemployment in
its train.
The Measure of 1911 which, as I have
said, was the first Measure that the State
was responsible for, brought into insurance on a contributory basis those engaged
in several industries-the industries which
at that time were considered to be the
ones which were most liable to industrial
depression, and, consequently, to unemployment. Only about two and a quarter
millions of the industrial population
were brought within the scope of that
great Measure. It, however, was a step,
I feel at any rate, in the right direction
in order that our working people when
anxious for work and unable to find it
should get the means of carrying on.
The next Measure which was placed on
the Statute Book was passed in 1916.
It brought into insurance munition
workers who had been engaged in war
work during the period of hostilities. It
was felt that these people, being recruited
for that particular purpose, would be sure
to be thrown out of employment when
the necessity for making munitions no
longer existed. In addition to that, a year
or so later it was felt that the insurance
scheme was not adequate to meet the
needs of what would occur when the war
was over, and when our troops were disbanded, and so tacked on to unemployment insurance we find what was called
out-of-work donation. It was on a noncontributory basis. It brought within.
its scope many thousands of those who
had been in the forces of the Crown during the war as well as other industrial
workers who were principally engaged in
war work during the war. It cost the
State £62,000,000, and I do not think
anyone will grudge the money when we
reflect what would have undoubtedly
occurred if this money had not been made
available to help those to whom we were
so deeply indebted.
So legislation proceeded up to 1920
when what was called the principal Act
was passed at Westminster. The reason
I feel it is desirable that I should refer
to the history-if I may call it by that
name of unemployment insurance is because anyone who has studied the matter
must be aware of the fact that one Measure has been built on the top of the
other, year after year, and to understand
completely what we are doing to-day we
must have a certain knowledge at any rate
of what has gone before. Besides, I am
aware of the fact that there are many
Members in this House on both sides who
were not in the House when I had the
privilege of bringing before it the principal or major Measures on other occasions. Therefore, I feel it will be helpful
to hon. Members if I give a summary
of the legislation which has taken place
in pretty quick succession year after year.
was
Since 1911 there have been no fewer than
22 Insurance Bills passed. I myself have
been responsible for no fewer than 15
Measures since this Parliament
established. It is a record of ups and
downs, of advances and retreats, I readily
admit, but on the whole I am glad to
think that it has been an advance along
the road of progress leading to better
things. The Act of 1920, to which I have
already referred, brought into insurance.
on a contributory basis about twelve
millions of the industrial population. It
included within its scope all industrial
workers over 16 years of age, except farm
labourers and domestic servants, and it
also brought into insurance for the first
time clerical workers, provided their salary
did not amount to more than £250 a year.
As I have said, it was on a contributory basis, and it was designed on a strict
actuarial basis, in other words, the
sanctity of the insurance principle was
preserved in that Measure, but it has
frequently been departed from since.
2059 Unemployment Insurance Bill- HOUSE OF COMMONS

Second Reading
[Mr. Andrews]
What I mean by the insurance principle
is simply benefits paid on a strict relation
to contributions paid. Benefit was paid
for one week in consideration of six weeks'
work having been done, or, in other
words, six contributions having been paid
to the Fund. The benefits were small,
the contributions were small, and benefit
was only payable in any one year for a
maximum period of fifteen weeks, but it
was found that when the industrial depression fell upon these islands with great
severity during the years 1921 and 1922
this principal Act was quite inadequate
to deal with the position which was then
created as the aftermath of the war, and
so quite a number of other Measures were
passed at Westminster dealing with the
matter.
They were most of them of minor
importance, and I do not want to take
up the time of the House by alluding to
them. There was one, however, in which
I was particularly interested. It
happened that it was introduced at Westminster between the time our Parliament
was opened by His Majesty the King in
June, 1921, and when we took over our
powers in January, 1922. That Measure,
amongst other things, introduced for the
first time the payment of what is known
as dependants allowances.
I remember reading in the paper one
morning that Mr. Lloyd George, the then
Prime Minister of England, had been
asked in Parliament if that Measure
would apply to Ireland. I can quite
understand his being at that time quite
fed up with Ireland, to use a homely expression, and so on the spur of the moment
he said it would not. The position that
we here were placed in was that Westminster did not propose to include us
within the Measure, and we had not the
power to pass a similar Measure ourselves.
After consulting our Prime Minister and
some of my other colleagues it was decided
that I should go to Westminster and point
out the reasonableness of things to Mr.
Lloyd George, and I am entitled to say
that he met me very fairly. On the day
I had the interview with him he stated
in the House of Commons that on reconsidering the matter the Measure would
apply to Northern Ireland.
The reason I mention that is this. It
was at that time the Government's decision was taken here to keep in step with
Great Britain in connection with unemployment insurance, and from that date
up to the present we have never varied
from that decision. I can easily convince
any impartial person that it was a wise
decision to have taken, and that it is a
wise decision to adhere to, and that if we
had taken any other course we would have
done a great injustice to the working
people of Northern Ireland as well as to
the employers and the community
generally.
Mr. HEALY: You have not convinced
your own paper, the "News-Letter."
Mr. ANDREWS: Papers do not worry
me, provided I feel I am doing the right
thing. That brings me to the Act of
1924, which was introduced by the
Socialist Government. It was a most
important Measure. It increased the
rates of benefit, it did away with refunds,
it made what is called the fourth statutory
condition, that is the much-disputed "not
genuinely seeking work" condition, applicable for the first time to both forms of
benefit. Still it was an important step
forward in many respects, and I readily
admit it held the field for a considerable
number of years.
It
Later on, however, it was considered
that it was not a Measure which for many
reasons could be looked upon as a permanent one, and so a committee called
the Blanesburgh Committee was set up.
It was composed of representatives of the
general community and representatives of
the employers and workers, and the present Minister of Labour in Great Britain
was a member of that Committee.
produced a unanimous Report, and on
that Report was passed the Act which
has held the field ever since, called the
Blanesburgh Act. It did a great many
things. For example, it laid down the
existing rates of benefit. It widened
the class of dependants and substituted
one class of benefit for two. It settled
the procedure for the determination of
claims to benefit. It did away with
rota committees and the ministerial discretion.
The
It set out definitely two main conditions
for the receipt of benefit, the fulfilment of
which the applicant had to prove.
first one was that he should have 30 contributions to his credit in the last two
years previous to the date of his claim,
and the second was that he was genuinely
seeking work. As regards the second condition I propose to speak later on.
gards the first it was felt that to apply it
immediately would involve for a great
many unemployed persons considerable
hardships. There was therefore estab-
As re-
Unemployment Insurance Bill- 18 FEBRUARY 1930
Second Reading
lished what was known as the transitional
period, when this 30 contribution qualification was not applied to those over 18
years of age, and unemployed persons
could obtain benefit on much easier tests.
That Act also established a thirteen week
review, and it did away with the family
income test.
That is the Act which has been
administered ever since, but I think I
ought to point out at this stage, because
it is a matter of supreme importance, that
our Government for many years felt that
we in Northern Ireland were not a safe
insurance risk, that we had too few industries to depend upon, and in addition
to that our two main industries had been
so engaged in war work that after the war
they found themselves in a particularly
unenviable position. It was felt also that
in the preparation of the White Paper
which set out the financial relations between Great Britain and Northern Ireland, unintentionally an injustice was
done to us here, because no allowance had
been made in that White Paper to enable
us to bear an excess of unemployment over
that which at any time existed in Great
Britain.
We appealed as a Government to several
successive Governments at Westminster in
order that they should help us out of the
position as we felt they were entitled to
do, but we appealed in vain until 1926,
when the Government of that day, after
an exhaustive inquiry, agreed that our
claim was just and that we were entitled
to expect financial assistance in order that
we might bear the burden. Had we not
obtained that agreement the effect would
have been that we could not have gone on
as we were going, because we had pledged
our Unemployment Fund to the extent of
three-and-a-half millions, and had borrowed money to carry on to that extent.
We were then faced with this position,
that we would have to consider lowering
benefits to the extent of one-third and at
the same time increasing contributions to
the extent of double if we were to keep
our Fund from getting further into debt,
or else we would have to get assistance
from Great Britain, which we felt we were
entitled to obtain.
Well, as I say, we succeeded, and so
the Re-insurance Agreement came upon
the scene. It was made an Agreement
which was to last for four and half
years in order that the experiment might
a
have time to show what its effect would
be. But in 1928 we felt that we were in
a somewhat insecure position owing to
certain eventualities which might occur,
and so, believing that a bird in the hand
was worth two in the bush, we appealed
to the same British Government to make
the Agreement permanent, and, all
honour to them, they did it. I say that
apart altogether from party considerations. I look upon this Agreement as the
charter of our working people here, because it ensures for them that so long as
we here pay equal taxation and pay contributions equal to those of our friends
on the other side of the Channel our
working people will receive equal benefits
when unemployed.
Before I deal with the Measure which
it is my duty to bring before the House
to-day, I would like to say a word or two
of a general character in connection with
unemployment insurance. I scarcely ever
open a newspaper, I scarcely ever meet
many people assembled together without
seeing or hearing appeals being made
to the Government on the grounds
that the dole, as ill-informed people
call it, should be discontinued, that
it should be wiped off the slate so
far as legislation and administration
are concerned. These people take the
view that it was not necessary in days
gone by, and that it ought not to be
necessary to-day. They forget, in my
opinion, that industrial conditions have
changed entirely, that large public companies have taken the place of private
firms, that in days gone by private firms.
continued to struggle on notwithstanding
difficult industrial times, and that nowadays it very often occurs, although not
always, that when it does not suit a firm
to work full time it is simply placed on
short time or stopped altogether.
Under these changed conditions changes
had to be made in legislation to meet
the new conditions created. Obviously,
people cannot be allowed to starve. We
are all agreed on that, and if they cannot
obtain work surely it is better and less
demoralising to carry them for a time on
an insurance scheme than to drive them
on to the rates, as was too frequently done
in days gone by. Therefore, I say, and I
say advisedly, that in my opinion, for
what it is worth, unemployment insurance in some form or other has got to
remain
the Statute Book, and the
payment of unemployment benefit
upon
can
Unemployment Insurance Bill- HOUSE OF COMMONS
Second Reading
[Mr. Andrews]
only stop when the happy time arrives
when there is work for all.
Coming to the Bill itself, hon. Members will see that the first Clause reduces
the insurance age to 15, when it is reduced to that age in Great Britain. If
I may say so, there has been a great deal
of loose thinking and equally loose talking about this Clause. It has been said
by people who profess to be authorities
that this means paying unemployment insurance benefit to persons of 15 years of
age. It does nothing of the kind. What
it does do is this: It brings them into
the insurance scheme. It means that if
they are in work they will have to pay
thirty contributions and then become unemployed before they can get any benefit.
It means that if they stay on at school
they will be credited with up to twenty
contributions on the basis of one contribution for every two weeks they remain
at school, but even when they have received gratis these twenty contributions,
or rather, to express it more correctly,
when they have been credited with these
twenty contributions, they will not be entitled to draw benefit but they will have
to do at least ten weeks work and then
become unemployed through no fault of
their own before they become entitled to
draw benefit. Personally, I do not hesitate to say that I do not think this provision is at all unreasonable, because,
after all, it is hard to draw the line and to
say that a young person of 16 years, if
unemployed, is entitled to draw benefit,
at a reduced rate, of course, compared
with an adult, and that an unemployed
person of 15 years of age is not to have
a similar advantage.
The next provision of the Bill to which
I desire to refer is Clause 2. It increases
the rates of benefit for certain young persons of twenty years and under, and in
some instances it increases the dependants' rate. Again I approve of this
Clause. I do not hesitate to say it. The
increases given to young persons are not
extravagant, and it should be remembered in this connection that they are less
than they were prior to the Blanesburgh
Act being passed. The additional persons who are brought into the scheme of
things as dependants I fully approve of.
Again I do not hesitate to say so.
Clause
3 is an unimportant Clause dealing with
the question of the stamping of cards, and
that brings me to Clauses 4, 5 and 6,
which I propose to deal with together as
they all deal with the same thing,
namely, the conditions governing the receipt of benefit. Clause 6 repeals the old
fourth Statutory condition around which
has centred for a considerable number of
years a great deal of controversy directed
from different angles. Personally, I am
very pleased, and I know many hon.
Members on both sides of the House are
pleased that we have heard the last of
this condition for the receipt of benefit.
The reason I am glad it has disappeared
is that I never felt happy in having to
administer it. It was a most difficult
condition to administer, because, after
all, it was very largely a psychological
test directed to discover, so far as it is
possible to discover-and that, in my
opinion, is not very far-what the mind of
another person is; in other words, to
ascertain whether a claimant was really
earnestly looking for work, and whether
or not he was available for it and was
willing to accept it. I am quite sure that
the Statutory Courts, in administering
this condition, felt themselves under very
serious difficulties on many occasions. It
is true that they brought to their aid all
the evidence they could obtain. They
took into consideration, for instance, the
claimants industrial record, they took into
consideration the opportunities for employment that the claimant might reasonably be expected to accept, and they took
into consideration quite a number of
other matters, amongst which was any
proof of a reliable character which the
claimant could bring forward to show
that he had been looking for work prior
to his claim being reviewed. The effect
of this condition, I quite admit, was this;
that it often drove claimants to look for
work which they knew was not there, and
a most demoralising process it must have
been. That brings me to express the

There is another provision to which I
wish to refer and that is Clause 7. In the
past it is too true that workers who were
insured persons were afraid to accept employment of an uninsurable nature for
fear that later on it might be held that
they were no longer insured persons.
This Clause rectifies that wrong,
and, in future, workers who are
in insured industries need have no
hesitation in accepting employment if they
desire to do so as farm workers or in connection with other occupations which do
not come within the insurance field.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear).
Clause 6 is also one of considerable importance, because it provides the machinery for the determination of claims.
It removes the insurance officer's discretion. In the Act of 1924 the Ministerial
discretion, as I have said, disappeared,
very much to my satisfaction. Now the
insurance officer's discretion disappears
and the whole responsibility will rest in
future, with the exception of the question
of unemployment created by trade disputes, upon the court of referees and the
umpire.
Unemployment Insurance Bill- HOUSE OF COMMONS
Second Reading
[Mr. Andrews]
Clause 9 provides that benefit shall be
continued until the claims have actually
been disallowed by the court or umpire.
Here again I feel that there is a great
deal to be said in support of this change.
Before the practice was that the claimant
lost his benefit before his case was submitted to the court and only had it restored to him if the court found in his
favour. Very frequently the absence of
benefit for one, two, or three weeks
created a great hardship in the homes of
unemployed people and this provision will
prevent that regrettable circumstance occurring in future.
Clause 16 is also a very important one
and it is the last one to which I feel it
will be necessary for me to refer. It extends what I have already referred to, the
transitional period, for another year and
it transfers from the fund to the Exchequer in respect of transitional claims
the liability for the cost of the
benefit and administration as from 1st
April last. I have already explained that
the transitional period was introduced so
as to prevent hardships that would occur
if the provision making it necessary for
the claimant to prove or show that he had
30 contributions to his credit in the two
years prior to his claim being made had
been in force under existing conditions.
This provision, as I have already said,
makes it easier for the claimant to receive
benefit than it would otherwise be.
The reason the liability is being transferred to the Exchequer is this: The fund
in Great Britain was in debt a few weeks
ago to the extent of 36 million pounds.
The maximum borrowing power was 40
million pounds, and, therefore, the Government was up against either asking for
further borrowing powers, which would
simply have been putting off the evil day,
or arranging that the burden of this
transitional provision would be removed
from the fund and placed upon the Exchequer. And I do not think it is unfair that the change should be made, because, after all, when persons have been
deemed to be outside the insurance field,
at any rate for a time, and when the
community decided that these men must
continue to receive financial assistance it
does not appear to me to be unreasonable
that the community should bear the cost,
rather than it should be placed principally
upon the workers who are employed and
upon their employers. Of course I am
sorry to admit that it puts a heavy burden
upon the Exchequer.
I do not propose to allude to the financial position at any great length because
that will be dealt with very fully, I am
sure, to-morrow by the Minister of Finance
or his Financial Secretary when introducing the financial Resolution. I
think it is sufficient that I should say this
that this provision which I have referred
to to-day will place an additional burden
upon the fund of approximately £404,000
per annum on the basis of 16 per cent. unemployment continuing. On the other side.
of the account we must remember that in
July last we helped the fund considerably
by increasing the State's contribution from
.4 of the combined contributions of employers and workers to half the combined
contributions of employers and workers.
That augments the revenue of the fund to
the extent of approximately £70,000 per
annum. In addition to that it will be
observed by those who have studied the
White Paper that the transfer to the
Exchequer of this benefit payable under
this transitional condition will relieve
the fund of £120,000 this year and it
will relieve the fund, on the same basis,
of £400,000 next year.
It is hoped that these changes will keep
the fund, at any rate in Great Britain,
in no worse state than it is in to-day.
Whether that will be so or not, only the
future can tell. However, in that connection, I do not think we need have any
very great anxiety, because, owing to the
Re-insurance Agreement, to which I have
referred at considerable length, our fund
is kept in parity with the British fund.
The debt upon our fund at the present
time is round about £800,000. Of course
we have in addition the debt of £3,000,000
which stands in a suspense account, and
which is being gradually reduced by the
annual payments made by the Exchequer
of £100,000. That was incurred in the
early days, for reasons that I have already
explained to the House, and it is unnecessary to repeat what I have already
said in that connection.
I should like to say that, personally, I

I have the facts from the "Spectator".

At the present time we are living in an

nation, because to-day we have our young
people coming on and work is not
going to be obtained for them. I am sure

the workers of Northern Ireland. I
believe after all-and I am going to say
it
without reservation-that the time has
come when the unemployment question
Iwill have to be tackled and when there

I gladly support this Bill to-day. I am

The FINANCIAL SECRETARY OF
THE MINISTRY OF FINANCE (Mr.
Barbour): In moving the Resolution
which stands in the name of my right hon.
Friend (Mr. Pollock) I propose to follow
the order of the Resolution itself, and
I would ask hon. Members in this connection to refer to the last page of the
Financial Memorandum which appears on
the White Paper which deals with this
Measure.
The provisions of the Bill have two
main financial effects:-
(1) A permanent increase in the
charges on the Unemployment Insurance Fund; and
(2) A temporary increase affecting
the Exchequer, due to the extension for
a further year of "transitional" benefit, coupled with a transfer of liability
for such expenditure from the fund to
the Exchequer.
The second of these imposes directly a
heavy charge upon the State funds, but
both changes have their repercussion on
the amount of the Equalisation Payment
payable under the provisions of the Insur-

To explain paragraph (b) (i) of the
Resolution I should perhaps reiterate to
the Committee that under present legislation transitional benefit would cease to
be payable on the 18th April, 1931.
Furthermore in the year ending on that
date transitional benefit would be paid
only on those claims dated prior to 19th
April, 1930. The Bill postpones the
closing date for payment until the 18th
April, 1932. The net effect of this postponement is that the fund becomes liable
for one additional full year's transitional
benefit spread equally over the two years
1930-31 and 1931-32. Against this liability the Bill provides for the fund being
recouped from the Exchequer, the amount
of all transitional benefit paid on claims
in benefit years commencing on and after
1st April, 1929, until the expiry of transitional benefit, and it is this charge for
which the Resolution proposes to make
financial provision, namely, the transfer
from the fund to the Exchequer of all
liability for benefit payments to
sitional claimants, including the cost of
administering such benefits. The assumption of this liability by the State is really
an alternative to allowing the fund to
drift into an insolvent position.
tran-
It is estimated that the Exchequer will
have to find £120,000 in the current
financial year under this head; £400,000
in 1930-31, and £200,000 in 1931-2, and,
in addition, the cost of administering the
benefit in question, which is estimated to
amount to £10,000 in the current year,
£30,000 in 1930-31, and £15,000 in
1931-32.
I need not dwell upon the magnitude of
these charges, save to say that they will
undoubtedly operate as a very serious
burden on the finances of the Province.
Reference has already been made to the
effect of the present proposals upon the
calculation of the equalisation payment
under our Insurance Agreement with
Great Britain, and, in this connection, I
would refer you to the last paragraph of

at the end of the White Paper in hon.
Members' hands. The calculation of
equalisation payment which is designed to
achieve parity between the state of indebtedness of the British and Northern
Irish funds and of the resultant contribution from Great Britain is an extremely
complicated affair, and hon. Members will
probably be content with the statement
made in the White Paper that the effect
under our Insurance Agreement will be to
reduce the net charge on the Exchequer of
Northern Ireland by an estimated sum of
£23,000 in 1929-30 and £33,000 in 1930-
31. These estimates will come under review on another occasion when the estimates for the Ministry of Labour are under
consideration. I beg to move.

Mr. BEATTIE: I want to be definite
about this, because there is a big question

Member seems to be under the impression that there is a flat period of hours
which is applicable to all clubs. That is
not so.
Mr. BEATTIE: For Sunday?
Sir DAWSON BATES: I think the
hon. Member will find that it rests entirely with the magistrates. Clubs must
make certain rules for carrying on their
clubs, and when a club makes application
for the renewal of its licence it is entirely a matter for the magistrate to say,
"I am not satisfied with those rules, and
you will have to alter them to suit my
views." Therefore it is absurd to suggest that the same rules as regards hours
of closing are applicable to every club.
I recollect the question being asked by
the Member for North Antrim, and I
prepared a certain return which was
mainly based on a return that had previously been laid on the Table of this
House. Those were the latest returns
we had. If the hon. Member wants further information I shall be only too glad
to furnish him with it, but I do not know
whether he refers to the recent licensing
sessions or the previous sessions.
Mr. BEATTIE: The licensing sessions
of January, 1929, when the rule was
made that no club should be open after
10-30 p.m. on Sunday.
Sir DAWSON BATES: I am not
aware of that declaration, and I should
say, speaking off-hand, that it is entirely
ultra vires for a magistrate to lay down
that rule. He might have said, "I am
not going to grant a licence to the club
unless the rules provide that the club
shall close at 10-30 on Sunday." I am
not aware that that has been given effect
to at all, because each case is dealt with
entirely on its merits. It is a matter
entirely for the magistrates whether or
not they approve of the rules passed by
the club. One club might be 9-30 and
another club might be 11 o'clock.

ASSISTANT SECRETARIES,
MINISTRY OF AGRICULTURE.
1. Lieut.-Colonel GORDON asked the
Minister of Agriculture whether he can
state why it is now considered necessary
to have two Assistant Secretaries in this
Ministry instead of one?
Mr. POLLOCK: In view of certain retirements which have already taken place
or are due to take place within the next
few years, it has been considered desirable
to reorganise the administrative staff of
the Department. In order to facilitate.
this reorganisation, one Assistant Secretary and one Principal Officer have been
replaced by two Assistant Secretaries,
but merely as a temporary measure. No
permanent additional charge is involved.

The MINISTER OF COMMERCE
(Mr. Barbour): The quantities of the

Linen, 111,983 cwts.

TEXTILE FIRMS IN LIQUIDATION.
3. Mr. NIXON asked the Minister of
Commerce whether he can state the number of firms engaged in the various
branches of the textile industry in Northern Ireland which have been closed
since 1923 ?
Mr. BARBOUR: I find, on reference
to the records kept by the Registrar of
Joint Stock Companies, that 55 limited
companies engaged in the textile industries have gone into liquidation within.
the period 1st January, 1929 to 31st
December, 1929. I should mention,
however, that this numerical loss has
been more than offset by new registrations within the same period. My Department has no information in regard to
the liquidation of unincorporated firms
which, as the hon. Member will be
aware, are not registered under the
Companies Acts.

on the buses belonging to the Belfast and

ROYAL ULSTER CONSTABULARY
-HOSPITAL TREATMENT.
Mr. NIXON asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether he can state if there
are any instructions requiring members
of the Royal Ulster Constabulary when
undergoing hospital treatment to go to
Craigavon Hospital?
Sir DAWSON BATES: With a view
to making improved arrangements f
hospital treatment for members of the
R.U.C. in Belfast, an agreement was arrived at with the authorities of the Craigavon Hospital for the reception and treatment of such members of the Force.
Instructions were consequently issued to
the medical attendants in Belfast providing that members of the Force requiring hospital treatment were to be sent in
the ordinary course to the Craigavon
Hospital or Mater Hospital. This, of
course, did not preclude any members of
the Force from selecting any other hospital in which accommodation could be
secured, and instances of this kind have
from time to time occurred.
ENNISKILLEN PETTY SESSIONS.
Mr. NIXON asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether his attention has
been drawn to a report in the "Belfast
Evening Telegraph" of a scene between
the magistrates at Enniskillen Petty Sessions on the 17th February, 1930, and
whether he can inform the House as to
what steps he proposes to take to terminate
these scenes.
Sir DAWSON BATES: My attention
has been drawn to the incident referred to
by the hon. Member, in which difference
of opinion arose between the magistrates
at the Enniskillen Petty Sessions in regard to the chairmanship of the Court,
and I may say that, while I greatly
regret that such difference of opinion and
unseemly incidents should have occurred,
the selection of a chairman at petty sessions is a matter for mutual agreement
between the magistrates present at petty
sessions, and is not one in which I have
any power to interfere.
I have, however, conveyed these views
to the magistrates, and can only express
the earnest hope that mutual accommodation on both sides will result in good
feeling being restored.

ARREST OF MRS. M. RAFFERTY,
OMAGH.
Mr. HEALY asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether he has had anv
report from the County Inspector of the
Written Answers
Written Answers
24 FEBRUARY 1930
Royal Ulster Constabulary concerning the
arrest of Mrs. M. Rafferty, Castle Street,
Omagh, on the 7th November last, on a
charge formulated against another person
of the same surname at Westport; whether
he can say who was responsible for identifying Mrs. Rafferty with the offence, and
bringing her all the way to Co. Mayo;
whether a warrant was issued for her
arrest in the North; and whether he is
aware that Mrs. Rafferty has received a
letter from the Free State authorities saying that the fault lies with the Royal
Ulster Constabulary?
Sir DAWSON BATES: I have received
a full report on the matter in question.
The warrant was received from the Free
State authorities for the arrest of a woman
who was wanted at Westport and whose
description answered that of the woman
referred to in this question. The warrant
was executed and the woman was conveyed by the Free State police to Westport where the principal witness failed to
identify her and she was released.
I am not aware that any such letter as
that referred to in the latter part of the
question has been received.
I am fully satisfied that the Royal
Ulster Constabulary did not act improperly in the steps which they took to
execute the warrant.
POLICE INQUIRIES IN BELFAST.
Mr. CONNELLAN asked the Minister
of Home Affairs whether, during the past
few months numerous visits have been
paid by members of the Police Force, at
various hours of the night, to the homes
of several young men in various parts of
the City of Belfast; whether these men
and their relations were questioned as to
their whereabouts some time prior to the
police visits; whether the police visits had
reference to supposed political activities,
and if any assurance can be given that
such visits and questionings have now
definitely ceased?
Sir DAWSON BATES: I am aware
that the police have found it necessary to
institute inquiries of the nature indicated.
It would not, however, be in the public
interest to disclose either the reason for
these inquiries, or their result, nor can
I give any such assurance as that asked
for in the latter part of the hon. Member's question.
I may, however, say that I am entirely
satisfied that in carrying out these investigations the police in no way exceeded
their duty.

HOUSE OF COMMONS
Sir Dawson Bates]
The rate of wages paid by a local
authority to surfacemen is a matter entirely within the province of the local
authority concerned, and is not one in
respect of which the Ministry has any
jurisdiction. The hon. Member will appreciate that the Ministry could not,
therefore, take into consideration the
wages paid in respect of any claim when
determining whether or not assistance
should be afforded from the Road Fund.
I understand that an application for
an increase of wages was recently made to
the Londonderry County Council by the
Transport Workers' Union on behalf of
the surfacemen, and that the Council did
not see its way to grant the increase.
The wages paid to road surfacemen in
the various counties are as follows:-
County Antrim.-25s per week in certain rural districts, and 30s per week
in other rural districts. Labourers
engaged in tar spraying, etc., receive
extra payment of 6d, 1s and 1s 6d per
day according to the nature of the
special work.
County Armagh.-27s 6d per week.
County Down.-27s 6d per week in the
Banbridge Rural District, 28s per
week in the Newry No. 1 Rural
District, and 30s per week in the remaining six rural districts in the
county.
From the 1st April next the rate of
wages to be paid in the Banbridge and
Newry No. 1 Rural Districts will be 30s
per week.
The above particulars apply to surfacemen engaged on Class III roads. Surfacemen employed on Class I and Class II
roads in County Down are all paid 30s
per week, and men engaged at tar spraying and similar jobs receive either 6d,
9d or 1s per day extra according to the
nature of the work on which they are
engaged.
County Fermanagh.-30s per week.
County Londonderry.-Surfacemen are
paid according to a scale beginning at
18s per week for boys, and rising to
25s per week. 78 out of 97 labourers
receive the maximum wage of 25s per
week.
County Tyrone.-Surfacemen start at
25s per week, rising to 27s 6d per
week after six months' service. Six
men in each road gang receive 1s per
day extra for work connected with
tar spraying.
REGISTRATION OF CLUBS.
Mr. BEATTIE asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether he can state how
many clubs are registered in the Six
Counties under the Registration of Clubs
(Ireland) Act, 1904; how many of these
clubs are registered in the City of Belfast
and how many outside Belfast; whether
there are any restrictions regarding hours
for the sale or supply of excisable liquors
for consumption on the club premises to
members of the club or visitors; what are
the hours for the sale or supply of excisable liquors for consumption on the club
premises to members of the club or visitors
for each registered club in the Six Counties and total sales of each club for the
calendar year ending January, 1930?
Sir DAWSON BATES: The annual
return in respect of the calendar year
1929, which will shortly be laid before
Parliament in pursuance of Section 11
sub-section (4) of the Intoxicating Liquor
Act, 1927, will contain the particulars
which the hon. Member seeks.
This return is almost ready for presentation, but certain particulars will not be
available until the early part of next
month, and I suggest, therefore, that possibly the hon. Member would prefer to
await this return, which will contain all
the information he requires, and I would
ask him, therefore, to postpone this
question.

Prorogation
The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.
Andrews): The Belfast City and District Water Commissioners are at present
engaged on one relief scheme towards
which my Department is giving financial
assistance, and my latest information is
that the watchmen employed on the

Sir DAWSON BATES: The Ministry
has just received the minutes of the meeting at which the appointment was made
by the Belfast Board of Guardians to the
position of inspector under the Children
Act, 1908. No special qualifications were
laid down for the post. The Board decided to have a man appointed to do this
special work, although the Child Welfare
Committee recommended that the person
appointed should be a woman having

the actual appointment is one that can be
approved, the matter will be fully inquired into.
TEMPORARY RELIEVING
OFFICER.
Mr. BYRNE asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether he is aware that
the Belfast Board of Guardians, at their
last meeting, proceeded to appoint a temporary Relieving Officer; whether the post
only became vacant on that day; whether
proper notice was given to the members or
the post advertised for; whether this is
the usual and correct practice; whether
the person appointed to this position
made any application either oral or
written, and whether it is the intention of
the Ministry to sanction these appointments without a searching enquiry!
Sir DAWSON BATES: The Belfast
Board of Guardians, at their last meeting, made an appointment to the post of
temporary Relieving Officer which became vacant on that day. This appointment has just been reported to the

Mr. NIXON asked the Minister of
Labour whether he can state the number of unemployed persons in Northern
Ireland, as shown by the Register, and

1923 ?
Mr. ANDREWS: The latest return,

number of persons registered at Employment Exchanges in Northern Ireland as
42,893. The corresponding figure for

STATE MEDICAL SERVICE.
Mr. HEALY asked the Minister of

The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.
Andrews): I desire to explain to the
House, at the very beginning of the remarks which I feel it is necessary that I
should make on this occasion, that this
House could not have been called together
sooner, because the British Bill, of which
this is a counterpart, did not receive the
Royal Assent until about a fortnight ago.
Since then our Measure had to be drafted
and modified in certain instances so as to
make it applicable to Northern Ireland.
A White Paper of an explanatory nature
-which no doubt hon. Members have received-had to be prepared. I was
anxious that hon. Members on both sides
2057 Unemployment Insurance Bill-

Second Reading
of the House should have the Bill and
this explanatory statement in their possession for approximately a week before
being called upon to consider the Measure here to-day.
In the first place, I would like to point
out that I do not intend to say one word
of a party character to-day, because I
have always felt that Unemployment Insurance, and in fact the unemployment
problem generally, should be lifted above
ordinary party politics and placed upon
a higher level. It may be said that the
Measure, which was considered "Red"
at Westminster, has turned "Blue"
owing to the fact that it has crossed
the Channel. That does not worry me
to the smallest extent, because what
really counts is what the Measure contains. Unemployment Insurance dates
back a very long time. The State first
felt it its duty to deal with the matter in
1911, but as far back as 1905 we find that
122 friendly societies and 80 trade unions
were paying unemployment allowance to
their members during periods of trade depression which brought unemployment in
its train.
The Measure of 1911 which, as I have
said, was the first Measure that the State
was responsible for, brought into insurance on a contributory basis those engaged
in several industries-the industries which
at that time were considered to be the
ones which were most liable to industrial
depression, and, consequently, to unemployment. Only about two and a quarter
millions of the industrial population
were brought within the scope of that
great Measure. It, however, was a step,
I feel at any rate, in the right direction
in order that our working people when
anxious for work and unable to find it
should get the means of carrying on.
ment insurance we find what was called
out-of-work donation. It was on a noncontributory basis. It brought within
its scope many thousands of those who
had been in the forces of the Crown during the war as well as other industrial
workers who were principally engaged in
war work during the war. It cost the
State £62,000,000, and I do not think
anyone will grudge the money when we
reflect what would have undoubtedly
occurred if this money had not been made
available to help those to whom we were
so deeply indebted.
The next Measure which was placed on
the Statute Book was passed in 1916.
It brought into insurance munition
workers who had been engaged in war
work during the period of hostilities. It
was felt that these people, being recruited
for that particular purpose, would be sure
to be thrown out of employment when
the necessity for making munitions no
longer existed. In addition to that, a year
or so later it was felt that the insurance
scheme was not adequate to meet the
needs of what would occur when the war
was over, and when our troops were disbanded, and so tacked on to unemploy-
So legislation proceeded up to 1920
when what was called the principal Act
was passed at Westminster. The reason
I feel it is desirable that I should refer
to the history-if I may call it by that
name of unemployment insurance is because anyone who has studied the matter
must be aware of the fact that one Measure has been built on the top of the
other, year after year, and to understand
completely what we are doing to-day we
must have a certain knowledge at any rate
of what has gone before. Besides, I am
aware of the fact that there are many
Members in this House on both sides who
were not in the House when I had the
privilege of bringing before it the principal or major Measures on other occasions. Therefore, I feel it will be helpful
to hon. Members if I give a summary
of the legislation which has taken place
in pretty quick succession year after year.
Since 1911 there have been no fewer than
22 Insurance Bills passed. I myself have
been responsible for no fewer than 15
Measures since this Parliament was
established. It is a record of ups and
downs, of advances and retreats, I readily
admit, but on the whole I am glad to
think that it has been an advance along
the road of progress leading to better
things. The Act of 1920, to which I have
already referred, brought into insurance
on a contributory basis about twelve
millions of the industrial population. It
included within its scope all industrial
workers over 16 years of age, except farm
labourers and domestic servants, and it
also brought into insurance for the first
time clerical workers, provided their salary
did not amount to more than £250 a year.
As I have said, it was on a contributory basis, and it was designed on a strict
actuarial basis, in other words, the
sanctity of the insurance principle was
preserved in that Measure, but it has
frequently been departed from since.
2059 Unemployment Insurance Bill- HOUSE OF COMMONS

Second Reading
[Mr. Andrews]
What I mean by the insurance principle
is simply benefits paid on a strict relation
to contributions paid. Benefit was paid
for one week in consideration of six weeks'
work having been done, or, in other
words, six contributions having been paid
to the Fund. The benefits were small,
the contributions were small, and benefit
was only payable in any one year for a
maximum period of fifteen weeks, but it
was found that when the industrial depression fell upon these islands with great
severity during the years 1921 and 1922
this principal Act was quite inadequate.
to deal with the position which was then
created as the aftermath of the war, and
so quite a number of other Measures were
passed at Westminster dealing with the
matter.
They were most of them of minor
importance, and I do not want to take
up the time of the House by alluding to
them. There was one, however, in which
1 was particularly interested. It
happened that it was introduced at Westminster between the time our Parliament
was opened by His Majesty the King in
June, 1921, and when we took over our
powers in January, 1922. That Measure,
amongst other things, introduced for the
first time the payment of what is known
as dependants allowances.
I remember reading in the paper one
morning that Mr. Lloyd George, the then
Prime Minister of England, had been
asked in Parliament if that Measure
would apply to Ireland. I can quite
understand his being at that time quite
fed up with Ireland, to use a homely expression, and so on the spur of the moment
he said it would not. The position that
we here were placed in was that Westminster did not propose to include us
within the Measure, and we had not the
power to pass a similar Measure ourselves.
After consulting our Prime Minister and
some of my other colleagues it was decided
that I should go to Westminster and point
out the reasonableness of things to Mr.
Lloyd George, and I am entitled to say
that he met me very fairly. On the day
I had the interview with him he stated
in the House of Commons that on reconsidering the matter the Measure would
apply to Northern Ireland.
The reason I mention that is this. It
was at that time the Government's decision was taken here to keep in step with
Great Britain in connection with unemployment insurance, and from that date
up to the present we have never varied
from that decision. I can easily convince
any impartial person that it was a wise
decision to have taken, and that it is a
wise decision to adhere to, and that if we
had taken any other course we would have
done a great injustice to the working
people of Northern Ireland as well as to
the employers and the community
generally.

Mr. HEALY: You have not convinced
your own paper, the "News-Letter."
Mr. ANDREWS: Papers do not worry
me, provided I feel I am doing the right
thing. That brings me to the Act of
1924, which was introduced by the
Socialist Government. It was a most
important Measure. It increased the
rates of benefit, it did away with refunds,
it made what is called the fourth statutory
condition, that is the much-disputed "not
genuinely seeking work" condition, applicable for the first time to both forms of
benefit. Still it was an important step
forward in many respects, and I readily
admit it held the field for a considerable
number of years.
Later on, however, it was considered
that it was not a Measure which for many
reasons could be looked upon as a permanent one, and so a committee called
the Blanesburgh Committee was set up.
It was composed of representatives of the
general community and representatives of
the employers and workers, and the present Minister of Labour in Great Britain
was a member of that Committee. It
produced a unanimous Report, and on
that Report was passed the Act which
has held the field ever since, called the
Blanesburgh Act. It did a great many
things. For example, it laid down the
existing rates of benefit. It widened
the class of dependants and substituted
one class of benefit for two. It settled
the procedure for the determination of
claims to benefit. It did away with
rota committees and the ministerial discretion.
It set out definitely two main conditions
for the receipt of benefit, the fulfilment of
which the applicant had to prove. The
first one was that he should have 30 contributions to his credit in the last two
years previous to the date of his claim,
and the second was that he was genuinely
seeking work. As regards the second condition I propose to speak later on.
As regards the first it was felt that to apply it
immediately would involve for a great
many unemployed persons considerable
hardships. There was therefore estab-

lished what was known as the transitional
period, when this 30 contribution qualification was not applied to those over 18
years of age, and unemployed persons
could obtain benefit on much easier tests.
That Act also established a thirteen week
review, and it did away with the family
income test.
That is the Act which has been
administered ever since, but I think I
ought to point out at this stage, because
it is a matter of supreme importance, that
our Government for many years felt that
we in Northern Ireland were not a safe
insurance risk, that we had too few industries to depend upon, and in addition
to that our two main industries had been
so engaged in war work that after the war
they found themselves in a particularly
unenviable position. It was felt also that
in the preparation of the White Paper
which set out the financial relations between Great Britain and Northern Ireland, unintentionally an injustice was
done to us here, because no allowance had
been made in that White Paper to enable
us to bear an excess of unemployment over
that which at any time existed in Great
Britain.
We appealed as a Government to several
successive Governments at Westminster in
order that they should help us out of the
position as we felt they were entitled to
do, but we appealed in vain until 1926,
when the Government of that day, after
an exhaustive inquiry, agreed that our
claim was just and that we were entitled
to expect financial assistance in order that
we might bear the burden. Had we not
obtained that agreement the effect would
have been that we could not have gone on
as we were going, because we had pledged
our Unemployment Fund to the extent of
three-and-a-half millions, and had borrowed money to carry on to that extent.
We were then faced with this position,
that we would have to consider lowering
benefits to the extent of one-third and at
the same time increasing contributions to
the extent of double if we were to keep
our Fund from getting further into debt,
or else we would have to get assistance
from Great Britain, which we felt we were
entitled to obtain.

a
Before I deal with the Measure which
it is my duty to bring before the House
to-day, I would like to say a word or two
of a general character in connection with
unemployment insurance. I scarcely ever
open a newspaper, I scarcely ever meet
many people assembled together without
seeing or hearing appeals being made
to the Government on the grounds
that the dole, as
as ill-informed people
call it, should be discontinued, that
it should be wiped off the slate so
far as legislation and administration.
are concerned. These people take the
view that it was not necessary in days
gone by, and that it ought not to be
necessary to-day. They forget, in my
opinion, that industrial conditions have
changed entirely, that large public companies have taken the place of private
firms, that in days gone by private firms
continued to struggle on notwithstanding
difficult industrial times, and that nowadays it very often occurs, although not
always, that when it does not suit a firm
to work full time it is simply placed on
short time or stopped altogether.
Under these changed conditions changes.
had to be made in legislation to meet
the new conditions created. Obviously,
people cannot be allowed to starve. We
are all agreed on that, and if they cannot
obtain work surely it is better and less
demoralising to carry them for a time on
an insurance scheme than to drive them
on to the rates, as was too frequently done
in days gone by. Therefore, I say, and I
say advisedly, that in my opinion, for
what it is worth, unemployment insurance in some form or other has got to
remain upon the Statute Book, and the
payment of unemployment benefit
can
Unemployment Insurance Bill- HOUSE OF COMMONS
Second Reading
[Mr. Andrews]
only stop when the happy time arrives
when there is work for all.
Coming to the Bill itself, hon. Members will see that the first Clause reduces
the insurance age to 15, when it is reduced to that age in Great Britain. If
I may say so, there has been a great deal
of loose thinking and equally loose talking about this Clause. It has been said
by people who profess to be authorities
that this means paying unemployment insurance benefit to persons of 15 years of
age. It does nothing of the kind. What
it does do is this: It brings them into
the insurance scheme. It means that if
they are in work they will have to pay
thirty contributions and then become unemployed before they can get any benefit.
It means that if they stay on at school
they will be credited with up to twenty
contributions on the basis of one contribution for every two weeks they remain
at school, but even when they have received gratis these twenty contributions,
or rather, to express it more correctly,
when they have been credited with these
twenty contributions, they will not be entitled to draw benefit but they will have
to do at least ten weeks work and then
become unemployed through no fault of
their own before they become entitled to
draw benefit. Personally, I do not hesitate to say that I do not think this provision is at all unreasonable, because,
after all, it is hard to draw the line and to
say that a young person of 16 years, if
unemployed, is entitled to draw benefit,
at a reduced rate, of course, compared
with an adult, and that an unemployed
person of 15 years of age is not to have
a similar advantage.
The next provision of the Bill to which
I desire to refer is Clause 2. It increases
the rates of benefit for certain young persons of twenty years and under, and in
some instances it increases the dependants' rate. Again I approve of this
Clause. I do not hesitate to say it. The
increases given to young persons are not
extravagant, and it should be remembered in this connection that they are less
than they were prior to the Blanesburgh
Act being passed. The additional persons who are brought into the scheme of
things as dependants I fully approve of.
Again I do not hesitate to say so.
Clause
3 is an unimportant Clause dealing with
the question of the stamping of cards, and
that brings me to Clauses 4, 5 and 6,
which I propose to deal with together as
they all deal with the same thing,
namely, the conditions governing the receipt of benefit. Clause 6 repeals the old
fourth Statutory condition around which
has centred for a considerable number of
years a great deal of controversy directed
from different angles. Personally, I am
very pleased, and I know many hon.
Members on both sides of the House are
pleased that we have heard the last of
this condition for the receipt of benefit.
The reason I am glad it has disappeared
is that I never felt happy in having to
administer it. It was a most difficult
condition to administer, because, after
all, it was very largely a psychological
test directed to discover, so far as it is
possible to discover-and that, in my
opinion, is not very far-what the mind of
another person is; in other words, to
ascertain whether a claimant was really
earnestly looking for work, and whether
or not he was available for it and was
willing to accept it. I am quite sure that
the Statutory Courts, in administering
this condition, felt themselves under very
serious difficulties on many occasions. It
is true that they brought to their aid all
the evidence they could obtain.
They
took into consideration, for instance, the
claimants' industrial record, they took into
consideration the opportunities for employment that the claimant might reasonably be expected to accept, and they took
into consideration quite a number of
other matters, amongst which was any
proof of a reliable character which the
claimant could bring forward to show
that he had been looking for work prior
to his claim being reviewed. The effect
of this condition, I quite admit, was this;
that it often drove claimants to look for
work which they knew was not there, and
a most demoralising process it must have
been. That brings me to express the
opinion that the pendulum had swung too
far against the claimants. Now it is
going to swing right in the other direction.
Mr. COLLINS: Too far?
Mr. ANDREWS: Whether it is too
far or not I am not prepared to say today. Only the test of time can give a
verdict on that, and if it swings too far
in the other direction for a time, as sure
as we are dealing with this matter to-day
it will swing back again to, I hope, what
will be a happy medium.
In the meantime I venture to-day to appeal to employers and to workers in Northern Ire-

Now if I may take it that we are all

There is another provision to which I
wish to refer and that is Clause 7. In the
past it is too true that workers who were
insured persons were afraid to accept employment of an uninsurable nature for
fear that later on it might be held that
they were no longer insured persons.
This Clause rectifies that wrong,
and, in future, workers who are
in insured industries need have no
hesitation in accepting employment if they
desire to do so as farm workers or in connection with other occupations which do
not come within the insurance field.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear).
Clause 6 is also one of considerable importance, because it provides the machinery for the determination of claims.
It removes the insurance officer's discretion. In the Act of 1924 the Ministerial
discretion, as I have said, disappeared,
very much to my satisfaction. Now the
insurance officer's discretion disappears
and the whole responsibility will rest in
future, with the exception of the question
of unemployment created by trade disputes, upon the court of referees and the
umpire.
Unemployment Insurance Bill- HOUSE OF COMMONS
Second Reading
[Mr. Andrews]
Clause 9 provides that benefit shall be
continued until the claims have actually
been disallowed by the court or umpire.
Here again I feel that there is a great
deal to be said in support of this change.
Before the practice was that the claimant
lost his benefit before his case was submitted to the court and only had it restored to him if the court found in his
favour. Very frequently the absence of
benefit for one, two, or three weeks
created a great hardship in the homes of
unemployed people and this provision will
prevent that regrettable circumstance occurring in future.
Clause 16 is also a very important one
and it is the last one to which I feel it
will be necessary for me to refer.
It extends what I have already referred to, the
transitional period, for another year and
it transfers from the fund to the Exchequer in respect of transitional claims
the liability for the cost of the
benefit and administration as from 1st
April last. I have already explained that
the transitional period was introduced so
as to prevent hardships that would occur
if the provision making it necessary for
the claimant to prove or show that he had
30 contributions to his credit in the two
years prior to his claim being made had
been in force under existing conditions.
This provision, as I have already said,
makes it easier for the claimant to receive
benefit than it would otherwise be.
The reason the liability is being transferred to the Exchequer is this: The fund
in Great Britain was in debt a few weeks
ago to the extent of 36 million pounds.
The maximum borrowing power was 40
million pounds, and, therefore, the Government was up against either asking for
further borrowing powers, which would
simply have been putting off the evil day,
or arranging that the burden of this
transitional provision would be removed
from the fund and placed upon the Exchequer. And I do not think it is unfair that the change should be made, because, after all, when persons have been
deemed to be outside the insurance field,
at any rate for a time, and when the
community decided that these men must
continue to receive financial assistance it
does not appear to me to be unreasonable
that the community should bear the cost,
rather than it should be placed principally
upon the workers who are employed and
upon their employers. Of course I am
sorry to admit that it puts a heavy burden
upon the Exchequer.
I do not propose to allude to the financial position at any great length because
that will be dealt with very fully, I am
sure, to-morrow by the Minister of Finance
or his Financial Secretary when introducing the financial Resolution.
think it is sufficient that I should say this
that this provision which I have referred
to to-day will place an additional burden
upon the fund of approximately £404,000
per annum on the basis of 16 per cent. unemployment continuing. On the other side
of the account we must remember that in
July last we helped the fund considerably
by increasing the State's contribution from
.4 of the combined contributions of employers and workers to half the combined
contributions of employers and workers.
That augments the revenue of the fund to
the extent of approximately £70,000 per
annum. In addition to that it will be
observed by those who have studied the
White Paper that the transfer to the
Exchequer of this benefit payable under
this transitional condition will relieve
the fund of £120,000 this year and it
will relieve the fund, on the same basis,
of £400,000 next year.
It is hoped that these changes will keep
the fund, at any rate in Great Britain,
in no worse state than it is in to-day.
Whether that will be so or not, only the
future can tell. However, in that connection, I do not think we need have any
very great anxiety, because, owing to the
Re-insurance Agreement, to which I have
referred at considerable length, our fund
is kept in parity with the British fund.
The debt upon our fund at the present
time is round about £800,000. Of course
we have in addition the debt of £3,000,000
which stands in a suspense account, and
which is being gradually reduced by the
annual payments made by the Exchequer
of £100,000. That was incurred in the
early days, for reasons that I have already
explained to the House, and it is unnecessary to repeat what I have already
said in that connection.
I should like to say that, personally, I
feel very much indebted to my right hon.
Friend, the Minister of Finance, for the

have hesitated to accept, and he has done

capacity for production, thanks to the introduction of machines, is so enormous

The FINANCIAL SECRETARY OF
THE MINISTRY OF FINANCE (Mr.
Barbour): In moving the Resolution
which stands in the name of my right hon.
Friend (Mr. Pollock) I propose to follow
the order of the Resolution itself, and
I would ask hon. Members in this connection to refer to the last page of the
Financial Memorandum which appears on
the White Paper which deals with this
Measure.
The provisions of the Bill have two
main financial effects:
(1) A permanent increase in the
charges on the Unemployment Insurance Fund; and
(2) A temporary increase affecting
the Exchequer, due to the extension for
a further year of "transitional" benefit, coupled with a transfer of liability
for such expenditure from the fund to
the Exchequer.
The second of these imposes directly a
heavy charge upon the State funds, but
both changes have their repercussion on
the amount of the Equalisation Payment
payable under the provisions of the Insur-
2117 Unemployment Insurance-

19 FEBRUARY 1930
Committee
ance Agreement with Great Britain, and
consequently on the amount of that payment which is debited to Northern Ireland.
Turning now to the detailed provisions
of the Resolution, paragraph (a) (i)
authorises the payment of normal State
contribution in respect of children who
are now to enter the insurance scheme as
from age 15 instead of from age 16. My
right hon. Friend has enlarged upon the
main purpose of the provision, and it only
remains for me to acquaint the House
that the amount of the Exchequer grant
in respect of employed juveniles between
15 and 16 years of age is estimated to be
approximately £5,700. Unemployment
and entitlement to benefit being low in
this group it follows that the receipts of
the Unemployment Fund in respect of this
new class of insured person will be considerably in excess of the disbursements,
and the gain which the fund will thus
achieve will diminish proportionately the
equalisation payment. This latter relief to the Exchequer will almost counterbalance the £5,700 increase to which I
have referred.
Paragraph (a) (ii) refers to Clause 13
of the Bill, which takes power to continue
insurance for those workers who are sent
outside Northern Ireland under contract
and who, when the contract ends, come
back to this area. At present such men
may lose all their insurance rights, and
consequently have to requalify on their
return. Only a small sum is involved.
Paragraph (a) (iii) arises from the repeal of Section 5 (5) of the Unemployment Insurance Act, 1920, which relates
to the question of contributions payable.
in respect of persons in receipt of old-age
pensions under the Old Age Pensions
Acts, 1908-19. The reference to this
change in the Bill will be found included
in the second schedule the italicized
portion. My right hon. Friend has explained that this repeal is necessary to
bring the law into conformity with the
present practice, and I would limit my
remarks to the statement that the financial
implications are difficult to estimate, but
may be taken as inconsiderable.
To explain paragraph (b) (i) of the
Resolution I should perhaps reiterate to
the Committee that under present legislation transitional benefit would cease to
be payable on the 18th April, 1931.
Furthermore in the year ending on that
date transitional benefit would be paid
only on those claims dated prior to 19th
April, 1930. The Bill postpones the
closing date for payment until the 18th
April, 1932. The net effect of this postponement is that the fund becomes liable
for one additional full year's transitional
benefit spread equally over the two years
1930-31 and 1931-32. Against this liability the Bill provides for the fund being
recouped from the Exchequer, the amount
of all transitional benefit paid on claims
in benefit years commencing on and after
1st April, 1929, until the expiry of transitional benefit, and it is this charge for
which the Resolution proposes to make
financial provision, namely, the transfer
from the fund to the Exchequer of all
liability for benefit payments to transitional claimants, including the cost of
administering such benefits. The assumption of this liability by the State is really
an alternative to allowing the fund to
drift into an insolvent position.
It is estimated that the Exchequer will
have to find £120,000 in the current
financial year under this head; £400,000
in 1930-31, and £200,000 in 1931-2, and,
in addition, the cost of administering the
benefit in question, which is estimated to
amount to £10,000 in the current year,
£30,000 in 1930-31, and £15,000 in
1931-32.
I need not dwell upon the magnitude of
these charges, save to say that they will
undoubtedly operate as a
very serious
burden on the finances of the Province.
Reference has already been made to the
effect of the present proposals upon the
calculation of the equalisation payment
under our Insurance Agreement with
Great Britain, and, in this connection, I
would refer you to the last paragraph of
the financial memorandum which appears
at the end of the White Paper in hon.
Members' hands. The calculation of
equalisation payment which is designed to
achieve parity between the state of indebtedness of the British and Northern
Irish funds and of the resultant contribution from Great Britain is an extremely
complicated affair, and hon. Members will
probably be content with the statement
made in the White Paper that the effect
under our Insurance Agreement will be to
reduce the net charge on the Exchequer of
Northern Ireland by an estimated sum of
£23,000 in 1929-30 and £33,000 in 1930-
31. These estimates will come under review on another occasion when the estimates for the Ministry of Labour are under
consideration. I beg to move.

and the liquor trade, and the answer

fact. the answer was obsolete, because

Antrim was as follows:-
a

Affairs can state how many clubs are
registered in the Six Counties under

Act, 1904; how many of these clubs

premises to members of the club or
visitors; what are the hours for the sale
or supply of excisable liquors for consumption on the club premises to members of the club or visitors for each
registered club in the Six Counties?

from the opinion expressed by Mr.

open until 1 a.m. on Monday morning.

correct, and if they were not correct why
he issued information that was obsolete.
Subject to the explanation that may be
given by the Minister, I am satisfied that
the hours of closing stated in the answer
to the question were not those in existence at that time.

ASSISTANT SECRETARIES,
MINISTRY OF AGRICULTURE.
1. Lieut.-Colonel GORDON asked the
Minister of Agriculture whether he can
state why it is now considered necessary
to have two Assistant Secretaries in this
Ministry instead of one?
Mr. POLLOCK: In view of certain retirements which have already taken place
or are due to take place within the next
few years, it has been considered desirable
to reorganise the administrative staff of
the Department. In order to facilitate
this reorganisation, one Assistant Secretary and one Principal Officer have been
replaced by two Assistant Secretaries,
but merely as a temporary measure. No
permanent additional charge is involved.

YARN IMPORTS.
2. Mr. NIXON asked the Minister of
Commerce whether he can state the
quantity of yarn imported into Northern
Ireland in 1929, and the names of the
firms importing it?
The MINISTER OF COMMERCE
(Mr. Barbour): The quantities of the
various kinds of yarn imported into
Northern Ireland in 1929 as shown by
the returns of the Board of Customs
and the Harbour Authorities were as
follows:
Linen, 111,983 cwts.
Cotton, 81,996 cwts.
Wool, 12,198 cwts.
Coir, 7,617 cwts.
Jute, 6,755 cwts.
Hemp, 56 cwt.
There is no information in the possession of my Department which would
enable me to reply to the latter part of
the hon. Member's question.
TEXTILE FIRMS IN LIQUIDATION.
3. Mr. NIXON asked the Minister of
Commerce whether he can state the number of firms engaged in the various
branches of the textile industry in Northern Ireland which have been closed
since 1923?
Mr. BARBOUR: I find, on reference
to the records kept by the Registrar of
Joint Stock Companies, that 55 limited
companies engaged in the textile industries have gone into liquidation within
the period 1st January, 1929 to 31st
December, 1929. I should mention,
however, that this numerical loss has
been more than offset by new registrations within the same period.
My Department has no information in regard to
the liquidation of unincorporated firms
which, as the hon. Member will be
aware, are not registered under the
Companies Acts.

ENNISKILLEN PETTY SESSIONS.
Mr. NIXON asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether his attention has
been drawn to a report in the "Belfast
Evening Telegraph" of a scene between.
the magistrates at Enniskillen Petty Sessions on the 17th February, 1930, and
whether he can inform the House as to
what steps he proposes to take to terminate
these scenes.
Sir DAWSON BATES: My attention
has been drawn to the incident referred to
by the hon. Member, in which difference
of opinion arose between the magistrates
at the Enniskillen Petty Sessions in regard to the chairmanship of the Court,
and I may say that, while I greatly
regret that such difference of opinion and
unseemly incidents should have occurred,
the selection of a chairman at petty sessions is a matter for mutual agreement
between the magistrates present at petty
sessions, and is not one in which I have
any power to interfere.
ROYAL ULSTER CONSTABULARY
-HOSPITAL TREATMENT.
I have, however, conveyed these views
to the magistrates, and can only express
the earnest hope that mutual accommodation on both sides will result in good
feeling being restored.
Mr. NIXON asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether he can state if there
are any instructions requiring members
of the Royal Ulster Constabulary when
undergoing hospital treatment to go to
Craigavon Hospital?
Sir DAWSON BATES: With a view
to making improved arrangements for
hospital treatment for members of the
R.U.C. in Belfast, an agreement was arrived at with the authorities of the Craigavon Hospital for the reception and treatment of such members of the Force.
Instructions were consequently issued to
the medical attendants in Belfast providing that members of the Force requiring hospital treatment were to be sent in
the ordinary course to the Craigavon
Hospital or Mater Hospital. This, of
course, did not preclude any members of
the Force from selecting any other hospital in which accommodation could be
secured, and instances of this kind have
from time to time occurred.

Mr. HEALY asked the Minister of

report from the County Inspector of the
Written Answers
Written Answers
24 FEBRUARY 1930
Royal Ulster Constabulary concerning the
arrest of Mrs. M. Rafferty, Castle Street,
Omagh, on the 7th November last, on a
charge formulated against another person
of the same surname at Westport; whether
he can say who was responsible for identifying Mrs. Rafferty with the offence, and
bringing her all the way to Co. Mayo;
whether a warrant was issued for her
arrest in the North; and whether he is
aware that Mrs. Rafferty has received a
letter from the Free State authorities saying that the fault lies with the Royal
Ulster Constabulary?
Sir DAWSON BATES: I have received
a full report on the matter in question.
The warrant was received from the Free
State authorities for the arrest of a woman
who was wanted at Westport and whose
description answered that of the woman
referred to in this question. The warrant
was executed and the woman was conveyed by the Free State police to Westport where the principal witness failed to
identify her and she was released.
I am not aware that any such letter as
that referred to in the latter part of the
question has been received.
I am fully satisfied that the Royal
Ulster Constabulary did not act improperly in the steps which they took to
execute the warrant.
POLICE INQUIRIES IN BELFAST.
Mr. CONNELLAN asked the Minister
of Home Affairs whether, during the past
few months numerous visits have been
paid by members of the Police Force, at
various hours of the night, to the homes
of several young men in various parts of
the City of Belfast; whether these men
and their relations were questioned as to
their whereabouts some time prior to the
police visits; whether the police visits had
reference to supposed political activities,
and if any assurance can be given that
such visits and questionings have now
definitely ceased?
Sir DAWSON BATES: I am aware
that the police have found it necessary to
institute inquiries of the nature indicated.
I may, however, say that I am entirely
satisfied that in carrying out these investigations the police in no way exceeded
their duty.
It would not, however, be in the public
interest to disclose either the reason for
these inquiries, or their result, nor can
I give any such assurance as that asked
for in the latter part of the hon. Member's question.
