The rate of wages paid by a local
authority to surfacemen is a matter entirely within the province of the local
authority concerned, and is not one in
respect of which the Ministry has any
jurisdiction. The hon. Member will appreciate that the Ministry could not,
therefore, take into consideration the
wages paid in respect of any claim when
determining whether or not assistance
should be afforded from the Road Fund.
I understand that an application for
an increase of wages was recently made to
the Londonderry County Council by the
Transport Workers' Union on behalf of
the surfacemen, and that the Council did
not see its way to grant the increase.
The wages paid to road surfacemen in
the various counties are as follows:-
County Antrim.-25s per week in certain rural districts, and 30s per week
in other rural districts. Labourers
engaged in tar spraying, etc., receive
extra payment of 6d, 1s and 1s 6d per
day according to the nature of the
special work.
County Armagh.-27s 6d per week.
County Down.-27s 6d per week in the
Banbridge Rural District, 28s per
week in the Newry No. 1 Rural
District, and 30s per week in the remaining six rural districts in the
county.
From the 1st April next the rate of
wages to be paid in the Banbridge and
Newry No. 1 Rural Districts will be 30s
per week.
The above particulars apply to surfacemen engaged on Class III roads. Surfacemen employed on Class I and Class II
roads in County Down are all paid 30s
per week, and men engaged at tar spraying and similar jobs receive either 6d,
9d or 1s per day extra according to the
nature of the work on which they are
engaged.
County Fermanagh.-30s per week.
County Londonderry.-Surfacemen are
paid according to a scale beginning at
18s per week for boys, and rising to
25s per week. 78 out of 97 labourers
receive the maximum wage of 25s per
week.
day extra for work connected with
tar spraying.
County Tyrone.-Surfacemen start at
25s per week, rising to 27s 6d per
week after six months' service. Six
men in each road gang receive 1s per
REGISTRATION OF CLUBS.
Mr. BEATTIE asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether he can state how
many clubs are registered in the Six
Counties under the Registration of Clubs
(Ireland) Act, 1904; how many of these
clubs are registered in the City of Belfast
and how many outside Belfast; whether
there are any restrictions regarding hours
for the sale or supply of excisable liquors
for consumption on the club premises to
members of the club or visitors; what are
the hours for the sale or supply of excisable liquors for consumption on the club
premises to members of the club or visitors
for each registered club in the Six Counties and total sales of each club for the
calendar year ending January, 1930?
Sir DAWSON BATES: The annual
return in respect of the calendar year
1929, which will shortly be laid before
Parliament in pursuance of Section 11
sub-section (4) of the Intoxicating Liquor
Act, 1927, will contain the particulars
which the hon. Member seeks.
This return is almost ready for presentation, but certain particulars will not be
available until the early part of next
month, and I suggest, therefore, that possibly the hon. Member would prefer to
await this return, which will contain all
the information he requires, and I would
ask him, therefore, to postpone this
question.
BELFAST BOARD OF GUARDIANS.
INSPECTOR UNDER THE
CHILDREN ACT.
Mr. BYRNE asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether he can state if an
appointment of an inspector was made
under Part I of the Children Act, 1908,
at the last meeting of the Belfast Board
of Guardians, and, if so, what qualications, if any, were laid down for the
appointment; whether it is a fact that the
Child Welfare Committee, which deals
specially with matters arising under the
Children Act, 1908, made certain defined
recommendations respecting qualifications;
whether this Board eventually turned
down these recommendations of this Committee, and whether any special reasons
were given for this action?
Written Answers
Prorogation
24 FEBRUARY 1930
Sir DAWSON BATES: The Ministry
has just received the minutes of the meeting at which the appointment was made
by the Belfast Board of Guardians to the
position of inspector under the Children
Act, 1908. No special qualifications were
laid down for the post. The Board decided to have a man appointed to do this
special work, although the Child Welfare
Committee recommended that the person
appointed should be a woman having
The Board of
nursing qualifications.
Guardians, on further consideration, adhered to their original plan, and the
Ministry saw no reason to question this
arrangement. Before deciding whether
the actual appointment is one that can be
approved, the matter will be fully inquired into.
TEMPORARY RELIEVING
OFFICER.
Mr. BYRNE asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether he is aware that
the Belfast Board of Guardians, at their
last meeting, proceeded to appoint a temporary Relieving Officer; whether the post
only became vacant on that day; whether
proper notice was given to the members or
the post advertised for; whether this is
the usual and correct practice; whether
the person appointed to this position.
made any application either oral or
written, and whether it is the intention of
the Ministry to sanction these appointments without a searching enquiry!
Sir DAWSON BATES: The Belfast
Board of Guardians, at their last meeting, made an appointment to the post of
temporary Relieving Officer which became vacant on that day. This appointment has just been reported to the
Ministry with a request for sanction, and
I am not fully aware of the circumstances
under which the appointment was made.
Before any sanction is given, the usual
investigations will be made.

THE UNEMPLOYMENT REGISTER.
Mr. NIXON asked the Minister of
Labour whether he can state the number of unemployed persons in Northern
Ireland, as shown by the Register, and
the corresponding number in November,
1923?
Mr. ANDREWS: The latest return,
which is for the 17th inst., shows the
number of persons registered at Employment Exchanges in Northern Ireland as
42,893. The corresponding figure for
the 5th November, 1923, was 42,169.

discontent on the part of tenants and
leaseholders, arising out of the unsatisfactory conditions of their tenure in
Northern Ireland, and in view of the
fact that the committee appointed to
inquire into this grievance issued a
report as far back as 31st January,
1929, recommending remedial legislation, he is prepared to introduce legislation dealing with this matter during
the present Session of Parliament."
To this the Minister of Home Affairs
replied:-
"The matter is engaging the close
attention of the Government, and I
hope to be in a position to introduce a
Measure at no distant date."

I have another letter. It is not very

Rent Restrictions Bill-

12 MARCH 1935
I do not pretend to bind myself to
every detail of this Bill, but I do say that
in its broad features it will draw attention
-Parliamentary attention at least, and
public attention probably-to the
grievances of a very numerous body of
tenants whose cases have been illustrated
by the hon. Member for Falls. The broad
objective of the Bill is to reduce the rents
payable by these tenants to something
like a just level. That, I take it, is the
fundamental and underlying principle of
the Bill, and I am sure that the hon.
Member for Falls would not be
unreasonable as to reject any reasonable
or well-considered amendments which
may be put forward.
so
There is one point which I do think is
a matter of great public interest. A
tremendous number of these tenants in
the city of Belfast hold and occupy houses
of valuations formerly under £8. These
valuations of £8 and under have now
practically disappeared. They are gone.
At the present moment you will find them
by the thousand. In the coming years
you will find them by the dozen. They
are almost all obliterated. Then the
valuations of houses which were formerly
£26 and under have in many, many cases
been raised above the £26 level. I do
think it would be well, it would be in
the public interest if the responsible.
Minister, who will deal with this Bill later
on, could indicate whether or not, in view
of these revaluations, the position of these
tenants has been worsened or in any way
prejudiced. It is a matter of very great
public perturbation and public anxiety,
because these tenants represent probably
85 or 90 per cent. of the tenants of the
dwelling houses in the city of Belfast.
Therefore, I do suggest to the Minister
that when he comes to reply it would be
desirable and to the public benefit if he
could state what the Government view is
with regard to the exposure of that
tremendous body of tenants to an increase
of rent and other charges connected
with their household expenses, such as
electricity or gas, in view of the recent
sweeping alterations in the valuations.

Mr. GRANT: I would have supported
this Bill whole-heartedly if it had been
confined to one Clause, namely Clause 3
which proposes that a fair rents court
should be set up. I have always
advocated the setting up of a fair rents
court because I think it would be
absolutely fair both to the tenant and to
the landlord. But there are so many
other things embodied in this Bill that I
am afraid I could not agree to it, though
I certainly am strongly in favour of
Clause 3 and hope that the Government
will give serious consideration to this particular Clause.
I would like to emphasise if possible the
remarks that were made by the last
speaker on the question of the position of
houses of under £8 valuation under the
Rent Restrictions Acts. If a fair rents
court were set up I would not be afraid
for those houses, but, owing to what has
taken place within the last few days,
thousands of tenants in Northern Ireland
are very much concerned about their
position, not only on the question of
valuation, but whether the valuation is
going to affect them to such an extent
that those houses will probably come out
of restriction altogether if the Government are not going to take that matter
into consideration. Like the hon. and
learned Member who has just spoken I
would appeal to the responsible Minister
to give us some indication in the House
this afternoon of how those houses are
going to be affected by the recent revaluation. That is about all I have to
say on this particular Bill. I am rather
disappointed about some of the other
Clauses in it, but I would like the Government to give special consideration to
Clause 3 and if possible to bring it into
operation at the earliest possible moment.

support of this Bill with a full knowledge
of the many evils that exist through the

which at the moment stand upon the

are 11,000 of those houses of valuations of

of those 11,000 houses, as a result of the
new revaluation, are now outside the
scope of the Rent Restrictions Acts.
Mr. POLLOCK: No.
Mr. BEATTIE: In accordance with
their new valuations yes.
Is there any
person who can say that only 10 per cent.
has been added to the valuations of
houses of £20 valuation? I am prepared
to say that the valuations of those 11,000
houses are now in the region of £30.
Mr. POLLOCK: It will not affect the

Mr. BEATTIE: Let us get down to it.
It will not affect the rents of those
houses-
Mr. POLLOCK: Restricted houses.
Mr. BEATTIE- -if the Government

on new property.
Mr. GRANT: You are encouraging
them.
Mr. BEATTIE: I am not encouraging
them. And I want to tell the Minister of
Finance, who interrupted just now, that
the moment he does that the reception of
the revaluation of Ulster and the criticism
of that policy will be nothing to the
upheaval that will take place if the
Government dare to interfere with the
Rent Restrictions Act as it stands on the
Statute Book at the moment
in any
direction other than to widen the scope of
it. A Select Committee of this House
gave eighteen days to the consideration of
this question, and made recommendations
to the Government, but the recommendations were ignored or pooh-poohed by the
Government as being impracticable. Today the Government are as determined as
ever they were gradually to squeeze off
the Statute Book laws that were in
existence prior to their coming into power
in Northern Ireland, and as long as I am
in this House they will not be allowed to
go off gently.
What does this Bill purport to do?
The Mover has admitted that the Bill is
not all that it could be or should be. I,
as a member of the Labour Party, presented a Bill in this House for the acceptance of the Government. In that Bill
I incorporated ideas that were accepted
by the Select Committee of this House.
The Government ignored my Bill, and
they ignored the recommendations of the
Select Committee. I should have
reached my foolish days if I expected the
Government to accept a Measure of this
kind in the year 1935. Not likely. The
Government will not accept a Bill of this
description. The Government will be
compelled to do something in regard to
the rents of homes in Northern Ireland.
If they do not do something in regard to
rents they will have to apply themselves
to increasing the purchasing power of the
working classes.
I have always contended that the rents
charged in Northern Ireland were far too
high. I have been repeatedly told that
this is a poorer country than Great
Britain. If it is a poorer country how
can you expect to get a return equal
to that of Great Britain? It is impossible. You went to the hidden
treasure to get £250,000 for the Derry
Bridge; we never found out where you
got that money. If you have hidden
treasure still in your possession I think
you should use it now for the purpose of
assisting the people, provided that you
wish the law allowing a landlord to

charge a rent which cannot be borne from
wages to remain on the Statute Book.
The rent is borne by the lives, the bodies,

Men should not have to deprive themselves of something in the interests of
landlords.
I have got a lead from the Government. They value their property on

of Northern Ireland could pay in rent.

Mr. BEATTIE: But the damage was

I watched a case proceeding through the
High Court. The party with whom I
sympathised was ably represented by
Members on the other side of the House,
whose sympathies were on the side of the
tenant; nevertheless, in their professional
capacity they had to push forward the
case on behalf of their clients. That was
their job; I have no fault to find with
them for doing their duty. But after
that experience I saw that the safeguards
in the Rent Restriction Acts were not
what I want; they are not what the hon.
Member for Falls wants, they are not
what the people want. They want an
Act of Parliament that is bullet-proof,
something that will make the landlords
toe the line.
The object of the Bill before the House
is to alleviate the grave distress that
exists owing to the extortion of rents on
a scale that people are unable to pay.
The hon. Member for Falls holds that a
man who is unemployed should never be
evicted because of his failure to pay his
rent. Would the followers of the
Government agree with that? Would
they agree that the victim of circumstances should be compelled to leave his
home because he cannot pay his rent?
If they agree that that should be so, I
have not heard a voice. I say it should
not be so. If the conditions that prevail
in the industrial world are due to causes
for which the workers are not responsible,
as the Minister of Labour said in his
Dundonald speech last night, the workers
should not be treated as if they were
responsible for unemployment, and they
should not be held responsible for the
things that follow unemployment.
the reduction of their purchasing power
they are unable to meet the requirements

Mr. POLLOCK: They are very lucky.

Mr. BEATTIE: These houses were

houses. It is an outrage to suggest that

the demand for houses was greater than

God
help the owner of that property when he

I would now like to refer to the recommendations made by the Select Committee which was set up to consider the
Rent Restrictions Act. We who served
on that Committee resented very much
the comments of the Parliamentary Secretary of the Ministry of Home Affairs
on the occasion of the presentation of the
Report of that Select Committee to the
House. At that time I had not an
opportunity of saying a word about the
comments of the Parliamentary Secretary. He pooh-poohed the very idea of
the recommendations contained in the
beginning of the Committee's report.
One of our recommendations was that all
houses that had been decontrolled beween the years 1925 and 1932 should be
re-controlled. There were between 5,000
and 7,000 such houses under £26 valuation, and we asked the Government to
re-control those 7,000 houses, but our
recommendation was brushed aside. The
only concession we got was that houses
with a valuation of between £8 and £26
which became vacant from 1932 onwards
should still be controlled, but the tenants
of those 7,000 houses which had become
decontrolled between 1925 and 1932 were
still to be allowed to be fleeced and exploited by the landlords of the property.
That is the reason for the anomalies that
exist to-day all over the city. You have
accomtwo houses of exactly the same
modation, the tenant of one paying a rent
of £1 a week, and the tenant of the
other paying 10s a week.
If you desire to foster this discontent
amongst the people it is all the better for
me, because I rejoice at the number of
rebels the Government are making. I
know they are beginning to realise their
foolishness in having supported the Government at past elections, and if you wish
that state of affairs to continue you have
it in your power to continue it. However, I am asking you to discontinue it
by accepting this Bill now before the
House. I hope you will take a little
advice from one who perhaps you might
say is unable to give any advice. I think
the Bill speaks for itself. It has been
designed to remedy the many grievances
which have been created by the policy
of the Government. In trying to legislate without giving due consideration to
the purchasing power of the working
people, and without considering what percentage of wages can properly be
allocated for rent. I read in a Unionist
newspaper comments about the housing
scheme of the Leeds Corporation, and
they wrote about the very idea of so many
people living free of rent. I say that
that idea is old. Surely the Northern
Government do not suggest that people
who cannot afford to pay rent should lie
in the ditches, in the fields, and in the
roadways. The roads are public property and they could be arrested for
vagrancy. Most fields are private
property, and the farmers could have
them prosecuted for trespassing.
We have no Crown common rights in
Northern Ireland. In England you can
go to the commons and sleep out and
no notice is taken of you. In Northern
Ireland, if you cannot pay your rent you
have to get out, and if you walk the
streets you are arrested for vagrancy.
The result is that people are driven into
the workhouse, where they have to be
maintained at a cost of 11s 74d per head.
You are prepared to pay that so long as
you are able to destroy the homes of
people unable to pay their rent. Is not
that an outrageous mentality for a Government that is supposed to represent the
working people of Northern Ireland.
They do not represent Pottinger Division,
that is certain. I think it is only a fool's
way to deal with this question in the
Rent Restrictions Bill-
Second Reading
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Beattie]
manner in which the Government has
dealt with it in the past. The people
have got to be housed, and it is better
to let them remain in their own homes
free of rent than to drive them into the
workhouse and maintain them at a cost
three times as much as their rent.
When the Leeds Corporation brought
forward this scheme it was criticised by
the Northern Tory as a scheme that was
never thought of in the history of the
world before. As a matter of fact it was
thought of long before our day and
generation. Although I admit there are
anomalies in it, I believe the idea of the
Leeds scheme will spread, and when
America brings forward its great idea of
technocracy perhaps you will become inspired with the idea that not only will
you have to keep people in their homes
without paying rent, but you will have
to keep them clad and provide them with
plenty of recreation without any return.
In conclusion, I ask the Government to
seriously consider this Bill in conjunction
with the recommendations of the Select
Committee on Rents, and if it is given a
Second Reading we will, on the Committee stage, assist in making the Measure
one worthy to be placed on the Statute
Book.

713 Rent Restrictions Bill-

Second Reading
to which the Bill applies, but there is no
definition in it as to which or what houses
the Bill does apply to. But I am not going
to make any small points of draftsmanship or matters of that kind. I look at
the Bill and as far as I can see there are
two main features or objects in it. The
first is to extend the protection of the
Rent Restriction Acts to all premises
irrespective of class or character, whether
they be dwelling-houses or whether they
be business houses, no matter whether the
houses were built before 1914 or since,
and irrespective of all valuation.
The second matter that the Bill purports
to do is to establish a fair rents court.
At the present the benefits of the Rent
Restriction Acts, speaking generally, are
restricted to dwelling-houses where the
valuation does not exceed £26. The
Rent Restrictions Act was introduced as
a purely expediency measure to deal with
the very abnormal circumstances that
introduced themselves in 1914. The policy
of this Government has always been to get
rid of these expediency laws, and this
House has on a number of occasions
indicated by hon. Gentlemen opposite in
their speeches, taken the opportunity to
relieve houses of a certain valuation from
the protection of the Rent Restrictions
Act, so that we might get back to what
was the normal condition of things prior
to August, 1914. But this Bill is not
only the negation of that policy but it
goes a good deal further, because it proposes to offer the protection of the Rent
Restriction Acts to all buildings of every
class, not for a limited period of time,
but for all time.
Why as a matter of principle this
should be directed to rent I cannot understand. If as a matter of principle it
could be or should be directed to rent
surely it ought as a matter of principle
be applicable to every other necessity such
as food. Well, I need scarcely tell the
House that this Government is not prepared to recommend any such step.
Where does the necessity for this Bill
arise? It cannot be said that it is to
supply houses or to allow people to remain
in houses of the working class because
they are protected by the £26 valuation.

number.

I have asked why this matter should be

the idea of the Bill is that all houses built
since 1914 and all houses that are to be
built in future have got to have a rent
comparable to the rent payable in 1914
in respect of premises offering similar or
comparable accommodation. Pre-war one
of these houses, corresponding to the
subsidy house, could have been built for
about £100. In 1924 that same house cost
£400 to build, and now at the present
moment is costing £250. How can it be
said that if these houses are comparable
in the accommodation they afford that the
rent of a house that cost £400 to build
and the rent of a house costing now £250
to build should be the same as the rent
payable before the war in respect of a
house built for £100? Surely hon. Members if they will only reflect upon that
for a moment will see the futility and
impossibility of the Government accepting

Mr. HENDERSON: This Bill contains
matters that are going to do justice to
the working classes. If passed it will be
a delightful piece of Parliamentary legislation. It would be far better than the
Cockabillion Bill or the Fish Bill that the
right hon. Gentleman introduced. Is it not
more necessary to help the workers than
the Bills that right hon. Gentlemen bring
forward and that help no one? The hon.
Member (Mr. Byrne) also deserves credit
for bringing forward the matter of those
landlords who furnish houses. They put
a table and chair in a house and then
charge an exorbitant rent. A landlord
who is guilty of a crime like that has
every right to be looked after by the
State, and the only way to do that is by
setting up a fair rents court. The Parliamentary Secretary did not do justice to
this Bill which contains eleven Clauses
which go to protect the people who are
being exploited and who are asked to
pay rents of from £40 to £50. These
are all working-men. According to the
Parliamentary Secretary you would think
there was no working-man living in
Belfast who has a house of over £8 valuation. Thousands are struggling to pay
rents, with no hope of any protection
from the Government. I am in a house
with a £30 valuation, and what am I but
a working-man? What are the Members
on this side only working-men? I have
great pleasure in supporting the hon.
Member in this splendid Measure which
he has introduced so ably, and I hope
that all Members will go into the Lobby
and vote for it.
Mr. BYRNE rose.
I
am
Mr. DEPUTY-SPEAKER:
afraid that the hon. Member has already
spoken, but if there is anything he desires
to explain as a matter of courtesy I will
be glad to hear him.
Mr. BYRNE: There are one or two
points on which I feel very much. There
are those houses which became vacant
between 1925 and 1933, and which are
decontrolled for all time if something is
not done. Then there is another point.
The British Government have passed a
Landlord and Tenant Bill, and the same
thing had happened in the Free State.
Is this Government not going to do something for those leaseholders who have
built up businesses at great expense and
who, when their leases expire, are at the
mercy of the landlords, who can charge
whatever they like? Surely the Government is not going to leave this area in
that position for all time?
Question put, "That the Bill be now
read a Second time."
The House divided: Ayes, 6; Noes, 19.

His Grace the Governor of Northern

House to attend in the Senate forthwith.

ELECTIONS.
Ordered, That all Members who are
returned for two or more places in any
part of Northern Ireland do make their
Elections for which of the places they will
serve, within one week after it shall
appear that there is no question upon the
Return for that place; and if anything
shall come in question touching the
Return or Election of any Member, he is
to withdraw during the time the matter
is in debate; and that all Members returned upon double Returns do withdraw
till the Returns are determined.

WITNESSES.

endeavoured to deter or hinder any person from appearing or giving evidence,

misdemeanour; and this House will proceed with the utmost severity against
such offender.
Resolved: That if it shall appear that
any person hath given false evidence in
any case before this House, or any Committee thereof, this House will proceed
with the utmost severity against such
offender.

the Royal Ulster Constabulary do take.

leading to this House be kept free and

during the Sitting of Parliament, and
that there be no annoyance therein, or

KING'S SPEECH.
Mr. SPEAKER: I have to report that
the House has this day attended in the
Senate to hear his Grace's Speech, on behalf of the Crown, to both Houses of
Parliament; of which I have for greater
accuracy obtained a copy. The Speech is
as follows:-
Members of the Senate and of the House
of Commons.
to
I have noted with gratification the
continued progress of our great Shipbuilding Industry, and I am glad
to observe also that within our Linen
Industry action is being taken
examine new methods for advancing its
prosperity. It is my sincere hope that
success may attend this effort and that
a practical solution may be reached of
those problems which have beset this
important Industry for so many years
past.
It will continue to be my Government's special endeavour to assist by
every means in its power Agricultural
and Industrial undertakings, and to
encourage, so far as is possible, the
development of new sources of employment in order that useful and productive work may
be available for the
People.
I am glad to learn that the need
for co-ordinated effort to widen our
industrial basis has been met by the
creation of an Industries Development
Association. This body has undertaken
the dual task of encouraging the
demand for home products within our
area, and of attracting to Northern
Ireland such new Industries as offer a
prospect of successful development. As
complementary to these activities, my
Government proposes to continue to
foster the marketing of produce from
Northern Ireland by participating in
Exhibitions in various industrial
centres organised by the
the Empire
Marketing Board.
A Bill will be submitted to you proposing certain amendments and additions to the Education Acts for the
King's Speech

11 MARCH 1930
Debate on Address
purpose of making secure the position
of simple Bible teaching in public
elementary schools and making further
provision for representation on regional
and borough education committees,
the better regulating of school management committees, and for other
purposes calculated to increase the
usefulness of the Measures taken by
Parliament since 1922 to improve the
educational system. The success which
has attended these Measures and the
improvement in the facilities provided
in all classes of schools since the passing
of the Education Act of 1923 have
afforded me much satisfaction.
My Ministers view with concern the
serious extent to which sickness has
prevailed over a number of years
amongst persons insured under the
National Health Insurance Scheme,
and the general mortality figures
which are regrettably high. A Measure is being prepared for your consideration to make a more extensive
provision for the medical treatment of
insured persons with the object not
only of improving the health of the
working population but also of facilitating the ratification by His Majesty's
Government of the United Kingdom of
the International Convention on Sickness Insurance.
Proposals will be laid before you for
according to Local Authorities powers
in connection with Town Planning.
Proposals will also be laid before
you designed with the object of effecting
certain necessary reforms in the Lunacy
Laws and of ensuring a more systematic
provision for the care and treatment of
mentally defective children.
My Government in the development
of its policy for the better marketing of
agricultural produce will introduce two
further Measures dealing with the
preparation of meat for export and
with the marketing of fruit.
Bills dealing with the following
matters will also be submitted for your
consideration:—
The amendment of the Law relating to Joint Stock Companies.
The amendment of the provisions
of the Railway and Canal Traffic
Act, 1888.
The amendment of the Law relating to Weights and Measures.
Electricity supply in
Ireland.
Personation at Elections.
Tenancies in Urban areas.
Northern
Provision of Labourers' cottages in
Rural areas.
Members of the House of Commons.
The Estimates for the Public Services
will be laid before you in due course.
Members of the Senate and of the House
of Commons.
My Government has arranged for an
Industrial Census to be taken in
respect of Production in Northern Ireland during the year 1930. I trust
that this enumeration, when considered
in conjunction with the results of the
corresponding Census of 1924, will produce results of the highest value to the
Industries of Northern Ireland.
A comprehensive survey designed to
ascertain the possibilities of providing a
supply of electrical energy on a large
scale is now in progress.
It is my
earnest hope that this may result in
a scheme of Electrical Development
which will confer wide benefits upon
our Industries and our People.
I pray that the blessing of Almighty
God may rest upon your deliberations.

Debate on Address
Debate on Address
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Captain Chichester-Clark]
back bencher, have been given the
great honour of moving the Address
to the Speech from the Throne. The
honour is more especially marked, I
think, because it has seldom, possibly
never, been before accorded to one who has
spent his life in what is called the
"Silent
Service." The "Silent Service" prefers
to teach men to meet many eventualities
in life, but it does not teach them to be
orators, nor does it encourage them to make
speeches, and I hope the House will be
lenient with me to-day.
I am glad to know that the Gracious
Speech opens in an auspicious way. It is
pleasing to note that our great shipbuilding industry is continuing in its progress.
In these days of fierce competition in the
shipbuilding industry, in the cutting of
prices and in the grabbing for orders, that
is surely a great feather in the cap of our
shipbuilders and the many skilled workers
who go to make up the numerous trades
that are necessary to turn out the great
liners of to-day. And it is not least a
feather in the cap of the Government that
through the Loans Guarantee Acts they
are able to attract orders to Belfast. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear.) Long may this
shipbuilding prosperity continue and increase, for we all know how much it means
to the inhabitants of our Province. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear..)
I note that in connection with our linen
industry action is being taken to examine
new methods to advance its prosperity. It
is needless for me to explain what the linen
industry means to our Province, and I only
hope and pray that these new methods will
bring back that prosperity which will so
greatly help to decrease our unemployment.
en-
That we
That the Government's special
deavour will be to assist by every means
in its power agricultural and industrial
undertakings is only what we should
expect from this Government.
agriculturists and industrialists can hope
so soon for some more of that rare and
refreshing fruit which we had during the
last Session of this Parliament in the
great Derating Act is more, perhaps, than
we can expect. But I see in connection
with agriculture that we are going to have
two new measures, the Marketing of
Fruit, and the preparation of beef for
export. Other measures at first were
seemingly tiresome and irksome, but at
the same time we now from experience
that these measures of a similar sort have
greatly helped the particular section of
the industry to which they are applied.
Now as the representative of an agricultural constituency it is not unnatural
that under this heading I should talk
about agriculture, and I will leave the
hon. and gallant Member (Major Hall-
Thompson), who is going to second the
Address, and who is an old captain of industry, to comment on the industrial
situation.
Now agriculture-I do not want to
labour the point-is in a very bad way,
but I think that can be said of a great
many of our other great industries.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear). However, to me there seems to be one very
distinctive feature between the ills of agriculture and the ills of most of the other
great industries which are in the doldrums. In the other great industries, if
one reads the reports of their meetings, it
is not always easy even for the directors
themselves to put their finger exactly on
the root cause of the depression. They
say that the depression from which this
particular industry is suffering is due to
a variety of causes such as seasonal depression, changes of fashion, increases of
wages, and many things of that sort.
They cannot very often absolutely and
exactly diagnose the cause of the
depression.
Now, in agriculture I think it is very
different, and at the present time we can
put our finger on to the root cause, on the
plague spot, that is causing the depression
in the industry. I think it is this: The
depression is caused by the dumping in
the United Kingdom of Continental
bounty-fed surplus cereals, oats and
potatoes, with the unfortunate result that
at the present moment no farmer can sell
either his root or cereal crop, except at a
price considerably under what it costs him
to produce it. As long as this state of
affairs continues, as long as production
costs greatly exceed selling prices, the
farming industry cannot improve.
Those small Acts, such as the Marketing of Fruit Act, etc., are useful in their
way, but they are something like offering
a piece of sticking plaster to a man who
has got a broken leg. I know the Government are going to make every effort in
their power, but we well understand that
their power is not infinite, and I feel,
therefore, that the efforts which they must
make will take the form of attempting to
Debate on Address
Debate on Address
11 MARCH 1930
secure a reasonable amount of some sort
of protection for agriculture and, at any
rate, to stop this grossly unfair foreign
competition. (Hon. Members, Hear,
hear).
In considering the legislation foreshadowed in the Gracious Speech, there
can be no doubt that the amending of the
Education Act will be one of the most
important items. The Education Act of
1923 effected a complete change in our
education system. The magnitude of this
change was such that to produce there and
then a perfect Act, an Act that would require no amending, would have called for
a breadth of vision and a political insight
not yet given to mortal man. The Government have, I am glad to say, not been
hasty. They have tried this Act out for
seven or eight years, and I think when all
is said and done we may congratulate ourselves that the Act has, generally speaking, been most successful and most
beneficial.
Many of us in this House have served
from the beginning on regional committees or borough committees, and speaking for myself I have certainly seen great
improvements.
(Hon. Members: Hear,
hear). I would like to quote from my
own observation. The building of schools
has certainly improved; education, speaking of education in its technical form, has
improved; and, what is more important
still, in some cases the health of the
children has greatly improved. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear). A great deal of
this Act is administered by regional committees, by borough committees, and by
local school committees. It is proposed to
strengthen and improve these committees.
Obviously, the working of this Act must
in its efficiency be in exact ratio to the
efficiency of the committee working it,
and, therefore, anything that will
strengthen these committees will unquestionably strengthen and improve the
Act.
In looking through the remarks on the
amending of the Act I see in the Gracious
Speech that it is
"for the purpose of making secure the
position of simple Bible teaching in the
public elementary schools."
Of all the many happy and harmonious
phrases in the Gracious Speech this phrase
in all its simplicity pleases me the most.
It rings true. It is simple, it is direct,
and I believe it could only have been
written by an Ulsterman. We at the
present time, and I speak in no contentious or sectarian spirit, all know that
Bible teaching is the foundation on which
the principles of Christianity are built up.
At this moment a religious persecution, a
persecution of every form of religion, is
being conducted with a venom and
brutality horrifying to the whole civilised
world in a country that we thought was
civilised. It is something that, I think,
we of all classes and creeds in this community ought to be thankful for, and to
congratulate ourselves on the fact that
there is one corner of the world where we
stick to religion, and where we are true to
our simple faiths, whatever they may be.
The next Bill which seems to me to
be of great importance to this Province
is the extension of medical benefits to
insured persons. I believe this Measure
came into operation in Great Britain in
1912, but in those days I was in better
employment than dealing in politics, and
so I am not aware of the reason why
Ireland was left out of the benefits conferred. I know many people will say
that this is a time of great depression and
that we ought not to indulge in any
further expensive legislation. Up to a
point perhaps one may agree with that.
We have had legislation which may tend
to form an unemployable class and possibly to stabilise idleness. But I look
on this legislation, or any form of legislation which will definitely improve the
health of the community from quite a
different viewpoint. If I could be born
again, if I could become a small baby
once more, and yet retain my present
experience of life, and a fairy godmother
were to offer me the choice of gifts such
as wealth, brains, beauty, and health, I
should, with the experience of 45 years,
choose health without the slightest hesitation, for it seems to me that in health
you combine all the other gifts.
Of course, I have not seen the Bill
which is going to be laid before us, but
I hope very much that our dispensary
system is still going to be continued as
there are many people who will not come
under medical benefits and who will be
too poor to pay for their own treatment.
I hope, therefore, it will be possible, and
I say it after considerable thought, even
though it will result in a certain amount
of overlapping, to continue the dispensary system, and I hope that in drafting
the Bill provision will be made for assistance to that hard-working profession.
the dispensary doctors.
Debate on Address
Debate on Address
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Captain Chichester-Clark]
are
Of the other legislation to come before
us I am glad to see that town-planning
has not been forgotten. Many prospective residential suburban areas
often spoilt from lack of foresight
in this direction. I am also glad to see
that more systematic revision of the
treatment of mentally deficient children
is going to be undertaken. I think we
in this Province are a little behindhand
in this respect.
Now, my experience of politics is small,
but in thinking over what I should say I
felt that no acrimonious matter or contentious sentiments should be brought into
the speech moving the Address in Reply.
I have done my best, and I hope I have
succeeded in saying nothing that could be
taken as being contentious or that would
hurt the feelings of anybody. I suppose
no Government can please everybody unless everybody happened to be of one
opinion, and that, of course, cannot
always happen. We know it is the duty
of the Opposition to oppose, and we know
that the Opposition will oppose and will
criticise in a healthy, constructive
manner.
I will end on this note, and I hope it
will be agreed to by all in this House. I
want to congratulate the Government on
the fact that the question of unemployment has not been mentioned in the
Gracious Speech. Every thinking man
and woman regards this terrible question
as the most pressing problem to-day. We
have seen during the past twelve months
the unemployment question discussed
most fully and from every aspect on
similar occasions across the water, and the
discussions have ended in what can only
be described as failure. We have seen,
alas, great hopes, high endeavour and
many promises on this subject end in
nothing but failure, in those ever-increasing numbers of the weekly lists of the unemployed.
At the same time all this talk of unemployment has possibly exaggerated, at
any rate it has most definitely emphasised,
our difficulties in foreign countries. It
has lowered our national credit. It has
lowered our national prestige. It
obviously has reflected badly on our trade
and on our commerce. Indeed all this
talk merely goes to diminish our trade
and so keep on swelling the ranks of the
unemployed. That is the situation which
seems to me to have been produced by a
great deal of talk on this most distressing
subject. Deeds and not words obviously
are what are wanted, and that is why I
have no hesitation in congratulating the
Government on not having mentioned the
term "unemployment" in the Gracious
Speech. They themselves have concentrated on finding means of employment
and of advancing and improving our commerce and industries; they are going to
increase and improve our educational
system; they are also going to bring in a
Bill to do something to help our national
health. These methods are much more
likely to bring back the prosperity which
we have lost and which is the only way
to get rid of the spectre of unemployment.
I beg to move. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear).
Major HALL-THOMPSON (in morning dress): I beg leave to second the
motion so ably proposed by the hon. and
gallant Member for Derry. In doing so
I do not propose to dwell upon points
appertaining to agriculture or rural areas,
as the mover of the Address has already
dealt much more effectively than I am
qualified to do with these phases of the
most Gracious Speech.
Hon. Members are, I am sure, much
gratified that one of our shipbuilding
yards has been restored to its usual
activity and is now fully occupied, while
the other is rapidly regaining its old
prestige. None the less, I cannot but
look to the future with apprehension in
view of the slowing down of demand for
shipping due to shortage of freights estimated at 16 per cent. below pre-war,
while working expenses have increased by
70 per cent.
I hope that as a result of the report
of a delegation of linen manufacturers
to the U.S.A. and Canada, steps will
be taken to mitigate some of the difficulties of that industry, reduce unnecessary local competition and lead to greater
co-ordination of effort. (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear.) I would suggest that, provided the linen industry re-organises and
co-ordinates its efforts, the Government
should be willing to guarantee loans to
it, so that that industry and other vital
industries may be revived and placed on a
sound footing. I think a policy of this
nature would be better than only assisting
new industries which in some cases are
injurious to those already in existence.
Debate on Address
Debate on Address
11 MARCH 1930
Nothing but good can come from the
well directed efforts of the Industries
Development Association. The extension
of the Safeguarding Act to many British
industries would. in my opinion, be very
helpful to that organisation. (Hon Members: Hear, hear.) Hon. Members
know as well as I do how we suffer from
unfair competition. It is our duty to
safeguard our manufacturers and help
them to recover their competitive power.
I am glad that our own Prime Minister,
whom we shall all be pleased to welcome
home in a few days, full of "New-
Zeal-and" energy, (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear.)-has declared that he will
press at the appropriate time for a
measure to safeguard the linen industry,
in the belief that such a measure would
do much to restore prosperity to the
thousands of workers who are normally
engaged in the manufacture of our worldfamed staple export.
I should like to congratulate the
Government upon its educational policy
which is working so satisfactorily. New
schools are being rapidly provided and
old buildings re-modelled. In a short
time the children attending elementary
schools will be as well provided for as in
any part of the United Kingdom. The
teachers are loyally and efficiently carrying out their duties, and I understand
there is not a Protestant child attending
the transferred and provided public elementary schools who does not daily receive
Bible instruction. It is the Government's
intention to ensure that nothing shall
interfere with this daily Bible instruction,
now given so faithfully by the teachers,
and to provide adequate safeguards to
secure that transferred schools shall be
conducted in accordance with the principles of the parents of the children who
attend them.
It is only right that I should here say
that much of the progress made in elementary education in Belfast has been
due to the energy and ability of an ex-
Member of this House, I refer to Alderman Duff, who has, unfortunately, just
resigned from the position of chairman
of the Belfast Education Committee.

It may be said that the working classes
are now provided for from the cradle to
the grave. Free education is provided,
provision is made for them in sickness and
in health, when employed and unemployed, when old, when widows
orphans, and subsidised houses are available in which to live.
All these provisions; even if good in themselves, are a
heavy burden on industry, which I hope
will be borne in mind when the estimates
for the public services are being framed,
with the object of obtaining counterbalancing economies.
You will observe it is intended to accord
to local authorities ample power in connection with town planning and to aid towards the abolition of slum dwellings in
town and country, with a view to the
further amelioration of the conditions of
the poor and distressed. I am sure Hon.
Members will agree that this is a step in
the right direction.
We are also promised legislation dealing with the marketing of agricultural
produce, which is likely to make Ulster
goods still more popular across the
Channel, alterations in the lunacy laws,
the law re joint stock companies, Railway
and Traffic Act, 1888, weights and
measures, personation at elections,
finances in urban areas, labourers'
cottages, and, last but not least, electricity
supply in Northern Ireland.
If we are to manufacture economically
an ample and cheap power supply is
essential. Electricity in the home and on
the farm is a great convenience and
labour-saving device, but is much cheaper
to produce in one large station, where
there is an ample supply of fuel and
water, than in a number of small units.
I, therefore, congratulate the Minister of
Commerce (Mr. Barbour) upon looking
well ahead in this matter, and in having
already secured the services of an eminent
consultant to advise as to the most ad-

It is a matter for sincere regret that the

this Province and the whole of the

benefit and relief schemes do not cure the

cheaply and marketing them more efficiently. I trust that all parties, creeds

revive industry, bring back prosperity,

I was profoundly disappointed, and I

Throne. After the professions of goodwill

It was with surprise, therefore, that we

which removes the minor grievances of

secure the position of Bible teaching in

task that you are absolutely unequal to.

than we in Northern Ireland?
take the United States of America, that
land of the free, that my hon. Friends opposite are so fond of quoting? In America
public schools are provided in exactly the
same way as they are here in Northern
Ireland. Roman Catholics in the United
States have asked from time immemorial
that Roman Catholic schools should be
built and paid for by public money, and
the United States Government have consistently refused to take such a step.
They submit, just as we do here, that
there are public schools provided that are
entirely undenominational, that there is
no fear for the faith of any of those who
attend them, and if the Roman Catholics
do not wish to take advantage of the facilities for education so provided they can
build their own schools at their own cost,
and run them in any way they please.
These are the conditions obtaining in
civilised countries that have really been
born under British traditions.
I hear economy preached. I seldom see
it practised. If I may begin with the
first speech that was delivered to-day
from the opposite side, that is by the hon.
Member for South Fermanagh (Mr.
Healy), upon a variety of subjects relating to matters contained in the King's
Speech, I would join issue with him at
once on many of the statements-indeed
the platitudes, if I may say so that fell

matters which he discussed. The grievances of Roman Catholics, of course, is a
very old story. We have had it periodically in this House and it has been within
the memories of most people in this House
probably from the beginning of their
careers. But I think there is less ground
for the charge of discrimination in Northern Ireland that in any country in the
world. It is not the case, as was stated by
the hon. Member, that the conditions
here in regard to Roman Catholic education are less favourable to that faith than
in Great Britain. I think it right to
make this explanation and to make the
matter clear apart altogether from any information which may be given by my hon.
and learned Friend (Mr. Robb), who
represents education in this House.
The British Government do not contribute to the building of schools for Catholic
purposes except on the basis of a Fourand-Two Committee in every case. There
are some 1,100 Roman Catholic schools in
Great Britain. These schools are all worked
under Four-and-Two Committees, and, of
course, they get their grants for school
building in the normal proportions.
Roman Catholics in Northern Ireland are
treated in exactly the same way, that is to
say, that if they consent to come under a
Four-and-Two Committee they can have
all the advantages that accrue to any other
denomination. That cuts the ground entirely from any charge that there is any
hardship in regard to the treatment of
Roman Catholics.
But is there a country in the world that
is so liberal in its views in regard to the

in the world that shows greater consideration or greater sympathy for such people

When the hon. Member speaks of freedom, using that word in a rather curious

Would anything so ridiculous or fantastic.
come from the lips of any reasonable business man? Would protection imposed by

population of Great Britain, which forms

Mr. HEALY: There are some over

Apart altogether from that, it was a free
gift of the British Government, and it
might be conceivable, under certain circumstances, that the British Government
would withdraw it. I do not think they
ever will; I am sure they never will withdraw it. But at the same time it is their

could be discussed. Whatever form of relief could be given to farmers, the land

held on that subject, that we can relieve

every kind.
In the face of economic laws, it is inconceivable that we should have a standard price for commodities. It would
hardly be possible to standardise the price
of any commodity that we produce.
If
we had the money we might subsidise a
particular crop, but what advantage would
accrue from that? There are many difficulties in the way of subsidies as we know,
varieties of quality, varieties of every
class, which would operate against any
such policy. I was on safe ground when
I said somewhere that until the mentality
of the British people changed we can have
no hope whatever that we can influence
the price of the articles raised by our farmers, or improve their position from that
point of view, because Great Britain is
our market, the market for all our agricultural commodities, and until the
British people change their policy in regard to the free introduction into their
country of all the agricultural commodities that are shipped by foreign countries
we cannot affect the price.
Economic laws are just as rigid as the
laws that govern the heavenly bodies, and
no Government is able to fly in the face
of those laws. Is there anything conceivable that the British Government
would not do at the present moment to
help industry and business generally?
They have tried every panacea they can
think of, and their great champion of
the relief of unemployment, Mr. Thomas,
has had to stand up in a white sheet in the
House of Commons, and admit that everything he has tried has failed, and that
there is only one method by which industry can be improved, and that is by hard.
work.
There is another difficulty in respect of
industry that I may mention when I have
the opportunity. While unemployment
has been increasing in Great Britain,
measures are being taken there by those
who are engaged in industry which must
necessarily have the effect of increasing unemployment, that is, the rationalisation
of industry. Rationalisation is the very
Debate on Address
Debate on Address
HOUSE OF COMMONS
{Mr. Pollock]
big word that is being used to describe
the methods that are being tried in industry. Rationalisation means in effect
amalgamation. In addition to that, the
machinery that is being brought into
operation from day to day, by which numbers can be curtailed and the cost of production reduced, can necessarily have no
other result than the increase of unemployment.
I have mentioned from time to time a
gentleman I know in America-in the
Falls River district, where cotton spinning
and weaving are carried on in a very large
way-who saw one girl operating 47 automatic looms. When one thinks of that
in connection with the development of
modern industry, one can see how greatly
that must contribute to unemployment
momentarily, until the conditions change
and additional people can be absorbed in
industry. Apart altogether from these
measures, we do find that Great Britain
is endeavouring to fight the tariffs of the
world, and that, in my judgment, is an
impossible thing. As I have said, not
until the mentality of the British people
changes and they impose such tariffs as
will level up the difference in the cost of
production here and the cost in those
countries where longer hours are worked
and lower wages paid, will there be any
hope in my opinion of reducing unemployment to any material extent. That is the
answer I give to the hon. Member for
South Fermanagh (Mr. Healy), who
would introduce a number of nostrums
that could not possibly have the slightest
effect on that great problem.
My hon. Friend, the Member for North
Antrim (Sir Robert Lynn), dealt with a
number of features of the problem as if
they were of some influence in promoting
employment. He mentioned the question
of sea fishing. Unfortunately our people
here are not sea fishermen in the general
sense that the term implies nowadays.
Fishing, like every other industry, is being
carried on by methods that in the olden
days were not possible or even dreamt of.
Large steam trawlers go far distances and
return with enormous cargoes of fish for
the British markets. We have no great
market for fish here.
Our men around the coast fish in
their little yawls, but they have not the
capital to provide trawlers, and even if
they had the capital their trawlers would
not be of any great value for this reason:
Our country is so sparsely populated that
there is no market for any considerable
sale of fish to justify trawling on
a large scale. It has been tried. I
know it has been tried. I have been interested in it myself, and it has failed.
Trawlers landed their fish at Larne, and
they could find no market for the fish.
What encouragement is there under those
circumstances for any Government to undertake enterprise of that kind? I cannot see it myself. But I do suggest that
these little harbours around our coasts
offer facilities, and the Government is applying itself to that aspect of the matter.
The fishermen who go out in their yawls
are being encouraged by the Government
in that direction, and my hon. Friend behind me has sufficient knowledge of the
world's fishing operations to enable him
to see the facts in regard to our own
coast.
The hon. Member also spoke of the
comparison of France and Great Britain
in regard to the cost of administration. I
presume he meant Great Britain, because
I do not think he could have been referring to Northern Ireland. I think that
if he will investigate the cost of administration here relative to our own area, our
own revenue, and our own population, we
will be quite on safe ground in comparison
with Great Britain. I am not so sure
that possibly we might not bear favourable comparison with foreign countries.
Economy can be effected much more
radically by changes of policy than by any
changes in administration. The cost of
administration here is a relatively small
thing. I do not mean to suggest that it
is unimportant, but I do suggest that it is
a small thing compared with the vast expenditure which we make as a result of the
work of this Parliament in passing
different Measures of reform of various
kinds and classes. Therefore, until the
policy changes no real substantial relief
can be given in regard to taxation, because
if we reduce the cost of our administration
20 per cent., 25 per cent., or 50 per cent.,
it would make no difference in the taxable
arrangements of the country, if this
House, in common with the Imperial Parliament, insists upon passing Measures of
social reform such as the derating scheme,
costing us a vast sum of money, and the
Widows' and Orphans' relief scheme, costing us £150,000 to £175,000. There is
not a word spoken in regard to the expenditure on these things when economy
is talked of. I do not think that economy
Debate on Address

exercised in that direction is desirable. I
am not suggesting that, but I do suggest
that until we realise that it is only in
change of policy that we can effect any

I think, reserve the question of economy
for discussion elsewhere.

am satisfied no Member wishes to make

trouble that one can scarcely give utterance to in public.
There are men and women who through
financial trouble, or domestic trouble, or
trouble of various kinds lose their balance
for the time being. I do not think that
people like that should be put into institutions of this kind where they are
branded as insane. There ought to be
some sort of what we might call observation houses or homes of rest for these
people to remain in for three or four
weeks, where, in the providence of God,
their mental balance might perhaps be
restored. I do think that the Minister
of Home Affairs should see that in whatever arrangements he makes something of
that description will be provided.
Then there are people who have perhaps
temporary attacks of insanity. They are
unbalanced in mind for a short time. I
understand from people who have given
great study to this matter that it is a
recurrent disease with a great number of
persons. There should be some arrangement made whereby the very best medical
expert knowledge could be obtained in
such cases.
It would be better to take
the risk of keeping in some people suffering from a recurrent form of insanity than
to allow them out however much they desired to be out. It would be better, in my
opinion, to inflict a slight injustice on some
few than to run the great risk of perhaps
transmitting to a great number of people
the form of trouble under which they
suffer. This matter is bristling with difficulties. I know something about it. I
do hope that these unfortunate people
will receive the greatest care and consideration from the Minister of Home
Affairs when he is drafting this Bill.
Then there is the question of domicile.
The creat city of Belfast sends patients
down to their friends in the country to
recover. When they become troublesome
again they are perhaps arrested, and we
are bound to put these Belfast patients
in the county asylum and support them
there. We ought to have the power to
settle absolutely the place where the
patients will go, and not allow them to be

am not competent for such a task. I admire the way in which my hon. Friend on

Debate on Address
Debate on Address
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. McNeill]
Chancellor of the Exchequer pointed out
yesterday most admirably, the displacing
of man power.
The Chancellor went on to express the
opinion yesterday that the workers would
be displaced only temporarily, but I differ
from him in that respect. The workers
are gradually being displaced permanently. I remember in 1920 reading certain figures that were published in the
London "Times." They were figures
which were prepared by a very eminent
statistician, Mr. Ernest Crammond, as a
result of inquiries which he made from
leaders of industry throughout England
and Scotland. He received answers to
the effect that the productive capacity of
the machine was-I think I am correct in
saying at least 75 per cent. greater than
it was in 1914.
com-
Those of us who read the results of the
great Economic Conference which was
assembled at Geneva in 1927, and which
was composed of 200 representatives from
Europe, representatives of trade,
merce, industry and economics, were astonished by the fact that all those eminent
men were agreed that the only problem
for humanity at the present time is the
problem of distribution-not the problem
of production. They were not dealing
with the potential power of production,
such as the figures which I have just
quoted of Mr. Crammond's.
They took as the basic year 1913. They
compared the condition of world affairs
in 1913 with the condition of world affairs
in 1927, and they showed that the production of raw material had advanced
enormously and out of all proportion to the
increase in population, that the production.
of food supplies had also increased to a
very large extent, and that the world's
shipping, which had been destroyed during
the war by German and other enemy submarines, was now 38 per cent. greater on
a tonnage basis than it was in 1914.
It was perfectly clear from the evidence
which they published that the only problem to-day with which we are saddled is
not the problem of production at all-it
is the problem of distribution. Industry
exists not for the purpose of providing employment. Industry exists to-day for the
purpose of providing goods, and if we have
industry which provides goods, irrespective
of the question of employment, we must
distribute the products and the fruits of
that industry.
What we are suffering from to-day is not
over-production, but, to put it in a different way, under-consumption. If every
man in Belfast had £1 handed to him today, and if he were to go with his pound
in his pocket to the shops and factories
and warehouses, what would be the effect?
The effect would be that he could immediately get his wants supplied. That
pound would encourage the small shopkeeper. He would have to get into contact with the manufacturers, and the
wheels of industry would again be set in
motion because of the effective demand
represented by that pound. I throw out
those suggestions on the question of unemployment, a question in which I am
profoundly interested, and one in which I
know every Member of this House is also
profoundly interested.
I should like to deal with another problem which is mentioned in the King's
Speech. I refer to the modification of the
Education Act of 1923, and the proposed
change. I cannot believe that hon. Members opposite are really genuinely concerned regarding the future of simple
Bible instruction. I believe they want to
have Bible instruction continued, but I
believe that every Member sitting opposite
me, perhaps with the exception of two, is
perfectly well aware that simple Bible instruction, in so far as Protestants are concerned, is already guaranteed by the Act.
It was guaranteed by Section 26 of the
Act of 1923, which made in incumbent
upon the local authorities, in whom the
control of education was vested by the Act,
to provide religious instruction according
to the tenets of the parents of the children
attending those various schools.
There is an obligation, and the obligation is further strengthened by the
Statutory Rules and Regulations of 1924,
which provide or set forth the hours during
which the religious education was to be
given. Furthermore, an Amending Act
was passed in 1925, with which, as far as
I recollect, the Protestant Churches expressed entire agreement. They were
satisfied with the Amending Act. What
has happened between 1925 and this year
of grace 1930 to cause such an alarm in the
breasts of a large section, or perhaps only
a small section, of the population of Ulster
with regard to the future of religious
education?

The taxpayer in many cases has got to

severely taxed on 15th April. We will
then all get an increase of taxation. I
think there is very little doubt about that.
Those who are working-class people are
also in a bad way, because the depression
in trade puts them on the dole, which
means a distinct reduction in their income,
while the better-class people will also be
worse off. I hope the Government will do
their utmost to exercise rigid economy. I
would like to mention another thing they
can do.
There is a great deal of waste or unnecessary expenditure in connection with
printing. I do not know whether it is a

that one flea bite does not do very much

they are very severe. (Laughter).
the Chancellor of the Exchequer would
