best they can for the agricultural
labourers, but with the present position
of the agricultural industry it is impossible for the agriculturists to do all they
should like to do for the agricultural
labourers. I am quite satisfied that agricultural prosperity will bring happiness,
not only to the agriculturist himself, but
to the agricultural labourer as well. We
want to see the agricultural labourers in
better houses.
Mr. CONNELLAN: So do we.
Mr. ELLIOTT: I say "we." I am
not disputing the fact that hon. Members
opposite are interested in this question as
much as we are. We all want to see the
agricultural labourers in better houses,
and we want to see them better paid; but
if we are going to do that we must first
of all put the agricultural industry in a
position to do more. However, I am
glad that the Government are going to
do something for the agricultural
labourers, and I anticipate big things in
connection with the housing of those men.
I hope the Government will make it possible for those who reside in agricultural
areas to provide a decent cottage for every
agricultural labourer, and that the hovels
in which they are sometimes compelled
to live will disappear from the face of
Northern Ireland for all time.
I disagree with the suggestion of the
hon. Member for Mid Derry (Mr. Leeke)
that agricultural labourers' cottages
should be built in colonies. Agricultural
labourers' cottages must be erected near
the place where the men are going to get
work. There is no use in building a number of labourers cottages ten miles away
from the farm in which the men will be
employed. These cottages should be built
in pairs, or singly if necessary, so that the
labourers will not have to travel miles to
and from their work. I find that when it
comes to taking land for this purpose the
Government valuer does not put a very
high valuation on the land, but I am quite
satisfied that if the Minister of Finance
can find the money there will be no difficulty at all in providing the land. Agriculturists through the rural councils and
urban councils will facilitate in every way
they can the erection of suitable houses
for labourers and working-class people.
There are other Measures outlined in
the King's Speech, but in regard to some
of them I have to make some little investigation before I can bestow my blessing
and benediction upon them. I believe
that the Government, in the programme
they have outlined in the Speech, have
nothing but the best interests of the people
at heart, and so far as I am concerned I
shall give them my whole-hearted support
in any Measure which will go to increase
the prosperity of Northern Ireland.
Mr. McCARROLL: As I listened to
the hon. Gentleman who has just sat
down, I came gradually to the conclusion
that those little paragraphs that appear
in certain sections of the Press are
not wholly unwarranted. I think he is
rapidly qualifying for preferment, and
the tone of his speech would indicate, as
I say, that he is trailing his coat, so to
speak, so as to ensure that when the
occasion arises the Government will recognise his splendid qualities.
Mr. ELLIOTT: Hear, hear.
Mr. McCARROLL: In addition to the
trailing of coats, we have had an exhibition of the trailing of what is called the
National flag.
Mr. ELLIOTT: You do not like that.
Mr. McCARROLL: What flag?
Mr. ELLIOTT: The Union Jack.
Mr. McCARROLL: What flag for us?
Mr. ELLIOTT: The Union Jack.
Mr. McCARROLL: Here you make it
a party flag. Here in the Six Counties
crime has been committed under it. We
have not made it a party flag. It is your
flag. You have constituted it a party flag,
and if I speak the Catholic mind and the
Debate on Address
Debate on Address
HOUSE OF COMMONS
(Mr. McCarroll]
National mind there is not a child that
will ever enter a school in which it is
compelled to salute that flag, so long as
you maintain it as a party flag and a
partisan flag. It is a substitute for the
Orange flag.
Mr. CONNELLAN: An illegal substitute.
Mr. McCARROLL: There is not a
demonstration held in any part of this
area at which you do not trail the Union
Jack. I have always maintained this, if
we did adopt that flag you people would
spurn it.
Mr. ELLIOTT: Try it.
Mr. McCARROLL: Any person who
comes from the city in which I live can
recall, as I can, the time when in the
Orange quarter of that city they had
"Papish Ned" put up in terms of scorn
in regard to His Majesty the late King.
There is not a doubt that the Union Jack
is a partisan flag. You have made it
such. It is not the National flag of Ireland. Frankly, I do not know what the
National flag of Ireland is at the moment,
constituted as the country is. It is a pity
that any Member should endeavour to
continue the spirit of bitterness which was
engendered yesterday by the Minister of
Finance by raising this question of the
flag at all.
The hon. Member for South Tyrone
(Mr. Elliott) has asked are we prepared
to accept the same status in regard to education as exists in the United States of
America? He seems to forget that the
Minister of Finance frankly admitted in
the speech he delivered yesterday that the
schools in America were undenominational. Of the schools that have been set
up, and of the school system that is going
to be set up now as a result of the new
Bill, can it be said they are undenominational? I challenge any member of the
Government
party to say that the
educational system that you are now imposing upon the Six Counties is an undenominational system.
The Act upon which your Government
is established compels you not to endow
any religion. I suggest to you that the
proposals you are now bringing into this
House are a direct endowment of the
Protestant religion. I take one of your
papers published this morning. I know
that it said that all you claim is simple
"News-
Bible teaching. I take the
Letter" of this morning and what does it
say? It says:
"We are confident that the new Bill
when it becomes law will remove any
apprehension about the continuance of
religious instruction in schools."
I frankly say that the schools you are
setting up here are denominational schools,
and by reason of that fact, if for no other
reason, and there are other and substantial reasons, Catholic parents conscientiously cannot send their children into
them.
The hon. Member (Mr. Elliott) said
We
that we seek preferential treatment.
do not. We seek to have definite religious
instruction in our schools, as you are now
going to have it in yours.
It does not
matter whether it was the Orange Order
or any other Order that succeeded in establishing that system, you are now going
to endow religion in your Protestant
schools in the Six Counties. We ask for
nothing more, we ask for nothing less. It
is quite a simple proposition. I know it
will be met with the argument that there
is an absence of democratic control. I
answer it, and I say that the system of
control which has existed in this country
for one hundred years is ample. It is a
system which is quite satisfactory to onethird of your population. The Catholic
people of the Six Counties are quite content with it. They want nothing else.
The teachers are also content.
The other day we had a declaration by
the leader of the Labour party of the
Free State, who said that if he thought
by advocating that the State should be
responsible for the building of schools,
he
was in any way interfering with
or endangering the managerial system,
he would not advocate it for one moment,
because he knew of no representative
body in the country that had any desire
to interfere with or put an end to that
system. He believed he was voicing the
opinion of the teachers when he said that,
if there was any attempt to do away with
the system, the first to resist such an
attempt would be the teachers, because
they were satisfied that the system had
worked as well as any other system in
operation in any other country.
The Catholic teachers on the 14th of last
month assembled in Belfast passed a resolution declaring:
"That we, the Catholic teachers of
Northern Ireland, desire to place on
Debate on Address
Debate on Address
12 MARCH 1930
record at this juncture that we prefer
the system of Catholic clerical management of our schools to the control of
any committee.
"We therefore call on the Government in the coming Amending Bill to
make provision for the same financial
aid for schools under Catholic clerical
management as is given to transferred
and provided schools."
I say that the Catholic parents throughout the Six Counties are quite satisfied
with the system of control that exists.
But what is the position created by
derating in regard to control? One contention is that the Ministry have the most
absolute control of the entire educational
system of the Six Counties, and that all
the money, save, I think, 2 per cent.,
necessary to finance education is voted in
this Parliament having regard to the fact
that derating is now in operation. As a
result, why is it contended that you should
hand over the control of schools to committees and establish what you call democratic control when they are not paying
rates?
When the sod was being cut for a new
school in Limavady it was declared that
in future probably all the money, save
2 per cent. would be voted by Parliament.
Is the control that the Ministry exercises
not deemed sufficient? I suggest there is
a much more serious reason behind this,
and the reason is that the Orange Order
and the Churches, and I think they have
admitted it in some of their statements,
are quite afraid-I do not say they are
justifiably afraid-that in certain areas
the Catholics would maintain or secure
that control in local affairs which by
gerrymandering you have now deprived
them of.
In one of the manifestoes they issued
they declared the fear was that some day
in places like Londonderry a Catholic
Corporation would get into power, or
that in Tyrone and Fermanagh Catholic
bodies would secure control of local
affairs, and that consequently the religion of Protestants in the schools would
be interfered with. There is no ground
for such a suggestion, it is absolutely
baseless. There is no desire on the part
of any Catholic in the Six Counties to interfere with the religious education of
Protestants.
This Government in its wisdom, and
as a result of pressure from different
sources is now going to endow religion in
its Protestant, and Presbyterian, and
other schools, and it is going to insist
that Catholics are to contribute taxes
for the maintenance of those schools.
Our demand is simple, and it can be conceded without detracting in any way
from democratic or popular control.
Our demand is that we get an equal
share of all the moneys required for the
building, the maintenance, and the extension of our schools.
I do not wish to follow the Minister
of Finance into the rather embittered
speech which he delivered yesterday, in
which he challenged entirely our whole
case, but I do say that we have legitimate
grievances. It does not matter a straw
whether in 1922 we did not come in here.
I can retort that your people did not recognise the Boundary Commission. For
a time we did not recognise this Parliament, but that is not an answer to the
simple, legitimate demand we make. It
is a demand for equality, not, as the hon.
Member for South Tyrone (Mr. Elliott)
said, one for preferential treatment in
the funds distributed by this Parliament
for the building and extension of schools.
We ask nothing more and we will be
satisfied with nothing less. Unless that
simple demand is conceded the world will
know that there is an injustice, and that
an iniquitous system is being perpetrated
to the disadvantage of the Catholics who
constitute one-third of the population
of this area.
Mr. STEWART: I wish to join with
the other Members in congratulating both
the proposer and the seconder of the
Address in Reply. I propose to deal very
shortly with the plight of the farmers
mentioned in the King's Speech. I will
deal solely with that. I represent a rural
constituency, and my business brings me a
good deal into contact with the farming
community. I would like to tell the
House that the small tenant farmers are
not in too rosy or healthy a condition. In
the last three or four years, with bad
weather, with not getting their crops
saved, and with bad prices for their produce, they are in a practically hopeless
position to-day.
On the first occasion on which I spoke
in this House, in June last, I suggested
that the land annuities, if it were at all
possible, should be split in two and spread
over a term of years. I was replied to by
someone who said that that was a reserved
service. I subsequently learned that the
Debate on Address
Debate on Address
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Stewart]
land annuities come back here for the purpose of keeping the Government functioning. Now, if ways and means could be
devised whereby the expense of running
this Government could be curtailed something could be done in the way of reducing
the annuities and giving a small measure
of relief to the tenant farmers.
As to the crops, the price for produce is
practically nothing. This morning, coming down in the train I was told by a man
that he was offered 10/- a ton for his
potatoes. He was told that if he did not
take it he would possibly take less before
the end of the month. That is a very bad
state of affairs. There are a tremendous
lot of potatoes in the country and there is
no sale for them. The same thing applies
to corn and other commodities for which
the farmers are responsible.
In one of the districts in my constituency, which is fairly mountainous, I am
told that in order to put the land into
condition it is desirable that lime should
be put on it. In the old days when the
landlords had control they supplied lime
to the tenant farmers. Some of the landlords, bad and all as they were, and they
could not have been much worse, supplied
lime to the tenant farmers at one period
or another, and I would suggest to the
Government that they should supply lime
to the tenant farmers in those districts in
which it is required. There are any
number of lime kilns in the country, and
with a small outlay lime, which would be
of immense value to the farmers for their
crops, could be supplied.
Colonel GORDON: Do you want the
landlords back?
Mr. STEWART: No, we are glad to
see them away. Unfortunately the position is very serious for the farmers. I
want to take this opportunity to tell you
that throughout the country they are in a
most parlous condition. They cannot pay
their rents. You have only to look at the
records of the quarter sessions for the last
two or three years to see that each year
the number of civil bills issued by the
Ministry of Finance against farmers in
respect of land annuities is growing.
It is growing to an extraordinary
extent. After all if the Irish tenant
farmers. no matter what may be said
about them, have the money they will
certainly pay.
We must give them
credit for that. The position is that they
cannot possibly pay because they have
not the money. They are leaving the
land. I know several farms that have
been left derelict. Farmers' sons are
emigrating, and if this state of affairs
goes on in my opinion you will have
nobody left in the Six County area but
Cabinet Ministers, Government officials,
and old-age pensioners.
Mr. BYRNE: I join with other hon.
Members in congratulating the mover
and seconder of the Address. There are
many things mentioned in the Speech,
but there are some things not mentioned.
We rejoice that the shipbuilding industry
is in a prosperous state, and we sincerely
hope that that will continue. As far as
agriculture is concerned I thoroughly
agree with those who have spoken that
something must be done to assist this industry. I know something about the
state of the farmers in certain parts of
the country. and I know that unless
something is done for them these people
will have to leave their places. I would
congratulate the Government on what
they have done in the interests of the
farmers. I would congratulate them on
introducing derating, but I believe that
derating is not enough. It is a relief to
the farmers, but the prices they get for
their produce mean everything to them.
We all know that not many years ago
a farmer could take five tons of pot atoes out of a field and get £5 a ton for
them. Ile got 1 a stone for his flax,
and good prices for other crops. As 1
say unless something is done to protect
the farmers I am afraid the country will
go into a bad state. I for one would
strongly advocate a form of Protection.
We find that German oats, which are
subsidised by the German Government.
are dumped into this country. What
hope have we for the farmers here in
such circumstances? So long as you have
depression in the farming industry
you will have depression all over.
Go down Corporation Street and
will see hundreds of people
round the Labour Exchange, and
if you go to the country you will see
thousands of acres of land untilled. Is
it not possible for those who are sent to
this House to do something for the
people they represent, to devise some
means by which the farmers can be
helped in this terrible time? I was
sorry to hear the Minister of Finance say
you

of labourers' cottages. I know that the

would like these people to get some information as to the period when they are

are ex-
The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.

I wish some further reference had been

I suggested in the last Session of Parliament that owing to the extreme depression in trade people will not be able to

It would be a good thing if the Government were to give a grant for the reconditioning of houses. If a little money

I want for a short time to refer to the
Education Act, which is very near and
dear to those Members on this side of the
House. We have heard many discussions
about that Act. I wish to point out that
in any references I make to this Act I do
not want to hurt the feelings of any
person of any other denomination. We,
as Catholics, feel we have a responsibility
to discharge. Over 70,000 children of our
people in the Six Counties are to be
Debate on Address
Debate on Address
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Byrne]
educated, and our conscientious conviction is that these children in order to be
brought up in their faith must be educated in Catholic schools under Catholic
management. Yesterday I felt quite relieved when the hon. Member (Sir Robert
Lynn) mentioned that he would like to
sce every section of the community
satisfied with regard to the Education
Act.
Would it not be possible yet to have
a conference between representatives of
the Government and of our people in
order to bring about some arrangement so
that we would be able to educate our
children under the same supervision as at
the present time?
It may be said, as it was said to-day,
that we are looking to be subsidised in
order that we may get our own wishes as
regards education, but I say to the
Government, "Do you want us to subsidise your Protestant schools?" We are
taxed the same as you are taxed, and
if our conscientious convictions tell us that
we cannot allow our children to be taught
in schools under the Four-and-Two Committees or any other supervision except
under the Catholic bishops and priests,
then I say you should give us some consideration. Yesterday the Minister of
Finance, who I regret is not here, stated
that in England the schools were under
the control of Four-and-Two Committees.
I happened to get a paper which gives an
explanation about the Education Act in
England. It says:
In England, the Education Committees are adjuncts of the Urban
Councils or the City Corporations, to
which are co-opted representatives of
religious bodies or other interested
parties.
Catholic elementary schools
governed by priests have no rights to
building and administrative grants, but
by an act of grace any such schools
which comply with the Committee's
building specifications, etc., generally
obtain the grants. Yet the appointing of the teachers therein (who are
paid by the Education Committee) still
remains fully in the priest's hands.
This is, of course, only possible because
of the entire absence of that bigotry
which makes a similar arrangement entirely impossible in Northern Ireland.
That is in England. There is about to
be a conference between the representatives of the Government and the Catholic
clergy in England in order that some arrangement may be come to whereby they
will be satisfied with the control of the
schools. In the constitution of the 1920
Act and the Acts we are living under it
is stated with regard to the two Parliaments:
In the exercise of their power to make
laws under this Act neither the Parliament of Southern Ireland nor the
Parliament of Northern Ireland shall
make a law so as either directly or indirectly to establish or endow any
religion, or prohibit or restrict the free
exercise thereof, or give a preference,
privilege or advantage, or impose any
disability or disadvantage, on account
of religious belief or religious or
ecclesiastical status.
We
Now I say that in the Free State where
about 7 per cent. of the people are non-
Catholic, they have the same conditions
as they had under the British Government and they are quite satisfied.
are 35 per cent. of the people of the Six
Counties. Are you going to deny us what
is granted in the Free State? Is it fair
for us to pay rates and endow Protestant
schools? I am delighted to see these
schools erected. There is a great need for
schools in Belfast. I sincerely hope that
even at this late hour something will be
done that will meet the appeal from this

to satisfy our religious beliefs.
We hold very strong convictions, and
without giving any offence to any Member
in this House, I would say we are taught
to think more of our souls than of our
bodies, and that is why we feel so strongly
on this matter. I sincerely hope something will be done. It is our duty in this
Parliament-one of our principal duties—
to assist you in every Measure in the
interests of the people generally, but over
and above that we have a very serious
duty to discharge and that is to look after
the interests of the faith to which I am
proud to belong. I think that is all I can
say. I repeat what I said before. I
hope, as Sir Robert Lynn said yesterday,
that this matter may be settled by a conference. I was going to say that there
is very little use of our people attending

Oral Answers
HOUSE OF COMMONS
HOUSE OF COMMONS.

Thursday, 13th March, 1930.
The House met at Three of the Clock,
Mr. SPEAKER in the Chair.
Oral Answers to Questions.
MARKETING OF AGRICULTURAL
PRODUCE.
1. Mr. McALEER asked the Minister
of Agriculture whether he is aware that
the Agricultural County Committees of
Derry and Tyrone passed resolutions
calling upon the Government of Northern
Ireland to urge upon the Imperial Government the extreme necessity of some measure
whereby agricultural produce could be
marketed at a remunerative price to farmers, especially in such main crops as
potatoes, oats, and flax; and whether representations have been made to the
Imperial Government on this very vital
question?
The MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE
(Sir Edward Archdale): I have received
a copy of the resolutions passed by the
Londonderry and Tyrone County Committees of Agriculture regarding the
marketing of agricultural produce at
more remunerative prices. As my hon.
Friend will realise, the problem is not
one which is confined to Northern Ireland, and although very effort has been
made by my Department to secure an
outlet for Northern Ireland potatoes, and
to facilitate the marketing of this crop,
the present over-production in
in Great
Britain has necessarily curtailed our
market there.
Some time ago the Ministry made representations to the Empire Marketing
Board regarding a potato advertising
campaign, which has since been inaugurated. The Ministry has also made
representations to the Imperial Government urging that the Governments of
Canada and the United States should be
approached with regard to the removal
of the existing embargo upon the importation of potatoes into those countries.
I can assure my hon. friend that, in
consultation with the Imperial Authorities, every effort is being made to further
the marketing of Northern Ireland agricultural produce.
LICENSED PUBLIC HOUSES IN
BELFAST AND LONDONDERRY.
2. Mr. CRAWFORD asked the
Minister of Finance whether he can state
the number of licensed public houses in
each of the Wards in the Cities of Belfast
and Londonderry, and in each of the Six
Counties in Northern Ireland?
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Pollock): I propose to circulate in the
Official Report a tabular statement giving
the number of licensed premises by
Counties and County Boroughs. I regret
that as the collection of licence duties is
not related to Local Government Electoral
sub-divisions, I am not able to supply
statistics for Boroughs by Wards.
Mr. CRAWFORD: May I ask where
we might expect to have an answer to the
question?
Mr. POLLOCK: It would only be by
my Department investigating the subject
with the local authorities and such other
bodies as keep records of the numbers by
wards in the community. I think if my
hon. Friend would communicate with the
Town Clerk he would probably get the
information. I certainly do not know of
any other method by which it can be
acquired, as we have no record of the subdivisions such as are asked for.
Mr. CRAWFORD: We will have the
information as to the counties?
Mr. POLLOCK: Yes.
The following is the tabular statement
referred to:

Debate on Address
Debate on Address
13 MARCH 1930
Question again proposed.
The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.
Andrews): Although this is the last
stage of the general debate on the
Address to his Majesty I would like to
join with those hon. Members on both
sides of the House who have so fittingly
congratulated the mover and seconder of
the Address during the past two days.
Both, as we all feel, made most excellent
speeches worthy of the highest traditions
associated with this honourable House.
In the first place, I would like to say
how gratified I personally feel that the
proposal contained in the Gracious
Speech in reference to medical benefits
has been received by every Member who
has spoken on the subject with feelings of
satisfaction. It gives me confidence to
realise that when the Measure itself
comes to be introduced in a few weeks
time we will be able, I hope, to give it
our united blessing as a great beneficent
Measure intended to right a wrong which
was done to the insured persons in Northern Ireland in 1911, when the Act of
that year, so far as medical benefits were
concerned, did not apply to Northern
Ireland.
The Government feel that they can no
longer remain inactive in connection with
this matter because both the general death
rate and the sickness experience amongst
insured persons are admittedly higher in
Northern Ireland than across the
Channel. I would like very briefly to
assure hon. Members on both sides of
the House that the proposed Measure
will not entail an additional burden
upon the rates, nor will it in any way
cause over-lapping with the existing
services. The hon. Member for North
Antrim (Sir Robert Lynn) and the hon.
Member for Mid-Antrim (Mr. Crawford)
did suggest that perhaps it would be
wiser if the Government delayed introducing this Measure until the matters
investigated by the Local Government
Commission were dealt with all together.
I would point out, however, that the
Government take a different view. We
feel that it is desirable to deal with a
service such as this, as it must obviously
be dealt with, along lines similar to
those on which it operates in Great
Britain.
The hon. Member for South Fermanagh
(Mr. Healy) made several what I might
call astonishing statements. I am afraid he
is cultivating a reputation for making
extravagant statements in this House. For
instance, he said on Tuesday last that unemployment in Northern Ireland was now
worse than when the Government took
over powers in 1921. That statement is
obviously incorrect. I do feel it is wrong
of hon. Members, in a reckless sort of way,
to circulate reports of the kind without
giving either facts or figures to back them
up, reports which necessarily tend to
create dissatisfaction and unrest amongst
our people. Sometimes I am driven to
feel that some hon. Members oppositeand only some of them-desire to paint
the picture darker than it is, and the only
explanation I can see is that they are
doing so for political reasons. I hope
not, but that is the only explanation I
can give of the extravagant statements
such as that made by the hon. Member
on Tuesday last.
The next matter I would like to refer
to is safeguarding. I am glad to know
that like the Members on this side of the
House he approves of safeguarding in its
application to our industries, and, under
certain conditions, I understand, to agriculture; but the strange thing is that
while he and others who sit beside him
advocate safeguarding in this House
a Member of this House who is also
a Member of the Imperial House is supporting the present Socialist Government
at Westminster in not declaring its intentions as regards the McKenna duties
and the safeguarding duties, which are so
often under consideration in the Imperial
House at the present time. The failure
to declare their intentions is, admittedly,
creating unemployment and misery in
many homes where unemployment would
not exist if the Government could make
up their minds in the right direction and
stick to it.
The hon. Member for Shankill (Mr.
Henderson) made a
very remarkable
speech, but one that was not so amusing
as his speeches generally are. He referred principally to roads and housing.
I dare say he is not aware of the fact
that no less a sum than over £1,000,000
is being spent on the roads of Northern
Ireland every year, and that approximately half that sum is being provided from
Government sources. In the second place,
I wonder if the hon. Member is aware of
the fact that grants have been approved
for ΤΟ fewer than 20,000 houses in
Northern Ireland and that over 15,000
houses have actually been completed. To
give a better idea of what this means T

The
Now I come to the hon. Member for
Pottinger (Mr. Beattie). I am not going
to say very much about his speech because
he really left me very little to say. He
spoke for fifty minutes, but his speech
consisted mainly of rather ungenerous
attacks upon hon. Members on this side
of the House, and he also made a very
untactful and ungracious reference to that
greatest of all shipbuilding firms in the
United Kingdom, Messrs. Harland and
Wolff. My opinion is that we as a community are deeply indebted to the chairmen and directors of our two local yards
for the enterprise, the courage, the public
spirit, and the humanity they have displayed in unselfishly, in many instances,
obtaining as much work for our shipyard
employes as it was possible for them to do.
I know that very frequently they have
taken orders when, apart from any profit,
they were not able to obtain even their
standing charges. For the hon. Member
to say they were making large profits and
underpaying their workers is quite, in my
opinion, unfair. They are paying the
standard trade union wage which is
paid not only here but in Great Britain.
In the second place, it is all too true that
no dividend is being paid on the ordinary
stock, and the greater part of their preference shareholders are also obliged to do
without a dividend. But the position
in the shipbuilding industry has improved, thank God, enormously. As recently as 1926 in the shipbuilding and
engineering industry there was unemployment to the extent of 37.1 per cent.
To-day the percentage is 13.3. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear.)
Then, again, the hon. Member went on to
refer to the linen trade as if it were down
and out too, and also as if those whose
families have been engaged in that great
industry for generations knew nothing
about how that industry should be controlled. The linen industry is not down
and out. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear).
But I maintain that these repeated statements to the effect that the trade is down
and out have a most injurious effect, because they take away, or tend to take
away, that security and confidence upon
which only can an industry prosper and
survive. The percentage of unemployment in the linen trade as recently as 1925
was no less than 45.7 per cent. To-day
that percentage has been reduced to 16.2.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear).
The hon. Member for North Armagh
(Mr. J. Johnston), who sits behind me,
referred to the all-important question of
electrical development in Northern Ireland. I am sure the House will be glad
to know that my right hon. Friend, the
Minister of Commerce (Mr. Barbour), has
engaged the services of one of the best
electrical engineers in the Kingdom to adadvise him and the Government as to the
best course they can pursue in order that
an electrical supply shall be available

Debate on Address
13 MARCH 1930
throughout the Six County area at as
early a date as possible.
The hon. and learned Member for the
University (Mr. McNeill), who always
speaks in a thoughtful and reasonable way,
which I am sure we all appreciate, dealt
very ably with quite a number of matters
yesterday. He referred to the fact that
machinery was replacing men, and that,
consequently, unemployment was being
created. That is perfectly true in some
directions, but he and the House generally
will admit that machinery frequently
creates employment. For instance, motor
transport has provided employment for a
tremendous number of people in Northern
Ireland, and has been most beneficial from
that standpoint. I only give that as one
example of how the introduction of
machinery can provide, and does provide,
employment, and useful employment.
And, in addition, if cheaper methods of
production were not introduced here in
keeping with the cheaper methods of production introduced in other countries, we
would be hopelessly out of the race.
Therefore, I feel that our employers are
entitled to be congratulated on the enterprise they display in obtaining the best
machinery to turn out the best work, and,
consequently, place themselves in a position to obtain new orders to replace
those which they execute from time to
time.
The hon. and learned Member for the
University also stated that he regretted
that no mention of unemployment had been
made in his Majesty's Gracious Speech.
Well, what I think is equally important—
mentioned
employment is
in his
Majesty's Speech, and, after all, that is
only another way of expressing the same
thing. It will interest the House to know
that, if you take into consideration our
farm workers and our domestic servants
who are in employment, and couple those
with our insured workers, at least 90 per
cent of our industrial workers in Northern
Ireland are continuously employed. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear). What of the
other 10 per cent? Some of them are not
eligible for employment owing to illness.
They are receiving Health Insurance benefit or disablement benefit as the case may
be. A considerable number are getting
the Old Age Pension, while some are receiving widows' and orphans' pensions,
and, again, great numbers of them are
receiving unemployment benefit. Proof
that not many of them are being left high
and dry or unaided from Government
sources is to be found in the fact that
at the present time we are spending no
less a sum than £81,000 each week in
these various forms of relief in Northern
Ireland.
The hon. and learned Member went on
to tell us that he thought the question of
distribution was more important even than
the question of production. He and I,
no doubt, could have an interesting argument on that, but I am not quite clear
to what he refers when he speaks of distribution. If it be to transport I would
like to say that as regards most of our industries the cost of transport forms a very
small part of what may be called the cost
of production. On the other hand, if he
referred to credit problems, as I think he
did, it is, of course, an economic problem
which obviously cannot be settled across
the floor of this or any other House.
The last speech to which I would like
to refer is that of the hon. Member for
Falls (Mr. Byrne), who always speaks in
a reasonable and thoughtful manner which
especially appeals to me. He asked me a
question which I am glad to be able to
answer satisfactorily. That was what is
to be the position of those farmers who
have bought under our compulsory Land
Act of recent date, and whose agreements
have not been completed. I am glad to
be able to inform the hon. Member that
those farmers are not going to be placed
at any disadvantage, because the appointed day for them is to be the same as
the appointed day for those whose transactions have been completed, namely, the
27th May, 1929. It is true that those
farmers whose farms have not actually
been transferred are still paying rents
which are slightly bigger than the land
annuities which they would be paying if
the transactions were completed, but, on
the other hand, provision has been made
by which when the transactions have been
completed those farmers will be recouped
for such over-payments as they may have
made. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear).
The only other matter to which
I feel that it is necessary for me
to refer to-day is that of education.
If I were pursuing the line of
least resistance I admit that I would
say nothing about it at all, but, on the
other hand, if I were to adopt that easier
course a wrong impression might be created
in the country, because it might be said
that the Government have no answer to
the arguments which have been put forward by hon. Members opposite during

HOUSE OF COMMONS

the last few days. In referring to education it seems to me somewhat strange
that those hon. Members did not make
a single reference to the education of the
children apart from the religious aspect
of the problem. I do think it is a pity
and rather derogatory to this House that
this religious question should be so frequently dragged into our discussions. It
is deplorable. After all, we are all
Christians going the same journey by somewhat different ways. I would be the last
to say anything to-day which I thought
would in any way wound the natural susceptibilities of hon. Members opposite. If
they are out for equality and equality
alone they can take it from me that the
Government are quite anxious that they
should receive it. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear). But if, on the other hand, they
are out to be placed in a position of privilege, in a special position of their own,
if they are out to be placed in a position
of ascendancy, that is a demand which the
Government will not and cannot grant.
I would just like to say this in conclusion:
Very often we are told that the minority
in Northern Ireland are not being fairly
treated. My opinion, for what it is
worth, is that no minority in any country
in the world is as fairly treated as the
minority in Northern Ireland. Look for
a moment at the position in the Free
State. There the minority are bound,
whether they like it or not, to learn
Irish. (Laughter.) Hon. Members may
laugh, but it is true. Further still, that
is only the means to an end-

Counties, with a population of

In my judgment the reason why we use so
much more potatoes according to the
population than they do in Britain is because we have fed them with poor potatoes. And in that respect to some extent,
if not to a large extent, the Ministry of
Agriculture is to blame. They have advocated the planting of a class of potatoes
that gives a large yield. They have induced the farmers to plant these potatoes
and they have prevented them from planting others because of their alleged susceptibility to black scab. The potato that
was well known to be one of the finest
a

toes known as Dates, Lochars, and other

Mr. POLLOCK : What do they do

Mr. O'NEILL: We send them to the

all. According to the figures of the

head in Northern Ireland as they do
in England. Therefore I think that in

Now, if we take the question of flax, we
produce, also according to the figures of
the Ministry, something like 5,000 tons of
flax per year and we import something
like 20,000 tons of flax per year. According to the figures given in the Senate
only yesterday we imported 3,000,000 lbs.
or to be absolutely correct 2,999,993 lbs.
in the year 1929 of flax, yarns, and linen
goods. It does seem strange that in a
country that has always had the name
-and I think rightly-of being well
adapted for growing flax and in an area
that has practically a monopoly of the
manufacture of linen we cannot produce
flax sufficient for them, and for what we
do produce we are not in a position to
pay the farmer even an economic price.
Is it defensible, I ask this House, that
under these conditions we should subsidise
the linen industry by paying them
£20,000 a year of the taxpayers' money
as we are doing now for the purpose of
advertising linen, and allow them to import flax and linen yarns and linen goods,
and yet not be able to pay your own
farmer who raises the stuff at your door an
economic price? There is surely something wrong, and there is something that
the Government should be able to rectify
if an effort, was made in the right direction.
Mr. POLLOCK:
How?
Mr. O'NEILL: That is for the Government. But it is surely not a defensible
thing that they should spend the taxpayers' money to assist the linen industry
when they are not in a position to give

economic price for it. No one suggests
that the farmers in this country do not
work as well as they do in other places.
No one suggests that they are better fed or
better cared than in any other country. I
think it is a crying scandal that a farmer
after the labour of himself and his family
producing flax cannot get a price for it
to pay even a quarter of the wages earned
in any other industry in any other country
in any part of the world. I am sorry that
I am not in a position to go any further

Mr. McALEER: I beg to second the
Amendment proposed by the hon. Member for Mourne. The Department of
Agriculture was established to foster and
encourage the development of the farming industry in this Northern Province.
Its function was to train and educate the
farmers and the farmers' sons in the most
up-to-date methods of husbandry. The
Department appointed a great many inspectors to give advice as to the proper
seeds to sow, the best and most useful
fertilisers to apply to the soil, and to see
that the people of the Six Counties got
approved breeds of horses, cattle, sheep,
pigs, and poultry. There was a big staff appointed to promote the interests of the
farming community in the Northern
Province. All this meant a very big
drain on the public purse.
There are some very able men connected
with the Department of Agriculture and
very estimable men. But I must say that
they must go one better if they want to
get and retain the confidence of the
farmers and other people of Northern
Ireland. Times are no better. They are
infinitely worse. The farmers have not
had such a bad year since the year 1879.
There is a poor demand for the produce
of their farms and the prices are very
bad.
Take for instance the egg trade. The
egg trade is a very important moneymaking industry in this country and in

cold weather such as we have been having

Take flax at 6s 9d a stone or 7s. That
would never pay any farmer.
It is one of
the most difficult crops to manage on a
farm, the ploughing of the land, reducing the soil to a nice tilth to take in the
small seeds of flax, buying seed, sowing,
the pulling of the crop, placing it in the
dams and looking after the retting and
spreading. It is one of the nastiest jobs
on a farm, and then the farmer will only
get 6s 9d to 7s a stone. There is not
much margin of profit in that. We hear
a great deal of sympathy with the linen
manufacturers. I think sympathy should
be extended to the farmer who is working
flax and only getting 6s 9d to 7s a stone
for it.
Cattle are a pretty good price but the
supply is limited. It is limited for this
reason that since the introduction of this
Government infertility and abortion has
been very common. That is the reason
why cattle have been scarce in this
country. At the present time farmers
are unable to make ends meet. They are
heavily in debt, in debt to the banks,
in debt to the auctioneers, in debt to the
shops and unable to pay the tradesmen.
The outlook is very bad as we see evidenced in the increasing flow of emigration of the young and the strong to the
United States, Canada, Australia, New
Zealand and other colonies. They cannot get a living in this country. I cannot congratulate the Government on this
state of affairs. The farmers are in bankruptcy, and the Government has been
weighed and found wanting. I beg to
second the Amendment.
The MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE
(Sir Edward Archdale): The two hon.
Members who proposed and seconded this

a little bit inaccurate in their statements.
The Member for Mourne (Mr. O'Neill)
seemed to think that the Government has

money was for the benefit of agriculture
in the various counties. There was a sum
of £9,000 given for live stock improvement, which included loans for the purchase of stud animals, and large sums of
money were also given to the dairy recording societies to help them to increase the
sale of milk. A sum of £6,000 was given
for schemes for the improvement of pastures, country grass-land, and for the improvement of mountain sheep. Last year,
£14,000 was given for the improvement of
holdings by drainage, work which absorbed
unemployed labour.
A sum of £5,000 was given last year in
loans for the improvement of land and
roads up to the farms and the clearing

a sum of £14,000 will be given for those

is a very considerable sum of money. The
hon. Member who seconded the Amendment talked about the education we provided for young farmers. I consider that
the education we provide for the young
farmer is the best that is given in any
country. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear).

them to Canada?

HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Sir Edward Archdale]
The Member for Mourne said the potato
industry was the greatest money-making
industry in the Six Counties. That is not
the case at all. The cattle industry is a
far more valuable industry than the potato
industry, and even the poultry industry
is greater than the potato trade.
Mr. NIXON: Question.
Sir EDWARD ARCHDALE: If the
poultry industry is not greater than the
potato trade it is at least as great. I believe myself that there is more money coming into the country from the sale of
poultry and eggs than there is from the
sale of potatoes. There is no doubt at
all that both the egg trade and the cattle
trade produce much more than the potato
industry, and what the Ministry want farmers to do is to go in for mixed farming
and not follow the example of the farmers
in one or two districts of County Down
where they go in solely for potatoes. I
know plenty of small farmers who are not
so badly off as hon. Members make out.
A man with a sow which produces two
litters in a year can get £3 for a young
pig and 104s. a cwt. for pork, so that he
is not so badly off. If he has a cow which
produces a calf which at twelve
months old is sold for £10 or £12
it is a considerable help on a small
farm worked by the tenant himself and
his family. There are plenty of small farmers working their farms with the labour
of their sons who have only two or three
healthy cows producing good milk, and
with a calf bringing £12, and by feeding
the pigs and poultry with the skim milk
they can make sufficient to keep the farm
going in a comfortable state.
I would also like to say that the Government have inserted in the newspapers a
notice that loans will be granted to farmers
for the purchase of livestock, a subject
on which the Ministry were recently interviewed by hon. Members opposite, including the Member for East Down
(Lieut. Col. Gordon) and Mr. Speaker.
These loans will be granted to farmers to
enable them to purchase livestock.
They
will be issued at 5 per cent. interest, and
are repayable in four years in equal payments on 31st December, 1931, 1932, 1933,
and 1934, or they can be paid off at once
if the borrower chooses to do so. There are
also short term loans available for the purchase of seeds and manures. These will
have to be paid off in one year at 5 per
cent. interest. I consider that these loans
will be of great advantage to farmers, as
they will enable them to re-stock their
farms. Considering the amount of money
that the Government have given to the
farming industry in the past, and the
amount they are giving at the present
time, I do not think it compares badly
with any
other country. The state of agriculture is certainly bad everywhere, but

stone. I cannot urge any farmer to grow
flax when he only gets that price for it,
because it would not pay him to do so when
the cost of labour is so high.

Colonel GORDON : The question of
subsidies was raised. The Member for

is out of the question. The taxpayer
has reached the limit and can pay no
more money and can stand no more strain.
It is quite useless to ask for a subsidy for
any industry. Will the Member for
Mourne go back to Warrenpoint and advocate a tax or not? I think the answer
is no.
I think in the agricultural industry
there are two main remedies, and the first
is the keeping out, as everybody has said,
of county fed foreign produce. We all
know that that is outside the province of
this Government to deal with. Whether
the Opposition like it or not we are bound
up with the fiscal system in England and
with that system we get the benefits of
derating and the social services which
would be otherwise far less than they are
now. I take it that that being outside the
power of this Government we can only wait
until the people across the water change
their minds, which I hope they will do very
shortly.
I noticed that the hon. Member for
Falls (Mr. Byrne), yesterday advocated
protection. I am very glad to hear him
say so. I hope he will go a step farther
and take his colleague, the hon. Member
for Central Belfast (Mr. Devlin), by the
hand and try to wean him from the
Socialists on the other side of the water,
and get him to his way of thinking, for
I am afraid he is not in favour of protection.
The next remedy is one that can be
dealt with here, and that is marketing
reform, trying to put our products on the
market in the best way and in the best
condition. We can also try to eliminate
every extra charge between producer and
consumer. I think that is one thing we
can and must pay attention to.
Now, I come to the potato question.
The Members who have spoken from the
other side of the House one and all seem
to blame the Government for this glut of
potatoes. No Government can be blamed
for a glut in any one product. The
Government is not responsible. I have
worked the figures out in regard to
England as compared with Northern Ireland. The facts and figures are these.
We grew in Northern Ireland last year
18 cwt. per head of the population. In
Great Britain in 1928 the crop per head
of the population was 1 cwt., and last
year, 1929, the crop was 24 cwt. You
will see that that is an increase of nearly
cwt. Therefore, the people across the
water, as everyone knows, have far too
many potatoes to dispose of.
The exports for the last three years
averaged 215 tons. No Government can
be blamed for being unable to dispose of
a crop that is over-produced. I think
the only remedy is, as the Minister of
Agriculture has said, to turn the attention of those farmers who have grown
potatoes solely to general tillage. I hope
they will make use of this loan which is
now being passed. I should like to say
that the private Members on this side of
the House are forming an agricultural
committee, and I hope when we get
started we will be able to give the Minister of Agriculture every assistance we
When Bills come forward we shall

we can to get them put through properly.

House. I think it is rather a pity that
such an important subject should be
brought down to such-I can
nothing but scandal-in this House.
The Amendment to the Address regrets

Measure of alleviation for those engaged

to be the "Government's special endeavour to assist by every means in its power
agricultural and industrial undertakings."
There is no Member of this House
who has a better knowledge of agriculture or who comes in closer contact with
the agricultural communities than I do
in my public and business capacity.
When the hon. and gallant Member for
Derry (Captain Chichester-Clark) said.
that the farmers are in a bad position in
regard to their industry I do not think.
he painted the picture any blacker than
it is, but I would like any hon. Member

we are going to better the condition of
the farmers.
Mr. FOLLOCK: Hear, hear.
Mr. MINFORD: It is quite true that
the prices of agricultural produce have
come down to a very low level, and it is
beyond the wit of man to see how farmers
can carry on at those low prices, but,
bad and all as it is, the farmers are not
yet down and out. The saving of the
situation lies not with the people in this
House, but with the people across the
water in the Imperial Parliament.
If
hon. Members on the opposite side proved
themselves just as anxious as we are to
get their representatives in the Imperial
House to try to solve this problem I believe
they would do more good than they do
now by coming here and criticising the
Minister of Agriculture. In my opinion
the only means of solving the trouble is
by closing the floodgates of foreign competition and bounty-fed produce. I was
amazed that the hon. Member for Mourne
(Mr. O'Neill) should have blamed the
Minister of Agriculture (Sir Edward
Archdale) for compelling the people to
plant potatoes that were not suitable or

-we were never compelled to do so. I
think the hon. Member said that the
Ministry compelled them to grow potatoes
called Up-to-Dates. I should like to tell
this House that that potato is the most
popular that goes to the English market.
The hon. Member for Woodvale (Mr.
Nixon) blamed the Minister of Agriculture for having such a number of inspectors going round the country. It is not
to the farmers' credit that these men
should have to go about the country in
this way.
We must have our stuff in
proper condition in order to secure a
market for it, and as a farmer myself I
agree that the inspection carried out by
the Ministry at the present time is just
and fair.
The hon. Member for Shankill (Mr.
Henderson) stated the other day that the

is employed on those farms. The reason

HOUSE OF COMMONS

the farming industry is in the position in

I would like to impress upon Members on

for protection. As long as we have Free
Trade and as long as we go on allowing
these foreign goods to come into our
markets, we cannot face the competition.
I am one of those who believe that the
farmers of Ulster can meet fair and equitable competition, and I hope that before.
many months have passed the Imperial
Government will see their way to adopt
the opinion of Mr. Baldwin, and to impose
a system of protection.

of this side of the House to do our best

(Hon. Members: Hear, hear). I am not

I am
speaking as a practical farmer and as one
who comes into contact with them, not as
some hon. Members who sometimes do not
know what they are talking about. What
the farmer wants to-day is a fair field.
What he wants is protection and to be able
to put his produce on the market in a
decent way.
I think it was the hon. Member for
Shankill (Mr. Henderson) who said that
the farmers did not pay their workers a
reasonably fair wage. As a farmer myself, and as a representative of farmers
and industrial workers, I say that it is
the object of the farmers to be able to

perhaps better-for their labour as any
other industry in Northern Ireland, but
the position to-day will not allow us to
pay the wage we would like to pay, especially after all the great losses we have
had in potatoes and other crops this year.
Our potato exports used to amount to
250,000 tons per year. This year we have
exported a very small quantity of
potatoes. Our export of this crop has
fallen very considerably, and I think I
am right when I say that the potato crop
represents a loss to the farmers of
Northern Ireland of approximately
£1,500,000.
But I am not going to throw the blame
for that upon the Ministry of Agriculture
or upon this Government. If I did I
would be most ungrateful, and I take this
opportunity of conveying to the Government the sincere thanks of the farmers
for what they have done in the interests
of agriculture. The Derating Act is
something of which we should be proud.
In this morning's paper I see that the
Minister of Agriculture has issued a
notice that men who want loans for stocking their farms or for buying seeds or
manures can have them if they apply
before a certain date. What more could
the Minister do?
The hon. Member for Woodvale (Mr.
Nixon) talks about some Biblical man
living on grass, and about the Hillsborough Experimental Farm. If we had
not that farm at Hillsborough then the
hon. Member would say that we were not
giving the farmers any chance of getting
proper scientific instruction or training.
The Minister is blamed sometimes for not
doing things for the farmers, and then
when he does them hon. Members blame
him again. I do not want to take up the
time of the House, but I am very glad to
have had this opportunity of taking the
part of the Minister of Agriculture, for
some people in this House seem to take
pleasure in saying most unkind things
. about him and the Members of the
Cabinet.
As well as for the farmers I feel very
much to-day for the farm workers. Unfortunately quite a lot of farmers are
letting their farms go into grass, instead
of tilling them, and these unfortunate

workers have now to go out to seek employment. To these men my sympathy

I will close by expressing the hope that

tons going to loss and cannot get rid of

With regard to flax, I know the price.
is still very bad. Indeed, for the moment

Members opposite will not throw the

through a most depressing time, but I believe that with perseverance and endurance we will still be able to carry on.
With the sympathy of the Minister of

back to the prosperous state in which it

The Ulster Year Book gives the average
yield per acre all over the Six Counties
as 32 stones per acre. I always have been
told that an average good crop was six
stones to the peck, and that there were
seven pecks of seed sown to the statute
acre. That meant a yield of 42 stones
to the statute acre. Even if you take the
price mentioned by hon. Members of the
Opposition, namely, 6s 9d, which is not
the average price, but about the very
lowest price-if you take 7s to make an
easier calculation, you get on those 42
stones about £15 per acre. 7s a stone is
not the average price, but the very lowest
price. Quite a common price this season
was nearer the average of 10s, which on
the same basis of 42 stones to the acre
would be about £20 to the statute acre.
I should be surprised if the Irish farmers do not grow as much flax in the
future as they have done in the past.
Members on both sides of the House who
are not familiar with the flax trade are
always inclined to look upon these prices.

Reference has been made to the Derating Bill. I think there is a great impression in the country that the derating
scheme has been of immense service to the
farming community. I do not wish to
belittle its effects, but, looking at it from
the point of view of the small farmer, I
think he would be satisfied if he could get
a fair price for his commodities. In one
instance a farmer's valuation was £40,
and the agricultural rating was 7/- in the
pound. Take it at £1 an acre.
The result is he is derated to the extent of £14.
The suggestion was made in this way that,
although he pays nothing in rates, in
times of stress he is pretty far down
financially. Say he had 28 tons of
potatoes a very small quantity for a
farmer-if he could get 10/- more per ton
than he is getting now it would make up
that £14. In other products the same
thing applies.
I do not believe the farmer is one of
those grasping individuals who is always
whinging and crying. The farmer is up
against a great deal, and Nature deals
hardly with him. I know something about
farming. I had a farm for many yearsnot in this country. I had the nasty experience of paying two dollars for my seed
oats, of putting them in, of having a good
harvest, of hauling my grain with horses
to the town, a matter of 25 miles, and of
getting 25 cents a bushel for it-oneeighth of the price of the oats I bought.
I then decided that I would feed my hogs
with the balance. I did so, and raised a
fine lot of young pigs. I brought them to
market, and to my intense mortification
found that everybody had been feeding
hogs. I could not give them away at 3
cents a lb. It was in that grand country
of Canada, a country in which as a rule
farming is a profitable enterprise. I want
to show you, and that example shows it,
that farming in any country all over the
world in any land has its ups and downs.
At best it is a very hard game to play,
because, as I said, Nature sometimes deals
hardly with the farmer. The times of the
most prolific crop are the times of the
lowest prices. To sum up my experience
of farming, the farmer can grow his crop
but he cannot say at what price he will
sell it. The manufacturer largely makes
the price of his article or commodity
against costs and profit before he sells it.
That is, as a rule.

I will refer to the town of Newry, the

enormous sum has been expended on

All we ask
is that we shall get the same terms as the

In these schools of ours we seek to control the religious teaching of the children.
We must take teachers for them who will

Mr. ANDREWS: Mr. Samuel Kyle
did not go over as the Leader of the

as a trade union leader to join with the

The employers' representatives and the
workers' representatives were told in the
clearest possible way that any assistance
which this Government could give to bring
about the desired object would be given.
I have a letter here which I will not
bother reading. It is from the Minister,
dated 21st November, 1924, and it is to
local authorities urging them to do
their duty in finding employment for the
unemployed. It shows a good heart, but
it is passing on your duty to other people.
That has been going on ever since. I
think we have come to the time of day
when we should be told something about
this great subject. Is it to go on as it
is? Is there a remedy? If there is a
remedy, why is it not applied? If the
Prime Minister had a remedy on the 28th
November, 1923, he should have applied
it. If he had not a remedy, he should
not have said he had. He should not
have misled the people, even on the eve
of an election. Nothing would justify
it. Nothing justifies misleading a starving man.
The hon. and gallant Member for St.

Mr. DONNELLY: I would like to
add my voice to the chorus of condemnation from these Benches with regard to
the education policy of the Government.
The principle of the Act of 1923 was
pure secularism in education. It is a
bad policy because it subordinates
religious training and religious teaching
to training and teaching that is purely
secular. If this policy is carried to
its logical conclusion it is just possible
that at some date we will have the state
of affairs existing in Northern Ireland
that exists in Russia to-day. That
policy has been objected to by the
Catholic Church and also by the heads
of the Protestant Churches in Northern
Ireland. The Government, by the proposed introduction of legislation to amend
the Act of 1923, evidently admit that
that policy is bad. They propose to introduce an amendment, as has been outlined in the King's Speech, but instead
of dealing with this thorny subject in a
statesmanlike manner and a manner fair
and equitable to all sections of the community, the Government propose to
satisfy the demands of the Protestant
Churches alone. The claims of the
Catholic community are absolutely ignored. I think it has been pointed out
to the Government time and again that
the religious education of the children is
a matter of paramount importance to
the Catholic Church, and that Catholics
require Catholic schools under Catholic
management.
The last speaker made reference to the
Act of 1920 and the powers of the
Government under that Act. Section 5
of that Act reads as follows:
Debate on Address
Debate on Address
13 MARCH 1930
In the exercise of their power to
make laws under this Act neither the
Parliament of Southern Ireland nor
the Parliament of Northern Ireland
shall make a law so as either directly
or indirectly to establish endow
any religion, or prohibit or restrict the
free exercise thereof, or give a preference, privilege or advantage, or impose any disability or disadvantage, on
account of religious belief or religious
or ecclesiastical status.
What I say with reference to this matter
is that the Government propose to meet
the demand of the Protestant Churches,
or some of the Protestant Churches, and
entirely ignore in their proposed legislation the claims of the Catholic Church,
and they commit a distinct violation of
this Section of the Act under which they
were created as a Government. It is interesting to know the treatment that is
meted out to Catholic schools by the
British Government and compare the
treatment that is given to them under
the Government of Northern Ireland.
The old system of National Education in
Ireland was not perfect. It did not meet
the Catholic demand in full, but on the
whole it worked fairly and satisfactorily
because in the parishes where all the
children, or a majority of the children,
attending the schools were Catholic the
parish priest was the manager of that
school and they got the usual grants of
two-thirds if it was a new school, or twothirds for enlargement, and in some
cases even larger grants were made with
the addition of the usual percentage for
cleaning, lighting, and heating.
Under the Northern Government there
is no Catholic management of any school
no matter how much the Catholic people
desire it. There are no schools provided for
Catholics which they can conscientiously
attend. This matter has been explained
to the Government time and again. There
will be a distinct violation of the Act of
1920 if the claims of one section of the
community are conceded and the legitimate claims of another section ignored.
We have had many things done by the
Northern Government since they came
into power to which we have taken serious
objection and to which we will always
object. In the matter of the electoral
franchise Proportional Representation has
been abolished. In the matter of local
government franchise the electoral divisions have been gerrymandered to such an
extent that substantial majorities are deprived of the control of local bodies to
which their majority entitled them. But
this matter of education is probably the
most serious. The manner in which the
Government are dealing with it is a matter
to which the Catholic community take the
strongest possible objection. We press
this matter that our legitimate demands
should be met, and that schools should be
provided under such management that
there will be no conscientious objection on
the part of Catholics to sending their
children to the schools.
Major McCORMICK: I rise to take

HOUSE OF COMMONS

their schools as it is. There is no compulsion on them to take advantage of this
Act. As a matter of fact at the present

The Member for South Armagh (Mr.
Connellan) spoke about the conscience of
the Roman Catholic community. Have not
the Protestant people got a conscience? I
say here that the conscience of the Roman
Catholic people is not dearer to them than
is the conscience of the Protestant people
to us. As I said, there is no compulsion
on Roman Catholics to take advantage of
the Act, but surely if they do so they cannot claim prior rights or preferential treatment.
The Member for South Armagh-
I am sorry he is not in his place-said
much about democracy. Apparently he
was not in favour of democracy or democrats, because this Education Act of 1923
was a very democratic Act and is said, not
by the people of Northern Ireland only but
by people in other countries, to be one of the
finest Education Acts ever passed. But it
was too democratic for the Member for
South Armagh. It does not suit his
Church. He likes a one-man show, and
we do not. That is the difference. We
fear autocracy, and we want more say in
the management of schools. We are
living in the spirit of the age. It is a
democratic age, and it is a democratic
movement that permeates the Education
Act.
I should tell the hon. Member and his
newspaper that the Protestant conscience
feels perfectly clear that the Education
Act is fair in its working in every way.
The fact that the people are taxed gives
them representation. It gives them the
opportunity to make use of the benefits of
the Act, and if they do not take these
benefits it is their own fault. I take it
there is no objection to simple Bible teaching, and in that respect I should pay a
tribute to the Member for South Tyrone
(Mr. Elliott) for his efforts to make it
clear to the minds of the people that simple
Bible teaching in the schools should not remain in doubt. I think that in all
countries general religious instruction.
should be confined to the Church, but that
simple Bible teaching should be given in
the elementary schools in accordance with
the views of the parents of the children
attending the school.

Member's question is in the affirmative.

sending a copy to the hon. Member.

such a Committee.
The various local authorities in Northern Ireland, that is, the County Councils
and County Borough Councils have ample
powers under the Blind Persons Acts to
make suitable provision for Blind Persons
within their respective areas.
Generally speaking, the conditions.
differ in each area, and it is a matter for
the local authority concerned rather than
for central authority or a Central
Advisory Committee to determine what
steps should be taken in each area to meet
the situation.

8. Mr. McBRIDE (for Sir Robert

whether a deputation from the County

this question?
Sir DAWSON BATES: The answer to
the first part of the question is in the

therefore, arise.
BAG-NETS FOR SALMON FISHING.
9. Mr. McBRIDE (for Sir Robert
Lynn) asked the Minister of Commerce
whether he is aware that around the coast
of Northern Ireland there is a strong feeling that bag-nets should be used in place
of draft nets for the capture of salmon,
and whether, in view of the fact that there
has been no legislation on the subject
since 1863, and that bag-nets are generally
used throughout the world, he will set up
an impartial Committee to inquire into
the subject?
The MINISTER OF COMMERCE
(Mr. Barbour): I have received representations from time to time in favour of
restoring the right to use bag-nets in
certain places around the Ulster Coast to
those whose right to use such nets was
taken away, and a right to use a fixed
draft net substituted therefor by the
Fisheries Act of 1863. Looking to the
history of salmon fishing in Ireland
generally, I have hitherto felt myself
compelled to decline any suggestion of repealing the 1863 Act, my views on this
matter being apparently the same as those
held by the former Irish Fisheries Authorities almost since that Act was passed.
While I should be reluctant to take any
step which might suggest that my Department has altered its view on the
fundamental facts underlying this matter,
I have come to the conclusion that, in
view of the lapse of time since the Act in
question was passed, it may be expedient
to investigate the subject afresh, and to
this end I propose to appoint a Committee of Inquiry, as suggested by the
Hon. Member in the last part of the
question.

The FINANCIAL SECRETARY (Mr.
Barbour): The most important items for
which supplementary provision is now required appear under Section II of the
Vote, and relate to the new Law Courts
Supply-
Committee
18 MARCH 1930
Building. As the two items in question

Ireland Estimates, and as they will recur
in subsequent years, it is desirable that
hon. Members should be fully informed

The first item of £2,400 relates to the
contribution from Northern Ireland funds
towards the provision of accommodation
for the Incorporated Law Society, that is
to say the Northern Ireland Solicitors'
Society which corresponds to the former
all-Ireland Law Society. When the requirements for accommodation in the building were first scheduled there was general
agreement that there should be provided
some accommodation for the use not of
the Society as such, but for the use of
solicitors having business at the Courts,
many of whom I understand are not members of the Society.
The Imperial Government accordingly
arranged for a certain amount of accommodation of the nature to be embodied in
the plans, and provided free of charge.
Representations were, however, made by
the Society that, in addition, accommodation should be provided for the Society's
purposes comparable to similar accommodation which the all-Ireland Society
had in Dublin, but the Imperial Government refused to admit any liability in
the matter on the ground that the Dublin
accommodation had not been provided
directly out of Government funds.
The Northern Ireland Government,
after careful consideration, came to the
conclusion that such accommodation was
necessary for a Society charged by Statute
with certain definite functions of a public
character, that a newly-formed Society
could not be expected to find all the
money necessary for such a purpose from
its own resources, and, therefore, that
some contribution from the N.I.
chequer was essential. It was, therefore,
arranged with the Imperial Government
that this further accommodation for the
Society was to be provided for in the
plans, on the clear understanding that
the Imperial Government would not have
to bear any part of the cost involved.
Ex-
The estimated cost of the provision is
£10,500, and as a result of negotiations.
which have been proceeding for some time
as regards the apportionment of the cost
as between the Government and the
Society, this Government will contribute
the sum of £7,000, and the balance will
be borne by the Society, payment of the
full amount being made in the first instance by the Northern Ireland Government as the building of the Law Courts
proceeds. The sum now asked for is the
first instalment.

The first item in Sub-head K is for a
new road on the Madden Estate in County
Fermanagh, to permit of tenants having
access to turbary. The labour employed
by the Fermanagh County Council is recruited mainly from tenants the
estate who have been in arrears with

them to pay off their arrears in whole or
part. The County Surveyor's Office of

improving holdings. The turbary thus
provided is expected to last for fifty
years.
The second item is also in connection

County Tyrone. The survey has necessitated an examination of hundreds of
holdings by a Land Commission inspector
acting as agent of the Ministry of
Finance. The preparation of this scheme
is not yet completed. I beg to move.

Mr. HEALY: No, it was not the

With regard to the construction of

CLASS III. No. 1.
MINISTRY OF HOME AFFAIRS.
Motion made and Question proposed,
That a supplementary sum not exceeding
£815 be granted to His Majesty for the
service of the year ending 31st March,
1930, to defray the salaries and expenses
of the Minister of Home Affairs (15 and
16 Geo. V, c. 3, s. 4 (N.I.); 16 and 17
Geo. V, c. 31 (N.I.), etc.
Sir DAWSON BATES: The Committee will see that we are asking for a
small supplemental vote of £815, and that
this amount is arrived at after giving
credit for certain savings amounting to
£200. The details under each Sub-head
are given in the Estimate, but, for the
information of the Committee, my right
hon. Friend has already explained the
£715 under C1. With regard to the next
item a sum of £240 is required to recoup
Down County Council and the Newtownards Urban District Council for works
undertaken for the safety of competitors
and spectators in connection with the International Motor Race.
When preparations were being made
for the race it was agreed by the representatives of the Royal Automobile Club,
the local authorities, and the Ministry,
after inspection of the course, that certain
measures for the improvement of the
course and the safety of competitors and
spectators were essential. The necessary
work included such items as the erecting
of barricades, which cost no less a sum
than £150; the lifting and relaying curbs.
and marking edges of footpaths, which
cost £50, and touching up level crossings,
drainage pipes, gratings, etc., at a cost of
£40. For this work, which was of use
only for the race and had no permanent
utility, the Government quite properly
undertook to reimburse the local authorities; on that understanding the local
authorities proceeded with the work.
