CLASS III. No. 7.
GRANTS TO LOCAL AUTHORITIES.
Motion made and Question proposed:
"That a supplementary sum not exceeding £66,000 be granted to His Majesty
for the service of the year ending on 31st
of March, 1930, to provide for grants to
local authorities, etc., in respect of health,
housing, etc., including annuities in respect of housing grants, and for grants in
relief of local rates."
Sir DAWSON BATES: There are two
heads under which the provision made
in the original Estimate has proved insufficient; firstly, the annuities in respect
of subsidies paid to private builders erecting houses; and, secondly, the amount required for the purposes of derating for
the current year. The sum required under the first head is £7,900, and under
the second £60,800.
The reason why we have to come to
the Committee for further money for
housing subsidies is that our policy has
been even more successful than was anticipated, and houses are being provided
in greater numbers than we had hoped
for. It will be remembered that when
the Estimates for the current year were
being presented provision was made therein for approximately 3,000 houses being
completed during the course of the year.
The Committee will no doubt be interested
and gratified to learn that up to the 11th
of this month-that is, for a period of 11
months-no less than 4,352 houses have
been completed, and this number will be
considerably exceeded before the end of
the financial year. In other words, our
Estimates have been exceeded by practically 50 per cent., and this number will
be considerably increased before the end
of the financial year.
It may interest the Committee to know
that for the financial year ending on the
31st March, 1928, the number of houses
completed was 2,092; for the year ending
on the 31st March, 1929, the figure was
3,829; and by the end of the current
financial year we anticipate something like
4,500 houses. Hon. Members will, therefore, see that there has been an enormous
increase, and I do not think any apology.
is necessary for asking the Committee to
vote this additional sum.
With regard to derating, when I presented the original Estimate I asked for
a sum of £765,000. When that Estimate
was prepared we were naturally not in
a position to form an accurate estimate of
the actual amount which would be necessary. We had made our scheme, but the
details on which an estimate of the actual
cost for the current year could be framed
were not available. In the first place,
the work of the Valuation Department in
determining what was agricultural land
and what were industrial hereditaments
had not been completed, and in the second
place, after we had received the valuation
books, much detailed information had to
be obtained from the local authorities before we could obtain a reliable estimate.
As was laid down in the Act passed by
the House last year, all local authorities
are recouped their actual loss of rates for
this year, and this estimate deals only
with the recoupment of losses on that
basis. As the House has already approved of the principle, I hope the Committee will vote this money. I beg to
move.
Mr. HEALY: There is one item
here, sub-head B, £1,350, which shows
a decrease on the original Estimate.
That, I take it, relates largely to the
operation of the Labourers Act (Northern Ireland).
It repre-

KING'S SPEECH.
GOVERNOR'S ANSWER TO THE
ADDRESS.
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Pollock) (at the Bar) reported that his
Grace the Governor having been attended.
with the Address of 13th March, has been
pleased to give the following answer:
I have received with great satisfaction
the expression of your thanks for the
Speech with which the present Session of
Parliament was opened.
ORDERS OF THE DAY.
Supply (1st Allotted Day.)
VOTE ON ACCOUNT, 1930-31.
Considered in Committee.
[Mr. MOLES in the Chair.]
Motion made, and Question proposed.
"That a sum not exceeding two million
three hundred and nineteen thousand
nine hundred pounds be granted to His
Majesty on account, or towards defraying
the charges of, the several services for
which a Vote on Account is required for
the period ending 31st March, 1931."—
(The Minister of Finance.)
Colonel GORDON : On this Vote on
Account I wish to discuss the policy of the
Government in having increased the
substantive salaries laid down for the
Permanent Secretaries of Departments.
On 24th February, when this House was
prorogued, the Minister of Finance in
answer to a question said that these scales
had been increased and, therefore, they
must be now included in this Vote on
Account. If it was passed without a protest it might be taken that the principle
had been approved. I have no intention
of going into details, but I wish to protest
against this policy and the manner in
which it was carried out.
The Committee will recall that in June,
1929, we passed the Estimates, and in
Hansard I see no reference to or hint of
an increase, yet I understand that three
months later, in October, an increase was
made. This seems, in my opinion, to
show a lack of candour on the part of the
Government to this House, which I think,
should have been informed at the time
this increase was made in October last.
I will now deal with the possible
reasons there may be for the policy of
giving such increases. First, it may be
that five or six years ago higher scales
may have been recommended and on the
grounds of economy may not have been
sanctioned. I consider now there is all
the more reason for not sanctioning an
increase as every trade is depressed and
money is short. I see no reason at the
present juncture for making this increase.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
Again, it may be said that the salaries
paid might be compared with those the
Corporation or the county councils pay.
Comparisons, I think, are odious, and 1
Supply-
Committee
19 MARCH 1930
hold that we are now paying ample
salaries. Again, it may be said that the
Government wish to retain the services
of some of these Permanent Secretaries
by granting this increase.
The CHAIRMAN: Is that a reduction
of £100 or a reduction to £100?

During the
war there was a famous saying and a

We must remember that our area is equal
to that of Yorksnire and that our population of one and a quarter millions is
less than 3 per cent. of that of Great
Britain. I believe in paying a just and
fair wage, no more and no less, and the
present scales are ample. We cannot
compete with larger countries. In saying

I will add that in case a reduction in

did not ask for and do not want this increase.

Royal Ulster Constabulary has been of an
idiotic kind. Just imagine in these peaceful days, when judges are going through
the country being presented with white
gloves, coming into the City of Belfast and
seeing a policeman on duty directing the
traffic armed with a revolver, ammunition,
and a baton. Did anyone ever see a more
ridiculous picture than that which I have
illustrated? A pointsman with revolver,
ammunition, and a baton-a man who requires to have all the weight possible
taken away from him owing to the strain
caused by long standing. I hope the
Parliamentary Secretary will take note of
this overburdening of weights, because
there are lumps of steel hung to the policeman's belt for no useful purpose, for he
has no power to use them. Then take the
day duty men. You have them running
about in a similar manner, with everybody
alive and looking to the best interests and
peace of the city. Those men have the
protection of the citizens, and yet the
Government decorate them also with
revolvers, ammunition, and batons when
all they require is a note-book and pencil.
If you are a peaceful country, if all is
well with Ulster, why do you maintain the
policy of arming the constabulary? Does
that policy tend towards peace? I say
that you must desire the country not to

put these men on their rightful work,

Mr. POLLOCK: I think it would be
convenient at this point in the debate that
I should reply to the statement that has
been made by my hon. and gallant Friend
(Lieut.-Colonel Gordon) behind me in respect of matters concerning my Department, and especially in regard to the small
increases that have been made in the
salaries of a few servants in the employment of the Government. In giving a
full explanation of this subject it will be
necessary that I should revert to the beginning of things in connection with the
establishment of our Government. It will
be quite understood by the Committee
that when Northern Ireland was constituted an autonomous unit in the Kingdom
there were not many of us who had much
experience in administrative matters, and,
therefore, it was necessary to consult the
Government on the other side as to what
their views were as to the emoluments
which the different officers in our service
should receive for their work.
The information we received at that
time was that the Permanent Secretary of
the Ministry of Finance should receive a
salary of £2,500, and that the salaries of
the Permanent Secretaries of the other
Departments should be based on £1,500
to £2,000. As I was the Minister responsible for the arrangement of these matters
I felt it was desirable that, at any rate,
we should start our establishment on a
scale as economic as possible. My hands,
of course, were fettered very much, in fact
almost altogether, by the fact that a large
body of our officers were taken over from
the Imperial service which had operated
for so long in Dublin. Their salaries were
determined and fixed, and it was not
within our competency to reduce them.
But in the case of the higher officials it
was clearly within my purview, and it was
my duty, to see that their scale of remuneration was based not only upon the
value of the services rendered, but also
upon such a scale as could be justified from
the position that our Province occupied in
its relation to the United Kingdom.
In face of some difficulty I stood firm
on the £1,200 to £1,500 basis for the
heads of our departments, with the exception of the Permanent Secretary of
the Ministry of Finance, who occupied a
very responsible position at that time.
He was my main support and assistant in
the matters under discussion. I refer to
Sir Ernest Clark, a very distinguished
civil servant, one of the best friends
Ulster ever had, a man who rendered
immense service to Ulster, and I am very
proud to be able to stand here to bear
testimony to that, because the assistance
I received from him in the matters now
under discussion cannot be overestimated.

activities. The inspectors of the Ministry and their advisers are the experts, and
they ought to indicate to the country and
to this House the condition which while
it is responsible for such a decrease in
Northern Ireland has produced an increase in the Free State.
I would also like to point out to him
the fact that Denmark, in the same period,
secures no less than 2,204,000 cwt. of the
import butter trade of Great Britain.
That is an extraordinary disparity between
what Northern Ireland can supply to the
British market and what a little country
like Denmark can supply. I would also
like to ask the Minister why it is that we,
a pork producing country, have had to
import in the month of January this year
no less that 5,863 cwt. of bacon, and
6,269 cwt. of butter. Why is it necessary
that we, a pork and butter producing
country, were obliged to import these
large quantities of products in the month
of January? It seems like sending coals
to Newcastle to send butter or bacon into
Northern Ireland.
Between 1925 and 1928 live stock and
live stock products fell in value from
£14,671,000 to £13,456,000. That is
something that indicates that all is not
well with the state of Denmark in regard
to the Ministry of Agriculture. I have no
doubt that applies to a good many of the
other Ministries as well.
From the beginning I have been of the
opinion that the policy pursued in this
House is not a policy conducive to the
prosperity of what you describe as the
Province. Your policy here from the beginning has been "the more you spend the
more you get." Now, the Imperial contribution in 1921 was the surplus of revenue over expenditure. That reckoning
has gone by the board some time, and I
take it for granted there is no Imperial
contribution at present. But they have
saddled you with a certain legacy. They
have saddled you with an expensive Parliament House fit for an empire, and they
have saddled you, or are about to saddle
you, with a very expensive courthouse fit
for a great country like France, instead of a
small country with a population equal to
that of the City of Glasgow.
These are going to entail permanent expenditure in the future by way of upkeep so that that animal which my hon.
Friend (Mr. Henderson) the other evening indicated from these benches was a
white elephant may be more real than
many of you suppose. You have Government buildings at the moment dotted over
Belfast everywhere. There is hardly a
district of the city where there is not some
department of the Government housed,
and it sometimes happens that one department is housed in three or four buildings. I do not know how the landlords
may be circumstanced in that respect, but
I imagine it must have been a very good
thing for the owners of property when
the Northern Government was set up and
you began allocating the various streets.
and localities in the way you have done.

The MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE
(Sir Edward Archdale): I only wish to
occupy a very short time. When the hon.
Member for Mourne (Mr. O'Neill) gets

am afraid that his remarks do not affect
me as much as the hon. Member would

Newry with the potato merchants, I still
hold to what I said previously, that there
was a case proved that potatoes were run
down to the ship without any inspection
at all. That case was known and proved
in my Ministry. We did our best to
facilitate them, and at that meeting in the
Newry Chamber of Commerce, of which
the hon. Member spoke, we agreed to go
to the stores again, but the final inspection
has to be in the ship. You cannot always
depend on potatoes going through the
stores. I had not heard about the other
disturbance the hon. Member referred to
where potatoes were refused to be shipped.
I will find out about that and let the hon.
Member know the result.
As regards the complaint about the
price of eggs being bad at the present
time, the blame cannot be laid on the
Ministry. Our eggs secure the top price
for eggs in England. As to the Estimates
we are putting in, there is a sum of £5,500
for the improvement of holdings under
the Unemployment Relief Scheme. There
is also a sum of £4,000 in relief of drainage in consequence of the damage done a
short time ago by a cloudburst in the
Sperrin Mountains.
The figure in Class I is a little up, because we have included there an Estimate
for £1,275 which is to provide for an
agricultural census which we hope to take
this year. The last agricultural census
was in 1925. We find it most useful in
a great many ways to get a census of the
output from the country of the commodities of the agricultural community.
The hon. Member for South Fermanagh
(Mr. Healy) complained about the imports of butter and bacon, and the hon.
Member for Mourne (Mr. O'Neill) said.
that we were bragging about the improvement in milk while less butter was exported than before. The farmers are
badly off, and do sell their best cows. If
the farmers of the country sell their best
cows at a good price to England you cannot expect as much milk and butter to be
exported as in ordinary times. Notwithstanding that, our milk recording societies
have increased the amount of milk in every
district where they are in operation during the last five years by over 100 gallons
per cow. I say we are entitled to take
credit, and do take credit for that.
Importation of butter at this time of
the year is necessary, because, as the hon.
Member for South Fermanagh (Mr.
Healy) or anyone living in the country
knows, you cannot get the farmers to
have their cows calving in the autumn.
We cannot have winter dairying in this
country, and the reason the Danes have
such a pull over us in this matter is because they send nearly the same amount
all the year round. Our people in this
country are in the habit of getting New
Zealand and Australian butter, which
comes in our winter and their summer,
and they sell that to keep their customers
going during the time they have no
butter from the creameries.
There is an item in our estimate of
£1,500 in connection with the World's
Poultry Congress, which is to take place
in July of this year in London. There
all the best poultry from almost every
country in the world are to have a sort of
séance for ten days. There will be lectures and exhibits of work of every kind
in connection with poultry.
Mr. BEATTIE: Who is to be the
medium?

spiritualism. We are taking part in the

As things stand at the present time our
poultry hold a very high place in the

entitled to help that on as much as we
possibly can.

The increase of these salaries was uncalled

public and private companies to-day doing

Sir DAWSON BATES: I desire to
reply to the remarks made by the Member
for Pottinger (Mr. Beattie) on the question of whether or not the Royal Ulster
Constabulary should be an armed force
and should carry arms in our streets. I
listened very carefully to the hon. Member, and he has not given me one valid
reason why arms should be taken away
from the police. I will give him one valid
reason why the policy we have adopted in
the past should be continued, and that is
that it is in the interests of the peace of
the community, and also for the protection of the police themselves that they
should carry arms, and the Government
propose to continue that policy.
Mr. BEATTIE: On a point of Order.
You will also have to consider whether
they are now to use arms.
The CHAIRMAN: Of course the hon.
Member knows that that is not a point of
Order.
Mr. BEATTIE: The point of Order
refers to whether the Minister should
make a statement which is a half truth
and not the whole truth.
The CHAIRMAN: A point of Order
relates to some real or imaginary breach
of Order in procedure of debate. The
hon. Member has not even alleged that,
but has asked for additional information.
Sir DAWSON BATES: I have some
difficulty in following what the hon.
Member means, because my reading of the
situation is that if you supply arms to
men they are supposed to use them if the
occasion should arise. It is perfectly true,
I am glad to say, that we are living in a
period of comparative peace and quietness,
and that is due solely to the precautions
taken by the Government and not, I am
sorry to say, to any change of sentiment
in the minds of certain groups of persons
who caused trouble in the past. One has
only to follow the endless propaganda
that is going on by the I.R.A. to realise
that if we as a Government were to relax
any of our precautions the earliest opportunity would be taken to repeat what has
happened in the past. Therefore I feel
that the present is not the proper time to
relax any of our precautions, and I think
the Government that succeeded in producing order out of chaos are very much
better judges of the precautions that should
be taken to maintain peace than is the
hon. Member opposite. With regard to
the remarks of the Member for South

Criminal Law and Prevention of Crime

Order for Second Reading read.
Motion made and Question proposed,

The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): As hon. Members
will see, the Bill which I now introduce
is a short one of three Clauses, and deals
with two distinct subjects. The first is
the time limit for prosecutions for offences
against female persons under the age of
16 years, and the second the maintenance
of discipline in our Borstal Institutions in
Northern Ireland.
In connection with Section 1, perhaps
I should just say a word as to the
necessity for its introduction. Under the
Criminal Law (Amendment) Act of 1885,
it was provided that prosecutions in cases
of defilement of girls between 13 and 16
years of age must be instituted within
three months from the date of the commission of the offence. This time limit
was subsequently extended to six months
by the Prevention of Cruelty to Children
Act, 1904, and again to nine months by
the Criminal Law (Amendment) Act,
1922, the provisions of the latter Act
having been applied to Northern Ireland
by the Criminal Law (Amendment) Act
(Northern Ireland), 1923. In the year
1928 the Imperial Parliament passed a
further measure in connection with this
matter, the Criminal Law (Amendment)
Act, 1928, under which the time limit was
again extended to twelve months. It
most certainly seems desirable that the
law in Northern Ireland should, in a
matter of this sort, be identical with that
in Great Britain.
Hon. Members may be aware from
cases within their own knowledge of the
necessity of this amending legislation,
and, undoubtedly, cases have arisen
where, owing to the inevitable delay
which must occur in instituting proceedings, the offender could not under the
existing time limit be brought to justice.
I am supported in the introduction of this
measure by many religious and social
bodies in Northern Ireland, who have
passed resolutions asking that the law in
this respect may be brought into line with
that in England. I do not anticipate that
there can be anything, but unanimous
approval of this proposal.
Section 2 deals with another matter in
which at the present moment we differ
from England. We have no power in Northern Ireland to cane Borstal boys who
merit such punishment by acts of gross
insubordination and other grave offences.
May I say, that I do not anticipate,
neither does the Visiting Committee of
Malone Training School, that it will be
necessary to utilise the powers which it is
proposed should be given under this
Section except on very rare occasions.
There can be very few schools in the
British Isles that take boys from the ages
of 16 years to 20 years which do not on
occasion have to resort to the cane as a
means of enforcing discipline, and it is a
strange anomaly that caning can be administered in almost any school, whereas
in Ireland up to the moment Borstal
inmates, who in the early stages of their
training, at any rate, are not always the
best characters, are not in a position to
receive this salutary treatment.
Mr. BEATTIE: Would the right hon.
Gentleman define what he means by
caning? Is it flogging?
Sir DAWSON BATES: Certainly not.
My Hon. Friend ought to give me credit
occasionally for speaking the truth.
Mr. BEATTIE: What does caning
mean?
Sir DAWSON BATES: If my hon.
Friend had received a caning in his youth
it might have done him a great deal of
good.
Mr. BEATTIE: Perhaps I got too
much of it in my youth and that is the

Gentleman.
Sir DAWSON BATES: There is no
doubt that the fact that the boys cannot be
caned at the present time means that
there is no deterrent to really bad be

Sir DAWSON BATES: Anybody who
has studied this question will be aware
that there is hardly a school in the British
Isles taking boys of sixteen years of age
and upwards where the power of caning
is not provided for. It is most necessary
that the boys in these Borstal Institutions
-and they are practically public schools
--should receive the same benefit-and
I regard caning as a benefit under certain
circumstances as a boy in a better walk
of life. I want to emphasise the fact
that under no circumstances is it intended that the boys should either be
flogged or birched. It will be pure caning, and when I explain to hon. Members opposite that regulations will have
to be drawn up prescribing the conditions.
under which this punishment is to be
inflicted, and that these regulations will
have to be laid upon the Table of this
House, I hope my hon. Friends will see
that ample protection is provided against.
bad temper on the part of the masters as
well as anything else. After all I think
this House should pay a certain amount

such a representative committee as our
Visiting Board. I hope, under these
circumstances, the House will give unanimous approval to this Measure.
Before I sit down I would like to take
this opportunity-it is seldom I have an
opportunity of doing so-of expressing
my thanks to the members of this Visiting Committee. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear). They visit this institution
constantly. They look after the boys
and help them in every possible direction.
Not alone do they help them during the
time they are in the school-because I
am glad to say it is a school, and not in
any sense a penitentiary-but they try
to get work for the boys when they
leave the school. I am only sorry that
more hon. Members of this House do not
visit the school from time to time and see
for themselves what goes on there.
The boys have their swimming baths and
their playing fields. I think the best
illustration I can give is to tell the House
that on one occasion I took my own boy
up there for the presentation of prizes.
I had told him that he would have to go
to school himself before very long, and
had taken him up to see the place. I
asked him what he thought of the school.
He, in turn, asked me would the school
to which he would have to go be any worse
than that. I said "No. Why" and
his reply was "If it is not any worse than
this school I would not mind going." I
beg to move.

I suggest that it is not likely to improve
him but that it is likely to engender in
him sentiments of resentment and bitterness.
I understood some time ago that there

Governor of the Belfast Prison, as I understood it, was that the men might get a
little remuneration for their work in the

thought have in view. Remember that
the poor beetle, that we

Public Roads Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.

Sir DAWSON BATES: This is a very
short Bill, and a very few remarks on my
part will be sufficient to explain the
matter to the House. The Grand Jury
Act of 1836 limited the extreme width of
roads to 50 feet. If a Road Authority
wished either to widen an existing road or
to make a new road, they were limited to
an extreme width of 50 feet. This limit
governs the extreme width of road, including the space required for the boundary fences. It is, of course, in the great
majority of cases sufficient, as it would
permit of a carriageway of 36 feet and
two footpaths of 6 feet each. It is unlikely that a greater carriage width than
36 feet will be required, but the provision
of surfaces of a permanent or a semipermanent character has raised new
point. Where you put in a surface of
this kind, such as reinforced concrete, it
is undesirable and expensive to have to
break it up again for the purpose of laying
pipes and so on.
a
If, therefore, a local authority were
undertaking any considerable scheme of
widening or of making a new road where
it is desirable to have a 36 feet carriageway with a permanent surface, it is important that it should not be necessary
to lay pipes for public services under the
surface of the road. This could be avoided
if the width between the two boundary
fences were sufficient to allow of a strip
or grass verge being left which would admit of pipes for water, sewage, gas mains,
or electric light mains, etc., being laid
without disturbing the surface of the
road. It is entirely a permissive Bill,
but we thought local authorities should
not continue to be handicapped as they
have been. For these reasons we have
thought it desirable to remove this limit of
50 feet, though it is unlikely that there
would be many cases in which 50 feet
would be insufficient. I beg to move.

Sir DAWSON BATES: The evil of
personation is one which for some considerable time has been causing concern
to the responsible members of all parties
in the State. I do not think that it is as
prevalent as it was some time ago, but
at the same time we cannot shut our eyes
to the fact that cases of this kind still
exist and that the number of instances in
which the offenders are brought to justice
is comparatively small.
It will be within the recollection of the
House that last year I appointed a Departmental Committee of Inquiry with a
view to having the question examined.
This Committee promptly set to work, and
after hearing evidence and making inquiries came to certain conclusions which
were embodied in the report which was
published in June of last year. I desire
to take this opportunity of expressing the
thanks of the Government to the members of this Committee for the able manner
in which they carried out the task entrusted to them, and for the excellent
report which has proved of the greatest
assistance to us in framing this legislation.
My object in appointing this Committee was to have the position examined by
a body of independent and experienced
persons so that we might ascertain in what
way the present law was defective and
devise means for improving it so
secure the prevention of the evil.
as to
The Committee recommended certain
changes in the law, all of which have been
embodied in the Bill now before the
House, but before indicating in general
terms to the House the main provisions
of the Bill, I would like to draw the attention of hon. Members to paragraph 12
on page 15 of the report of the Committee,
where they say that--
"The existing law as to personation
and other matters more or less directly
connected therewith appears to us to be
in need of simplification, and indeed in
some cases of a clearer elucidation of its
intent. In the course of our inquiry we
have been struck by a number of discrepancies and anomalies affecting not
only the form but also the substance of
the law."
The present law as to personation is contained in five Acts of Parliament extending from the year 1850 to the year 1884,
and it is undoubtedly somewhat difficult.
to follow the law as contained in these
various Statutes. We have, therefore,
seized this opportunity of not only amending the law but of consolidating it and
of bringing it together into one Statute.
I think I can confidently claim that one
merit of this Bill is that it contains practically no legislation by reference and
that it is easily intelligible.
20 MARCH 1930
Elections Bill-

Second Reading.
Fourthly, the Committee recommended
that the duty of deciding whether a person accused of personation should be
committed for trial should be entrusted
to a Resident Magistrate, and the Government feel that there are very special
reasons for this course, having regard to
the nature of the offence and the fact
that it is committed whilst elections are
in progress and whilst political feeling is
running high.
The first recommendation of the Committee was that the definition of personation for local government elections
should be made the same as for parliamentary elections. The main difference
was that in a parliamentary election a
person committed the offence of personation if he applied for a ballot paper in
the name of some other person, whereas
in a local government election before the
offence was completed he must have
actually voted. The person who takes all
the preliminary steps to vote wrongfully
but desists because he finds that suspicion
has been aroused seems to be just as guilty
as the man who succeeds in voting before
being caught. The existing provisions
with regard to parliamentary elections
seem to be more just and in accordance
with common sense.
The second recommendation was
directed towards making the procedure
once personation was detected more
effective. At present the prosecution is
undertaken by the agent, and is in the
nature of a private prosecution. It was
felt that if the Crown undertook the
responsibility for prosecution, as in the
ordinary case of an indictable offence,
there would be less likelihood of offenders
escaping, as there is undoubtedly a natural
reluctance on the part of a private person to undertake a prosecution in respect
of what is really an offence against the
State.
The third matter dealt with by the
Committee related to the proof to be required to sustain the charge. Section 95
of the Representation of the People
(Ireland) Act, 1850, requires the
evidence of not less than two credible
witnesses to prove a charge of personation. It is difficult to see why there
should be a distinction between the provisions of the law in this respect in regard to personation and those which
govern other indictable cases. The
better course seems to be to remove this
restriction and to leave it to the Courts
to say what evidence will satisfy them
that the offence has actually been committed. The accused has adequate protection in that the magistrate must first
be satisfied that there is evidence upon
which he should be put upon his trial.
Then the Attorney-General must be
satisfied that the case is one which ought
to go to a jury. Thirdly, the grand
jury must be satisfied that there is a
prima facie case, and finally, the ordinary
jury must be satisfied as to his guilt.
The last recommendation of the Committee to which I need to refer is one of
somewhat minor importance.
At
present if the personation agent makes
a declaration undertaking to prove a
charge of personation against an
individual the presiding officer must
order that individual's arrest, but the
power of doing so is confined to the presiding officer, and should he be absent
from the polling station temporarily
there is a deadlock. I know some hon.
Members may say that in the City of Belfast a polling station usually consists of
a large number of presiding officers and
polling clerks, but in the country it is
different. The Committee recommend
that the presiding officer should be entitled to depute this power to the polling
clerk assisting him during his temporary
absence, and the Government feels that
this recommendation should be accepted,
because the duty of ordering arrest
followed automatically upon the completion of certain formalities by the personation agent, namely, a declaration undertaking to prove that the accused has been
guilty of personation.
Clause 1 defines the offence of personation both for parliamentary and
local government elections to include not
only voting in the name of any other
person living or dead, but even applying
for a ballot paper in the name of some
other person.
The Clause further reenacts the existing penalties, namely,
imprisonment for a term not exceeding
two years. This penalty may be inflicted
not merely upon the person who actually
commits the offence, but on anyone aiding
or abetting him in doing so.
Clause 2 merely re-enacts the existing
law empowering candidates to appoint
personation agents.
Clause 3 deals with the machinery
to be used when a charge of personation
has been made, and provides for the
arrest of the person accused upon the

If there was a Clause in the Bill to make
it illegal for any person at an election to
have in his possession the name and
address and number of a voter you would
practically wipe out personation. It is not
necessary. If I or any other man here
come forward surely to goodness I know
my own name and address. If I give my
name and address to the presiding officer
he gives me the vote. Take away the tally
room. It is not necessary at all. That is
the root and branch of the whole personation.
Another thing I think might usefully be
done, and every Member will agree with
it-every Member from Belfast anyhow.
The time for an election to terminate
should not be 8 p.m.; it should be 9 p.m.
The franchise has been extended and now
you will have at some polling booths over
5,000 voters, more than there used to be in
a division altogether. They are trying to
get in their votes by 8 p.m. There is absolute congestion and no agents could watch
it. But if the time is put back to 9 p.m.
it would do a lot of good. Take a man
working in a shipyard. He may be working a little bit of overtime. You deprive
him of his vote because he has not time
to go home and get a meal and get in
his vote by 8 p.m. Sometimes people send
down a motor-car or a char-a-banc to bring
up voters. They do not bring up their
own, as men get into them, no matter
whose vehicles they are. I do not blame
them. I think the Minister would and I
think every Member from Belfast would
agree to make the time 9 p.m. That would
give the agents a better chance.
There are other things. I saw a man

who will give the best service to the State.
The present system of electioneering exploits and robs the individual, because it
is an outrage that a person who fights an
election should be called upon to meet the
liabilities he is called upon to pay when
the election is over. I have fought an
election in East Belfast for £152, and I
had as good propaganda, and as able
assistance in every way as my opponent.
What did it cost my opponent? I really
had four opponents running as one, and
it cost each of them about £600. It is
a crying shame that anyone should have
to pay that sum of money for something
he could have got for £152.
Therefore, it is in the interests of the
supporters of the Government that they
should be protected against this electioneering exploitation, or electioneering blackmail. They do not blackmail me because
they know they get nothing from me. They
came to me at the last election and told
me about a certain thing they wanted,
and I told them to go to those who could
give it to them because I could not. I
know Members on the other side who had
to make a large contribution before they
got "For he's a jolly good fellow." That
is not playing the game towards people
who come into public life, because many
of them make great sacrifices, and it is
not fair that they should be made the
victims of election blackmail every time
an election comes round. I have been in
public life for many years, and I have
fought six elections. As long as I live I
do not expect to get a walk-over, but I
would sacrifice my seat before I would
stoop to the methods adopted by some of
the political hacks who go round at
election times. Decent men are sometimes put out of public life by the
methods adopted up to the present, and
those are the methods that were brought
to perfection by the Unionist party in 1921.
Your attempt to remedy the evil by means
of this Bill will not be a success.
At the last election my opponent
thought it would be a good thing to do
away with tally rooms. I accepted his
offer to abolish tally rooms and agents inside the polling booths because I put my

That has been done in Ballymacarrett.
I do not say it occurs all round; I do not

to get doubtful votes recorded for the

and they make no challenge; they allow

Then there is also the interference with

man, or the old woman, as the case may

That is the state of affairs that prevailed
at my last election. I say that is illegal.
No one but the officers should be allowed

all that are required inside to see that
everything was carried out in accordance

and unfettered in the casting of their

Another point I want to make is this.
When a man is arrested the candidate is
sometimes fleeced. I am stating this from
practical experience. We made an arrest
at the last election of a Unionist representative. There was an arrest made in my
name; it was done at the instance of an
agent who, I was given to understand, was
not in the box when the arrest was made,
but he was bribed. I think that sort of
thing should never occur in any locality
where an election is being carried out.
From that day to this that man never
came to see me again. I had to pay £5
for the wrongful arrest of that man, and
I felt it very much.
Un-
The magistrates can impose a fine for not
going on with the case, but the system is,
if you arrest one of ours we will arrest
one of yours, and the levelling takes
place on the day of the prosecution. That
is corruption of the worst kind. If I had
a case that I thought was right, I would
go the whole hog; I would not withdraw
it, but I would not arrest any man until
I was satisfied that he was not the person
he had represented himself to be.
fortunately this man of whom I am speaking should not have been arrested, and I

Then I discovered that the

menace to the candidates themselves and
a menace to the electors, and the sooner
you place confidence in the people behind
the counter the sooner you will purify
electioneering in Belfast.
I go so far as to say that until we have

send in my resignation, and say I had no

of this Bill being improved.

Each Member on this occasion takes that
part which comes nearest to his heart,
and, therefore, I am taking the Unemployment Insurance (Amendment) Act, which
this House passed, and which is now, if I
may say so, being badly abused through
the methods adopted by the Minister.
The Unemployment (Amendment) Act,
for which provision is made in this Bill,
was brought in for the purpose of alleviating distress caused by unemployment
among those workers who were driven out
of work through no fault of their own.
Therefore, the fewest qualifications possible
were put in in order that all classes of
workers who were at any time within the
category of normally employed persons
should be covered by the Amendment
Act; in other words, the principle of the
Amendment Act is the right to work or
maintenance.
That is a very small portion of the
principle of that Act, but it is really the
intention embodied in the Act of 1930 as
passed by the Labour Government in
Great Britain. We all welcome that
Measure into this House, I am sure every
Member on that side and every Member
on this side welcomes it as much as I do.
That Act of Parliament is on the Statute
Book, and if you cannot get the mentality
to administer an Act you can turn a good
Act of Parliament into a bad one, one
that will have an adverse effect upon the
principles it was established to advance.
I had the pleasure of being at the first
court of referees last Friday. I went
again on Saturday morning, I was there
yesterday, and I was there again this
morning. I want to say that the principle
of the Act is being violated. I am not
saying it is violated deliberately, it may
be unintentional, but it is being violated.
For the Minister's information I will give
him the grounds.
I was told yesterday of a woman of 60
years of age who had been 40 years employed in the Belfast Rope Works. For
the past five years owing to age and the
nature of the occupation she was denied
work although willing to work if given an
opportunity. Although five years unemployed she has maintained her signature
at the employment exchange since 1928
earnestly seeking for work. The chairman of the Court told me this was
border-line case, and it was so questionable that it took him upwards of twenty
minutes in deciding whether she was a
a
normally insured person within the meaning of the Act.
I was speaking to a representative of

20 weeks. He had 20 contributions to

a normally insured person within the

Mr. Hayden, a British Member of Parliament, who took such a keen interest
in the Morris Committee, and who is

Act then the whole question as regards

Act. I want that mentality to prevail
in the Courts of Referees. That is the

an Act of Parliament.

The next point I wish to raise is that
I object strongly to criticism of expenditure on social services. Ulster's asset is its
people. The State is not of much importance without the people, and you are
not going to ruin and destroy the State's
only asset. To-day you are doing ruin by
driving out of Ulster its youth. The
only busy places in Northern Ireland are
the shipping offices and the Queen's
Bridge jetty on Saturday mornings. If
you go there, which is at the extreme end
of my constituency, you will find tenders
duly timed to leave at certain periods
with cargoes of human freight-the youth
of Ulster going out to the Colonies to develop the lands of Colonial Governments.
That is what is being done instead of
employing these people on our own land.
Instead of Ulster being built up she will
in a few years be left with a population
of old age pensioners. That is the chaos
and disaster which are brought about
since the establishment of this Parliament. I think it is deplorable. Let
the Government make a real effort to find

published by the Ministry of Agriculture

dition of affairs. But instead of tackling
the things nearest to their hands, the
Government keep their eyes on the horizon. Undoubtedly the cause of this originated 100 years ago, when our forefathers here started to decry their native
land in every possible way. Now when we
have got this portion of the country
segregated from the rest of the country,

that it is not fit to stand on its own legs.
Last night the Minister of Labour-I
do not know whether he was at the
Unionist Labour Association or whether
he was rotarying-said:
They recognised-some of them with
regret that the results of Free Trade,
which the Manchester School prophesied, had never been realised. All
they had to-day was, on the one side,
free imports and taxed exports; so that
the theories put forward by the economists in bygone years had no practical
effect to-day. Those theories had proved
to be all wrong. Instead of the
countries of the world lowering their
tariffs, they had been, without exception, including even our own Dominions,
raising their tariff walls against us.
His forefathers-the forefathers of the
Minister of Labour-held the exact views
which his words would lead us to believe
he holds to-day. They knew when they
went to Dungannon that this country
should have a seperate fiscal system from
England; they fought for it, and carried
it.
Now we are told that all will be well

a meeting of the Wholesale Merchants'
Association in Belfast the other evening,

strong case that the products of Ulster
that were produced for the people should
be consumed by the people of Ulster, and
in that way, he said, great relief would
be given to the Province as a whole.
I thoroughly agree with that gentleman,
but while human nature is as it is a lady
will buy from any part of the world if
the goods she wants are d cheaper than
the home product. That wholesale gentleman wants help; he wants help that
he can get from this Government,
and that this Government can give
him, by refusing to work the Act
of 1920, and demanding the same
freedom as even the Isle of Man has.
Within the past fortnight the Isle of
Man took action. They had the same
difficulties about agriculture as we had in
Northern Ireland. The farmers went
forward to the House of Keys and pointed
out that the market of their little island,
to which so many visitors came, was killed
by the import of meat not only from
foreign countries, but from the Free
State and from Northern Ireland, the
territory in which we live. The House
of Keys decided to keep out all meat, alive
or dead.
Mr. POLLOCK: From where?
Mr. COLLINS: From all over the
world, including Northern Ireland and
the Irish Free State, and Great Britain.
No meat will be allowed into the Isle of
Man until the House of Keys makes an
order in the event of the price of meat
exceeding the price of meat in the Liverpool market by a certain percentage.
That is what that little Government has
done for its own people. The Prime
Minister, fresh from his world tour, will
be the first to admit that he has no power
in this great area of the Six Counties to
protect his farmers in the same way. The
Prime Minister has gone round the world.
I understand that, except when he was in

Trade? He said this:-
The Dominions will not have it.
Canada and Australia are self-governing

creating and expanding their manufacturing industries behind their own
tariff walls. Britain might prefer that
they should be content to produce food
and raw materials and to buy their
manufactured goods from her, but they
have decided to become manufacturing
nations on a basis of protective duties.

Rev. Professor CORKEY: I rise to
support this Bill. I think every Member
of the House feels that the Government is
making a brave effort to manage this
country in the interests of the welfare of
the people as a whole and is doing its best
to solve the great problems that confront
it. Anything which I may have to say

to details. I have heard it said that the
Imperial House of Commons is the finest
club in the world, and if so I think it would
be a fair inference that this House of
Commons is the second finest club in the
world. If the spirit of this club is anything like a fair sample of the spirit and
atmosphere that pervades club life generally I am not surprised that men frequent
clubs and that clubs are inclined to grow
and increase in number.
What I want to say is that I am afraid
the advantage of the good fellowship and
fraternity fostered in club life is in many
instances being vitiated by the main type
of entertainment which the club members
seem to persist in. I have had before me
recently a governmental return giving details on this subject, and some of those
details are very surprising. They would.
suggest to me that some of these clubs
would require a little more careful supervision than they get. For example, I find
that a working men's club in Belfast-I
am not going to give any name although
I might spends, how much do you think?
on liquor. Last year it spent over £3,000.
And there were 92 members of that club.
That suggests to me that this club is
really being used as a public-house, and
is competing unfairly with the decent publicans in the neighbourhood-(laughter)
-who have to pay licence duty and who
have to maintain a reputable character
before the community.
I could give other lamentable instances,
and I am sorry that clubs, at least registered clubs, have increased to the extent
they have. I think it ought to be made
a little more difficult for any group of
people to get together, to have their club

day or night, and in any quantity they
like. I particularly regret that so many

would be a brave man who would suggest

Let me refer briefly to another subject,
that is unemployment. Reference has
been made to the plight of the unemployed here very frequently recently.
For myself I have no panacea for this
great misfortune which has befallen great
numbers of our people. It will prove to
be a very stubborn problem. It is an
international problem. May I say in
passing that a great deal is being done
by the League of Nations through its
International Labour organisation to
solve this problem for us, for the aim of
that organisation is to raise the standard
of life, and the standard of industry
throughout the backward countries of the
world up to the standards of life and
standards of industry that we enjoy here.
That will make for equality, and will prevent our having to compete with sweated
labour in backward countries in the way
we have to do to-day.
It was said the other day by an
hon. Member that a solution of the
problem would be to provide the
people with more purchasing power. So
far as my knowledge of economics carries
me that seems to be a way of describing
the situation rather than affording us any
insight into a reasonable and practical
method by which we are to get rid of the
evil.
May I venture to say that I cannot
help regretting that people do not use the
purchasing power which they possess more
wisely. It seems to me a pity that the
people of the Six Counties should still
spend £4,000,000 a year-about £10,000
a day-on-shall Ï say--a powerful
lubricant which does very little for them
or anyone.
My point is not that the
elimination of this expenditure would be
a permanent panacea for all our unemployment. I do not believe a word of it,
but I do believe that it would be a help
in the right direction. (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear).

were spent in any other way on

particular material.

every penny was used up. The bulk of
our money comes in in January and
February. I think 60 per cent. comes in
during that period, and only the rest
comes in during the year.
In the meantime we. have to meet the
claims of the county councils. We pay
no less a sum than 50 per cent. in respect
of the maintenance of first-class roads, 30
per cent. on second-class roads, and 15
per cent. on third-class roads. We also
pay 72 per cent. on the reconstruction of
first-class roads. Hon. Members will
agree that we have done our utmost. My
hon. Friend has criticised an item of
£40,000 in regard to the services of
the police. I think the House will agree
that it is a reasonable thing that the Exchequer ought to be reimbursed the heavy
additional burden that falls on the
Exchequer by reason of the increased
traffic caused by the improved roads. My
hon. Friend knows that we are
experimenting with the automatic signals,
and if these increase in time we may be
able to reduce that expenditure. It
would be useless to have good roads unless
we have proper traffic regulations.
My hon. Friend (Professor Corkey) referred to clubs. May I say I entirely
agree with him. I am sorry I have not
the papers with me, but I accept his
figures as correct. They certainly show
that there is too much alcohol used. 1
think, however, he does not do the Government fair justice when he suggests that
anybody can get a licence. That is not
so. I know that in England and Scotland
the law is that any group of persons can
get a licence, but here no one can get a
licence unless he first goes before two resident magistrates and satisfies them that
the premises are suitable, and that it is
necessary that there should be a club. I do
not think that the number of clubs has increased by more than two during the year.
There has not been such an extraordinary
increase as is suggested. Many a plications
for club licences have been turned down
as the result of the evidence produced before the court. I am sorry my hon.
Friend belongs to a a club where the

manner. When the club comes up again
for a renewal, and the hon. Member shows
that the licence should not be renewed I

full justice to' the evidence adduced.

The FINANCIAL SECRETARY (Mr.
Barbour): The approval of the Committee
to the Resolutions which appear on the
Order Paper is required before the House
can be called upon to consider the text of a
Bill covering the points dealt with in the
Resolutions. It will be noted that certain
charges on the Consolidated Fund and
upon Votes are involved, and, in addition,
minor amendments in the law affecting a
particular Exchequer transaction and the
powers affecting the making of advances
from the Government Loans Fund.
I propose first to deal with new expenditure arising out of the Resolutions.
Section 1 (a) provides for the payment of
an additional sum of £5,000 to the Irish
Sailors' and Soldiers' Land Trust in respect of the housing subsidy of £80 per
house. Houses erected by the Trust are
not entitled to the Government subsidy
under the Housing Acts, and the Exchequer and Financial Provisions Act of 1927
provided for the payment to the Trust,
at the rate of £80 per house in respect of
houses completed on or after 1st January,
1926, of a sum not exceeding £30,000.
Owing to the accumulation of interest on
the Trust's funds, the Trust has been able
to build more houses than was thought
likely in 1927, and the maximum of
£30,000 has been reached. Accordingly,
it is proposed to increase the maximum to
£35,000. The additional sum now to be
provided represents a subsidy for about
62 houses.
Section 1 (b) of the Resolution proposes
to amend the scale of salary payable to
the Comptroller and Auditor-General by
providing for annual increments of £100
within the scale instead of £50 increments,
and for an increase in the maximum of
the scale from the existing figure of £1,500
to £1,600.
The new scale proposed for application
to the Comptroller and Auditor-General
is that which will be found in the Estimates for the coming year for the Secretary
of the Cabinet and Secretaries of
Ministries, and a special resolution, to be
ultimately confirmed by Act of Parliament, is necessary in his case by reason of
the fact that unlike other officials of the
Government the salary of the Comptroller
and Auditor-General, who is an officer of
this House, is charged upon the Consolidated Fund.

case for those of us who sit on these
Benches. I do not object to a decent
salary being paid to a man who does a
decent job, and the Minister of Finance
has explained very fully that this gentleman should not be in a worse position
than the Permanent Heads of Departments. I quite agree with that. I do
not object to this gentleman's increase,
and I do not happen to know him at all.
The hon. and gallant Member for East
Down (Lieut.-Colonel Gordon) said he
thought the standard for the Permanent
Secretaries had been set on too high a
scale. I am sorry to say I must agree
with that; but, now that the standard
has been set, I think no case has been
made out for keeping the salary of the
Comptroller and Auditor-General on a
lower level than the salaries of the Permanent Secretaries. Certainly the hon.
Member who proposed the reduction was
not serious, I think, when he proposed to
do so, because his case simply was that
this gentleman was a member of a board
that did not give satisfaction so far as
he was concerned. I think that is a
rather unfair way of trying to hit back at
a man who has no opportunity of speaking for himself. He is a member of a
board, but that board does not give satisfaction to every Member of the House.
At different times I have been sorry that
some person in whom I was interested was
not appointed. I think there is not a
Member on either side of the Committee
who has not been dissatisfied on some
occasion or other.
The CHAIRMAN: I hope the hon.
Gentleman will not develop that argument, but will keep to the Resolution.
Mr. ELLIOTT: It is not fair that
blame should be hurled at this gentleman,
and I think it is a poor way to express
either appreciation or dissatisfaction to
move that a man's salary should not be
increased because a board of which he is
a member does not give satisfaction to
some Member or Members of this Committee.
The PRIME MINISTER: I intervene
only for a few moments on the question
that has arisen on the Benches behind me
as well as in the Opposition, with regard
to the small rises that the Cabinet thought
were due to the heads of the Departments
and to the Comptroller and Auditor-
General. In order that there may be no
misunderstanding in the matter, I may
say that this decision was reached before
I left for my trip abroad, and I fully
concurred in the conclusions that had been
arrived at by my colleagues with regard
to this matter. There has been no increase given to any of the heads of our
Departments during the past nine years,
and if hon. Members who have sat in this
House all that time will cast their minds
back to how we stood then as compared
with the present day, they will realise that
the work and responsibility cast upon the
higher officials and upon the Comptroller
and Auditor-General have increased to a
very considerable extent. Hon. Members
hardly realise that the Department, for
instance, that my right hon. Friend is responsible for has during the past few years
very considerably extended the building of
houses throughout the whole of the Ulster
area. He has extended a great many of
the social services and every Act ameliorating the lot of the poorer classes in our
community instantly places upon the
Department a very much heavier load to
carry and consequently a greater responsibility upon the head.
If I take my right hon. Friend the
Minister of Labour it will be realised by
anyone that the granting of old-age pensions, contributory and non-contributory,
widows' and orphans' pensions and the
general extension even during the short
time of my absence of services helping the
poorer classes in the last year has made the
work attached to the Department infinitely
greater. The head of the Department of
Finance, for instance, has to deal with all
the intricacies in connection with all those
great financial transactions that he has
carried out for the benefit of the country,
even in connection with the Loans Guarantee alone the responsibility and importance
of which no one can decry. If one takes
again the Road Fund which, I understand,
now has reached something like £400,000
a year, and which nine years ago was a
comparatively small sum, the division of
that amongst the county councils and the
responsibility for its fair allocation and,
indeed, all the ramifications that have
arisen in those years, in my opinion are
full justification for adding £100. It really
does not amount to £100 on account of the
decrease in the war bonus, but even call-

Mr. BARBOUR: Section 2 provides
for an extension in time and in scope of
the provision of Section 2 of the Exchequer and Financial Provisions Act of
last year, whereby bank loans for the purchase of seeds and artificial fertilisers were
guaranteed by Government. Under that
Act applications for loans had to be made
before 31st December, 1929, but it is now
proposed to make the scheme applicable
during a more extended period. Furthermore, the loans which may be
guaranteed will in future include loans
for the purchase of live stock and poultry.
In the event of ultimate default on the
part of a borrower and his sureties, the
State assumes liability for repayment and
accordingly provision is made in the Resolution in respect of this contingent
charge.
Turning now to the minor amendments
of the law which are covered by the
opening part of the first Resolution, a
reference is made to certain tithe Rent
Charges, which, under a Statute passed
in the year 1872, are redeemable at a
period of not less than 22 years' purchase. In view of the increased yield
from Government securities nowadays as
compared with the yield in 1872, a 221
years' purchase term is considered to be
too high and is hampering voluntary redemptions, and it is proposed to introduce in the Bill a clause to enable the
Ministry to accept redemption by means
of a payment of such sum as will yield,
when invested in Government securities,
an amount of interest approximately
equal to the amount of the rent charge.
A clause will also be included to provide
for the issue of a new type of loan from
the Government Loans Fund.
Hon. Members will recollect that in the
Supplementary Estimate for Public
Works and Buildings, which was recently
passed, an item was included as a contribution from Northern Ireland funds
towards the provision of accommodation

for the Incorporated Law Society. The

payable by the Incorporated Law Society
of Northern Ireland. The Society itself
has probably no power under its charter
to borrow this sum, and therefore it is
proposed to take power to enable this
sum to be advanced from the Government
Loans Fund to the Ministry, the latter
being recouped by the Society by means
of a terminable annuity. I beg to move.

If the governor (or, in his absence,
the chief officer) of a Borstal Institution for male young offenders within
the meaning of Part I. of the Prevention of Crime Act, 1908, reports to the
visiting committee of such Institution
that an offender detained therein has

any two members thereof, shall inquire

are of opinion that the case cannot be

The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.

right hon. Friend to reply.

Member, so far as they are available, are

94,203 cwts.

""

MORATORIUM ON LAND PUR-
CHASE ANNUITIES.
2. Mr. MINFORD asked the Minister
of Finance whether, in view of the continued depression in agriculture, and the
low prices being obtained for farm
produce, he would consider the granting
of a moratorium of all land purchase
annuities in Northern Ireland for at
least two years?
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Pollock): I regret that I am unable to
add anything to statements which I have
made on previous occasions. The question of foregoing land purchase annuities
has been raised frequently since this
Government was set up, and not only
would it be unwise in principle to agree
to any such suggestion, but I am advised
such action by this Government would be
an infringement of the Government of
Ireland Act, and it should, therefore, be
widely known that the hon. Member's
suggestion is quite impracticable.
Mr. MINFORD: As the Minister has
not given a satisfactory answer I wish to
give notice that I will raise the matter on
the adjournment.
MOTOR CARS ON BELFAST
STREETS.
3. Major McCORMICK asked the Minister of Home Affairs whether he has
approved of a by-law which prohibited.
owners of business premises in Belfast
from leaving their cars outside those
premises except for a reasonable time;
and, if so, whether he can state the meaning of the term "reasonable time"?
Financial Provisions Bill-
Second Reading
27 MARCH 1930
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): No by-law such as
is suggested by the question of the hon.
Member exists.
Section 167 of the Belfast Act of 1845
makes it an offence to cause any carriage
-an expression which would include a
motor-car-to stand in any street longer
than may be necessary for taking up and
setting down passengers.
I would also draw the attention of the
hon. Member to Article IV (2) of the
Motor Car (Use and Construction) Order,
1904, which makes it an offence to allow
any motor-car to stand on any highway
so as to cause any obstruction.
Major McCORMICK:
Would the
Minister state whether the Act referred to
by him or whether the by-law in that
case makes the policeman the sole arbiter
or judge of the law?
Sir DAWSON BATES: No. The
policeman is not the sole arbiter of the
law. The magistrate acts on the evidence
which is produced before him.
Major McCORMICK: Is the Minister
aware that this by-law or Act he refers
to is harsh and hurtful to the trade?
Sir DAWSON BATES: On the contrary, I have frequently had complaints
from owners of shops of motor-cars standing before their premises so that customers
could not get into the shops.

involved in the contents of the Bill itself,

Measure. I will, however, if I may, touch

to enable Members to understand more
fully the nature of the Measure itself.
The first Clause concerns itself with the
necessary power given to the Ministry of
Finance to provide the additional sum of
£5,000 for the Irish Sailors' and Soldiers'
Land Trust in order to complete the entire scheme of building houses for exsailors and ex-soldiers. Perhaps I should
give some additional information to that
which was furnished yesterday and let
the House know that while the original
amount was intended to cover the whole
of Ireland, when the separation took place
it was necessary naturally that some division should take place, and the number of
houses would be provided by the Imperial
Government for each area. On that
division it appeared that we were entitled
here to 1,066 houses to be built. As the
scheme further developed, however, the
Treasury offered us a capital sum sufficient to provide for the building of these
1,066 houses.
This money was vested in the Trust
formed by the Imperial Government, consisting of one chairman, who was an
Englishman, and one representative who

the erection of these 1,066 houses.

The second Clause deals with the
powers given to the Ministry of Finance
to guarantee loans to farmers for several
purposes. It would, perhaps, be convenient if I gave some information as to
these purposes and the terms on which
the money is lent to farmers, having
regard to the questions that were raised
during the discussion
Resolution yesterday. There are two
classes of loans, one for seeds and
artificial fertilisers, and the second for
the purchase of livestock including
poultry. Applications on the ordinary
forms can be made to the Ministry of
Agriculture in accordance with the
practice adopted in connection with other
loans in the past. These loans are made
by promissory notes, which are discounted
by bankers, and the Government's
guarantee is extended to these bankers
that in consideration of their advancing
the money they will be indemnified
against any losses that may arise in discounting the bills.
With regard to the loans for livestock
-I have spoken firstly of the loans for
seeds and artificial fertilisers, and the
methods by which they can be securedthis is quite a new service. It is intended
in the main to enable those farmers who
have been so badly hurt by the condition
of the potato market and the loss of
money so involved, to purchase livestock
with a view to making up some of the loss
they have sustained on potatoes. It will
be understood that this is a lesson, perhaps, to the farmers-though I am not
entitled to advise farmers-that they
should not rely solely on potatoes, because it would appear from the seasonal
difficulties that arise that they are a very
uncertain crop. However, that is a
matter for the farmers themselves, and I
only comment on it in passing.
These
loans are issued at five per cent. in the
usual way, and the Bill requires two
guarantors upon the backs of the bills
which are issued and discounted by the
banks.
Clause 3 deals with a very small matter.
It relates simply to the extinction of tithe
rent charges. It enables the Ministry of
Finance to purchase them outright at a
lower rate than that which was provided
by an Act in the year 1872 when a limitation of 22 years' purchase was imposed
upon the purchasers who extinguished
these rent charges. As the value of
money has changed so greatly since then.
it is desirable that the 22 years' limit
should be removed, and that whatever
bargain can be made by the Government
in the redemption of these charges should
be permitted, but in such a way as would
not reduce the return if the money were
invested in Government securities.
Clause 4 deals with the salary of the
Comptroller and Auditor-General. We
discussed that at considerable length
yesterday, and I have nothing further to
say on the matter beyond the fact that
this is intended to carry out the bargain
made with this officer when he assumed
charge of the Department for which he
is now responsible. From the opinions
expressed yesterday I think the House
will agree that that arrangement should
now become permanent.

to provide any

shown by the police, that the police took
a particular side, that they did not hold
their hand fairly, and that owing to their
neglect of their duties the election has
turned out how it may. I, myself, do not
believe that the police would take sides,
but I know that after every election the
charge would be made, and would be made
with all the insistence that the opponents
and those who dislike our police can muster, that the police were the agents of
a particular party and that they
favoured a particular party. That is a
position the police should never be placed
in. If personation is to be checked, the
only way it can be checked is by the appointment of official personation agents,
by imposing upon the personation agents
the duty of making the charge, and by
imposing upon the personation agents and
the actual candidates the responsibility of
seeing their charges of personation are
well founded.

If, at a parliamentary election or local
government election, after a person applies for a ballot paper and before he

is an offence of personation as in this

particulars of such act, or declares to
the like effect, then in every such case
the presiding officer shall immediately

When he knew a man not to be the person

that where the presiding officer has the

Mr. BLACK: One has a good deal of

that felony, and it is the duty of the
police to take proper action. The presiding officer has at least the same rights and
duties and privileges as a private citizen,
and if a presiding officer sees a felony
being committed in his presence it is his
duty to inform the police. I do not think
the Amendment proposed by the hon.

If any such Amendment were made in

He has not a very wide field of choice,

people who have not very great experience. If there is anything done wrong in
the performance of that duty there would

be an ultimate responsibility on the

offered by way of illustration is that of a

rights of an ordinary citizen-
Mr. COLLINS: On a point of Order.

Mr. HANNA: I was careful to say
that the illustration that the hon. Gentleman took was that of a schoolmaster in
the country. That was part of my hon.
Friend's very able advocacy in regard to
this matter. But now you are going to
impose upon a presiding officer a duty
that is altogether foreign to the duties
that he is selected to perform. The presiding officer must be kept free from influences either on behalf of the minority
candidate or of the majority candidate.
His simple duty is to conduct the election,
and to vest him with this added power of
making a note of an application for a
paper does not lead anywhere, because,
as the hon. and learned Member for
Willowfield (Mr. Black) has pointed out
his rights as a citizen are not at all interfered with.
If he knows that a man is committing
a felony-and that is the case the hon.
Gentleman has indicated--then no question of £5 or £10 compensation arises,
because he knows it of his own knowledge.
He is a perfectly competent witness, and
has a perfect right, as has been pointed
out by the hon. and learned Member for
Willowfield, to see that a prosecution is
instituted. It is the duty of the presiding officer in those circumstances to see
that such a prosecution is instituted. But
I can very well understand that if he were
a schoolmaster in a district where there
was a minority candidate in a very small
minority, and a majority candidate, his
life in that school afterwards might not
be very well worth living. The machinery
that has been set up under the law for
the conduct of elections has been found
by those gentlemen who investigated this
matter to be practically adequate for its
purpose. We have tried to adopt in this
Bill all the suggestions that those gentlemen have made in their report, and we
feel that, as we are giving a candidate
the right to have in the polling station
a personation agent, a man with local
knowledge will not stand by and allow a
person to commit this crime of personation. His duty is a perfectly simple one,
and that is to draw the attention of a
presiding officer there and then to the
fact that a person is committing a crime,
and it then becomes the immediate duty
of the presiding officer to order the arrest
of that person. I submit that no more effective machinery for the abolition of
personation could be conceived. In my
view it would be better and less harmful
that one man who personated should
escape than that an honest man who had
the right to vote should be prevented
from voting or impeded in exercising that
right. The State and all public institutions depend upon the free right to vote

priest came to the rescue to try to save
myself and others. Therefore, I say that
if you make it the duty of the local schoolmaster-I do not care which side he is on
-to take the action suggested in cases of
personation my experience of elections.
justifies me in coming to the conclusion
that his life would be made a perfect
misery.

THE SOLDIERS' AND SAILORS'
LAND TRUST.
2. Mr. HEALY asked the Minister of
Finance whether he can state when the
Soldiers' and Sailors' Trust, representative
of the Imperial, Northern and Free State
Governments, which began to function in
1924, was dissolved; whether the operations of the Trust in Northern Ireland are
carried out by the Ministry of Finance
now as an agency service?
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Pollock): The Irish Sailors' and Soldiers'
Land Trust has not been dissolved. The
operations of the Trust in Northern
Ireland are still carried out by my
Ministry as an agency service, under the
direction of the two Northern Ireland
trustees-Lord Dufferin and General Ross.
Mr. HEALY: Do I understand the
Imperial Government still act?
Mr. POLLOCK: The Imperial Government are represented how does it come the
James Brungate was, and is, chairman.
He still continues chairman of the Committee or of the Trust. The Northern
Government section is operated by the two
gentlemen I have mentioned.
Mr. HEALY: If the Imperial Government are represented how does it come the
Northern Government are acting for them
by way of agency service?
Mr. POLLOCK: The Northern Government are acting as agents in exactly the
same way as they do in several services
that are really under the control of the
Imperial Government, as
every hon.
Member knows.
WIDENING OF THE BANGOR
ROAD.
3. Mr. BEATTIE (for Mr. Henderson) asked the Minister of Home Affairs
if he can state whether his Ministry is
taking any action in regard to the
widening of the Bangor Road from the
Belfast City Boundary to Bangor, and
whether he intends to ensure that this
road shall be constructed so as to take
fast and slow traffic?
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): The road from the
boundary of the City of Belfast to Bangor is under the jurisdiction of the Down
County Council. The Council has prepared a scheme for the widening of this
road which is an undertaking of great
magnitude, and there are considerable
difficulties of various kinds to be overcome.
The Ministry has intimated to the
County Council that it would be prepared
to make grants from the Road Fund
towards this work at the appropriate
rates towards the loan charges for the
payment of interest and principal on the
money required. The Ministry is still in
correspondence with the County Council
with regard to the scheme.
The hon. Member may rest assured that
the scheme, which is under consideration,
is designed to meet all reasonable requirements of traffic between the two points,
now and in the future.
THE FIRE AT PURDYSBURN
MENTAL HOSPITAL.
Hen-
4. Mr. BEATTIE (for Mr.
derson) asked the Minister of Home
Affairs whether he is aware that a
serious fire took place at Purdysburn
Mental Hospital; whether the water supply failed, and water had to be carried
in pails from the pump to extinguish the
fire, and whether he can state what steps
the Ministry propose to take to see that
a proper water supply is provided, so as
to avoid a recurrence of this unsatisfactory
state of affairs?
Sir DAWSON BATES: I am aware
that a fire broke out on the 2nd instant
under the roof tiles of the officers' quarters
in the centre block of the Mental Hospital at Purdysburn. The quarters
Oral Answers
Oral Answers
1 APRIL 1930
occupied by the patients were not affected.
The fire was readily brought under control by the Brigade, and at no time was
the safety of any of the patients or staff
imperilled. I may add that the buildings
are fireproof in structure.
It is not a fact that the water supply
failed. The Fire Brigade authorities
were satisfied that their requirements
could be adequately met by the supply
available from the large tanks in the roof
of the building itself, and they did not
consider it necessary to lay down hose to
the hydrants in the grounds. The engine
was, therefore, supplied with water drawn
in buckets from the taps in the basement
of the building, and it is not a fact that
the water had to be drawn from a pump
as suggested. The supply thus obtained
was amply sufficient, and, in fact, the Fire
Brigade authorities are of opinion that
the use of more water would have increased the damage.
The Hospital authorities have been in
consultation with the Fire Brigade
authorities as to what further precautionary measures might be taken to cope with
possible outbreaks of fire, and as an additional safeguard it is proposed to provide a convenient means of access for
Brigade engines to the large underground
reserve tanks at the water tower so as
to enable the Brigade engine to be located
if necessary in the immediate proximity
of these tanks.
Mr. HEALY: That is a great article!
