HOUSING OF AGRICULTURAL
LABOURERS.
6. Mr. HEALY asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether the Omagh Rural
District Council disposed of sites acquired.
some years ago for the purpose of housing
agricultural labourers; and, if so, whether
there was any loss on this re-sale?
Sir DAWSON BATES: The Omagh
Rural District Council have disposed of
68 plots acquired for the purpose of their
Labourers' Order, 1913.
Under this Order the Council acquired
128 plots, and they utilised 60 of these
plots for the building of cottages. As a
result of the outbreak of war the building
of cottages on the remaining 68 plots was
deferred.
By Section 15 of the Labourers' (Ireland) Act, 1883, if cottages are not built
upon the plots acquired within two years
the sites must be reconveyed to the original
owners or sold by public auction.
To meet the emergency caused by the
war, the time within which pre-war
schemes might be carried out was extended
by Section 1 of the Labourers' (Ireland)
Act, 1918, to 31st August, 1924.
The Omagh Rural District Council did
not erect any cottages on the sites in question within the prescribed period as they
were of opinion that, in the interval, the
position had altered so that there was then
little need for the erection of cottages on
these particular sites. In the circumstances they were bound by law to dispose
of the sites in accordance with the provisions of Sections 15 and 16 of the
Labourers' (Ireland) Act, 1883.
Of the 68 plots, reconveyance was accepted by 19 owners at the prices paid,
but in the remaining cases the owners refused to accept the sites back, and they
were, therefore, put up for sale by public
auction.
The amount paid by the Council for
the plots in question was £2,119 12s 4d
and the amount realised by their sale was
£1,086 2s 10d. There was, therefore, a
loss of £1,033 9s 6d on the transaction.
Mr. HEALY: Arising out of that
reply, would the right hon. Gentleman
indicate where his sympathy for the working classes lies when he allows a transaction
of this kind to take place in Omagh where
there is a terrible dearth of houses? Are
you honest or are you not?
Sir DAWSON BATES: I think the
hon. Member entirely forgets that these
events happened before the Northern
Ireland Government existed.
Mr. HEALY: Some of these events,
I understand, have been sanctioned since
the Northern Ireland Government was
formed.

CLASS VII. No. 1
MINISTRY OF COMMERCE.
Motion made, and Question proposed,
"That a sum not exceeding £16,313 be
granted to his Majesty to complete the
sum necessary to defray the charge that
will come in course of payment during
the year ending 31st March, 1931, to
defray the salaries and expenses of the
Ministry of Commerce (15 and 16 Geo.
V., c. 3, s. 4 (N.I.); 16 Geo. V. C. 4
(N.I.))" (Note-£6,000 has been voted
on account).
The MINISTER OF COMMERCE
(Mr. Barbour): The scope of the work
of the Ministry of Commerce is sufficiently
indicated by the Estimates before you.
In the effort to encourage trade attention has naturally been directed to two
aspects, namely, trade within the Province itself and export trade. While it
would be erroneous to imagine that Northern Ireland, as we know it at present,
could subsist even to a large extent on
trade within her own borders, it would
be equally erroneous to suppose that the
home trade is of negligible importance.
A glance at our list of imports is
sufficient to correct such a misapprehension and, while, relatively, the home
market is of subsidiary importance to our
staple industries, its importance to our
smaller industries is surprisingly great.
For this reason, therefore, the Government has afforded assistance to the
effort now being made by the Ulster
Industries Development Association to
foster the consumption of Ulster-made
goods by the Ulster people. I am confident that the Committee will have
appreciated the zeal and energy with
which this campaign is being prosecuted.
With a view to stimulating in Great
Britain the demand for the produce of
4.99

Supply-
Committee
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Barbour]
our countryside my Ministry will continue to co-operate wholeheartedly with
the Empire Marketing Board in arranging exhibitions in London and Provincial centres in Great Britain. These
Exhibitions continue to be of undoubted
value to the Northern Ireland producer,
and beyond that I am convinced that
they afford a valuable means of bringing
home to the public at large in Great
Britain the true position of our Province
and its relation to the United Kingdom.
I may say that I had the opportunity
a few days ago of visiting a display in
Glasgow, and I was greatly gratified by
the manner in which this work is being
done by the Empire Marketing Board.
not only as regards the site which they
had selected for their exhibit, but also
as to the amount of space which they
devoted to produce from the North of
Ireland, and the taste with which they
exhibited their display. I feel it must
have a considerable effect in bringing our
produce before the consumers in the
United Kingdom.
So far as our larger industries are concerned we are endeavouring to assist in
every useful direction. The Government
may be able to assist an industry towards
prosperity, but it cannot of itself make
an industry prosperous. Industry, not
only in this Province but throughout the
world, is still having an uphill fight
against those economic conditions which
are the aftermath of war.
The peculiar difficulties of the situation
with which the linen industry is faced
are only too well known and I need not
enter into them here, but I do hope to
see a greater disposition on the part of
the industry than there has been in the
past to face the facts, and a greater
readiness to work together for the solution of the problem. The delegation of
the whole industry which recently visited
the United States was an earnest of what
might be done in that direction, but I
am sure that all will agree with me in
feeling that isolated efforts of this kind
are not sufficient to turn the tide towards
prosperity, and that what is necessary is
a sustained effort to get together and to
sink the individualism of the past in
closer co-operation in the future.
The Government is giving special assistance to the linen industry in respect
both to the assurance of its supplies of
raw material and the marketing of its
manufactured goods. With regard to
raw material, I should explain to the
Committee that the nature of the grants
which we have hitherto made through
the Linen Industry Research Association
has been changed.
The assistance given by the Government to the Linen Industry Research Association has in the past been by way of
subsidy of its general activities. We now
feel, however, that a stage has been
reached at which the industry as a whole
should be convinced of the utility of research on the purely industrial side and
be prepared to assume an increasing
measure of financial responsibility for
the carrying on of that particular form
of research work. In the matter of flax
and fibre production, however, different
considerations apply. The provision of
plentiful supplies of raw
raw material at
steady prices is a matter of vital importance to the trade, but anything which
tends to render the cultivation of flax and
the production of flax fibre easier and
more profitable is of equal and more immediate benefit to the farmer both here
and elsewhere, and the linen trade may
claim with some force that they should
not be expected to bear the whole brunt
of financing research work in these directions. At the same time, research work,
both agricultural and industrial, needs to
be carefully co-ordinated and the ideal
of linen research is to have tests extended
from the seed to the finished article.
We therefore propose, in conjunction with
the Empire Marketing Board, to support
financially the Flax and Fibre Production
Division of the Linen Industry Research
Association, and it is a contribution to
this end that I shall ask the Committee to
provide, when I come to Part 2 of the Estimates.
We are further in this connection amplifying the assistance which we have been
giving in conjunction with the Imperial
Government, to the Flax Industry Development Society in Somerset, in seconding the efforts which are being made there
to establish the industry of flax fibre production in Great Britain, and ultimately
throughout the Empire.
With regard to the marketing end, the
Government is prepared to continue for
another year its support to the publicity
campaign of the Irish and Scottish
Damask Advertising Association and its
sister body, the Irish Linen Guild.
are satisfied from the investigations which
we have made and the reports which we
have received that the campaign in the
We
Supply-
Committee
1 APRIL 1930
United States of America is being run
upon able and energetic lines. It is still
too early, however, for me to express an
opinion as to the efficacy of the campaign
which has been instituted in the home and
Dominion markets.
The Committee will be aware, of course,
that my Ministry is helping our manufac
turers and traders generally by means of
the Commercial Intelligence Service
which, as in the case of the Department of
Overseas Trade in Great Britain has been
a leading feature of our activities since the
inception of the Ministry. I am glad to
be able to inform the Committee that our
manufacturers and traders continue to
avail themselves of this voluntary service
with great readiness and that they have
repeately expressed appreciation of the
service which my Department is able to
give in this respect.
There is one item in the Estimates to
which I think I might now appropriately
draw attention, namely, that relating to
the census of production. Under Subhead D, provision is made for the estimated expenditure during the year on the
taking of a census of production of Northern Ireland in 1931 in respect of the
year 1930.
The Committee will recollect
that a similar census was taken in respect
of the year 1924. On that occasion, however, the work of taking the census was
performed by the Board of Trade under
an
agency arrangement.
The opportunity of making a similar arrangement
in regard to the forthcoming census was
again open to my Ministry, but after a
careful examination of all the considerations involved it was decided that it would
probably facilitate our traders and also
render the final returns more useful if the
census were taken by the Ministry itself.
A decision to that effect was, accordingly,
taken and the preliminary operations in
carrying out the work have been set in
motion. Here I should explain that a
census of production for Great Britain for
1930 will be taken simultaneously with
that for Northern Ireland.
In contrast to the procedure followed on
the previous occasion both the Board of
Trade, in the case of Great Britain, and
my Ministry, in the case of Northern Ireland, have issued preliminary return
forms to the firms affected by the census
which will enable them to see at the beginning of the census year the exact
nature of the information which they will
be required to furnish at the end of the
year.
I have no doubt that the adoption
of this procedure will enable many firms
to furnish the required particulars with
much less trouble than would have been
the case had no warning been given, and
will also ensure greater exactitude in the
bulk of the returns which we receive.
The Committee, I am sure, will scarcely
expect me to put forward any very lengthy
justification for the taking of the census.
In these days when every industrialised
community is facing increasing competition on all sides, and when every such
community is obliged to make a periodical
review of its industrial position, recurrent
Comcensuses have become a necessity.
pared with her competitors the United
Kingdom may be said to have been rather
backward in this respect. I understand
that in the United States an industrial
census is taken biennially, while in some
of the Dominions the interval between the
taking of the census is much shorter than
has hitherto been the case in the United
Kingdom. The Committee will readily
appreciate the uses to which the results
expected from the forthcoming census may
be put. In the first place, those results
will enable us to compare our industrial
output of to-day with that of 1924 and
to see in what respects progress or retrogression has taken place. Again, they
will afford interesting material for a comparison of production with export and
import figures, and might be of inestimable use if and when one or more of our
industries were involved in a safeguarding
application.
Before I leave the subject of trade and
commerce I should like to refer to a factor
in our economic life which exercises a
greater influence than is commonly supposed upon our balance of trade, and that
is the development of tourist traffic.
In
a sense we export our scenery and our
holiday facilities just as much as we do
our ships, our linen goods and our other
manufactured articles, and it is important that what may be called our invisible
trade in tourist facilities should not be
overlooked. There is a general movement
amongst the countries of Europe to exploit to the utmost the attractions which
they can offer to travellers and holiday
makers, and we here have noted with
considerable satisfaction the growth in the
tourist traffic to Ulster which has followed
the activities of the Ulster Tourist Development Association.

I have dealt hitherto with what I may
call the commercial functions of my Ministry. I now turn to functions which may
be broadly classed as statutory.
Such
matters as railways and canals, the registration of companies, friendly societies,
business names and moneylenders provide
little for comment, but, as the Committee are already aware, it will shortly
be my duty to introduce a comprehensive
Measure for the amendment of company
law in Northern Ireland. I should also
say that the duties assigned to the Ministry under the Industrial Assurance Act
of 1924 have resulted in a volume of work
which has steadily increased from year
to year.
In the calendar year 1929, the
number of disputes between policy holders
and companies or societies referred to the
Industrial Assurance Commissioner for
arbitration was 803 as compared with 737
in 1928 and 260 in 1927. This rate of
increase is being maintained.
There is no question about the necessity
for the simple, but efficient, method of
arbitration on disputes which the Act provides for the people by whom these cases
are brought forward. The figures themselves are ample proof that it has been
appreciated and, indeed, that it was essential. Much additional evidence is
afforded by numbers of letters received by
the Commissioner from policy holders in
all parts of the country, including even,
I am glad to say, appreciations from
claimants whose cases after careful and
patient consideration have been dismissed.
It is undoubtedly the desire of all persons affected that a system of arbitration,
which has served so well in the past,
should be continued. Provision is, therefore, made for carrying on the arrangement
whereby the assistance of a practising
barrister is secured in order to cope with
the very large number of cases coming up
for adjudication.
I shall deal at a later stage with the
matter of harbour improvements, and
with regard to the subject of electricity

difference in the prices is 7s 6d per ton.
I wonder will the Minister justify that increase in the price of coal. I do not say
that either of these prices-one was 30s
and the other 37s 6d- is anything at all
approaching the higher prices that are
charged for coal. As a matter of fact I
think most people in the place about
which I am speaking would be very glad
to get their coal even at 37s 6d per ton.
But the two prices-30s a ton in 1929 and
37s 6d a ton in 1930-occurred in the same
town and to the same individual, and I
would like to know if there is any justification for raising the price of coal by
7s 6d a ton.
That is one matter in connection with
which I think the Minister of Commerce
should be more alert. Indeed it seems to
me that the Government have not been
alert at all in this connection. All who
read the papers know that this matter was
ventilated in the Dail in Dublin and the
same suggestion made. As a matter of
fact I think it was mentioned that the
same individuals control the coal ring in
Dublin as control it here. If that be so
the Government should step in and, if
they have the power, stop it; and if they
have not the power then they should use
their influence to stop it, because it is unfair and unjust that any individuals who
are in a position to create a monopoly in
connection with any item that is in daily
use by the public should not be prevented
from making high and exorbitant charges.

As regards the dredging of the port at
Warrenpoint, that touches on the general
policy of the Government in respect of
dredging. The Government are not responsible in so far as the dredging of private harbours is concerned, but they realise the value of private harbours to the
Province, and where the owner of a private
harbour is anxious to have dredging done
the Government are very glad to place at
his disposal the dredging plant which the
Government own, charging only the actual
cost of the operation. So it is of no cost
to the Government, and it gives the owner
of the harbour the advantage of having
dredging plant near by and suitable for
doing that class of work.

I now come to the harbours round about
the coast. Those harbours, with the exception of the Royal Harbours and the
larger harbours like Derry, Larne and
Belfast, are entirely a matter for the
county councils. It is their duty to keep
them up,
and the Government
ready to assist them with the plant
and to come to their assistance
to the extent of half the expenditure.
The harbour at Warrenpoint is a privatelyowned harbour, and as a matter of fact
the owner of that harbour had opened
negotiations with the Government, asking

dredging plant at his disposal on the usual
terms, and the Government replied that

As regards coal, I should not like the
hon. Members of this House to think that
the Ministry of Commerce do not look into

to deal with that matter. My attention

and the loss of weight in transit from one
cause or another.
As hon. Members will realise, personally I am very much interested in the cost
of coal, and I should be very glad to be
able to buy coal cheaper than I am able to

the figures that have been put before me I

charges are made, or exorbitant profits

Northern Ireland.
I can say that, after
having looked carefully into such figures
as I have been able to command.
With regard to the linen industry, the
grant for the publicity campaign has been
criticised on the ground of insufficient
benefit accruing to the different parties
contributing to the trade in Northern Ireland. As regards flax, let me say that the
linen industry in Northern Ireland, I am
glad to say, still represents the biggest
part of the linen industry in the world.
I do not think there is any country in the
world has a larger share of the linen industry than Northern Ireland. When we
talk about flax, we must remember that
the 5,000 tons referred to by the hon.
Member for Mourne (Mr. O'Neill) is only
a contribution to a world supply of something like 500,000 tons.
The hon. Member must realise that in
the nature of affairs flax spinners must
look to other sources of supply than the
Irish farmers. Speaking as a trader, I
Supply-
Committee
1 APRIL 1930
may say that I am sure many traders
rather envy the Irish farmer in that
he never makes a bad debt in the sale of
his flax. The farmer may sometimes consider that he gets a poor price when he
takes his flax to market, but almost invariably he is able to find a purchaser.
The crop of flax grown every year in
Northern Ireland is practically sold every
year in Northern Ireland. It is a very
different matter with the producers of
other goods, who are not able to find a
market for the entire amount of their output. After all, the price of flax is determined by world conditions.
Hon. Members will know that in considering the price of flax that the Irish
farmer gets they must take into consideration the price that rules in Russia-the
greatest flax-producing country—the price
that rules in Courtrai, in Belgium, even
in France, or any other of the flaxproducing countries with whose products
we have to compete. After all, there is
one thing of which I
can assure hon.
Members-in fact it is a thing I regretthat there is very little combination
amongst spinners. The Irish spinner is
not the only spinner who uses flax. There
is no reason why, if he thinks his flax is
worth more, the Irish farmer should not
try to get flax spinners in other countries
to buy it. It is a world market. Speaking as a spinner, I think that Irish flax
really does command its relative value.

con-
They thought it would be much better
to see that the lines would carry current
of such capacity that when the towns
further out required electricity they
could simply be attached to the end of
the Lisburn wire. So the bargain which
this House made through my Ministry
was that the Government would in the
meantime bear the difference in the cost
of construction of the heavier cable that
would be required to be suitable for extension further out into the province,
and the cost of the cable which the
Lisburn people were going to put up
merely for their own use. The result is
that the cable now running between Belfast and Lisburn is capable of being extended to other parts of the province
when towns further out wish to take
their supply of electricity from Belfast.
As soon as current is used in excess of
the amount that the Lisburn people
would have provided through their lines
the Government will be able to make a
charge for such excess. I think that was
a wise provision to make, but in the
meantime the Lisburn people really
derive no benefit out of it at all.

endeavour to get as ample security

capital account will be for the purpose of
extending storage accommodation and enlarging retting tanks and also modernising
equipment generally. The extra working
capital is, of course, required for financing
the increased acreage and will be represented by the fibre produced.
I do not propose to detain the Committee with further remarks on the
subject of the Linen Industry Publicity
Campaign, with which I have already
dealt in introducing Part I. The Estimate in Part II provides for a further
grant on the same basis as that of last
year, namely, 15/- for every £1 collected
by the linen trade, and is based on the
Supply-
Committee
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Barbour]
assumption that trade subscriptions will
reach approximately last year's level.
The sum of £750 included in Sub-head
F3 (Grant in aid of Linen Industry Research Association for the development of
a scheme of research into the problems of
flax growing and fibre production), as a
grant-in-aid towards capital expenditure
represents one-fourth of the total contribution of £3,000, the Empire Marketing
Board having agreed to provide the remaining three-fourths. It is also proposed
to contribute from Northern Ireland funds
for a period of five years commencing
1st October, 1929, the sum of £1,250 per
annum towards maintenance expenditure
in connection with this scheme. The
Empire Marketing Board have agreed to
contribute towards maintenance expenditure to the extent of £3,750 per annum in
the first and second years and £3,000 per
annum in the third, fourth and fifth
years. The total Government grants for
the first three years will, therefore,
amount to £5,000 per annum, and for the
fourth and fifth years £4,250 per annum.
During the latter years the balance of
£750 per annum required to bring the
amount available for this work up to
£5,000 per annum will be provided from
the funds of the Research Association.
As to Sub-head F4 (Grant in aid of
Ulster Industries Development Association), it is too early yet for this campaign,
of which I have already spoken, to have
produced its maximum effect, or to have
won for itself that measure of support
from manufacturers of the Province
which we hope it will in the future
receive. The Government, accordingly,
proposes to contribute for a further year
towards the funds of the Association a
sum equivalent to £1 for every 10/-
collected in respect of subscriptions or
contributions from every source. The
driving idea behind the campaign that we
should support our home industries
wherever possible has, I think, found
acceptance in every quarter of this House.
Sub-head G (Grant in aid of Tourist
Development) makes provision for the
payment of a grant-in-aid to the Ulster
Tourist Development Association similar
in amount to that granted last year. The
basis of payment remains the same as
hitherto, namely, a sum equivalent to 10/-
for each £1 collected by the Association
in respect of contributions or subscriptions
from various sources. Hon. Members
will, I think, agree with me that the increase in the number of tourists who are
now visiting our Province is in a very
great measure attributable to the activities
of the Association.
I come now to statutory railway grants.
The total amount included under this subhead shows a decrease of £603, as compared
with the previous year. Provision is
required to meet the guaranteed dividends.
and loss on working the Clogher Valley
Railway. The amount payable in respect
of guaranteed dividends represents 2% per
annum on the paid-up capital of the
Company, which amounts to £123,310.
This amount remains constant from year
to year. As regards loss on working, the
contribution amounts to 45% of one-half
the amount by which the loss on working
exceeds the sum represented by a rate of
6d in the £ levied on certain baronies in
the Counties of Tyrone and Fermanagh.
This amount varies from year to year,
according to the extent of the loss on working during the twelve months in respect
of which the contribution is payable.
The next Sub-head is Receipts Appropriated in Aid. The amount of receipts
in respect of harbour dues, etc., depends
principally upon the success of the herring
fishing season at Ardglass. The season of
1929 was unfortunately disappointing, and
affected adversely the receipts from
harbour dues and dues payable in respect
of herring branding. The amounts recoverable from local authorities and from
the fees received by inspectors of weights.
and measures represent the total provision
made under Sub-head C. of the Estimate,
to which I have already referred.
sums payable by county councils are in
respect of contributions towards the cost
of works of improvement to be carried out
at various harbours by the Government
dredging and rock-breaking plant. I beg
to move.

Coming to the question of fishing, I do
not know whether I would be in order in
suggesting that the Minister ought to devote his attention for a little to the question of Toome eel fishery. It is unique,
I suppose, inasmuch as it is the only
fishery of its kind in this kingdom. The
fishermen there have a geniune grievance.
They have taken their case from one court
to another, until finally it landed in the
House of Lords, and there their contention was only overborne by a majority of
one. It has been held that the Toome
eel fishery exists for the benefit of a
private individual, and surely it is a
throw-back, as it were, to argue in these
days that a Government must help an
industry that is primarily a benefit to an
individual or a private company.
The fisherman ought to be the main
consideration both of the Ministry and of
the Government, and the fishermen
believe it is up to the Ministry to buy out
those private interests in the Toome eel
fishery. It may be said that these people
are not going to sell their rights unless at
an exorbitant figure, but this Parliament
would probably have something to say to
that. You could introduce legislation
here that would offer a reasonable figure
to the owners of the Toome eel fishery,
and that would at the same time put the
fishermen in that locality-and there are
a great number of them-in a better
position than they occupy at this moment
of earning a livelihood. There are very
few opportunities in Northern Ireland at
the moment of people making a livelihood.
The only alternative seems to be to rush to
some of the Colonies where things are
probably not as rosy as they are painted.

HOUSE OF COMMONS

publicity campaigners themselves. We give

The next question is the payment of the
chairmen of courts of referees, which is a

On the wording of the Unemployment
Insurance Act passed in Northern Ireland
it takes three to constitute the full court

is the legal chairman. There is not what
I would call extra responsibility upon that

three shares the same responsibility in
regard to the working of the new Act,

HOUSE OF COMMONS.

Wednesday, 2nd April, 1930.
The House met at Three of the Clock,
Mr. SPEAKER in the Chair.
ORDERS OF THE DAY.
Parliamentary and Local Government
Elections Bill.
Motion made, and Question proposed,
"That this Bill be now read the Third
time."—(Sir Dawson Bates).
Mr. GRANT: In rising to support the
Third Reading of this Bill I would like
to take the opportunity of expressing the
hope that all hon. Members of this House
are seriously of the opinion that personation should be done away with in connection with elections. But on analysing
some of the speeches made by hon. Members opposite I am afraid it is not their
desire to do away with personation.
During the course of the Second Reading
debate we heard charges made against the
right hon. Gentleman (Sir Dawson Bates)
that he was not honest in his intentions in
having this evil abolished. Those speeches
reminded me of an incident that occurred
in Belfast Police Court some time ago. A
very well known legal man in the city had
put up his case to the Bench and the decision had gone against him. Addressing
the Bench he then said: "I can understand why I have lost my case. I am
afraid I have produced too much evidence.
That is the reason I have lost my case."
I think hon. Members opposite have put
up far too much evidence. That is why
I do not believe they are serious in their
desire to have this evil abolished.
Take the speech of the hon. Member
for Woodvale (Mr. Nixon) who, I regret,
is not in the House. He put up the argument to the right hon. Gentleman that the
hours from 8 o'clock in the morning to
8 o'clock in the evening were not long
enough to give people, at any rate in the
city, an opportunity of exercising the
franchise. He gave reasons for that which
were very good from his point of view.
If he had finished there, he had put up
a fairly decent case. But then he went
on to say that he knew two ladies at an
election in the city some time ago who
were so honest and sincere in their desire
to have their particular candidate returned
that he was sure they voted at least 200
times. Now if we take it that even personators require some hours for meals on
election day, and we take two hours off
the 12, that means that in ten hours they
actually voted twenty times per hour. So
they voted at least once in every three
minutes during the course of the day. I
think that is absolutely absurd. Even
with all the dressing stations mentioned by
the hon. Member for South Fermanagh
(Mr. Healy) it would be a physical impossibility for any individual to vote 200
times. But not only that, his previous
argument for extending the time for an
hour was to give these ladies another hour
longer so that they might add twenty more
votes to the 200 they already had.
Mr. SPEAKER: The hon. Member
must remember that on the Third Reading he can only discuss what is actually in
the Bill. He is now making a Second
Reading speech. I must ask him to confine his remarks to what is in the Bill.
Mr. GRANT: My intention is to deal
with the evil of personation. I thought I
would have an opportunity of dealing
with that on the Third Reading speech,
because the unfortunate thing about it is
this that charges have been made against
people without any names being mentioned, and without their having an opportunity of defending themselves. I
think it would only be right if I ask hon.
Members who are making statements in
this House to go outside the House and
make those statements and give people an
opportunity of defending themselves.
However, passing from that point we go.
on to the hon. Member for Pottinger (Mr.
Beattie). He tried to point out that he
knew certain representative gentlemen in
the city-he mentioned an alderman, a
councillor, a publican, and a pawnbroker
-who paid for personation. Now no one
can charge me with defending people who
personate, and I think the hon. Member
who made that allegation ought to go out-..
side the House and mention those names,
thus giving these people an opportunity of
defending themselves in public. I have
no doubt they can defend themselves. On
the question of personation the hon. Member waxed very eloquent, and yet I make
bold to say both inside and outside this
House that he actually gained his seat in

Mr. O'NEILL: None.
Mr. HANNA: I will proceed to indicate some of the differences that it does
make. It used to be the case it is the
law as it stands at present-that a prosecution was initiated by the agent of a candidate undertaking to the presiding
officer that he could prove that a certain
person had attempted or had committed
personation. The continuation of those
proceedings was a matter to a very great
extent in the hands of either the candidate or his agent. But now that is taken
away, and the moment the basis of prosecution is laid by a declaration of the personating agent the police step in, and they
take up and carry on the prosecution.
One of the matters that has been commented on in the Press, at public meetings
and in this House, was this unfortunate
position that people afterwards could
make bargains and hand over one person
for another, with the result that so far as
personation was concerned the law was
practically annulled. That is ended now,
and the prosecution, once it is commenced,
will go on. I repeat what I have said
before. We must not, in trying to put
an end to the evil of personation, make
it impossible or difficult for an honest
voter to record his vote, because the
foundation of these public institutions of
ours rests entirely on the right of freedom
in the exercise of the vote. No longer
will people be able to make this bargain,
and if a candidate takes the responsibility
of instituting a prosecution against a voter
he must pay for it if he makes a mistake.
If he left the matter otherwise, what
would happen? It would be within the
province of any candidate, where he could
secure one or more personating agents, to
have half of the voters arrested without
incurring any responsibility. How could
any other Member get up in this House
and suggest that that protection that is
given to the voter should be taken away,
and that he should be at the mercy of any
personating agent when he came to offer
his vote? It is impossible to mix up the
duties that are allocated on the day of
election to different officers. Personating
agents are there for a particular purpose.
They know their duty; they have their responsibility. The presiding officer occupies his place one of strict impartiality.
He should not be mixed up in any shape
or form with either of the parties.
We have heard to-day that presiding
officers sometimes talk and make state-

ments to candidates after the election.

PRICES OF COAL IN BELFAST.
1. Mr. O'NEILL (for Mr. Beattie)
asked the Minister of Commerce whether
he can state the different classes of coal
imported into
into Belfast, the pit-head

The MINISTER OF COMMERCE
(Mr. Barbour): The principal classes of
domestic coal, to which I presume the
hon. Member's question refers, imported
into Belfast are: English, first, second
and third quality, and Scotch house
coal. The hon. Member will appreciate
that no official statistics are available on
the points raised in the question. I am
informed, however, that the Belfast coal
merchants normally do not buy these coal
at the pit head, but f.o.b. British ports,
and that the respective f.o.b. prices are
31s, 28s 6d, and 24s per ton for the three
qualities of English coal, and 21s for
Scotch house coal.
I am given to understand that average
freight rates may be taken to be 5s per
ton on the English coals and 3s 6d per
ton on the Scottish coal. The retail
prices per ton are: English, first quality,
52s; second quality, 49s; third quality,
44s; and Scotch house coal, 39s. The
hon. Member will, of course, understand
that the margin between the retail
price and the cost of coal on board ship
in Belfast includes the following items:
Discharge from steamer, cranage, harbour dues, quay rent, breakage, filling,
screening and weighing, cartage, delivery costs, bad debts, short weight and
overhead charges.

QUESTION OF PRIVILEGE.
Major SHILLINGTON: I desire to
raise a question of privilege. In today's leading article in the "Northern
Whig and Belfast Post," dealing with
the proposed new bridge over the River
Foyle, there appear the words-
"Everything had been beautifully
arranged. The Parliamentary Committee, as usual, had been complacent,
and had taken the simple course of
refusing to hear the other side."
I submit that these words can convey
no meaning other than an insinuation
against the integrity and honour of the
Members of a Select Committee set up,
not by this Government, but by this
House of which I had the honour to be
Chairman, and constitute a grave
breach of the privileges of this honourable House.
I would like to recall to the recollection of the House that this Committee
was composed of three Members of this
House, and three Members of the Senate. I was elected Chairman of the
Committee, and the other Members
appointed from this House were the hon.
Member for Clifton (Major Hall-
Thompson) and the hon. Member for
Falls (Mr. Byrne). One of the three
Members appointed by the Senate represented Labour interests. My recollection of the proceedings is that after
the Committee met there was an
objection made by Counsel for the promoters as to the locus standi of one of
the petitioners. Argmuents were
heard in regard to that objection, and
the petitioner himself was heard. The
Committee deliberated in private, and
they unanimously agreed that the
petitioner had no locus standi when he
came before the Committee.
I have no personal feeling in this
matter, but I think it is my duty as
Chairman of the Committee to protect
the other members of the Committee
from the insinuations made in this
Mr. SPEAKER:
I have read the
article in question, and I think the
passage complained of is most offensive
in its implications in regard to members
of the Committee. In my judgment
this matter could be quite suitably discussed by the Committee of this House
set up for that purpose, that is the Committee of Privileges, and I suggest that
the matter be referred to that Committee for their consideration and report.
If the hon. and gallant Member agrees
perhaps he would move accordingly.
Major SHILLINGTON: That is a
matter altogether for the House. I do
not know what the procedure is, but I
am prepared to fall in with your suggestion.
The PRIME MINISTER (Viscount
Craigavon): This House on all sides is
very jealous of any implication on the
honour of any single Member. You,
Mr. Speaker, have suggested the way in
which this matter should be dealt with,
and I think I would be voicing the
sentiments of Members in all quarters if
I were to move that the matter be referred to the Committee of Privileges.
I have the honour to move accordingly.

CLASS VI. No. 1.
MINISTRY OF AGRICULTURE.
Motion made and Question proposed:
"That a sum not exceeding £55,756 be
granted to His Majesty to complete the
Supply-
Committee
3 APRIL 1930
sum necessary to
to defray the charge
which will come in course of payment during the year ending on the 31st
March, 1931, for the salaries and expenses of the Ministry of Agriculture
(15 and 16 Geo. V, c. 3, s. 4 (N.I.);
16 Geo. V., c. 4 (N.I.)." (Note-
£20,000 has been voted on account).
The MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE
(Sir Edward Archdale): The presentation
of the Estimates affords a suitable opportunity for reviewing the activities of my
Ministry during the past year and also the
position of the agricultural industry
generally. No one regrets more than I
do that the past season was not a prosperous one for agriculture. The outstanding features of a depressing nature
were the low prices for potatoes, oats and
flax. The depression in the potato market is due in the main to two causes.
First, the fact that during the past 30
years the acreage under this crop in the
United Kingdom has remained more or
less constant, whilst the yield has increased 50 per cent. In Northern Ireland
the yield in 1900 was 3.7 and in 1929
7.4 tons. Therefore, being a bumper
crop in 1929 in England, Scotland and
Northern Ireland the result is a glutted
market. The second cause I have recently referred to, namely, a change in
fashion or taste and a consequential drop
in consumption.
The future of flax production is
problematical. As far as Northern Ireland is concerned it is a question of price,
and as long as prices to the farmer remain
round the present level, I think it is unlikely that we shall see any substantial
increase in the present acreage.
A glutted wheat market aggravated to
some extent by importations from the
Continent is mainly responsible for the
poor price of oats. At the present
moment there exists in the granaries of
the United States, Canada and England
the equivalent of the whole of the United
States and Canadian wheat crop for 1929,
and the 1930 harvest is merely a matter
of five months ahead. It is this fact more
than any other which has caused a very
heavy fall in the price of all cereals. As
far as Northern Ireland is concerned it
has its advantages as well as its disadvantages. The price of all purchased
feeding stuffs such as maize and the
various cakes and meals have fallen to
almost pre-war level.
Farmers all over the world have been
hit heavily by these economic disturbances
and the agricultural depression may truly
be said to have been world wide. Bad
though times have been it is some consolation to know that our farmers in Northern Ireland have not been so heavily
hit as their colleagues in England and
Scotland or, for that matter, the Continent, and the New World generally.
What has eased the burden so far as we
are concerned is the diversity of our
agriculture. Fortunately, with the exception of few relatively small areas,
our farmers do not depend upon the sale
of crops for the major part of their in-
Over 78 per cent. of our agricultural output takes the form of stock
and stock products, and for some time we
have felt that along that line lies the hope
for British agriculture. We have, therefore, bent and will continue to bend, in
spite of uninformed criticisms, all our activities along the direction of improving
our stock and our stock products, and developing our natural markets for such
goods in Great Britain.
come.
It should be the policy of all North of
Ireland farmers to concentrate on the livestock side and to market as far as is practicable all their crop products through the
medium of the animal. I am happy to
be able to record that the wisdom of this
policy is being recognised generally in
Northern Ireland. The recent slump in
the price of cereals has had the effect cf
accelerating this movement and farmers are taking to heart the advice to
trust to stock and stock products for the
salvation of their industry. During the
present season the quantity of oats sold off
Northern Ireland farms has been relatively
small. They have been fed to stock, and
when the returns are available I shall be
surprised if a substantial decrease is not
shown in the quantities of imported feeding stuffs purchased by our farmers.
May I emphasise the importance of the
livestock side of the industry by quoting
to you the figures based on an average of
three years (1925-1928) of the value of all
our crops and livestock products.
Mr. COLLINS: Sold?
Sir EDWARD ARCHDALE: No, the
output. The total value of output of all
crops was £3,200,000, and the total value
of output of all livestock and livestock
products £10,800,000. The values of our
Supply-
Committee
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Sir Edward Archdale]
poultry produce, cattle and beef and dairy
produce each exceed the total value of
all our crop output.
We hear to-day a great deal about the
depression in agriculture, but there is
another side to the picture, and it is quite
a rosy one. The prices which North of
Ireland farmers are receiving for store
cattle are better than they have been since
the immediate post-war period, and prices
for pigs to-day are such as to make pork
production a most profitable investment
and justify me in repeating the advice to
farmers which has been constantly given
by my Ministry to keep in pigs all the
time and to forsake once and for all the
mistaken policy of trying to jump in and
out of the pork market.
In
Sheep is another item in our balance
sheet of which we have no reason to complain. Ever since the war prices have
been good and they are still good. Moreover, Northern Ireland is the only part
in the United Kingdom which shows a
big increase in its sheep population.
1921 we had 400,000 sheep in Northern
Ireland, and in 1929 we had 654,000.
The sheep population in Great Britain
has increased since 1922 by only 17 per
cent., whereas ours has increased by almost 50 per cent. Add to this the fact
that prices throughout have been of a remunerative nature and you will see not
only the justification of the Ministry's
policy but the measure of its success. I
am glad to be able to report to the House
that the Ministry's scheme for the improvement of our sheep population is
meeting with success and its merits are
appreciated.
During the season 1929-30, 397 rams
have been standing under the Ministry's
scheme in our mountain and lowland districts. Their number has grown from 22
in 1921-22 and no interested person can
fail to see the steady improvement which
is taking place in our sheep population.
No review of the agricultural industry
would be complete without a reference to
poultry which bids fair to being the
largest single item of value in our agricultural output. I am not exaggerating
when I say that the year 1929 was the best
year that has yet been experienced in the
egg trade, and that thanks to our improved methods of marketing, due to the
Marketing of Eggs Act, we succeeded
throughout the whole of the year in securing the highest price paid for eggs imported into Great Britain. I may be told
that there has been a slump in prices recently. While that is true, it is due
mainly to the industrial and agricultural
depression in Germany and the temporary
deflection of Danish supplies from the
German to the English market. Here I
should like to refer to the immense help
which the poultry industry is receiving
from our research and experimental work.
The Committee will recollect that the Empire Marketing Board recently paid us the
tribute of establishing at Hillsborough an
Empire centre for poultry nutrition, and
I will now mention briefly a few of the
results which have been achieved at this
station in the short period of two years.
(1) Everybody interested in poultry
keeping is aware that heavy losses are experienced each year in rearing chickens.
Our research officers have now shown that
these losses are very largely a matter of
feeding and that they can be reduced
from 20 per cent. to 5 per cent. by the
simple addition of separated milk to the
normal farm ration.
(2) As a result of their experiments
these officers have also shown that it is
possible, by simple adjustments in the
ration, to raise the egg production of a
large proportion of the pullets in the
country to a figure as large as that obtained from the birds in the Stormont
laying trials, which represent the picked
birds in the whole country. Approximately 650 day-old white wyandotte chicks
were recently purchased by the Station
from eight breeders. The chicks were
reared at Hillsborough and from these
birds 260 pullets were drawn and fed
for egg production for a period of one year.
The remarkable egg average of 194 eggs
per annum over the whole flock of 260 was
obtained. 120 eggs per bird is
timated as being an average over our Six
County area. If we
could raise our
average to 194 eggs per bird, at 1s. per
dozen, it would mean an increased poultry
revenue of £1,133,000, which would pay
for a considerable amount of research.
es-
(3) Turning now to the third problem,
namely, that of the surplus cockerel, it
has been felt for a long time that if a
profitable method of disposing of surplus
cockerels of dual purpose breeds could be
found it would be of immense assistance
to poultry breeders and would add very
considerably to cur poultry income. Our
research workers claim to have found the
solution of this problem, which lies in the
Supply-
Committee
3 APRIL 1930
better utilisation of materials which are
often wasted on our farms.
All surplus
white wyandotte cockerels hatched during
the months of January and February at
the Hillsborough Station have during the
past two years been disposed of to wholesale and not retail merchants when 12-13
weeks old, at 5s 3d to 5s 6d a head,
leaving the handsome profit of 2s per bird.
Any one of the results I have mentioned
will amply repay all the money we have
ever spent on poultry research. Suffice it
to say that these are the sort of practical
problems which are being attacked successfully by our research officers, and information such as I have given as to the results of their investigations is now being
disseminated as rapidly as possible through
the medium of our poultry instructresses.
Before leaving this subject I should like
to refer to the rapid development which
is taking place in the industry. The funds
which were recently put at the disposal of
my Ministry have enabled us to increase
our poultry stations from 570 in 1928 to
983 in 1930, and it is interesting to study
the effect on the industry of the Ministry's
activities. This year, in spite of the fact
that the egg stations have increased from
570 to almost 1,000, it has been almost
impossible to meet the demand for hatching eggs, and before the end of January
many of our stations were unable to accept
further orders.
The research station at Hillsborough recently offered to supply a limited number
of sittings at from 7s 6d to 10s per sitting.
Within 24 hours the whole supply to the
end of the season was booked up. Everyone wanted the 10s sittings, and no one
would take the 7s 6d sittings until they
were convinced that there was no chance of
securing the 10s sittings.
Mr. COLLINS: Why did you not have
12s 6d sittings?
Sir EDWARD ARCHDALE: We
could, I believe, have got 12s 6d or 15s a
sitting if we had known there was going
to be such a demand. We certainly were
astonished, and I am sure the Committee
will be astonished, at the increase in
poultry equipment. We got particulars
from one town merchant and one country
merchant. The town merchant sold, in
1928-29, 241 incubators, and this year
473. The country merchant sold, in
1928-29, 230 incubators, and this year
450. We also went to a man who sold
Hoovers-I suppose hon. Members know
what they are-and his sales last year
were 176, and for the present year 263.
Such figures are an excellent demonstration of the remarkable development which
is taking place.
I do not propose to weary the Committee with further statistics. I wish
however, to point out that during the past
four years the poultry population has increased from 6 to 8 millions. The value
of the industry in 1929 was no less than
£3,569,000 and exceeded the value of the
gross output of our shipbuilding yards in
1924. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear).
This is a record with which we are frankly
pleased and it is more than an ample
justification of the policy we have pursued. I am absolutely convinced that it
is returning far more than a tenfold increase to the country of the money
expended.
When introducing the Estimates of my
Ministry for the past financial year I
dealt very fully with the cattle industry
and I do not intend to take up time in
recapitulating the facts then presented.
I should like, however, to refer to the
much debated problem of milk versus
beef. Some farmers have criticised my
Ministry for giving any encouragement to
the production of beef and seem to pin
their faith on the development of milkproducing animals and to ignore altogether
the suitability of their progeny for beef
purposes. Advocates of such a policy
overlook the fact that our beef and store
cattle trade is on the average of the four
years 1925 to 1928 worth £2,600,000, almost equal to our production of milk and
butter, which was worth £2,800,000.
The Ministry has always held the view
that it is a dual purpose cow which is of
the most service to Northern Ireland and
that both these trades must be preserved.
Considerable criticism of my Ministry
has recently been made in this Committee
and elsewhere regarding the decline which
has taken place since 1921 in the exports
of butter through Northern Ireland ports.
Those who contend that this decline in
the quantity of butter passing through
our ports reflects the reduction in the output from our creameries ignore completely
the great increase which has undoubtedly
occurred in the consumption of Northern
Ireland creamery butter within the Six
County area. I have had abstracted
from the accounts of forty-five co-operative
creameries the quantity of butter made by
Supply-
Committee
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Sir Edward Archdale]
them in each of the past eight years from
1921 to 1928. These are the figures:

47,555 cwt.

50,764


47,935

""

""
Far from these figures showing the decline
in our butter industry which
hon. Members opposite claim to have
taken place, it is apparent that our creamery output has been well maintained.
According to the Census of Production
taken by the Board of Trade in 1924 the
output of butter from creameries in
Northern Ireland amounted to 55,600
cwt., so that the sample of forty-five
creameries upon which the above particulars are based may be taken to cover
over 70 per cent. of the total output.
It is our settled policy to raise cows
which will produce an average of 800
gallons of milk and at the same time a
calf which will make a first-class store or
can be converted into baby beef at 14 to
16 months' old. This can and is being
done, and thanks to the pioneer work of
our Research Departments many of our
milk recording societies and an increasing
number of our farmers are concentrating
successfully on this policy. We have in
this Ministry followed closely the trend of
the world cattle position, and it was because we were certain that the future lay
with the animal and animal product side
of the industry that we have striven
steadily on towards our goal of improving
our cattle and our animal products until
we reach the pinnacle of quality, knowing
full well that we will be rewarded amply.
Prophets may have no honour in their
own country, but many of you may have
read what is really a vindication of our
policy in the article on the world's live.
stock position which recently appeared in
the "Times." Hitherto we have been
prone to consider the United States as
producing the whole of its food supply.
That is no longer so, and it is now realised
generally in the States that that country
has definitely entered the category of beef
importing countries and must continue in
future to look abroad for increasing proportions of her beef supplies. Already
she has drained Canada to such an extent
that the Canadian cattle population has
declined. Unable to satisfy her requirements from Canada, she is drawing
heavily upon the surplus beef production
of New Zealand, and has at last been
forced to turn to the Argentine and satisfy
her requirements by the importation of
canned beef. All the signs are, therefore,
very definitely in favour of relatively
higher prices for cattle. It has not the
appearance of a temporary boom-there
may be ups
and downs-but I am satisfied
that the future of cattle prices is well
assured, and I would ask these who represent agricultural divisions to assist the
Ministry in urging their constituents to
press forward with the policy of feeding
our crops to stock and thus marketing
them as stock and stock products.
Such
a policy means more and not less tillage,
and I am confident that it will bring to
Ulster many years of agricultural prosperity.
I would now like to make just a few
remarks on the various items in Vote 1.
There is really very little change. Salaries
and wages show an increase of £1,783, due
mainly to the normal increments. In the
headquarters division the Committee will
notice that an assistant secretary replaces
for the time being one principal officer
and one assistant principal. There is, in
consequence, a saving of £456 on that
Estimate. If the Committee turn to the
Accounts and Establishment Branch they
will see that owing to the increase of the
financial work of the Ministry, due chiefly
to the extension of the loan schemes, it
has been necessary to appoint a superintending officer to take charge of the
branch. As indicated in a footnote to
the Estimate it is intended as soon as possible to effect a reduction in the executive
staff of the branch. There has been no
increase at all in the total staff, notwithstanding the fact that recent and imminent legislation with regard to the
marketing of eggs, butter, and fruit has
added very considerably to the work of
the administrative staff. With regard to
the collection of agricultural statistics,
the Committee will notice on page 125 of
the Estimates that £1,275 has been added
to that to meet the cost of the Census of
Production which has to be taken in 1930
and 1931. I beg to move.
Mr. HEALY: From whatever side of
the Committee criticism is going to be
offered to the Minister of Agriculture on

we should like to congratulate him on his

health and vigour to-day. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear). There have been

The Minister in his speech-and I am
glad to support him-mentioned that store
cattle trade is our most important trade.
While he is not neglecting the milk and
butter trade he is all out to improve store
cattle. I think that is going to be one
of our mainstays in the future.
There is another thing in the Estimate
I would like to ask about. The average
number of potatoes exported in the last
three years was 215,000 tons a year. I do
not know what we exported during last
season, but I would like to ask the Minister if proper steps are taken to ensure
that when there is a reduction in the quantity of potatoes exported, a corresponding
reduction is made in the inspectors employed. I have heard criticisms on this
matter outside. I may be wrong in saying there are too many inspectors, but I
think when our exports fall, a corresponding reduction should be made in the inspectors' staff and so save money.
The Minister referred to the increase in
the staff of two assistant secretaries. He
has explained, I understand, that this
is partly a temporary measure and that
the Department is being reorganised. I
think he should have support in this
matter. As regards the coming season,
now that the farmers are putting in their
crops, I think the way we should look at
the whole thing is to turn our back on the
past, which has not been good, and look
forward to a better season in 1930-31.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear).

The Minister has told us that the bad

to some extent the Ministry themselves

They now find there is no market for

people in Great Britain. In my judgment that is due to the class of potatoes
we have been sending across the water.
We consume the finer class of potatoes ourselves. There is no doubt about it, the
people in Northern Ireland who consume
potatoes do not consume the class of potatoes they ask the English people to eat.
I am not at all surprised the English
people have refused to eat them. That,
I believe, is the premier cause of the decline in the consumption of our potatoes
in England. Until the farmers produce
the class of potatoes we eat ourselves there
will be no market for Northern Ireland
potatoes. If we send the right kind of
potatoes there will yet be a large market
for our potatoes in England.

That is not what I said. I said the outstanding features of the depression in
agriculture were the low prices for potatoes, flax, and oats. No one can deny that
we have had very low prices for these three
commodities. There will most likely be a
reduction in the acreage planted this
year, and therefore there is a chance of
a little better price being obtained. It is
most depressing to know that when you
have a good crop you nearly always have
a bad price. A big crop means overproduction, and the result is a bad price.
The hon. Member also suggested that
the land should be used to fatten livestock, but what the Ministry want is that
farmers, instead of selling their oats and
potatoes at an impossible price, should
feed their livestock with it and make
money out of their cattle, for which they
get a very good price. The hon. Member
went on to refer to the number of inspectors in the Ministry. We have reduced the number of temporary inspectors
by twelve owing to the reduced quantity
of potatoes that is being sent out of the
country. It is a curious thing that although we had such a bad demand for
potatoes this year, during the past five
months 46,500 tons have been exported.
In March-last month-11,000 tons were
exported; in February, 5,600 tons; in
January, 10,600 tons; in December,
11,000 tons, and in November, 8,300
tons. We do our best to induce the
farmers to export potatoes that will be
eaten in England. We took the trouble
to send men to the recent Birmingham
Exhibition with potatoes, and we not only
took prizes but we took all the prizes
against the potato growers of England and
Scotland. Our men at the exhibition
sold stone bags of potatoes so that the

While it is very easy for the hon.

Mr. BEATTIE: I want to draw the
attention of the House to the conduct of
the Minister of Labour (Mr. Andrews) on
Tuesday of this week and to-day by his
action in what I call treating the House
with contempt. The Minister of Labour
can show no justification for the contempt
into which he has brought this House.
There is not a Minister on the Front
Bench who has treated the House with
such contempt at the Minister of Labour
has with regard to the questions which
appeared on the Order Paper to be
answered on Tuesday and to-day. I have
gone fully into the position which he
occupies. I have made certain concessions
in regard to staff and in regard to the
conditions pertaining to his Ministry. I
have made allowances, but I find that,
with all those allowances, there is
ample staff at his command to get
the information for which I asked in my
question. But he has refused to do it.
and I will give you the reasons why he has
refused to do it.
He has at his command at headquarters a number of Parliamentary
Secretaries, permanent secretaries, assistant secretaries, principals, private secretaries, and so on, and the total cost of
these gentlemen is £8,095. Let me tell
the House that the administration of
this Ministry, according to the insured
population of Northern Ireland, is costing double what it is costing in Great
Britain according to the heads of insured
population there. As far as our cost is
concerned, are paying very high
salaries and fees to the headquarters staff
of this Ministry for carrying out duties
which I claim should be carried out
efficiently and well. When a question
is sent from this side or from that side
of this House they should be able to get
the information asked for and to give
the answers in accordance with Parliamentary procedure. But we have been ignored. It is my intention, and I take
this opportunity of telling the Minister,
to ask this question every week.

The PARLIAMENTARY

CATION (Mr. Robb): This Estimate will

of Education the sums required amount to
£1,989,126, nearly £2,000,000. That is
an increase of £27,532 on the Vote last
year. The increase arises practically and
entirely on two items in Vote 2, and I
do not deal with them at the moment.
I just want to say one or two general
words about the administration of the service of education during the past year. We
find this fact that all the education
authorities within the Six Counties are
already levying a rate of 1s. and over, the
highest of the rates being 1s 6d in the
£. As the Exchequer contributes only
the first shilling of the education rate it
will be seen that in a great many of the
areas heavy charges are falling upon the
ratepayers. The ratepayers having that
charge laid upon them are and we know
In this particular Vote the increases are
quite small and they are due entirely to
normal increases of salary given to
officers of the Ministry, and to the fact
that the bonus payable to civil servants
generally has risen during the past year
owing to the rise in the cost of living
figure. We have had during the year
a maintenance of the figure for good attendance at school. We are gratified to
know that the figure has risen ever since
the 1923 Act came into operation, and although it is not as high as we would like
or as high as in England and Wales, still
it is much more than what was in vogue
before this Ministry was established.
Medical inspection has been in operation during the past year in all but two
of the regions, and I am glad to say in
one of those two, since the present year
has begun, applications have been invited
for a medical officer and nurse. In Belfast there has been a development of the
effort to feed hungry school children, and
in Belfast we have had during the year
an alteration of the system. The Belfast
authority now provides a free mid-day
meal for five days of the week during the
whole of the year, except on bank holidays
and for one fortnight during the summer,
when the staff is given a holiday and when
the premises are overhauled.
The year has shown a remarkable increase in the number of pupils attending
secondary schools. The number for which
we have had to provide has gone up by
1,000. That comes on on Vote 2. On
Vote 1, I would like to explain two
things. Hon. Members have asked me
what is in the registry that appears on
page 112.
They asked what does it do
and what are these men paid for. Each
Ministry has a registry. Although I am.
not speaking for other Ministries I suppose
it is much the same with them. What the
registry does in our Ministry is it receives
the correspondence that comes to the
Ministry. It distributes it amongst the
various departments. It also keeps a register of the letters that go out from the
Ministry, and, most important of all, in
the registry are kept an enormous number
of files. It is the duty of the men in
charge of the registry to put their hand
Supply-
Committee
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Robb]
file at any moment.
on any
Without such
a system and such a department it would
be almost impossible to deal with matters
that come into the registry when you
recognise the fact that we have got 2,000
elementary schools, 75 secondary schools
and about 40 or 50 technical schools.
Questions are constantly arising on any
number of different subjects with regard to
education. It will be seen, therefore, it
is necessary to have some plan where you
can at any moment get the papers touching any subject without any delay. That
is the work of the registry.
Other hon. Members have asked me regarding a question of administration.
They want to know how our postage is
calculated. We do not, as you know,
stamp our letters. I have been asked
more than once how much we ought to be
charged, and what rate are we charged.
With regard to telegrams, telephone service, and registered letters, there is a record of that by the Post Office and we pay
on that.
With regard to the ordinary
correspondence of the Ministry, the way in
which it is worked is this once in every
quarter the Post Office sends in an official
who takes a census of the letters that go
out from our Ministry. We do not know
when they are coming. They come haphazard, and in each quarter they
take the number of letters that go out from
us, and we are charged on thirteen times
that in the quarter. It is a rough and
ready estimate, but the difference between
the estimate so arrived at and the actual
figures probably is so small that it is not
worth anybody's while doing anything
else. I beg to move.

Some people seem to think that we are
spending too much money on education.
I, for one, have always argued in this
Committee while being in favour of
economy-that, as far as this Province of
ours is concerned, the best investment we
could make is to invest our money in a
good sound educational service. Education lies at the root of our whole life.
We want to have the best educational
system that it is possible to get, and, believe me, you cannot get a good educational system unless you are prepared to
spend money.
Just the other day I was
looking over some statistics with regard
Supply-
Committee
S APRIL 1930
to & Dominion that has a population much
the same as our own-I am referring to
New Zealand-and I discovered that,
while our expenditure on education
amounted to two million odd poundsthat is for primary, secondary, technical,
and university education-in New Zealand
the amount spent on the same branches
reached £3,700,000. As a matter of fact,
in New Zealand there is about £500,000
more spent on primary education than we
spend on the whole of our educational services in Northern Ireland.
But it is not so much a question of the
money we spend as of the value we get for
it. It is not a wise thing for us to sit here
always and to throw bouquets at ourselves.
We ought to look the situation over from
time to time and see whether there are
any improvements we can make. We are
living in an age when you must either go
forward or go back, and that applies to
education as much as it does to any other
sphere of life. I want to ask the Parliamentary Secretary does he think we are
getting the fullest possible value for the
money we are spending. That would
open up a very wide subject and I am
not going to keep the Committee by dealing with it now. In fact it might even
take longer than my hon. Friend's narration of figures, and I am sure would be
much more uninteresting.
But I do think we ought to ask ourselves whether our system is the very best
that can be had. Personally I hold a very
strong view that we are trying to cover
too much, especially in our elementary
schools, that inside the small period from
six years to fourteen years we are trying
to get the pupils of that age to do something which it is quite impossible for a
brain of that age to do. Take the curriculum to-day and see how wide it is, see
how many subjects are brought in, and
they seem to be increasing day by day.
I suggest seriously to the Parliamentary
Secretary that he and his Ministry-and
he has the wisest and most experienced officials that any Education Secretary could possibly, have-should sit down
quietly some day and ask themselves if
the time has not come when there should
be a revision of the whole curriculum of
our elementary schools. I know you find
people asking you to give them a bias towards technical instruction, to give them
a bias towards agriculture, to give them a
bias in this direction or in that direction,
but what you really want to do, as far
as our elementary schools are concerned,
is to see that there is a sound foundation
laid. If you get a sound foundation,
then, undoubtedly, you can build on that
foundation in whatever direction you want
to afterwards. But I do say--and I know
that in this I would be cordially endorsed
by the heads of technical and secondary
schools that the pupils that come to them
from the primary schools are asked to do
so much that they really have not grasped
the great fundamentals on which education must be based. I do think the
Department ought to look into this thing,
and, if necessary, have a full investigation,
in order to see whether they cannot get
a system that will lay a far better foundation than is being laid at present.
Do not let anyone in this Committee or
elsewhere for a moment imagine that inside the eight years that are allowed for
primary education you are going to make
a university graduate. You cannot do it.
But do lay the foundation soundly, and
then those who want to go on to secondary,
technical, or university education will
have no barriers in the way. My hon.
Friend the Member for Woodvale (Mr.
Nixon) will realise that under the Education Act a great improvement has taken
place, and there is now no bright boy or
girl in Northern Ireland, who has sufficient brains and energy to go on, who cannot rise from the very bottom to the top
rung of the education ladder. That is
what every Member of this Committee
wants to help forward. The question is
how are we to do it. I just want to join
in congratulating the Ministry on their
work for the year. In Vote 2 there are
other matters that one may want to raise
later, but in the meantime the Minister
has the sympathy of every Member of this
Committee, and what is much more important even than having the sympathy
of the House of Commons is that he has
awakened sympathy throughout the
country where people are taking a much
larger interest in education than they have
ever done before. I am sure the Ministry
want to utilise that newly-found energy
and to turn it to good account, and not
only in this Committee but in the country
I am sure they will find sympathetic and
willing allies.

£18,000 less this year that it was last year.
Has this sum of £400,000 been done away
with, and if you are continuing to ask
local authorities to erect buildings for
which you are justified in giving grants
why are you not giving as much as last
year?
Mr. ROBB: To take the last point first,
we are only drawing £10,740 from the
£400,000 because that is all that is needed
to complete the buildings that are in course
of completion. The buildings will be completed and formally opened on the 1st of
May, and we only draw that amount because that is all we have to spend.
With regard to the question of teachers'
residences, that is a liability that we inherited from the old Commissioners of
National Education. There were some
200 teachers' residences in respect of which
advances had been made from public funds
and in respect of which the Commissioners
had undertaken to pay half the annuities.
That liability was handed over to us on
our establishment. The sum mentioned
this year is £950, as compared with £1,000
last year.
I think the hon. Member (Sir
Robert Lynn) wanted to know do we retain any control over these teachers' residences after the loans are paid off. Is
that it?
Sir ROBERT LYNN: Yes.
Mr. ROBB: Frankly, I do not know,
but I will inquire. With regard to the
model schools, under the Section of the
1923 Act all these model schools were to be
transferred to the local authorities.
Sir ROBERT LYNN: May be.
Mr. ROBB: As a matter of fact they
all have been transferred to the local
authorities and the amount which appears
here is only a continuing liability on our

in model schools, who continued to be employed, and who were paid certain grants
by the old Commissioners. The liability
still rests upon our Ministry to pay the
grants. They are diminishing from year
to year as the teachers resign, die, or
otherwise disappear. The hon. Member
for Woodvale (Mr. Nixon) has again
raised the question of extern degrees.
Frankly I do not know exactly what facilities do exist in Queen's University for
persons who are in employment during the
morning and afternoon to obtain degrees.
I am convinced that there are facilities,
but I do not know exactly what they are.
But if the hon. Member asks this Ministry
and the Government to force upon Queen's
University a system of granting extern degrees to students who do not attend lectures in the University then I will tell
him frankly that I will oppose it.
Mr. NIXON: If you will arrange the
lectures, or get them arranged, to suit the
people who have to work during the day
that will meet the situation quite well.
Mr. ROBB: I believe there are facilities, but what they are I do not know.
They may not suit the conditions of the
hon. Member's friends. I cannot help
that.
Mr. NIXON: They are not my friends.
I do not think that is a fair observation
to make.
The CHAIRMAN: In this case it is the
ordinary use of the word "friends," meaning people in whom the hon. Member is
interested, and not necessarily relatives.
Mr. NIXON: If he means everybody

right. I hope they regard themselves as

have no control.

HOUSE OF COMMONS.

Wednesday, 9th April, 1930.
The House met at Three of the Clock,
Mr. SPEAKER in the Chair.
Mater Infirmorum Hospital Incorporated (Extension) Bill.
The Chairman of Ways and Means reported from the Joint Opposed Committee
on the Mater Infirmorum Hospital Incorporated (Extension) Bill as follows:
That they had considered the said Bill and
examined the allegations thereof, which
were found to be true, and that the Committee had gone through the Bill and
