A Breach of Privilege.
Mr. BEATTIE: I have to report to
the House from the Committee of Privileges, which met this morning, as
follows:-
The Committee have investigated the
matter to them referred, and have decided
that the passage complained of in the leading article in the "Northern Whig and
Belfast Post" of the 3rd day of this instant
April, which passage was:
"Everything had been beautifully arranged. The Parliamentary Committee, as usual, had been complacent, and
had taken the simple course of refusing
to hear the other side."
constitutes a breach of the privileges of
this House.
Major SHILLINGTON: I raised this
question on Thursday last as Chairman of
the Committee referred to, and as I am
sure the House will agree with the report
given by the Committee of Privileges, I
beg to move the following Resolution:
"That the passage in the leading article.
in the 'Northern Whig and Belfast Post'
constitutes a breach of the Privileges of
this House."
Lieut.-Colonel GORDON: I beg formally to second that Motion.
Mr. NIXON: I hope I am entitled to
speak on this Resolution and to oppose
it. I came here to do that without any
consideration or preparation. I did not
know it would be arranged for to-day. In
the first instance it is nice to pay a tribute
to an hon. Member behind his back and
the hon. Member for Clifton (Major
Hall-Thompson) is not present. There is
no more honourable Member than he in
this House or elsewhere. I can say the
same thing about the hon. Member for
Falls, and I dare say the same thing about
the Chairman who was supposed to be attacked in this leader. But why are hon.
Members so thin in the skin, or is there
going to be no liberty here for the Press
at all? If I was to go into the courts
every time I am aggrieved by the Press
I would never be out of them. But I have
not sufficient money to go there
every time
I have a grievance against the Press.
I think the House is only lowering itself
by taking any notice of the article at all.
I do not mean that in any manner reflecting upon the particular paper concerned.
As a matter of fact it is practically the only
paper at the present time that gives both
sides of any question. I wonder is this
an attempt to suppress it altogether. I
wonder that some hon. Members are so
timid about their honour-Gentlemen who
in this House have voted against their own
Amendment. I never saw the like of it
done in any dark corner of the City of
Belfast. A man who is capable of voting
against his own Amendment after speaking
to it has, I think, nothing to complain
about when he is criticised.
I think this is about the last lap of the
freedom of the Press in Northern Ireland.
The "Northern Whig" may have gone a
little too far. I am not saying it did not.
But why should such a subject be taken up
and paraded before the world. Honour!
Honour! We are all honourable Members
when we are here. I do not know whether
we are all honourable outside the
House. (Hon. Members: Order). I
would like to know who said "Order."
As one of the Members of this House so
far as I know I have never broken my
word if I could help it. (Laughter).
Now that the laughing has subsided, hon.
Members who are laughing broke their
oath in the Covenant.
Mr. SPEAKER: I think if the hon.
Member proceeds on those lines I shall ask
him to resume his seat, as he has no right
whatever to attack the honour of this
House. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear).

Mr. NIXON: I bow to your ruling,

in connection with the Imperial Parliament. It may have occurred. I am not

I do not know if I would be in order.
Perhaps I would not. If I am not you
I will rule me out at once. Recently a

I think the House is going too far in

The PRIME MINISTER: I suggest
to the House that the wishes of every
Member here would be fully carried out if
this Resolution was passed without further
discussion. I think that the hon. Member who has just spoken really misses the
point, the point being that one of the
papers in our midst reflected not upon the

Members as Members of this House, but
upon a committee, a semi-judicial committee set up, not by the Government, but
by this House in order to deal with a very
important matter. The House is jealous
and should be jealous of any attack being
made upon it of that sort. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear.) Every hon.
Member is quite prepared to stand the

acting on behalf of this House.
Mr. DEVLIN: I have never heard
anything of this before, and I would like

what precisely is the language used in the

The PRIME MINISTER: Knowing,
therefore, the power that rests in your
hand, and every Member being
thoroughly familiar with it, I think myself personally that under all the circumstances we need not proceed further with
the matter. I think that would meet the
wishes of my hon. Friends behind me.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) Notice has
been taken of the matter, the Committee
have dealt with it, the Committee have
been unanimous in their finding, and this
House should also be unanimous in backing up the independent Committee that
decided accordingly.

Education Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.
Motion made and Question proposed:
"That the Bill be now read a Second
time."
The
PARLIAMENTARY SECRE-
TARY OF THE MINISTRY OF
EDUCATION (Mr. Robb): In asking
the House once again to consider a Bill
dealing with education I am conscious
that I am inviting it to enter into a field
of discussion covering a very difficult and
controversial subject, and I must beg for
its patience and indulgence while I endeavour to explain as briefly and clearly
as I can the exact purport of the Measure
now put forward for Second reading. I
do not propose to dwell at any length
upon the policy and basis of the Education Act of 1923, for that policy and that
basis are little altered by this Measure,
and what we now aim at doing is not to
strike out in any new direction, but to
Education Bill-
Second Reading
9 APRIL 1930
complete as far as we can and to give
better effect to the principles of administration of education embodied in the Act.
It is now almost seven years since the
Act passed into law, and when one considers the magnitude of the reforms introduced by it and the variety of subjects, many of which were quite new to
our educational experience, with which
it dealt, it is not surprising that lapse of
time and acquired practical experience
have revealed some defects in its working.
The Act contained no fewer than 111 sections, but the Bill I am putting forward
to-day leaves 96 of these absolutely unchanged and untouched, and in several of
those sections which we propose to amend
the alterations are of a trifling character.
Our Bill contains 30 Clauses, and I am
confident in declaring that more than
two-thirds of these will meet with general
approval from all quarters of the House.
There are only half-a-dozen Clauses
which may give rise to much controversy,
and even in regard to those I trust that
hon. Members will recognise that in
dealing with the various proposals put
forward by the Protestant Churches on
the one hand, and some representatives
of Education Authorities on the other,
the framers of the Bill have done their
best to steer an even keel, and above all
to take no step which might be prejudicial
to the interests of education. In the
preparation of many of the Clauses most
useful representations have been made to
the Minister of Education by the Education Authorities, teachers, school managers, and others, and I desire to offer to
all those who have tendered advice, the
warm appreciation and thanks of the
Minister and of the Government.
I should like to make it clear at this
stage that the Ministry is quite assured
that the general results of the policy of
giving the people themselves, through the
County Councils and Education Committees, a responsible share in educational
administration are in the highest degree
satisfactory. All over the Province the
new Authorities have shown great zeal
in providing new buildings of the most
modern kind, and in repairing and renovating many of the old school buildings
that have been transferred to them.
They have dealt generously in providing
scholarships for promising pupils of every
class and creed, and have in many cases
given substantial assistance to secondary
education.
Their long-established interest in the
welfare of technical education has been
intensified by the widening of their
powers, and they have effected a most
gratifying improvement in regularity of
school attendance. In varying degrees
they have shown interest in medical inspection of school pupils, and they have
already done much for afflicted children
whose education hitherto has been sadly
neglected in many parts of the country.
One of the Clauses in this Bill, which enables the Ministry to provide a central
school for mentally defective children,
and which, I feel sure, will receive the
warm approval of the House, will give
the Education Authorities the means of
further assisting the education and training of these unfortunate young people,
and I sincerely hope that all
Authorities will join heartily in
operating with the Ministry in sending
the mentally defective children in their
areas to the proposed new central institution.
the
co-
In addition to the good work which has
been done by the Committees the Ministry is most gratified to find that a great
increase in local interest in education has
been the result of the establishment of
the Education Authorities. I am sure
we are all sensible-sometimes perhaps
some of us too sensible-that on the platform, in the Press, and in the ordinary
discussions of daily life, educational
topics occupy a much larger space than
ever before. This is one of the most
valuable fruits of the policy of the
Education Act.
With evidence such as this before us,
it is impossible to contemplate for a
moment any grave interference with or
vital amendment in the system of local
control that was established by the Act
of 1923. Why then are we proposing
any changes? The answer is because we
feel that our education system is not receiving its full measure of support from
certain classes, and we believe that by
alterations in the constitution and powers
of School Management Committees, the
representation of transferors of schools
on Education Committees, the greater
surety of undenominational Bible teaching in provided and transferred schools,
and by giving those locally interested in
the schools a greater share in the selection of the teachers, we shall secure a
fuller measure of co-operation from many
who are to some extent now holding
aloof. It may be that the fears of
Education Bill-
Second Reading
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Robb]
secularism and other evils in our educational system, that might spring up at
some future time, are groundless, but
these fears are genuinely held by many
worthy and well-meaning people, and we
think it would be wise and useful to remove them so far as it can be done without prejudicing the success of the system.
These fears arise in connection with
three principal features of the system
established under the Education Act.
These are the want of representation on
Regional and Borough Educational Committees for managers and others who
transferred their schools, the danger of
appointments of teachers being made
which would be out of harmony with local
feeling, and the belief that the position
of religious and Bible instruction in provided and transferred schools is not yet
secure.
The Bill is an honest and
moderate effort to meet these fears and
to devise a system which will give satisfaction to the interested parties without
injuring the efficiency of the schools.
It will be within the recollection of
many Members of the House that the
Education Act of 1923 when first presented to Parliament contained provision
for the appointment of five persons to be
nominated by the Minister of Education
on the Borough and Regional Committees
but that at the Report stage of the
Measure this provision was withdrawn and
an Amendment proposed by the Minister
himself, who felt that it was better, in the
first instance at least, to leave an unfettered choice of representatives to the
County and District Councils in whom
the power of appointment was vested.
The House assented, though somewhat
reluctantly, to the change, and I see two
hon. Members present here to-day who
raised their voices against the Government proposal.
It was generally expected that many
of the more active school managers would
find places on the Committees, but events.
have so turned out that in a great many
cases managers who have transferred
their schools, and who represent interests
which have been primarily responsible
for the promotion of elementary education during the greater part of the last
hundred years have not obtained that
position on the Education Committees
which their services to Education and
their special experience and knowledge of
its administration seemed justly to entitle them to, and which it was anticipated
they would obtain when the Act was
passing through the House. I am sure
hon. Gentlemen will feel sympathy for
them, and will not consider those persons
unreasonable who have raised their voices
in criticism of the Act on this account.
If the expectations of Ministers in 1923
were not realised in the actual working
of the Act, I do not see that we can now
be blamed by the Education Authorities
for trying to give effect to these expectations.
The Government has, therefore,
decided that it is desirable and reasonable
to amend the Act by arranging for an
element of representation on the Regional
and Borough Committees of the transferors of schools, and this is effected
in Clause 1 of the Bill. In the interpretation of the expression "transferors of schools "
is taken
power
to include, not only the actual
managers who held office at the date of
transfer, but patrons and trustees and
all those in whom authority over the
school management was vested. The
definition of transferors also covers the
case of new trustees appointed to replace
retiring members and the representatives
and successors of the former managers.
Before selecting the persons
to
be
nominated the Minister will take counsel
so far as this course may be practicable
with the transferors of schools.
In order that the introduction of members nominated by the Ministry on the
Committees may not be the cause of any
possible disagreement or friction it is proposed that the education authorities
should be consulted before the Ministry
decides on its nominees. It may be asked
why the Bill does not leave the nomination in the hands of the committees themselves, and this point has been carefully
considered. It is believed, however, that
in view of the fact that in many cases the
authorities did not appoint ex-school
managers on committees, and thereby a
certain amount of feeling has been engendered in some quarters, it is a wiser
and more expedient course to place these
appointments in the hands of the Minister
of Education.
If it be objected to the intrusion of nonelected members into bodies that have
the spending of public funds, I think it is
a sufficient reply to this criticism to point
out that the control of expenditure on
education from the rates is reserved by
Education Bill-
Second Reading
9 APRIL 1930
the Act to the education authority, that
is, the county council, and that as all
the financial proposals of the regional education committees must receive the approval of that body, it will not be possible
for a committee to be led into extravagance
through the zeal or recklessness of members not responsible to the ratepayers and
contrary to the wishes of the council
elected by the latter to watch their financial interests.
As to the proportion of the nominated
element on the committees I should like
to point out that the Bill requires the
Minister in determining the number of
persons to be nominated to have regard
to the number of transferred schools in
the area, so that where these schools are
few and transferors are consequently not
numerous, the addition of members to the
committee will be correspondingly small.
It will necessarily follow that any section
of the community that thinks it best to
refrain from transferring will not be able
the comto secure representation on
mittees through the medium of the nominated element.
The Government recognises that this is
a part of the Bill that may not altogether
commend itself to some of the education
authorities. It would, however, impress
on these objectors, if there are any such,
that a concession of this kind to parties
who feel strongly on the subject is bound
to conduce to a more harmonious feeling
in regard to the transfer of schools and to
the committees' work for education.
I now pass on to the next two Clauses,
2 and 3. which are among the most important in the Bill. In framing these
the Government has had more regard to
what it is feared may happen in the
future, rather than to meeting any defect in the existing state of things. The
Clauses prescribe the constitution and
functions of school management committees and lay down a procedure for the
appointment of teachers in provided and
transferred schools which, though it may
appear cumbersome and complicated in
the precise and somewhat elaborate
language in which it is of necessity set
forth in the Bill, is in reality a very
simple matter. But the point I wish to
emphasise is that this framework of constitution and functions and this procedure
for appointment, except in regard to the
duty of intervention imposed on the
Ministry in a certain eventuality, are
very much what have spontaneously grown
up in the practice of these matters in
many education committees. And this
practice, which the Ministry thinks is well
devised, it wishes to see secured for all
transferred schools and extended to all
provided schools, so that it may not be in
the power of any committee in the future,
that might have hostility or prejudice towards the working of the system, to upset
arrangements which make for the successful administration of education, in harmony alike with legitimate local feeling
and the reasonable claims of an authority
representing the ratepayers.
The general advantages we claim for
these proposals are the following:-
Firstly, the initiative in the appointment of teachers being secured for the
Management Committee, it will be impossible that a teacher can be forced on the
locality contrary to the view of that committee;
Secondly, as the Management Committee by its constitution under the Bill will
be representative in a preponderating degree of the former school managers and
the parents of the children, its actions
will be in harmony with the opinions of
those primarily interested in the school;
Thirdly, by giving the Management
Committee a more definite place in the
scheme, local interest in education will be
developed and intensified; and
Fourthly, by making the Management
Committee definitely subordinate to the
education authority the control and responsibility of the latter will remain unimpaired.
It has been suggested that in altering
the position of the teachers' representatives on these committees by taking from
them the right to vote, a slight has been
inflicted upon the teaching body. I desire to assure the House that this is not
the case. The change became necessary
when, in place of performing merely advisory functions, these committees have
imposed upon them the duty of choosing
teachers. It can hardly be questioned
that the right to appoint a teacher could
not well be granted to members of the
teaching profession themselves. Except
for the inability to vote there is no reason
why teachers should not continue to play
an important part in the work of the
committees.
While the Bill proposes that each provided and transferred school shall be under a school management committee, it is

expected that it will be found convenient

Clause 4 deals with the important
question of Bible teaching and enacts that
if such teaching is not being given in a
provided or transferred school the education authority may be required to provide.
it on the requisition of the parents of
not fewer than ten children who are in
regular attendance at the school. In this
matter due regard shall be had to parental
right and authority and no child whose
parents disapprove may be present at the

and other arrangements must be such that

directly or indirectly, from the other advantages which the school affords.
It
will be seen, therefore, that there can be
no possibility of any child being forced
to attend any Bible teaching to which exception is taken by its parents, and in
view of this fact I do not understand how
the existence of such teaching in the
school can be regarded as an offence or
a grievance.
In another Sub-clause protection is
afforded to the teacher against any liability to dismissal in case his efforts to give
the Bible instruction, when made in good
faith, are not completely satisfactory. I
feel it due to our teachers to say they have
never taken any exception to being required to give this Bible teaching, and
I have no doubt it will be given by them
with even greater zeal and efficiency than
has been shown anywhere in the past.
I would like to draw the particular attention of the House to the definition of
Bible instruction set forth in the Clause.
It will be seen that the choice of the
version of the Holy Scriptures on which
the instruction is based is left optional,
so that there can be no question of the
pupils being asked to submit to instruction
based on a version of the Bible which is
not acceptable to their parents. In drawing up this Clause the greatest care has
been taken to see that the requirement
does not interfere with the legitimate feelings of any section of the community.
By Clause 5 it is laid down that no
teacher can be compelled, as a condition
of appointment or holding office in a provided or transferred school, to teach any
catechism or religious formulary distinctive of any particular religious denomination. This does not of course prohibit
a teacher in such a school from joining in
the imparting of such instruction if he
volunteers to do so.

Members will recollect that under the

authority are divided into duties which
they have to perform and powers which

exercise of a power conferred upon it as

to compel the authority to do what was
right. The new Clause seeks to remedy
this and to give the Ministry the power
which Parliament evidently intended in
1923 and to enable the Ministry to exercise compulsion on an authority acting
contrary to the spirit of the Act of 1923.
Section 98 amply protected the education
authorities by enacting that no order of
the Ministry can be made under it unless
and until a public inquiry has been held,
and the position and views of the education authority fully and publicly stated.
With this protection education authorities can rest assured that no Ministry
could take action unless they were supported by public opinion.
There are two further Clauses to which
I should like to direct particular attention.
These are numbers 8 and 9 dealing with
voluntary schools. Clause 8 introduces

In Clause 9 we have endeavoured to

authority may make grants towards the

a grant from public funds should be

on which the education authority of the

the trustees who provide the balance of the

the Government are of opinion that the
management of the committee should be
permanent in such a case, and that to
place a school temporarily under a committee in order to secure a grant, and
then to revert to individual management
in the following year after the money has
been paid out, would be a serious abuse of
the system of grants.

By Clause 16 the procedure for enforcing school attendance is speeded up
by the omission of the warning notice,

Clauses 21 and 22, relating to afflicted

22 deals with the notification to the Ministry of Home Affairs of mentally defective

Clause 23 is a new Clause to be substituted for Section 68 of the 1923 Act,
which deals with the question of teachers'

Clause 24 gives the Ministry power to

We have also heard from the Prime
Minister and his Cabinet Colleagues the
assertion that the Government stands for
fair play and full equality, that the Protestants and the Catholics are treated exactly alike, and that the scales are held between them with even-handed justice.
This Amending Act, to remedy a glaring
defect in what the New Zealanders were
told was one of the masterpieces of educational reform, gives the lie to that
declaration. The result of it is
manifestation of gross unfairness on the
part of the Government for which, I am
glad to say, there is no parallel in any
part of the British Empire. The Government declares its intention to meet
every conscientious objection of the Protestant section of the community, and at
the same time to outrage the most sacred
conscientious convictions of the Catholic
community.
a
Does the right hon. Gentleman who is
at the head of the Government realise
that on the rolls of the public elementary
schools in Northern Ireland the children
of this minority which he proposes to
treat with contumely and contempt, form
a larger percentage of those receiving instruction than the children of any other
religious denomination ? Here are the
figures which supply, I think, a damning
indictment of the policy of religious intolerance which the present Bill proposes
to intensify. The Catholic children on
the rolls of the elementary schools number
36.1 per cent.; the Presbyterians represent 32.3 per cent.; the Episcopalians represent 25.9 per cent.; the Methodists,
3.3 per cent., and all the others 2.4 per
cent. The Catholic children attending
the schools in Northern Ireland number
7,593 more than the Presbyterians, and
almost 9,000 more than all the others
combined.
These figures bring into startling relief the monstrous wrong which you are
about to perpetrate, and, if it were in

the injustice cannot endure. It is interesting to observe the way in which a
complete change in one respect in this

leaders of some of the Churches suddenly

Mr. McNEILL: I rise for the purpose

Education authorities, under the preceding Act, had a power which was real
and substantial and not merely a simulacrum of power. They had power to appoint regional committees, and their choice
was in no way limited. They had power
Education Bill-
Second Reading
HOUSE OF COMMONS

to appoint the education committees to

of their former powers. Yet the Bill still
refers to the education authority as an
authority.
Now, there are many features of this
Bill to which I must utter a word of
protest. I object profoundly to the composition of the new Education Committees.
Those new Education Committees, by
reason of Sections 2 and 3 of this Bill,
are to be turned into parochial or congregational committees. In no way will
such committees represent the education
authorities. They will be merely Presbyterian Committees in many cases, or, if
they are not Presbyterian Committees,
they will be Church of Ireland Committees. Those committees, which have
superseded the old system of management,
have the power of choosing teachers.
They can appoint or nominate a select list
of three teachers, and out of that
select list the education authority
must, of necessity, select one. I
hold that that inflicts a great injustice
upon the teachers themselves, and it is a
reversal back to the old principles of
clerical management which prevailed before 1923. There is no answer to that.
This Bill is a total reversion back to a bad
and antiquated type, and instead of advancing farther it shows an altogether
backward and retrogressive tendency.
I object profoundly to this Bill because,
for the first time I believe in human
history, it imposes upon the teachers the
obligation to give religious instruction.

It is quite obvious to every intelligent
Member of this House who has studied
the essential difference between Catholicism and Protestantism that the Roman
Catholics demand something more than
simple Bible instruction, whether it be the
Douai version or not. Protestants, on
the other hand, are quite content with
simple Bible instruction, and Protestantism, rightly or wrongly, allows private
individuals to interpose their interpretations, which the Roman Catholic Church,
wisely or unwisely, forbids. I have
quoted the Roman Catholic point of view
from the Council of Trent, and I propose to quote to the House the Protestant
view as put forward by a very eminent
educational authority, an eminent Irish
Presbyterian called James Godkin, who
wrote a book on "Education in Ireland."
which was published in the year 1862,
and which, I may tell Members of this
House, is a veritable classic as regards.
Irish education. In dealing with the
establishment of the National Board he
narrates the early history of the National
Board from its birth in 1831 until the
troublous times of 1852.
Members are well aware that for a long
time the greatest harmony prevailed between the two chief Commissioners of
National Education, Archbishop Whately,
the Protestant Archbishop of Dublin, and
Dr. Murray, the Venerable Roman
Catholic Archbishop. The most cordial
relations prevailed so far as they were concerned until 1852. Then Archbishop
Murray died and Dr. Cullen was appointed in his place. Dr. Cullen took up
a very different attitude on the education
question. He was profoundly opposed to
Protestant and Catholic children having
education in the same school, and he was
profoundly opposed to what he called
simple Bible teaching. Mr. Godkin has
a great contempt and dislike for his vicws,
naturally enough, looking at the question
from the Protestant point of view, and
he uses these words, summing up the
position:-
Yet it must be owned that Dr.
Cullen has rightly interpreted the
principles, spirit, and practice of his
Church on this subject. Protestants
and Roman Catholics rest the evidence
of Christianity on totally different
grounds. The former establish the
Divine authority of the Bible independently of the Church, proving its
authenticity and inspiration and the
right of private judgment to interpret
its contents, entirely without her aid;
whereas the latter receive the sacred
Scriptures from the Church, which
they acknowledge as the sole depository
and the infallible interpreter of revelation. The Protestant principle of inquiry upon this subject is, therefore,
if carried out, utterly subversive of the
Roman Catholic Faith.
I will read the last sentence again. It

stating the Roman Catholic point of view,

The Protestant principle of inquiry
upon this subject is, therefore, if carried out, utterly subversive of the
Roman Catholic Faith.

whether a copy will be issued to the Members of the House?
The MINISTER OF COMMERCE

Oral Answers to Questions.
GRANTS FOR AGRICULTURAL
RESEARCH.
1. Sir ROBERT LYNN asked the
Minister of Agriculture whether his attention has been drawn to the increased
grants that have been made in Great
Britain for Agricultural Research and
other purposes calculated to help the agricultural industry, and whether it is proposed to make similar grants to help
agriculture in Northern Ireland?
The MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE
(Sir Edward Archdale): The answer to
the first part of the question is in the
affirmative. As regards the second part,
I would refer the hon. Member to the
Estimates for Agricultural Services for
1930-31, which I recently presented to
this House. Any increase in the funds
already provided for agricultural research
and education will depend upon the
future general financial position of the
Province.
"READERS" IN PUBLIC ELE-
MENTARY SCHOOLS.
3. Mr. NIXON asked the Parliamentary Secretary of the Ministry of Education whether he can state if it is necessary
for the teachers of public elementary
schools to change the "readers' every
year; whether he is aware that this policy
imposes unnecessary financial burdens
upon the shoulders of poor parents;
whether it would not be more satisfactory for the "readers" in use in any
year to be used for the two years following, so that younger members of a family
could use those laid aside by the older
ones?
The PARLIAMENTARY SECRE-
TARY OF THE MINISTRY OF EDU-
CATION (Mr. Robb): It is usually
found in the smaller schools where the
staff consists of only two or three
teachers that the same reader is used in
the combined instruction of a group made
up of two or three standards, and in
nearly all schools some pupils have to be
retained in the same standard for a second
year.
Oral Answers
Oral Answers
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Robb]
As it is important that fresh reading
matter should be provided for such pupils,
it is not, as a rule, found feasible to use
the same reading book in a standard in
two successive years; but there is no reason why a book should not be used again
in the same standard after the lapse of
one year.
Subject to the consideration that it is
most desirable that pupils should have a
variety of reading during their school
course, the Ministry is strongly in favour
of efforts being made to minimise, as much
as possible, the cost to parents of purchasing school books.
NORTH ANTRIM REGIONAL COM-
MITTEE AND MARRIED WOMEN
TEACHERS.
4. Mr. NIXON asked the Parliamentary Secretary of the Ministry of Education whether it is proposed to inhibit
the North Antrim Regional Committee
from refusing to send down to Management Committee the names of married
women teachers who may be candidates
for vacant appointments in the schools
managed by these Committees ?
Mr. ROBB: Under the Bill now before
Parliament, the Education Authority
must transmit to School Management
Committees all applications for posts as
teachers.
NUMBER OF PENSIONED P.E.S.
TEACHERS.
5. Mr. NIXON asked the Minister of
Finance whether he can state the total
number of pensioned teachers of public
elementary schools in Northern Ireland
on the 31st March, 1930, and the total
sum paid to them in pensions?
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Pollock): In reply to the hon. Member,
the number of pensioned teachers of public
elementary schools as at the 31st March
last was approximately 1,072. I say approximately, because there are a few
additional teachers, who retired towards
the end of last financial year, and whose
claims for pension have not yet been received or the amounts of whose pensions
have not been fixed.
The total amount of pension paid to
such pensioners during the year ended
the 31st March last was approximately
£127,000.
DEPARTMENTAL COMMITTEE ON
MEDICAL BENEFITS.
6. Mr. MILLER asked the Minister of
Finance whether he has received the report of the Departmental Committee appointed by him in September last, with
reference to a scheme for medical benefits
for Northern Ireland and its effects on the
present dispensary medical services, and,
if so, whether he will have this report circulated to Members of the House?
Mr. POLLOCK: I have received the
report referred to by the hon. Member,
and steps are being taken to arrange for
its presentation and publication.
SUPPRESSION OF DONAGHADEE
URBAN COUNCIL.
7. Sir ROBERT LYNN asked the
Minister of Home Affairs whether he can
state his reasons for suppressing the
Donaghadee Urban Council; what were
the statutes under which he took action;
and whether he can state how long the
Council is to remain in a state of suspension ?
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): With regard to the
first part of the question, I would refer
the hon. Member to the answer which I
gave on the 14th November last to a
question put by the hon. Member for Pottinger (Mr. Beattie) of which I am
sending him a copy.
With reference to the second part of
the question, the Ministry took action
under the Local Government (Emergency
Powers) Act, 1921.
With regard to the third part of the
question, I am not yet in a position to
state how long it will be necessary for the
present arrangements to continue.
RELIEVING OFFICERS AND OUT-
DOOR RELIEF RECIPIENTS.
8. Mr. NIXON asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether he is aware that
some relieving officers require recipients
of outdoor relief to assemble on roads at
places assigned by them; whether in
numerous instances these places are at
considerable distances from the recipients'
residences; whether some of the recipients
are very weak and old, and unable to
walk long distances; whether some of
Oral Answers
Cral Answers
10 APRIL 1930
them have to walk on crutches; whether
they have to remain on the day of payment until the relieving officer finds it
convenient to attend, which often necessitates their remaining on the road for
hours in the rain; whether outdoor relief
is sometimes sent with postmen and other
messengers, to whom these very poor
people give tips for carrying it, and
whether he will issue instructions that the
relieving officers deliver the outdoor relief
personally at the address of the recipients,
or make arrangements for its payment
in the same manner as that of old age
pension through the Post Office?
Sir DAWSON BATES: I have no information that would suggest that the
practices mentioned in the first part of the
question are in existence, but if the hon.
Member will furnish me with information
in any specific case, I shall have the matter inquired into.
It is the duty of a relieving officer to
attend at such places in his district, and
at such times of the day and on such days
of the week as the board of guardians shall
from time to time direct for the purpose
of dispensing relief, as well as of receiving
applications for relief. He is required to
dispense the weekly allowances of all poor
persons belonging to his district, duly
and punctually, and, so far as possible,
at the home of the applicant. He is further required to visit all persons who are
in receipt of outdoor relief owing to temporary sickness at least once a week, and
all other persons in receipt of outdoor relief at least once a month.
I do not think it would be practicable
or desirable to issue instructions requiring
payment of relief to be made in all cases
at the recipient's home, and with regard
to the suggestion that payment should be
made through the Post Office, it would
not be feasible to make such an arrangement.
Mr. NIXON: Will the Minister inquire at Ballymoney?
COURT OF CRIMINAL APPEAL FOR
NORTHERN IRELAND.
9. Mr. BEATTIE asked the Prime
Minister whether he is prepared to make
representation to the Imperial Parliament with a view to having a Court of
Criminal Appeal set up for Northern
Ireland?
Sir DAWSON BATES: I have been
asked to reply.
I am glad to be able to inform the hon.
Member that as a result of representations
which were made some time ago in connection with the establishment of a Court
of Criminal Appeal in Northern Ireland,
a Bill for this purpose has been prepared
by the Imperial Government and I understand that this Bill will be introduced
in the Imperial Parliament as soon as
parliamentary business will permit.

DISCIPLINARY CHARGES
AGAINST MEMBERS OF R.U.C.
11. Mr. NIXON asked the Minister

number of disciplinary charges preferred
against members of the Royal Ulster
Constabulary which were denied and subsequently investigated by a sworn public
inquiry during the past three years, and

Court found the accused (a) guilty and (b)
not guilty?
Sir DAWSON BATES: The number of
disciplinary charges preferred against
members of the Royal Ulster Constabulary
which were denied and subsequently investigated by a sworn public inquiry since
the 1st January, 1927, up to the present
date is 288.
In 194 cases the accused were found
guilty, and in 94 not guilty.

Sir ROBERT LYNN: I do not presume that it is necessary for me to offer
any apology for rising to support the Bill
which is before the House for its Second
Reading. The Bill is only an amplification of the Act that has already been
passed, and is rendered necessary owing
to reasonable changes required in the
existing Act. I would like at the outset
to say that I appreciate the moderate tone
in which the hon. Member for the Central
Division (Mr. Devlin) approached this
question. I have often wondered why it
is that the question of education, like the
question of religion, is a subject on which
people often lose their temper, because if
ever there was a subject that calls for
quiet consideration it is this question of
education. I hope in anything I am going
to say to-day I will be as moderate
as the hon. Member for the Central
Division.

The Council of Trent was first begun in
the year 1545, nearly 400 years ago. Its
objects were the reform of ecclesiastical
abuses, the pacification of religious disputes on doctrinal decisions and discussions on a crusade against infidels. True,
it has a tremendous power on all Roman
Catholic thought, but it was completely
superseded and all its tenets were reversed
by a Council of the Vatican set up in 1869.

are striving to ram this Measure down
our throats. If I believed they were
acting conscientiously in the interests of
the Protestant people I would be only too
glad. We would be only too glad to see
the Protestant people receive the greatest
measure of fair treatment imaginable,
but when we ask for that fair treatment
for ourselves it is denied us. When we
make an appeal here--this is an extraordinary thing--based on the dictates of
our conscience we are told that conscientiousness must be subordinated all the time
to the reasoning of the conscience of
Members on the Government side of the
House.

priest as a school manager has practically

could be upheld would be on the score

That is limiting the manager's power
down to a very small extent indeed. And
is it because of the little power that he
possesses in regard to the moral conduct
of the school and in regard to the form
of religious instruction which the teacher
gives, is it because of that that the
Government are so hostile to Catholic
clerical managers?
Lots of parallels have been quoted for
us yesterday and to-day by the Prime
Minister and others as to the treatment
of Catholic schools in Scotland, England,
and in America. We are neither in Scotland, nor America, nor in England. The
Catholic people in Scotland and the
Catholic people in England are merely
rising, as it might be said, out of the catacomb of a long night of obscurity. They
could not really successfully put forward
the same claim that we put forward with
such a show of reason, although they are
travelling at a greater rate than we are in
this country. They have never lost anything, but our position has been worsened.
Therein lies our complaint, and we cannot
allow any parallel to be instituted with
the people of England, Scotland, America,
or any other place. If you adopt that as
a principle, you might go down to the
Carribean Islands, or the wildest part of
Africa, find a place where there is not a
breath of religion, where Christianity in
any form is not recognised, and say,
"Look how much worse off they are in
the Sandwich Islands or in Burton-on-
Trent." (Laughter). You cannot introduce comparisons of that kind.
We have heard a lot of flowery oratory
from the Government benches during the
past few days. We have heard a great
deal of sophistry and a united attempt to
obscure the real issue. The only thing to
which we can pay attention is the long
catalogue of woes to which the minority
in these Six Counties have been doomed,
that long catalogue of woes which this
Parliament has thrown on us. The
time surely has arisen, not to perpetuate
the bad blood of the past, not to create
new animosities, but to bring about some
measure of fraternisation amongst the
different peoples of the Six Counties, to
make this Bill a measure of achievement,
and to infuse into it something better than
the sword which gleams in every line of
it. If justice is not done now we are not
going to hear the end of this. If the catalogue of the woes of the Catholic people
of the Six Counties were published it
would form a very bulky volume, and
would make very interesting reading if
published to the outside world. The
world up to the present knows very little
of what the minority here have been condemned to, and if justice is to be done in
the matter of education and in other respects I hope there will be no necessity for
making them aware of it. But if this
thing continues, and if one wrong succeeds
another, there is no reason why the world
should not know what is going on in the
Six Counties.
Mr. ELLIOTT: Hear, hear.
Mr. CONNELLAN: I believe that it

Mr. McALEER: I do not intend to
intervene at any length, but the hon. and
gallant Member for South Derry (Captain
Chichester-Clark) said this afternoon that
no Member of the Opposition had any

had any experience of the administration
of education, or knew anything about the
spade work of regional committees. Possibly I am the exception to that rule. I
was principal teacher of a school for many
years, and since my retirement have
served on a regional committee for a number of years. My experience of regional
committees, and committees generally, is
such that it fills me, as it fills my coreligionists, with fear and trembling as to
the working of this new Bill if it ever gets
to the Statute Book.
The constitution of the Committee of
which I am a member is about one-third
Catholic and two-thirds Protestant. Since
its institution no Catholic has ever been
appointed to any paid position. I will say
that this Committee is no better and no
worse than any other of these committees,
and what is true of it is true of all the
committees. I know that the Protestant
people are the dominant people on them.
They are in the majority, they have the
appointments, and have in their hands the
ruling of all education within their
respective areas. Some people will say
that the Committee to which I am attached
has given something to Catholics. It did
give something in the way of University
scholarships, but why were those scholarships given? Because no Protestant boy
or girl qualified. No Protestant boy or
Protestant girl applied. Those University scholarships had to be given to
Catholics because nobody else qualified.
Mr. ELLIOTT: Do you object to that?
Mr. MCALEER I do not. We are only
getting what we should get.
Mr. ELLIOTT: Hear, hear.
Mr. McALEER: It was the same with
secondary scholarships. In the beginning
one or two were given with reluctance. In
recent years they were divided, though I
must say that the Catholics have had the
highest efficiency marks and only got part
of the scholarships. We have heard a lot
of talk about the transferring of schools.
I know a few schools that are transferred
in our area, but I want to tell the Prime
Minister that the reason why those schools
were transferred was that the Protestant
managers of them were careless or indifferent and did not want the trouble of
collecting money in order to keep the
schools in efficient order. That is a fact.
Education without religion is no education. We Catholics believe that to
divorce religion from education would
bring us into the position in which France,
Mexico, and Russia are to-day. In this
matter the Catholics of the Six Counties,
bishops, priests, and laity, are unanimous
as never before. We object to this Bill
because it saps the very foundation
of religion in the schools. We want
equality of treatment. We want the
same grants as are given to Protestant
schools. We want clerical management
continued, because under clerical management the schools were efficiently and well
kept up. The parish priests were instrumental in collecting large sums of money.
They appointed very efficient and welltrained teachers, and under their management the schools have been as well kept
up as those that have been more favoured.
We have complete confidence in the
clerical management and want it continued.
I want to say in reply to the hon.
Member for North Antrim (Sir Robert
Lynn), who trotted out the question of
the Vatican Council of 1869, and said that
it qualified some of the decrees of the
Council of Trent. I may tell him that he
is absolutely ignorant of the whole subject
because no decrees were ever issued by the
Vatican Council. The meetings of that
Council will be continued in the year
1931, but no decrees were ever issued in
connection with it. I beg to say that I
support my colleagues on this side, that
we want equality and fair treatment in
the matter of grants to our schools.

15 APRIL 1930
HOUSE OF COMMONS.

Tuesday, 15th April, 1930.
The House met at Three of the Clock,
Mr. SPEAKER in the Chair.
Paper Presented.
Ministry of Agriculture:
The Marketing of Potatoes (Northern
Ireland) Rules, 1930. (By Act).
Oral Answers to Questions.
IMPROVEMENTS AT BANGOR PIER.
1. Mr. HENDERSON asked the Minister of Commerce whether he would give
any information as to when the improvements to Bangor Pier are going to be
carried out, and whether he could state
the nature of the improvements to be
made?
The MINISTER OF COMMERCE
(Mr. Barbour): The nature of the improvements to be made at Bangor Harbour and the time of their execution are
matters primarily for the Bangor Borough
Council to determine. I may add,
however, for the information of the
hon. Member, that as the Government propose to make a Grant from Public
Funds towards the cost of these improvements, I have requested the Borough
Council to furnish me with full particulars of the scheme, together with
detailed plans and estimates.
TRAINING OF STUDENTS AT
STRAWBERRY HILL.
6. Mr. McALEER asked the Minister
of Finance whether it is a fact that a
higher capitation grant per student is
paid for the resident students of Strawberry Hill Training College than for the
students of Stranmillis Training College
in Belfast; whether it would be more desirable to have the entire grant expended
in Northern Ireland by establishing a
Training College for these students in this
area; and whether he does not consider
that this course would be more economical
both for the Government and the students?
The PARLIAMENTARY SERETARY
OF THE MINISTRY OF EDUCATION
(Mr. Robb): I have been asked by my
right hon. Friend the Minister of Finance
to reply to this question.
The capitation grant payable by this
Ministry for students in training at St.
Mary's, Strawberry Hill, is fixed annually
by the Board of Education, England,
which acts, in this matter, as agent for
the Ministry. The capitation grant last
paid was at the rate of £70 16s 3d. The
capitation grant for men students at
Stranmillis Training College is at present
£70.
The number of students from Northern
Ireland in training at Strawberry Hill is
40, and it would not be possible to conduct
a properly staffed residential training
college on the proceeds from fees and
capitation grants of such a small number.
ABOLITION OF WATER-BOUND
STREETS IN BELFAST.
7. Mr. HENDERSON asked the Minister of Labour whether he is aware that
the Belfast Corporation have approved of
a large number of schemes for abolishing
water-bound and pebble-paved streets, at
a cost of £300,000, for the relief of unemployment, and whether he can state
when the Government Inquiry into the
granting of this loan will be held?
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): I have been asked to
reply to this question.
I am aware that the Corporation have
a large scheme of street re-surfacing under
consideration, but the scheme has not yet
been submitted to my Ministry, nor has
any application been made for sanction to
a loan.
The hon. Member may rest assured that
if, and when, such a scheme is submitted
there will be no avoidable delay in holding the necessary inquiry, but, of course,
he will realise that a scheme of this magnitude must be carefully considered, and
that the necessary investigations will take
a little time.

CULTURE EXPERT.

number of ex-Servicemen who applied for

the position of physical culture expert for

RE-AFFORESTATION IN IRELAND.

drawn to the newspaper report, where it

millionaire philanthropist, of Indiana,
signified his intention of helping Ireland
in the work of re-afforestation, and if it
is the Government's intention to apply
for a big grant for Northern Ireland, so
that useful and profitable employment be
obtained for our unemployed in the
planting of trees in swamps and boglands,
and on exposed and bleak mountain
sides?
The MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE
(Sir Edward Archdale): I have not seen

Member refers, and, therefore, the second
part of the question does not arise. If
the hon. Member is in a position to furnish me with particulars of the offer of Mr.
Frank S. Betz to provide financial
assistance in connection with the work of
afforestation in Northern Ireland I shall
be happy to have the matter enquired
into.
Mr. HEALY: Arising out of the reply
will the right hon. Gentleman pursue
his investigations with regard to the possibilities of planting the waste areas of
Co. Fermanagh?
Sir EDWARD ARCHDALE: Most of
the waste areas in Fermanagh belong to
different people and they want rather
more money for those waste areas than
the Ministry are allowed to give.
GRANTS FOR AGRICULTURE IN
GREAT BRITAIN.
12. Mr. McBRIDE (for Sir Robert
Lynn) asked the Minister of Agriculture
whether he can state the amount of the
increased grant made for agriculture in
Great Britain, and whether he is aware
of the purposes to which the grant is put?
Sir EDWARD ARCHDALE: I understand that a special capital grant of
£500,000 has been made to the Development Fund for the extension of agricultural research and experimental work in
Great Britain. This grant is for capital
expenditure and is not applicable to maintenance charges.
In addition, a circular letter from the
Ministry of Agriculture and Fisheries has
been addressed to each county authority
for agricultural education in England
and Wales intimating that within due
limits that Department is prepared to
support a reasonable expansion of the
present work and organisation in connection with agricultural education. This
support will be given by means of grants
on the existing scale of two-thirds of the
approved expenditure.
an
I do not know what increased expenditure will be involved as a result of this
circular issued by the Ministry of Agriculture and Fisheries, but I notice that
the Estimates of that Department for the
current year show increase from
£584,975 to £750,385 in grants for agricultural education and research. There
are several other minor directions in which
increased expenditure on agriculture in
Great Britain is being made. An inquiry
into the field of marketing organisation is
being undertaken by the Ministry of Agriculture and Fisheries with a grant of
£12,000 a year from the Empire Marketing Fund. A farm management survey
on a large scale has also been instituted,
while an additional £20,000 has been
made available for the whole of England
and Wales for the assistance by way of
loans toward the erection of village halls.
