Message from the Senate.


The Senate agree to the Exchequer and
Financial Provisions Bill and the Housing
Bill, without amendment.
They agree to the Criminal Law and
Prevention of Crime (Amendment) Bill,
with Amendments, to which they desire
the concurrence of the Commons.
Ordered, That the Amendments made.
by the Senate to the Criminal Law and
Prevention of Crime (Amendment) Bill
be taken into consideration to-morrow.
ORDERS OF THE DAY.
SUPPLY (Fifth Allotted Day).
ESTIMATES, 1930-31.
Considered in Committee.
[Mr. MOLES in the Chair]
CLASS III. No. 1.
MINISTRY OF HOME AFFAIRS.
Motion made and Question proposed:
"That a sum not exceeding £44,159 be
granted to His Majesty to complete the
sum necessary to defray the charge which
will come in course of payment during
the year ending on the 31st March, 1931,
to defray the salaries and expenses of the
Ministry of Home Affairs."-(Note-
£15,000 has been voted on account).
Sir DAWSON BATES: In presenting
the Estimates for the Ministry of Home.
Affairs, I think that, as on previous occasions, it would be desirable that I should
give a general review of the activities of
the Ministry during the past year under
the separate heads of administration
which come within the purview of the
Ministry.
I have explained on former occasions
that the Ministry in effect comprises two
distinct departments; one, the Home Office
Department dealing with the activities
which are usually associated in the public
mind with the Home Office, that is to say,
law and order, crime, police, prisons, care
and training of Borstal boys, reformatory
and industrial schools, lunatic asylums,
etc., etc., and the other the Local Government Department which, as the Committee is aware, exercises general supervision
over the activities of local government
authorities in such matters as roads, road
traffic, poor law, public health, local
government, finance and audits, housing,
and the various other services coming
under the jurisdiction of local authorities.
As regards the particular Estimate,
Class III, No. 1, which makes provision
for the salaries of the staff of the Ministry,
the Committee will observe that so far
as the amount asked for is concerned there
is no appreciable change as compared with
the amount passed last year, the small increase of £134 being due to normal
fluctuations and increments of salary.
It will also be observed that the number
of members of the staff in the Ministry,
that is 150, remains the same as last year,
and I think that I am entitled to claim
credit for the Ministry that it has not
been necessary to ask for any additional
staff this year, having regard to the fact
that during the year in question two very
heavy additional services were imposed on
the Ministry, one in connection with the
arrangements for derating-to which I
will refer later-and the other in regard
to the new arrangements which have been
so successfully instituted in connection
with the control of motor traffic in Northern Ireland-a matter to which I will also
have occasion to refer at some length later.
I referred last year to the pending retirement of Colonel Dawson, late Chief
Medical Officer of the Ministry, and I
Supply-
15 APRIL 1930
Criminal Law Bill
think it well to inform the Committee that
the vacancy thus caused has been filled
by the promotion of Dr. Patrick, who has
been for so many years acting as a medical
inspector under the old Local Government
Board and under the Ministry, and who
is thoroughly conversant with all public
health and medical conditions in Northern Ireland. The vacancy caused by Dr.
Patrick's promotion has been filled by the
appointment of Dr. Deane, who has been
for so many years associated with the
County Down Mental Hospital, and whose
knowledge and experience of mental
diseases should be of considerable service
to the Ministry in his capacity as Inspector of Lunatics.
The vacancy caused by the retirement
of Mr. Moorhead from the position of
Chief Crown Solicitor has been filled by
the appointment of Mr. Carson, who for
many years had been acting as Crown
Solicitor and Sessional Crown Solicitor for
County Tyrone. It is with sincere regret
that I feel I must refer to the great loss
sustained by the Ministry, and, indeed,
by the whole Local Government Service in
Northern Ireland, owing to the death of
Dr. George Bryan, Inspector of Audits.
For many years past Dr. Bryan has been
closely associated officially with local
authorities in Northern Ireland and
there was no phase of local government activity and no official standing in the Local Government Service
with which he was not familiar. I
think I am voicing the views of
the officials of the local authorities in
saying that they feel his death is a great
loss.
I should refer to the item under subhead C4, namely, expenses in connection
with the international motor race, from
which it will be seen that we are provisionally asking for an amount of £350
towards the recoupment of expenditure
on certain works which are to be undertaken by the local authorities in connection with the race. It will be understood
that in connection with the course certain
works have to be carried out which, in
effect, improve the roads and are to the
benefit of the travelling public. The cost
of these works will be appropriately
borne by the Road Fund, but there are
other works which are incidental only to
the race and which are essentially a State
charge. I refer in particular to the provision of barricades at the dangerous
points in Comber, Dundonald, and Newtownards. These works are of a protective
nature and fall under the same heading as
the cost of the police employed in guarding the course.
I should say, however, that the item set
down in the Estimates is of a speculative
nature only and is based on last year's experience, and I think I should also make
it plain that since the preparation of the
Estimates other items have come under
consideration which will make the charge
on the Government Funds very much
heavier than was anticipated at the time
the Estimates were prepared. As far as
can be seen at the moment it will be necessary at
a later stage to introduce a
Supplementary Estimate covering the full
Government charge in connection with the
race as the Government has agreed to
bear the cost-approximately £1,175-of
widening the road opposite the Grand
Stand in order to give a larger pit area
and so minimise the risk of accident by
collision between cars emerging from the
pits and those in circulation.
Generally speaking, as far as can be
estimated at the moment, the cost entailed on Government funds in connection
with the race will be roughly £1,375.
While the Road Fund on its part will bear
the cost, approximately £1,320, of improving the actual road surface, apart
from that there will be expenses incidental
to the employment of the large force of
police which will be necessary to keep the
course-roughly speaking 800 men are required for this purpose, and the expense
may run from £800 to £1,000, which will
cover transportation, subsistence allowances and the emplovment of such members of the Special Constabulary as may
be necessary to supplement the regular
force.
as
I
These races have been successful to a
marked degree in the past and have attracted to Northern Ireland a considerable number of tourists with resultant
gain to the community a whole.
trust that the race this year will be a
greater success, if possible, and I am sure
that the Committee will give the Government their support in connection with the
making of the necessary provision for ensuring that the race is run under proper
circumstances with due regard to the
safety of the competitors and the spectators.
I will now turn to the activities of the
Local Government Department of the
Ministry, and perhaps in this connection
I might first refer once again to the ques-
Supply-
Committee
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Sir Dawson Bates]
tion of Local Government reform, which
has been in our minds for so many years
past. I have been asked from time to
time when effect is to be given to the
recommendations of the Local Government
Commission, and I would like once again
to explain that the problem is of such
magnitude and complexity that I am
satisfied that it would be impossible to
deal with the various recommendations
submitted to us by the Commission in one
Bill and that the proper course to adopt
is to take each different section in a
separate Bill.
As has already been announced in the
King's Speech, the first section of the reforms will be dealt with, it is hoped, during the present Session, namely, the
reform of the lunacy services. On a careful examination of all the proposals it
appeared to the Government that these
services appear to be in the most urgent
need of reform as they are being administered to-day on the same lines as
they were nearly 50 years ago, even though
public and medical opinion have advanced rapidly in recent years regarding
the question of mental diseases. It would
be improper for me to indicate the lines
of the proposed Measure dealing with
mental diseases, but I think it will be
sufficient to say that in framing our legislative proposals we have had under careful
consideration the recommendations put up
to us by the various organisations of local
authorities, etc., and have also been in
close touch with expert and technical
opinion in the country.
Further we are following with close attention the recent developments in Great
Britain, where this subject of the care and
treatment of mental diseases is under consideration by the Imperial Parliament at
the moment. I would also like to make
it clear that in framing our proposals we
will endeavour as far as possible to make
them dovetail in with the proposals which
we hope at a later stage to lay before
Parliament in connection with the reform
of our poor law, our public health and our
general local government services.
In connection with public health there
is no service which has such a bearing on
the life and well-being of the community
as housing. Housing has formed the subject of no fewer than eight Acts of Parliament passed by this Parliament, and this
fact alone. if no other, would show the
interest which the Government and Parliament take in this essential service. I need
hardly dwell once again on the situation
which confronted us when the Government assumed power in 1921. It was
estimated that we had a housing shortage
in Belfast alone of at least 10,000 houses,
and as similar conditions prevailed
throughout the rest of Northern Ireland it
would not be far wrong to say that the
housing shortage in Northern Ireland was
in the neighbourhood of 25,000.
I do not propose to weary the Committee with unnecessary statistics, but I think
that a short statement of the present situation will demonstrate to this Committee
that a short statement of the present situamade under the Government's subsidy
proposals towards alleviating, if
actually meeting, the housing shortage.
Up to the end of last month, that is, the
31st March, a total of 17,528 houses had
been completed with Government assistance. This includes 237 houses erected by
private builders and 502 houses erected
by local authorities between the years
1919 and 1923 under the Imperial Acts;
1,155 houses erected with the aid of unemployment relief grants, and 13,952
houses erected by private builders and
1,682 houses erected by local authorities
under the Northern Ireland Housing
Acts, 1923-1929.
Apart from the houses erected under
the Housing Acts and Unemployment
Relief Acts, no fewer than 1,902 cottages
have been approved for erection under the
Labourers' Acts, of which 1,540 were
actually completed on the 31st March
last. The total loans advanced from
Government sources for the provision of
labourers' cottages since the establishment of the Government of Northern
Ireland amounted to £506,782, while the
total free grants made by the Govern
ment in aid of the loan charges since the
same date and up to the 31st March, 1930,
were £111,515.
At the same time we have at present
in course of construction and approved for
grants 4,177 houses, of which 4,102 are
being erected by private builders and 75
by local authorities. This progress,
which I suggest is undoubtedly satisfactory, is due entirely to the very substantial Government assistance which is
accorded under existing Acts of Parliament to private builders and to local
authorities in connection with the erection
of subsidy houses, and I think that the
Committee will appreciate how substantial
this assistance has been when I say that
up to the end of March, 1930, no less a
Supply-
Committee
15 APRIL 1930sum than £1,332,840 has been paid out
in subsidies under the Housing Acts to
private builders and to local authorities,
the amount paid to private builders being
£1,205,720, and to local
to local authorities
£127,120. The sums which I have referred to are, of course, quite distinct
from the Government grants and subsidies
paid under the Unemployment Relief
Acts and the older British Acts.
I am glad to be able to say that the
progress of building still continues to be
satisfactory. During the month of
January last no fewer than 591 houses
were approved for erection under our
Housing Acts, 405 were approved during
the month of February, and 304 in the
month of March, making a total of 1,300
houses during the last quarter. The
Committee is aware that at the close of
last Session in Parliament a Housing Act
was passed which extended from 650 to 700
superficial feet the maximum floor space
for subsidy houses, and it will no doubt
interest the Committee to learn that of
the 1,300 houses referred to above, 714
exceeded 650 superficial feet in area, the
remainder approximately 600-being
650 superficial feet or under. It will thus
be appreciated that many of the builders
still find it necessary and desirable to restrict their operations to the smaller types
of houses which can be let at lower rents
to workers, and this fact in itself bears
out the statement which I made during
the debates on housing in November last
that the small type of house-650 superficial feet and under-is a type that is
very much required for our purposes.
It is impossible for me to give any particulars as to the working of the recent
Act passed by Parliament as there has not
been sufficient time to estimate its effect,
but the Committee can rest assured that
the operations throughout Northern Ireland will be carefully watched and that
any attempt to evade the spirit or the
letter of the Act will be severely checked.
As the Members of the Committee have
already seen from the King's Speech, it
is the intention of the Government to introduce during the present Session in Parliament a Bill conferring town-planning
powers on our local authorities in Northern Ireland. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear). The proposals in the Bill are still
the subject of conference and discussion
with the local authorities, who are more
directly interested in this particular matter, and it will be understood that it
would be improper for me at present to
enter into any discussion in regard to or to
enumerate the proposals which it is hoped
will be included in the Bill, but it will be
sufficient for me at the moment to say that
we propose to make a marked departure
from the principles which operate in Great
Britain in connection with town planning
at present in that it is proposed for Northern Ireland to give powers to the local
authorities to deal with built-up areas as
well as with undeveloped land. By this
means it will be possible where circumstances demand it for local authorities to
kill two birds with one stone by dealing
with the slum problem on the one hand
and by improving the amenities of their
cities or towns on the other hand.
As regards general public health administration, the year in question has
been marked by steady progress rather
than by the introduction of any new
special features. The health of the population has been normal and there have
been no considerable outbreaks of infectious diseases. Steady improvement continues to be effected in sanitary affairs,
and it is worthy of note that, generally
speaking, there is a strong move throughout the area of Northern Ireland towards
the provision of proper water supplies and
sewerage arrangements for the minor
towns in the rural districts where the arrangements hitherto have been somewhat
primitive. The provision of these services
is essentially a costly matter, and this fact
has in the past acted as a strong deterrent
against the installation of up-to-date services in the above respects. During the
year in question loans amounting to over
£44,000 were sanctioned for improvements in water supplies and sewerage
arrangements. The Ministry during the
year has continued to impress generally
on local authorities the need for increased
supervision of the meat and milk supplies,
and I think it only fair to say that the
authorities as a whole are now realising
in a greater degree than ever their responsibilities in this regard.
The question of the high death rate of
infants and mothers in childbirth has been
the subject of much interest and great
concern recently, and has been engaging
the serious attention of the Ministry and
many of the local authorities. As the
Committee is aware, the Ministry gives
encouragement to the promotion of
schemes for the welfare of young children
and their mothers in a practical fashion
by paying grants at the rate of, approximately, half the approved expenses of the
Supply-
Committee
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Sir Dawson Bates]
local authorities and voluntary associations which undertake such work. The
amount included in the Estimates for the
last two years for this purpose was approximately £5,000, and I can assure the
Committee that no money provided in the
Estimates of the Ministry of Home Affairs
is spent to better advantage. I would
like to bear testimony to the devotion
shown by the ladies and gentlemen who
throughout Northern Ireland give their
time and attention to this good work.
Schemes are in operation in 47 different
areas, which include practically all the
urban areas. In the larger towns, such
as Belfast, Bangor, Newry, and Portadown, the schemes are fairly comprehensive and make provision for centres or
clinics at which mothers can attend for
advice and treatment, health visitors to
visit mothers in their homes, and the provision of food of a nourishing character in
necessitous cases. As the Committee is
aware, the Belfast Corporation have had
recently under consideration the development of their scheme in this regard. It
is not possible for me at the moment to
say anything definite in regard to this
scheme. It is of a very comprehensive
and expensive character and before we can
give our approval to it we have to be
satisfied in the first place that it has been
framed in such a way as not to overlap
with other services of a similar character
which are in operation in the City of
Belfast. As the matter is still under
consideration both by the Corporation
and by the Ministry, I think it would be
inappropriate to make any further reference to it at the present.
The question of maternal mortality has
also been the subject of some concern
and consideration by me, and in order to
ascertain how the death-rate from this
cause might be reduced, I thought it well
to approach the medical profession in Northern Ireland with a view to obtaining
their assistance in endeavouring to ascertain the causes of death in childbirth. I
am glad to be able to say that I have been
met, as I have always been met, with the
greatest frankness and willingness by the
members of the profession, and steps are
being taken to have records kept which on
being collated and examined may, I trust,
be of some help and assistance to the profession who are engaged in this particular
aspect of their profession.
With regard to the question of the
treatment of tuberculosis, in respect of
which the Government contribute 50 per
cent towards the expenses of the local
authorities schemes for the treatment of
this disease are now in operation in every
county and county borough with the exception of Londonderry County Borough.
The County Council of Londonderry have
recently formulated a scheme of a tentative
character, and while it is perhaps modest
in its aims, it at least constitutes a beginning in that particular county. About
375 beds are available in Northern Ireland
for the treatment of tuberculosis in public sanatoria in addition to other accommodation in private institutions. There
are also 44 clinics at which outpatients
receive treatment, while domiciliary
treatment is provided for suitable cases
which cannot be dealt with in sanatoria
or at clinics. From an examination of
the reports received from the medical
officers in charge of this work there can
be no doubt as to the beneficial effect of
the measures which have been and are
being adopted for dealing with this
disease. The death rate from tuberculosis
has been steadily declining in recent
years, being only 1.40 per 1,000 in 1928
as compared with 2.54 per 1,000 in 1918.
As to the question of road traffic, the
improvement which recent legislation has
effected in traffic conditions in Northern
Ireland may be gathered from the fact
that in the calendar year immediately
folowing the passing of the 1926 Motor
Vehicles Act, that is, in 1927, the number
of road accidents reported by the police
to the Ministry amounted to 1,438.
following year showed an increase to
1,467, but for the year 1929 the total was
only 1,417.
The
The number of motor vehicles in the
Province in 1927 was 31,900, and in
1929 there were 34,900 consequently
were it not for the energetic action taken
to put in operation the provisions of the
1926 Act with respect to dangerous
driving, speeding, it is reasonable to
expect that the number of accidents
reported would have been much greater.
During the year 1928 convictions were
obtained in 66 cases of drunkenness while
in charge of a motor car, but during the
year 1929 only 60 such convictions are
recorded. During the year 1928 reckless
driving and that class of offence
occasioned 300 convictions, and in the
following year the number rose to 333
Supply-
Committee
15 APRIL 1930
Except in the Borough of Bangor and
the Urban District of Carrickfergus
motor vehicles not over 2 tons unladen
weight are not restricted as to speed,
consequently, apart from prosecutions
instituted for infringing the speed limits
fixed in these two areas, speeding convictions result only in connection with
omnibuses, char-a-bancs, motor coaches
and goods lorries. In the year 1928
convictions for speeding with such
vehicles were obtained in 603 cases, but
in the year 1929 the number was only
358. When it is remembered that the
increase in the number of convictions for
dangerous driving was mainly due to
speed cases being dealt with as dangerous
driving rather than as speeding, the
marked improvement which has been.
effected under these two headings will
readily be appreciated. A comparison
between the returns of convictions
obtained during these two years shows
that so far as omnibuses or char-a-bancs
are concerned the convictions for reckless driving decreased from 34 to 29, and
those for speeding from 354 to 231.
It may interest the Committee to be
told something of the Belfast traffic.
During the year 1928 the number of
accidents caused by vehicles was 580,
while in 1929 the total had fallen to
352, and this difference must be
attributed mainly to the withdrawal
towards the end of the year 1928 of the
omnibus competition which had been so
prominent a feature of the City's traffic
problems during that year. Regarding
the automatic traffic control which has
been installed in Belfast, this has been
in operation for over a month, and has
proved successful. I believe that this
principle should be extended, and with
such extension it will be necessary to
provide appropriate by-laws, which we
are engaged in framing.
The first meeting of the Roads
Advisory Committee was held on the
11th instant. It is hoped to be able to
obtain the advice and assistance of the
Committee at the first few meetings
which will be held on the following
matters:-Regulation of regular omnibus
services; Lighting of road vehicles;
Speed of heavy motor cars--both passenger-carrying vehicles and goods
vehicles. Other matters regarding traffic regulation, local and general, will be
brought before the Committee at an
early date.
I should like to refer to the question
of Reciprocity between Great Britain
and Northern Ireland as regards motor
traffic. The free circulation of private
motor cars and motor cycles between
Great Britain and Northern Ireland and
vice versa has continued uninterruptedly
since the transfer of services. Vehicle
licences issued in one area for such
vehicles are without question recognised
in the other, and so far an informal
recognition has also been afforded to
driving licences. It is desirable that the
inter-availability of such licences should
continue, and with that object in view.
negotiations were conducted with the
Ministry of Transport in London, and as
a result the Road Traffic Bill at present
before the Imperial Parliament contains
a provision for the recognition in Great
Britain of driving licences granted in
Northern Ireland. It will be necessary
for this Government to introduce a
similar Measure for Northern Ireland.
One of the most important aspects of
road traffic in Northern Ireland is the
increased importance which motor omnibus transport assumes in our social
system. I am glad to be able to say once
again that the system and principle
which was established over a year ago
with the approval of Parliament is working smoothly and satisfactorily. When
speaking on the subject of the regulation
of omnibus traffic from time to time, I
have drawn the attention of Members to
the list of casualties in which motor
omnibuses were concerned, and I have
expressed my conviction that the afrangements which I was making would have
an important effect in reducing the
casualty list by taking away from drivers.
of omnibuses the temptation to indulge
in dangerous practices on the road, such
as excessive speeding and racing on the
roads. The results in this respect have
exceeded my most sanguine expectations.
The figures for the years 1928 and 1929
make this very clear-they are as
follow :--


Persons Persons
Accidents. Injured. Killed.


The Committee will observe that the
numbers of accidents and the numbers
of persons injured have been reduced by
more than one-half, while the number of
persons killed also show a very considerable decrease.
Supply-
Committee
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Sir Dawson Bates]
People who continually travel on the
roads assure me that there is a most
marked improvement in the manner in
which these vehicles are driven, both
from the point of view of safety and
from the point of view of courtesy to
other road users. Indeed many private
motorists might well take example in
matters of courtesy and consideration
from the professional drivers of these
vehicles. At the present time there are
services being operated on 343 routes in
Northern Ireland, and this figure includes 20 new routes which have been
opened up within the past six months,
which seems to me to contradict the
statement which was so often made that
with the regulation of omnibus traffe
development would be arrested.
Throughout the year the work of improving the service to the public has gone on.
time-tables have been adjusted in many
cases so as to give an improved service
and to ensure that the existing services
are run at such times as will be of the
maximum convenience to the public.
I wish to take this opportunity of paying a tribute to the staff of the Ministry
which has been in charge of this work.
I have received much independent
evidence of their tact and efficiency, and
operators have gone out of their way to
express to me their appreciation of the
helpful manner in which they have been
dealt with by my staff. Reports have
appeared in the Press from time to time
of amalgamations of omnibus undertakings, and of acquisitions by the larger
operators and by railway companies,
and I am sure that the Committee will
expect me to say something on this subject, especially as some apprehension has
been expressed lest such amalgamations
should operate to deprive the public of
services which they have had. I am
satisfied that such fears are entirely
groundless. This process of amalgamation is not confined to Northern Ireland.
It has been suggested that it has resulted
from the system of control, but this is
obviously not the case as a similar
process has taken place in England,
Scotland, Wales, and the Irish Free
State, where competition at the present
moment is free and unrestricted. The
cause of these amalgamations must,
therefore, be common to all these
countries, and indeed it is easy to discern
the impulse which is driving the industry
in this direction.
It has been found that road passenger
traffic can be undertaken more cheaply
and more efficiently by large units rather
than by the small operator. An operator
who can spread his overhead charges over
a large number of vehicles and who can
buy his petrol, tyres and other necessities
in large quantities and therefore on good
terms, can run his vehicles at a smaller
cost per mile. A reduction in costs is
the best hope of maintaining cheap transport in Northern Ireland. The public
have had very cheap transport for a number of years, but the evidence is overwhelming that that cheapness was secured
by running services at less than the economic cost and at the expense of the
capital invested in the business. The
condition was, therefore, a purely artificial one, and would not have been maintained.
Members of the Committee will have
noticed from the Press reports that the
railways in Northern Ireland are now becoming important omnibus proprietors.
They have now realised that omnibuses
are an essential element in the road transport system of the country, and that they
are necessary to supplement the railway
services. They have, therefore. entered
seriously into the business and either by
the establishment of new services or the
acquisition of existing services they have
now become large operators. There are
many advantages in this for it ensures coordination of the various forms of transport and will enable the railways to offer
many facilities to the public, such as the
interchangeability of tickets, which was
an unheard of thing in the earlier days.
I would like to emphasise that in every
case in which services have been acquired,
whether by the railway company or any
other operator, the transaction has been
carefully scrutinised by the Ministry and
sanction has only been given where the
Ministry is satisfied that the transaction
will result in better service to the public.
It has been made clear, in the most
specific terms, to those responsible for the
management of railways in Northern Ireland that the road services must be maintained in the most efficient manner and
that they will not be allowed to deprive
the public of the road services to which
they are fully entitled, but at the same
time I must sav in all fairness to the
railway companies, that I have seen no
evidence of any attempt on their part to
use their position in this direction. On
the contrary, where they have acquired
Supply-

services, they have at once set to work to

may be allowed to quote from the issue

The paper, which is published in the Irish
Free State, is commenting on the acquisition of the control of the Irish Omnibus
Company by the Great Southern Railway
and of the acquisition of certain services
belonging to the Belfast Omnibus Company by the London Midland and
Scottish Railway. It says-and I cannot
put my own views in better language-
"Unlike the Great Southern Railway who, as the Free State law stands,
are free to close down all the Irish
Omnibus Companies and other services
of which they have obtained control,
the London Midland and Scottish Railway, under Northern Ireland law, must
not only continue the required road
services, but accept the decisions of Sir

to further future time tables and
rates of fares. Should they quarrel with such decisions the penalty
is clear. It will become the business of the Tribunal to throw the
L.M.S. road services open to other competitors. With a vigilant and active
travelling public keeping a close eye on
both the L.M.S. and the official Tribunal it is therefore safe to assume that
there is little, if any, danger that the
latest railway enterprise will have the
effect of crippling Northern Ireland
road operations."
That is the policy which I have set out
on many occasions in regard to road
traffic.

I would like to say a word or two about
the very important question of derating.
It is hardly necessary for me to dilate on
the benefits which this principle has conferred on the agricultural community as
well as on our productive industries in Northern Ireland, and I will simply confine
my remarks, therefore, to the steps which
under the Act recently passed by this Parliament it has been necessary for the
Ministry of Home Affairs to take in order
that full effect might be given to the principles embodied in the Act.
It will be remembered that the Act
made a clear distinction between the first
Supply-
Committee
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Sir Dawson Bates]
year of its operation and the succeeding
years. As regards the first year, it was
simply enacted that the Government
would recoup to local authorities the
actual losses sustained by them owing to
the operation of the principle of derating,
while as regards the succeeding years the
Act laid down that grants were to be paid
on the basis of the expenditure in each
area other than county borough and
urban district council areas during the
three standard years, namely, the financial
years 1926-27, 1927-28, and 1928-29.
The Act also recognised that local government services tend to develop and that
there might be under certain heads of expenditure an increase, and in order to
meet this increase it was laid down that
supplementary grants would be payable
with the approval of the Ministry up to a
specified limit calculated at the rate of 6d
in the pound. The working out of the
standard expenditures and the calculation
of the standard grants based on these
standard expenditures has been a work
of enormous labour and complexity, and,
to add to this work, it has been necessary
for the Ministry with great care to work
out the supplemental grants paid to each
local authority. In connection with this
very difficult work, here again I would
like to pay a tribute to the staff of the
Home Office in charge of the matter.
In order to appreciate the real benefit,
particularly in the rural areas, of the
principle of derating, I think it well to
specify in detail to what extent the Government is under present arrangements
shouldering the burden of expense in the
various counties. I think the best way of
showing this in a form that will be readily
understood is to give it in the form of
percentages
In County Antrim the Government
are bearing no less than 73 per cent.
of local expenditure.
In County Armagh the percentage is
84.
In County Down the percentage is 74.
In County Fermanagh the percentage
is 88.
In County Londonderry the percentage is 80.
In County Tyrone the percentage is
83.
I might point out that the difference between the percentages of County Antrim
and County Down and the other counties
is that these two counties possess a larger
proportion of non-derateable premises
than the other four counties.
It will thus be appreciated that the
whole aspect of local government has been
changed and that in the rural areas particularly the Government is the biggest
ratepayer. In the two county boroughs
the proportion of expenditure borne by
the Government under the derating principle is about 11 per cent., this being, of
course, in respect of the 75 per cent. relief given to industrial hereditaments,
while in the urban districts the Government's share of expenditure under derating varies from 6 per cent. to 16.5 per
cent.
In a review of the services which come
within the purview of the Home Office Department, the first aspect of this side of
administration which calls for notice is the
general question of the peace of the community, and here I think it is merely
sufficient for me to refer to the fact that,
as has been stated by the judges who presided over the various Assizes, there is a
strong downward trend in crime in Northern Ireland. When I come to the question of Prison administration the Members
of the Committee will see a corroboration
of this fact in our Prison Statistics, and
I am sure that all the Members
of the Committee will join with me in appreciating the fact that in our Northern
Ireland people there is this downward tendency as regards crime.
It would not be wrong for me to say
that, while to a very large extent this
gratifying feature is due to the moral influences exercised on the community by
the various Churches, and, indeed, by the
instincts of the people themselves, on the
other hand we cannot leave out of account
the fact that has been commented on by
the judges that this diminution in crime
is to a great extent due to the activities
and efforts of our police force, and here
I should also include the Special Constabulary who by their association with
the police force in the country exercise
such a steadying influence on the community as a whole.

With regard to illicit distillation,

for obvious reasons one of the most difficult offences to detect. While the number
of cases in which persons have been
brought to justice has substantially increased it is a deplorable fact that this
evil should exist to the extent it does.
The police are very severely handicapped
by the reluctance of some of the population to give information, and I would
appeal to all to help in stamping out one
of the greatest curses a country could
have. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear).

Before I sit down may I say a word
about prisons? The first feature of importance which calls for notice in connection with our prison administration is the
steady reduction in the numbers confined
in our prisons. Five years ago—that is
after the troubles had subsided in Northern Ireland-in 1925
3,142
we had
Northern Ireland prisoners committed
during the year. During the year 1918
the number committed was 2,928-a reduction of over 200, while for the year
1929 the number of committals had fallen
to 2,744-a very satisfactory figure.
The Home Office is, as has been explained to the Committee on previous
occasions, faced with considerable difficulty in the administration in connection
with the proper classification of prisoners
owing to the limited accommodation available in Northern Ireland. In Great
Britain and other centres where prison administration is on a much wider and more
extended scale it is possible for the prison
authorities to arrange for different classes
of institutions to which the different
classes of prisoners can be sent. With us,
unfortunately, it is necessary to confine in
the same institution not only convicts but

Reverting to the police, I have already
paid my tribute to the Force, and I want
to say this, not for the purposes of criticism, but with the object of procuring
a remedy. There are great complaints.
about discipline being too tight in the
City of Belfast. In regard to discipline.
the old proverb is ever true :-"Wide will
wear, but tight will tear." If men are
hauled over the coals and punished for
little things, it rankles in their minds,
and eventually it does not assist discipline. I quite agree that discipline must
be maintained, but it is quite possible to
make the discipline too tight, and a course
of that kind will finally do more harm than
good. I am sorry to say that I hear
some complaints in that respect. A little
more kindness would cure all that. If a
man makes himself impossible, by all
means deal with him, but punishing a
man for petty things never does any good.
Of
A man on the first relief in the early
morning may be smoking, and his officer
may see him smoking, but it would be far
better to pretend that he did not see him.
I am speaking from experience. It would
be appreciated. The man would probably
be more careful in the future. It would
be better for the man, better for the
officer, and better for the Service.
course the police should not gossip, but
that doctrine can be pushed too far, because if a policeman does not speak to
people he can never hear anything; he
never can know anything; he never can
be useful. If he has an ordinary conversation with a man coming out of a shop,
or something like that, he will perhaps
hear something that it may be useful for
him to know; it may increase his local
knowledge, and therefore it should not be
dealt with too seriously. That, of course,
is a different thing from a man gossiping
for gossip's sake, or from a man on point
duty gossiping. The man on point duty
has no time to gossip; he has enough to do
to look after his duty. If matters were
improved in these respects, the Service.
would be improved.

is at present before the Imperial Parliament. At any rate it is incorporating
principles along those lines. Some parts
of our city are in great need of clearing
up. A very distinguished literary Ulster
man said not very long ago that if he had
to live in one of the slum areas he would
probably drink and he would certainly
riot from one year's end to the other.
I think it rather a pity that the
Northern Government does not give
facilities to public utility societies similar
to those which are given in England, and
also in the Irish Free State. I am inclined
to think that according to the present law
the Government can make grants to public
utility societies up to two-thirds of the
value of any working-class houses that
may be built by such society. The Government as a matter of fact does not do it.
Now these societies are capable of doing
good work, and there is very little risk in
financing them in this way; and if there
is any difficulty or obstacle in the way of
facilitating such societies in supplementing
the good work in building houses that has
been done by the Government, I hope the
Government will be enabled to remove
those difficulties.

It has been said that the terms given to

In the 1927 Act the conditions were not so
favourable. The result has been that
rural district councils have been discouraged. It is said, perhaps with some
truth, that members elected to rural councils are elected for the purpose of keeping
down rates.

Mr. DEVLIN: I agree with my hon.

in some matters the English people are
a very timid people? Although a people
with a great deal of fundamental and inherent courage they are timid. Bernard
Shaw said about them that the Irish had
a reputation of being sentimental, but
they were not sentimental, it was only
the English who were sentimental. What
does a tourist, who comes over here to
Northern Ireland for a holiday, think

armed with revolvers? He gets the
conviction in his mind-it is one of the
usual ignorant ideas the English people
get about this country-that his life
would not be safe here.
I am, in fact, a sort of tourist agent
myself. I am always telling the people.
about the beauties of Ireland, and particularly of my own part of Ireland.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) And
sometimes, even at this time of the day,

over there now?" My own opinion is,
and I tell it to them, that it was always
safe to come here. We do not hate

each other. (Laughter.) Even in the

there was a most violent anti-English
feeling individual Englishmen were perfectly safe. We do not, either in the

bodies.

In my judgment what you ought to do

objection to a policeman if he is a policeman, but there are two classes of the community I cannot stand, one is a lay
preacher and the other is an ununiformed
policeman. You put the badge of
superiority, if it can be so regarded, upon
one citizen as against another. If I
lived in a country village or in a town,
and I am as good and peace-loving and
law-abiding as my neighbour, what right
has he to constitute himself or what right
have you to constitute him a policeman to
keep order, to be superior to me, and to
have a rifle in his house and sometimes a
rifle outside his house?
I read a case some weeks ago in which
bailiffs a class of people not very acceptable to me-went upon a farm to make a
seizure for debt or something of that sort.
They were obstructed in the due process
of carrying out the law, I think that is
the legal expression. What happened?
Out came the two sons of the person to
whom this writ was addressed with rifles
to shoot the two bailiffs. Shooting
bailiffs may have been a popular thing in
the old days. In these days of wide-spread
peace it is not just as acceptable as in more
primitive periods. I think these men
were prosecuted, and it was Lord Justice
Andrews, I believe, who made a strong
animadversion on their conduct.
What was their explanation when they
were asked where they got the rifles that
were being used to shoot to some extent
some reprehensible officers of the law?
They said they were specials and, as such,
got these rifles. I would ask the Prime
Minister to bear this in mind that these
specials when they got these rifles as
specials were, therefore, exercising that
due superiority, to which I have referred,
of the right to shoot anybody they do not
like, especially if he happens to be a
bailiff. That is a luxury to be entirely
confined to the "B" Specials for which
this Government is asked to pay £60,000
a year.
If a policeman is to be a policeman let
him be a policeman. Let him bear the
ordinary discipline which an ordinary

any other part of the world. That is
point No. 1. Then, the meanness of
their remuneration. What are they paid?
They are paid £2 a year. It is bad

Emigration is going on steadily from
the Six Counties, and that again does not
indicate that the people are content or
that the community is prosperous.
As an
indication of whether the people are saving more in recent years let me quote you
some figures taken from the Ulster Year
Book, figures which are therefore official.
In 1924-25 the average savings per
head of the population was £7. In
1927-28, which is the last year for
which statistics are available. the saving
per head remained the same, £7. In the
Free State in 1924-25 the average savings
were £2 per head, but they had risen by
300 per cent. in 1927-28 to £6 per head,
and last year I believe they were in excess
of that. There is a specific case of where
your people are not improving their conditions, and where the people across the
border are materially improving theirs.
I would direct the Parliamentary and
Financial Secretary's particular attention
to this fact. It is all very well for the
Minister of Labour to ascend a hill at
Comber. in County Down, and rhapsodise
about the Six Counties past and future,

know whether his forefathers had exactly
the same national feelings as he has, but
I rather imagine some of them had not.
You have staring you in the face the economic fact that people are leaving the Six
Counties and that those who remain are
not saving anvthing, and their position,
so far from being improved by a Government of their own, is actually being
worsened.

CLAUSE 2 (Infliction of corporal
punishment in Borstal Institutions.
8 Edw. 7, c. 59).
If the governor (or, in his absence,
the chief officer) of a Borstal Institution
for male young offenders within the
meaning of Part I. of the Prevention of
Crime Act. 1908, reports to the visiting
committee of such Institution that an
offender detained therein has been
guilty of grave misconduct for which no
appropriate punishment is provided by
the enactments, regulations and rules
which apply to the Institution, the
visiting committee, or any two members
thereof, shall inquire into the facts of
the case, and, if they are of opinion
that the case cannot be met except by
the corporal punishment of the offender,
may order the infliction upon
offender of such corporal punishment as
they consider necessary to meet the case,
subject, however, to such general regulations as may be made by the Ministry of Home Affairs under sub-section
(2) of section four and section eighteen
of the Prevention of Crime Act, 1908.

Criminal Law Bill
Adjournment
16 APRIL 1930
This Amendment, which was proposed
by the Government, and accepted in
another place, is of a purely drafting
character and does not in any way alter
the sense or the intention of the Bill. The
Clause as originally drafted provided that
the infliction of corporal punishment was
to be subject to such regulations as might
be made under the Prevention of Crime
Act, 1908, which requires regulations
made thereunder to be laid before Parliament. It was considered, however, as
open to question whether the section so
drafted did in fact carry out the intention
of the Government inasmuch as the Prevention of Crime Act did not confer the
power of imposing corporal punishment.
In order, therefore, to place it beyond
doubt that the imposition of corporal
punishment would be subject to regulations which would be laid before Parliament it has been thought advisable by the
Government that this Amendment should
be inserted.
Amendment agreed to.
Ordered: That a Message be sent to the
Senate to acquaint them that this House
has agreed to the Amendments made by
the Senate to the said Bill without any
amendment.

BREACHES OF LICENSING LAWS
DURING 1929.
2. Mr. CRAWFORD asked the Minister of Home Affairs whether he can
state the number of prosecutions against
licence holders for breaches of the
licensing laws during 1929, the number
of convictions and the number of cases
in which the licences were endorsed?
The MINISTER OF HOME AF-
FAIRS (Sir Dawson Bates): The
number of prosecutions of licence holders
for breaches of the licensing laws during
1929 was 200, during the same period
the number of convictions was 132, and
the number of cases in which the
licences were endorsed was 8.
It must be understood that the offences
in which convictions were obtained were
not all of the character involving endorsement on conviction.
NON-CONTESTED LOCAL GOVERN-
MENT ELECTIONS.
1. Mr. CRAWFORD (for Mr. Miller)
asked the Minister of Home Affairs
whether he considers it is necessary or
advisable in case of non-contested Local
Government elections to placard and disfigure the countryside with large bills
informing all and sundry that there will
be "No Poll," when everyone has known
of the fact weeks before through the
public Press, and, if not, whether he
would take the necessary steps to have
this expensive and useless practice discontinued?
Sir DAWSON BATES: The publication of the notice to which the hon.
Member refers is required by Rules 45
and 46 of the First Schedule of the
Ballot Act, 1872, which applies to Local
Government elections.
It is the official intimation from the
Returning Officer to the electors of the
area concerned that they will not be called
upon to exercise their votes in connection
with the election in question, and it could
hardly be considered proper that the
public should have to rely upon newspaper reports or hearsay for information
of such importance to them.
The cost of posting these notices is
small as it is an inconsiderable item in
the general contract taken by the county
council for all placarding of this kind.
ORDERS OF THE DAY.
Companies Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.
Motion made, and Question proposed,
"That the Bill be now read a Second
time.
The MINISTER OF COMMERCE
(Mr. Barbour): The Bill to which the
House will be asked to give a Second
Reading to-day is one which affects the
activities of our commercial and industrial community in a great variety of
ways.
The system of finance by joint stock
has made remarkable strides during the
past half-century, and nowhere have the
advantages of limited liability been more
keenly appreciated than in Northern
Ireland. It is, therefore, not surprising
to find that the greater portion of the
industry of our province is conducted
957 Companies Bill-
29 APRIL 1930

Second Reading
under joint stock principles either by
is more frepublic companies or, as
quently the case, by the private limited
company into which so many of our
"family" businesses have been formed.
This tendency is further illustrated by
the high proportion of Irish joint stock
companies which in the past were domiciled in Northern Ireland.
For example, while at the end of 1920
there were in all Ireland 2,520 living
companies having a paid-up capital of
almost £70,000,000, there were in Northern Ireland alone, at the end of 1925,
the first year for which authentic figures
for our area are available, 1,339 living
companies having a paid-up capital of
almost £50,000,000. In the succeeding
years, while there has been no marked
change in the amount of the paid-up
capital there has been a small but steady
increase in the number of living companies on the Northern Ireland Register,
and this must be regarded as a favourable feature having regard to the years
of depression through which we have
passed.
Apart from short Acts passed in 1913
and 1917, and the Act in 1923, providing
for the reconstitution of the destroyed
records, there has been no development
in joint stock company legislation since
1908, when the Consolidation Act, under
which we are working to-day, was passed.
This Act, excellent as it was at the time,
and well designed to cover every development of joint stock company enterprise
of the period, has been found to have
many shortcomings when applied to conditions and practices which have sprung
up in the period of post-war reconstruction; and so, here in Northern Ireland
as in Great Britain, it has been found
desirable to consider what Amendments
are necessary to bring the law into closer
relationship with commercial conditions
as they exist to-day.
In approaching this matter, I may say
at once that we have derived the greatest
assistance from the Report of the deliberations of the very able Committee, presided
over by Sir Wilfrid Greene, K.C., which
in 1925 and 1926 reviewed the whole field
of company law and practice, and presented a Report, the chief recommendations of which were embodied in a Bill
in the Imperial Parliament, which became
law in August, 1928, as the Companies
Act, 1928. This Act, with the exception.
of two Clauses-one dealing with share
hawking or share-pushing, and one relating to capital re-organisations did not
come into force until a Consolidation Act
was passed, and this latter Act came into
complete operation on 1st November last.
In Northern Ireland we propose to
follow, in the matter of legislation, the
scheme adopted in the Imperial Parliament, that is to say, we propose in the
Bill now before the House many changes
in the Company Law as it applies to
Northern Ireland at the present time, and
when this Bill has been passed we propose
to introduce a new Measure consolidating
Company Law in Northern Ireland. With
the exception of the provisions as to reconstruction and share-hawking or sharepushing, we propose to suspend the provisions of the present Bill until such time
as the second Bill shall have received legislative sanction.
I can-
In preparing the present Bill we have
sought to improve and to tighten up the
law without imposing restrictions that
would seriously impede the administration
of properly conducted companies.
not hold out the hope that it will be possible by the legislation put forward in this
Bill, or in any Bill, completely to prevent
frauds. The Committee to which I have
already referred pointed out that the idea
that fraud and lesser malpractices can be
stopped by legislation dies hard, and that
it is not possible either to make the Company Law perfect or to protect fools or
indiscreet persons from the consequences
of their folly. I cannot dissent from this
expression of opinion.
""
The fabric of our commercial system is
"interwoven with credit spun from character, good faith, and honest dealing,'
but, nevertheless, it will always be necessary for members of the investing public
to use their intelligence or seek advice
from those competent to give it if they
are to invest their capital and their savings
wisely. Happily, however, the objectionable practices that have in recent months
caused so much loss and uneasiness in
Great Britain have made but little headway in Northern Ireland, due in a large
measure, I have no doubt, to the natural
Hon. Members
caution of our people.
will appreciate, however, how essential it
is in view of our close commercial relations
with Great Britain that we should diverge
as little as possible from the code of Company Law in force in the other part of the
United Kingdom.
Companies Bil!-
Second Reading
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Barbour]
As hon. Members may have noticed, the
Bill is in the main a series of dissociated
amendments, and I, therefore, propose today to confine my observations to matters
of major importance and of general interest. In so doing, I should like to take
this opportunity of expressing to those
local professional bodies who have been
good enough to advise on various matters
arising out of the preparation of the
Measure, my keen appreciation of their
assistance.
Clause 1 deals with the names of companies. As regards the names of companies, the use of the words "Royal,"
'Imperial" and "chartered" in the
names of companies is already restricted
in Northern Ireland by Section 1 of the
Companies Act, 1928, which became
effective on 1st November, 1929, and
further restrictions are now placed by
Clause 1 of the Bill upon the use of the
words "Municipal," "Co-operative" and
"Chamber of Commerce," while the use
of the words "building society" by a
company as a part of its name is prohibited
altogether.
In regard to capital, which comes under
Clause 16, companies will be permitted to
issue redeemable preference shares in
cases where they take power in their
Articles of Association to do so. Such
shares may be redeemed out of profits
which would otherwise be available for
dividend, or, alternatively, out of the proceeds of a fresh issue of shares made for
the purposes of the redemption. The condition is attached that when profits are
employed to reduce capital there must be
transferred to a reserve fund to be called
"the capital redemption reserve fund" an
equivalent amount. This condition will
serve to protect creditors and to prevent a
reduction of capital without due sanction.
Under Clause 14 it will no longer be
possible to use the resources of a company
for the acquisition of its shares. I need
not emphasise the importance of this
amendment of the law or the mischief
which has been caused in some cases by
such use of a company's financial resources. Exception is made of the purchase of shares for the benefit of employees
or the making of loans to employees other
than directors for the purchase of a company's shares.
Under Clause 17 (3) of the Bill, repealing section 40 of the Companies (Consolidation) Act, 1908, it will no longer be
lawful for companies to distribute accumulated profits to shareholders by way of
reduction of paid-up share capital. This
section has seldom been availed of in
Northern Ireland, and its main use elsewhere was for the purpose of evading
liability to supertax.
Shareholders of registered companies
will be protected by Clause 3 from any
obligation being placed on them without
their consent to subscribe for additional
shares. This method of raising capital by
framing the constitution so as to place
shareholders under obligation to take up
additional shares was sometimes employed
in Industrial and Provident Societies but
cannot now be used by such societies
owing to an amendment made in the law
last year.
Turning to the matter of accounts and
balance sheets, in Clauses 37 to 42 of the
Bill we have provisions with respect to
accounts, balance sheets, audit and the
rights of members and debenture holders
to receive copies of balance sheets and reports of directors and auditors. Every
company will be obliged to keep proper
books of accounts, and directors will be
liable to imprisonment or to a fine not
exceeding £200 for failure to take steps
to secure compliance. (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear).
So far
Every balance sheet must under Clause
40 contain a summary of the authorised
share capital and of the issued share
capital of the company, its liabilities and
its assets, together with such particulars
as are necessary to disclose the general
nature of the liabilities and the assets, and
to distinguish between fixed and floating
assets, and to state how the values of the
fixed assets have been arrived at.
as the following items are not written off
there must be stated-the preliminary expenses of the company; any expenses incurred in connection with any issue of
shares or debentures, and the amount of
the goodwill and of any patents and trade
marks if ascertainable. Provision is also
made for the treatment of assets consisting
of shares in, or debts due by, subsidiary
companies.
A profit and loss account must under
Clause 38 be laid before the company in
general meeting once at least in each
calendar year and also a balance sheet and
a report by the directors with respect to
the state of the company's affairs.
961 Companies Bill—

29 APRIL 1930
Second Reading
Under Clause 42 every member of a
public company must be furnished with a
copy of the balance sheet and any holder
of debentures is entitled to have a copy of
the balance sheet and of the documents required by law to be annexed to it. Members of private companies and also debenture holders will be entitled to copies of
the balance sheets on payment for same at
a charge not exceeding 6d for every
hundred words. Hon. Members will observe that one result of the new legislation
will be to afford considerably more information to the investing public than has
hitherto been the case.
I now turn to the subject of offers for
sale and prospectuses. Clause 96 of the
Bill prohibits any house-to-house canvass
for the sale of shares, and imposes heavy
penalties for any infringement of the law.
This prohibition should have a salutory
effect, for, although it is a customary
method of selling sound shares in some
countries overseas, in these islands the
practice has generally been associated
with shares of little, if any, intrinsic
value. It has, accordingly, become necessary to protect the public in their homes
from the attention of eloquent but unscrupulous sharepushers. Restrictions
are also placed upon offers of shares made
in writing, such offers in future having to
be accompanied by a statement in writing
giving many particulars.
As regards prospectuses, hon. Members
will find the requirements set forth in
Clauses 30 and 31 and the First Schedule
to the Bill. A practice has grown up in
recent years of selling shares or debentures
in bulk to an issuing house so that the
latter may offer them to the public. In
some cases this was done with the object
of avoiding the onerous conditions attaching to prospectuses within the meaning of
the Act, and documents were issued which
the public regarded as prospectuses but
which were not prospectuses in the legal
sense.
Clause 30 provides that any document
by which such an offer is made to the
public shall for all purposes be deemed to
be a prospectus issued by the company and
that all enactments and rules of law as to
the contents of prospectuses and to liability in respect of statements in, and
omissions from, prospectuses or otherwise
relating to prospectuses shall apply and
have effect accordingly as if the shares or
debentures had been offered to the public
for subscription and as if persons accepting the offer in respect of any shares or
debentures were subscribers for those
shares or debentures. In other words, the
directors of a company will be liable to be
called to account for statements in, or
omissions from, documents offering shares
or debentures to the public in cases where
the company sold such shares or debentures in bulk with the object of their
being offered to the public. I regard this
as a valuable amendment of the law, and
I am sure hon. Members will agree with
that.
The particulars to be stated in a prospectus are extended and include-If the
proceeds are to be applied in the purchase
of any business, a report by an accountant
to be named in the prospectus upon the
profits of the business for each of the three
previous years; if the share capital of
the company is divided into classes, the
right of voting at meetings and the rights
in respect of capital and dividends attached to each class; a report by the
auditors of the company with respect to
the profits for three years and with respect
to the dividends paid on each class of
shares.
Clause 32 deals with the character of
the minimum subscription, which will
also be changed and must represent the
minimum amount which in the opinion of
the directors must be raised by the issue
of the shares to provide the sums required
in respect of (a) the purchase price of
any property purchased or to be purchased; (b) any preliminary expenses and
any commission payable on shares; (c) the
repayment of any moneys borrowed for
the foregoing matters; (d) working
capital. The minimum subscription will,
however, only attach to companies offering
shares to the public for subscription, that
is to say, to prospectus companies. Companies which file a statement in lieu of
prospectus will no longer have to fix a
minimum subscription.
Clauses 97 and 98 provide that any
prospectuses issued by foreign and
Dominion companies in Northern Ireland
will require to be registered and to conform to the requirements laid down in
the Bill. We do not propose, however, in
this connection to treat British companies
as foreign companies. Some changes will
be made by this Bill in the internal regulation of companies.
Companies Bill-
Second Reading
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Barbour]
Under Clause 5 every company having
more than fifty members will have to keep
an index of the names of its members unless its register of members already constitutes an index. A card index is permissible. In the annual return furnished
by a company to the Registrar of Companies the names of the members must
under Clause 6 be arranged in alphabetical order. Alternatively there must
be annexed to the return an index sufficient to enable the name of any person
in the list to be readily found. I may
mention at this point that companies other
than private companies will be required
to send in copies of their audited balance
sheets as part of their annual return, and
this requirement will attach to companies
limited by guarantee as well as to companies which have a share capital.
Under Clause 23 it will no longer be
necessary to hold two meetings for the
purpose of passing a special resolution,
and a resolution will be a special resolution
when it is passed by a majority of not less.
than three-fourths at a general meeting of
which not less than twenty-one days'
notice specifying the intention to propose
the resolution has been given. In the
case of an extraordinary resolution, a
three-fourths majority of those voting in
person or by proxy will be required instead of as hitherto a majority of threefourths of those present in person or by
proxy at the meeting.
Some changes are proposed in the Bill
concerning the rights of dissenting shareholders. Difficulties have sometimes
arisen in the past through the obstinacy of
a small minority of shareholders who will
not assent to a scheme or contract for the
transfer of the shares of a company to
another company.
Under Clause 52 of
the Bill, in cases where an offer by a transferee company is approved by the holders
of nine-tenths of the shares affected, the
dissenting shareholder will be obliged to
transfer his shares on the terms agreed by
the majority of the shareholders unless he
can persuade the Court to make an order
to the contrary.
Clause 15 provides that in cases where
the rights of a class of shareholders are
being varied by resolutions of the holders
of shares of that class, a minority consisting of the holders of not less than fifteen
per cent. of the shares may apply to the
Court to have the variation cancelled.
There are one or two other changes proposed in this Bill to which I should like to
make a passing reference. The scope of
registration of mortgages and charges is
extended so as to include mortgages on
ships or on goodwill, patents, trade marks,
and copyrights, and mortgages on lands
acquired subject to mortgages.
The powers of creditors and of liquidators will be considerably extended and
voluntary liquidations will fall to be
divided into two classes, one in the case
of creditors voluntarily winding up, covering liquidations where the directors cannot make a declaration that in their
opinion the company will be able to pay
its debts in full within twelve months;
and secondly, shareholders voluntarily
winding up where the directors are able
to make such a declaration.
The procedure set up to regulate creditors voluntarily winding up will be found in Clause
68.
I have referred to the principal Amendments embodied in the Measure now before
the House. As hon. Members will observe, the Bill, consisting as it does of
Amendments relating to a diversity of
matters, does not lend itself readily to a
Second Reading speech. I beg to move.
Mr. COLLINS: I am one of those who
would like to see plenty of business in the

to deal with the business that exists in it
and that will come to it in the future I
would just like to point to one Clause
which I observed while the Minister was
making his able speech. It will be found
on page 92. My attention was directed

I had with a merchant in the course of my
business yesterday in Newry. In talking

had had no less than seven representatives

Marsh's, our own little biscuit factory in

across the Channel, and also of Jacob's.

It struck me that it was an extraordinary thing that the representative of
our own biscuit factory, Marsh's, could

country, namely, the Free State, while

And then I thought of the new policy of

Just take the illustration of biscuits.

I say this-and this not only applies to

Great Britain as from the manufacturers

you are cutting across the whole scheme as

The Minister of Commerce (Mr. Barbour)
did not deal at length with this section
when he was introducing the Bill. I do
not blame him for not dealing at length

is a very voluminous Bill. But I would
like to know did Great Britain enforce this
upon us, have we to take this lying down,
because it is a thing that should be removed at once. I direct, or at least I request the Minister of Commerce, in the
interest of the people whom he is representing here, namely, the manufacturers
and traders of Northern Ireland, to give

Mr. BARBOUR: The brief Measure, to
the Second Reading of which I now seek
the approval of the House, has for its object the amplification of Section 45 of the
Railways and Canal Traffic Act, 1888,
The section in question makes provision
for the procedure to be adopted on the
abandonment of a canal. I am advised
that, in so far as the provisions of Section
45 relate to derelict canals, as distinct
from unnecessary canals as defined in the
Act, no amendement of the existing law
is necessary. It happens, however, that
since the passing of the Act forty years
ago there has not been any case of abandonment of an unnecessary canal, where
difficulties arose in regard to the settlement of compensation as between the canal
company and those persons entitled to
compensation by reason of the proposed
abandonment. Such a case has now aren
in Northern Ireland.
Railways and Canal Bill
Supply
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Barbour]
If hon. Members will turn to the
Measure which is now before them they
will observe that Clause 1 amplifies the
provisions of Section 45 of the 1888 Act.
I should perhaps mention that under the
1888 Act two stages were necessary in
acceding to the application of the canal
concern, namely:-
-
(a) the granting of a Warrant of
Abandonment after compensation had
been paid; and
(b) the issue of an Order of Release
from all statutory and other obligations
in respect of the canal.
This second step, of course, came at a date
considerably later than the issue of the
warrant of abandonment.
The procedure to which I have referred
as to the issue of the warrant and order
of release will still apply, but the Bill now
before the House makes provision whereby
compensation does not actually require to
be paid before the warrant is issued.
When the Bill becomes law it will be
sufficient that security for compensation
should be given. Moreover, a weakness
in existing legislation has been met by the
provision that the order of release shall
dispose of lands which may be in the hands
of the canal company at the time the warrant of abandonment is issued. Clearly
it is most undesirable that any such lands
should be abandoned and become in effect
a" no man's land."
The 1888 Act did not make any definite
provisions as to how compensation was to
be determined and I have accordingly
thought it well to have laid down a procedure involving the appointment of an
independent arbitrator."
There is one other provision to which I
might draw attention, and that is that
where you have adjoining landowners or
others who desire sections of the canal
lands it is eminently desirable that such
lands should be capable of transfer with
the minimum expense and trouble to all
involved. With this in view the Bill
provides for the award and order of release to operate as vesting orders, a short
and expeditious method of arranging for
the transfer of ownership in such cases.
Hon. Members will observe that such
vesting orders will, under the provisions
of the Bill, be exempt from stamp duty. I
beg to move.
Question put, and agreed to.
Bill read a Second time, and committed
to a Committee of the Whole House for
to-morrow.

The PRIME MINISTER: I am very
glad to give the House all the information at my command in connection with
the Hospitality Fund of the Government. I may say that there is no truth
whatever in the allegation of the hon.
Member that the hospitality that is paid
for by the Government is in the slightest
degree party in character. It may be.
on account of the long period that the
Conservatives were in office in England,
that the Ministers and the men connected with the Departments on that
side coming over here gave rise to au
assumption of that kind, but I can
assure the House that we make no distinction whatever as to what Government
may be in power at Westminster. During
the past few months we have had an
opportunity of entertaining out of Government Funds to a certain extent, and
also out of my own private purse, which
I am quite delighted to do, both Mr.
Lansbury, who came over here in connection with the laying of the foundation
stone of our new Royal Courts of Justice.
and Mr. Roberts and five of his staff from
the Imperial Ministry of Pensions, whom
I was just as delighted to have stopping
at Stormont, and to entertain in my own
humble way, as if it had been any of the
preceding Ministers of Pensions who
might possibly have been politically more
in accord with my own feelings than
either Mr. Roberts or Mr. Lansbury.
But this hospitality Fund rises above
all these petty considerations entirely.
The one consideration that I and my
Colleagues have is that as far as we can
we should do to other countries as they
do to us, and that Ulster should not be
behindhand in extending some form of
hospitality to distinguished strangers
who come over here. I may say that,
when I had the honour of visiting
Australia, Mr. Scullin and his Cabinet
invited my wife and myself to be their
guests at a luncheon, at which we were
able to discuss matters of common import
to all parts of the Empire, and that they
also placed at our disposal every facility
