,,
The FINANCIAL SECRETARY OF
THE MINISTRY OF FINANCE (Mr.
Barbour): The net total of the three
sections into which this Estimate is
divided shows an increase of approximately £132,000 over the figure for last
year. Hon. Members are already fully
informed of the distinction which exists
between the classes of expenditure covered
by the three sections of the Estimate, and
will observe at once that the major portion
of the increase occurs under Section I, that
is to say, expenditure on the provision of
accommodation for the staffs of our various
Northern Ireland Departments at Stormont and the Law Courts, which is ultimately a liability of the United Kingdom
Government. The balance of the increase
occurs under Section II, where provision
has been made for the first year's expenditure on the Bann Drainage Scheme.
Section III shows a very considerable
reduction, but this does not, of course,
affect the net total of this Vote, because
of the corresponding decrease in the
amount to be recouped to this Vote by
other Departments in respect of works
executed and supplies purchased on their
behalf.
Some of the items have been the subject
of recent discussion here, and I shall as
far as possible limit my remarks to those
which are either new services or which
require explanation because of developments. The most important item in
Section I is the sum of £261,290, which is
provided in Sub-head D to meet expenditure during the year on the erection of the
new Parliament Buildings and Depart-
HOUSE OF COMMONS

Committee

Supply-
[Mr. Barbour]
mental Offices at Stormont.
This sum
represents a very considerable increase
over last year's figure, and is an indication
of the acceleration of the building works.
If progress is maintained at the rate which
is anticipated, there is every indication
that the Departmental portion of the
building will be ready for occupation by
the Departmental staffs during the early
Summer of 1931. The Parliamentary
portion of the building, however, is unlikely to be ready for occupation until at
least a year
later.
The sum of £28,970 provided in this
Sub-head for that portion of the expenditure on the new Law Courts Building,
which relates to the provision of accommodation for that portion of the Departmental staffs which will remain in the City
is in the same category as the expenditure
on the administrative buildings, etc., at
Stormont. I am glad to say that building
operations at the Law Courts are now proceeding rapidly.
Hon. Members may possibly like to
have some indication, although at present
it can only be furnished in broad outline,
of the arrangements contemplated for
housing the various departmental staffs in
the Stormont Building, and in the new
Law Courts Building respectively.
The Ministry of Commerce, whose
duties obviously bring them into close
touch with the business community, will
be located in the city building, as will
also certain other Departments whose
duties render it necessary that the members of the public should have convenient
and direct access to them. These Departments include the Stamp Office, the
Estate Duty Office, the Office of the
Registrar General, the Public Record
Office, the Registry of Deeds, and the
Works Branch of the Ministry of Finance,
etc.
The remaining Departments of the
Government will be located at Stormont,
but provision has been made in the Law
Courts Building for the accommodation of
a small staff of each of these Departments
in order that they may deal with inquiries,
and give any necessary information to
callers and members of the public generally
on subjects concerning their particular
Ministry. I think it will be found when
the removals are completed that public
business will be much facilitated by the
concentration of staffs, and I have little
doubt, although at this early stage it is
not possible to indulge in
even
any
approximate estimates of savings, that
administrative economies will be effected
in due course.
I now turn from expenditure, which is
ultimately a charge on the British Exchequer, and come to Sections II and III,
that is to say, to our own "domestic" expenditure. Section II is made up of
Subheads E, F, G, H, I and J, on pages
30, 31 and 32, and hon. Members will
remember that, unlike Section III, Section II consists of items which cannot be
earmarked to and paid for by any particular Department. The first item in
Subhead E provides for a further instalment of the contribution payable out of
Northern Ireland funds towards the provision of Office accommodation in the new
Parliament Buildings for staff over and
above the number for which the Imperial
Government is providing accommodation
under Section 34 of the Government of
Ireland Act, 1920; this contribution has
been under the notice of the Committee
on previous occasions.
The next item relates to expenditure on
the scheme for the drainage of the River
Bann, under the Drainage Act of last
year. The contract for this large scheme
has now been let, after satisfactory competition, to the James Dredging, Towage
& Transport Company, Limited, of Southampton, an eminent firm of specialists,
who are at present carrying out an extensive dredging contract at Southampton
Water. Hon. Members will be interested
to know that, so far as can reasonably be
foreseen, the Bann drainage works will
be carried out for an expenditure within
the estimate of £650,000. It is hoped
that the operations on the Bann will be
commenced by June next, and it is anticipated that the work will be completed
within a period of five years.

former sum is the second instalment of

gards the remainder of the land, it is

As re-
The various items of maintenance and
other recurring expenditure provided for
in Sub-heads F, G, and H call for no
special comment. As regards Sub-head I,
the purchase of the dredging fleet has been
amply justified, the craft having been
fully employed throughout the year in
carrying out operations not only at the
Royal Harbour at Ardglass, but at several
other harbours including Portstewart,
Carrickfergus and Kilkeel. There is,

and requisition in due course the services
of the Government craft.
Turning to section 3 of the Estimate
(pages 33 to 37) which summarises the
works expenditure incurred on behalf of
the various Northern Ireland Departments, it will at once be observed that
there is a very
considerable reduction,
amounting to approximately £39,000 in

due to the fact that the schemes in connection with the prisons and the Training

end, while the works at the Criminal
Lunatic Asylum, Londonderry, and the
Juvenile Instruction Centre at Belfast

The works which are being carried out by

The erection of the cottages for the
staff of the Malone Training School has
been delayed pending consideration of the
type of cottages to be provided, and their
location within the grounds of the Training School. It is hoped, however, to
accept a tender for this work at a very
early date.
Owing to the difficulty of obtaining a

no progress with the provision of a new
Employment Exchange at Lisburn has up
to now been possible, but negotiations
have recently been completed for the purchase of a suitable site, and it is anticipated that building operations will be
commenced within the next few months.
Under the head of "Proposed Works"
the main item is the sum of £3,100 for the
erection and equipment of a new wing to

School. This addition to the building is
imperative as the number of cubicles at
present available in the school is quite inadequate for the number of boys who will
require to be accommodated. The cost
of this additional wing, as well as of the
staff cottages to which I referred just now,
is recoverable in full out of the Capital
Fund No. 2, which was established by the

The next large item is the sum of £900
for the instalment of central heating and
hot water supply at Malone Training

the people consider that a sum of

Reference was then made to what was
considered the extravagant size of the new
Parliament buildings. Hon. Members
must be aware of the negotiations which
took place in reference to them between
those representing Northern Ireland and
those representing the Imperial Government. At first the buildings
contemplated were on a much larger scale than
what was adopted eventually, but even if
buildings had been adopted as at first suggested the Government of Northern Ireland did not consider sufficient provision
had been made for possible requirements
in the future. Therefore, the building
would have been smaller than it is but for
the very prudent fear on the part of those
who had to deal with this matter, and so
reasonable provision was made for possible
future requirements. I quite agree it
would be a mistake from any grandiose
ideas to put up any larger or more extravagant building than is actually required, as no one is more alive to the inevitable burden of maintenance and upkeep of a building out of keeping with our
requirements than I am.

of distress unfortunately existing in our
midst? To be paid for productive work
is more to be desired, I think, even by the
people for whose benefit unemployment insurance is provided, than the mere payment of money without any work being
done in return. The work is not confined
to Belfast, as the hon. Member will see.
For instance, I think there is hardly a city

spreading, as far as is economically possible, the amount of employment that can
be given out of Government funds.

nearly three-quarters of a million for the

far as it is possible to deal out even-handed

Mr. BARBOUR: The first Clause of
the Resolution on the Order Paper derives its necessity from Clause 50 of the
Bill, under which the Ministry of Comis empowered, on request, to
appoint inspectors to conduct an investigation into the affairs of a company. There
are two contingencies under which the expenses of such investigation would be
defrayed by voted moneys, namely
(1) Where as a result of the investigation the Attorney-General decides that a criminal prosecution is
warranted; and
(2) Where there is no such prosecution and the Company makes default in
respect of its liability for the payment
of all or portion of the expenses which
the Ministry of Commerce has directed
it to pay, and the security of £100
given by the applicants for the investigation is insufficient to cover the default. The balance, if any, of the
costs of the inquiry are then chargeable
against voted moneys.
The second Clause of the Resolution relates to Clause 82 of the Bill. Under
that Clause, unclaimed dividends or unapplied balances of a company which has
been wound up voluntarily are proposed
to be paid into the Exchequer of Northern
Ireland after a reasonable lapse of time,
and in the event of any claim being made
in respect of such dividends or balances,
provision is made for the issue out of the
Consolidated Fund of the
claimed, subject to an order of the
Court approving of such payment. I beg
to move.

PROMOTIONS IN MINISTRY OF
FINANCE.
4. Mr. NIXON asked the Minister of
Finance whether he can state how many
officers in the employment of the Ministry of Finance have been promoted from
the grade of lower clerical officer to the
grade of junior executive officer since
the establishment of the Government of
Northern Ireland; how many of these
promotions were made from officers who
neither passed the entrance examination
nor were ex-Service men; how many of
those promoted were disabled ex-Service
men; and whether it is a fact that the
disability pension is a bar to promotion?
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Pollock): The answer to the first part
of the question of the hon. Member is
nineteen, of whom twelve were ex-
Service men; to the second part, two; to
the third, none; while the answer to the
last part of the question is in the
negative.
I may add that of the two officers promoted to the executive from the clerical
grade, who were not ex-Service men and
did not pass an entrance examination for
admission to the Civil Service, one had
been transferred to the Ministry under
the Government of Ireland Act as an
established clerical officer, while the
other was admitted to the service in 1922
under an interim arrangement whereby,
pending the inauguration of the present
system of recruitment by competitive examination, a number of clerical appointments were filled by a selection from
school-boy candidates with a satisfactory
educational record.
Mr. NIXON :
Would the Minister
state how many disabled ex-Service men
have, as a matter of fact, been promoted
within the past five years?
HOUSE OF COMMONS

CIVIL SERVICE COMMISSIONERS.
5. Mr. NIXON asked the Minister of
Finance whether he can state the names
of the gentlemen who constitute the body
known as the Civil Service Commissioners;
by what authority these gentlemen override Local Authorities in the matter of
fixing pensions for municipal officials;
and whether the decision of the Commissioners is liable to be reviewed, and,
if necessary, corrected by His Majesty's
Courts of Justice.
Mr. POLLOCK : The hon. Member
presumably refers to the Civil Service
Committee for Northern Ireland set up
under section 56 (2) of the Government
of Ireland Act, 1920, as amended by
paragraph 7 (1) of the First Schedule to
the Irish Free State (Consequential Provisions) Act, 1922.
The members of this body are:
Sir Alfred Dennis, K.B.E. (appointed
by the Lord Chief Justice of England);
Viscount Cross (appointed by the
Treasury);
Sir R. A. Johnson, K.B.E. (appointed
by the Secretary of State for Home
Affairs);
Sir W. B. Spender, K.C.B. (appointed
by the Government of Northern Ireland);
Mr. W. Crone, M.B.E. (appointed by
the transferred Civil Servants).
The authority under which this body
determines, in cases of dispute, the right
of an officer of a local authority to an
allowance or
retirement,
gratuity on
resignation or removal from office, and
the amount of such allowance or gratuity
is contained in Section 8 of the Local
Government (Ireland) Act, 1919,
amended by the Government of Ireland Act, 1920, and the Irish Free State
(Consequential Provisions) Act, 1922.
as
The Civil Service Committee is not
under the control or jurisdiction of the
Parliament or Government of Northern
Ireland, and I do not consider it proper
for me to express any opinion regarding
the last portion of the question.
6. Mr. STEWART asked the Minister
of Home Affairs whether he is aware that
on Sunday, 20th April, 1930, three
young men were arrested in the vicinity
of Dungannon, and detained for several
hours in the Dungannon Police Station
without any charge being preferred
against them; and whether in view of the
ignominy and inconvenience they were
subject to the Government is considering
the question of compensation.
The MINISTER OF HOME
AFFAIRS (Sir Dawson Bates): It is a
fact that on the 20th April, 1930, the
police found three men near Dungannon
wearing emblems indicating Republican
sympathies under circumstances and conditions likely to lead to a breach of the
peace. On being requested to remove the
emblems in question, these men refused
to do so and they were accordingly
warned that if they persisted in their refusal they would be arrested. As they
refused to comply with the request of the
police they were taken into custody and
detained at Dungannon Police Barracks
until all danger or further likelihood of
a breach of the peace occurring as a result
of their conduct had passed.
The question of a prosecution in these
cases was carefully considered by the
Attorney-General, and although there is
no doubt these men had rendered themselves liable to such, it was decided that
in all the circumstances, the fact of their
arrest and detention was a sufficient
warning and would suitably meet the requirements of the case, and further proceedings were consequently dropped.
The Government sees no grounds for
considering any question of payment of
compensation in this case.
Mr. STEWART: Arising out of the
reply of the right hon. Gentleman, is not
the real reason why these young men
were arrested that they were wearing this
emblem which I have in my hand. These
are the colours of the Free State-green,
white, and orange. I understand the
Free State were represented at the Naval
Conference, and that they have also been
admitted to the League of Nations. That
being so, does the right hon. Gentleman
think it a proper thing to insult these
colours of the Free State?
Oral Answers.
Oral Answers.

Sir DAWSON BATES:

pointed out these men were
arrested for wearing and refusing to remove certain badges which were emblematical of the Republican party.
The
police considered the wearing of these

Mr. HEALY: Am I to understand
from the right hon. Gentleman that no
one in Northern Ireland can give expression constitutionally to any view
opposed to the right hon. Gentleman's
view without leaving himself open to the
possibility of arrest?
Sir DAWSON BATES: I never
thought the Republican body was a constitutional party.
Mr. COLLINS: Is the right hon.
Gentleman not aware that if the majority
in Northern Ireland to-morrow constituted
themselves the Republican party they
would be constitutional?
Mr. ELLIOTT: Arising out of the
right hon. Gentleman's reply, may I ask
whether he is aware of the fact that
irrespective of creed or class the loyal
residents in the district in which this
occurrence took place, and which I have
the honour to represent in this House,
heartily approve of the action of the
Constabulary on that occasion; and is he
also aware of the fact that had it not
been for their prompt action a serious
situation might have arisen on account of
the injudicious action of the young men
referred to who displayed emblems which
aroused feelings of resentment amongst
the loyal people of South Tyrone?
Mr. HEALY: Is the right hon.
Gentleman aware that thousands of
people in Northern Ireland, including
myself, wore these emblems on this
occasion and nothing disorderly occurred?
Is it illegal to work constitutionally for
the same sort of government in this
country as prevails in France and the
United States of America?
Sir DAWSON BATES: My hon.
Friend misunderstands the situation.
It is not illegal to wear emblems, but it
is illegal to wear emblems under such
circumstances as may lead to a breach of
the peace.
I am quite satisfied that the
Royal Ulster Constabulary, as they
always do, acted in quite an efficient
manner.
Mr. STEWART: May I reply to the
right hon. Gentleman? (Hon. Members:
No, no). I disagree absolutely with
him-

Member disagrees, but this is not the

Mr. STEWART: Hear, hear,
Sir DAWSON BATES: I have never

Mr. O'NEILL: You are very simple.

CLAIMS MADE THROUGH LOCAL
EXCHANGES.
9. Mr. BEATTIE asked the Minister
of Labour whether he can state the
number of claims made through the
various local Exchanges of Northern Ireland from the 4th March, 1930, to the
22nd April, 1930; the number allowed,
and the number disallowed.
The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.
Andrews) Owing to the Easter holidays
the returns which would usually be furnished on the 21st April are included
with those furnished on the 28th April.
From the 4th March to the 28th April,
42,952 new claims (apart from claims
already in action) were made at the Exchanges.
The returns from courts of referees are
kept on a monthly basis, but an approximate estimate of the number of claims disallowed by the court of referees and the
umpire, for the period mentioned in the
question, would be 4,900, or an average
number of 700 per week. The average
number of claims paid each week during
the same period was 43,220.
"NORMALLY INSURABLE"
AND
NOT NORMALLY INSURABLE"
PERSONS.
10. Mr. BEATTIE asked the Minister
of Labour if he can state the total number of persons in Northern Ireland who
are classified as "normally insurable" and
the total number classified as "not normally insurable."
Mr. ANDREWS: I regret that it is
obviously not possible to give the exact
number of persons in Northern Ireland
who are "normally insurable," as persons
are constantly entering and leaving the
insurance field. The latest estimate, however, of the average insured population
of Northern Ireland is 258,000. At the
last census in April, 1926, the number of
persons in Northern Ireland between the
ages of 16 and 65 was found to be 765,859.
Deducting the insured population from
this figure, it would appear that there are
about 507,000 persons in Northern Ireland within the insurable age who are not
normally insured.
Mr. BEATTIE: Would the Minister
be prepared to make arrangements for an
industrial census of Northern Ireland in
order to get the question on the Order
Paper answered in the manner in which
it should be answered?
Mr. ANDREWS: I do not think such
a proposal is really practicable.
Mr. BEATTIE: Is it not a fact that
in Great Britain a similar thing has been
carried out, and in view of that fact is
the Minister not prepared, as we have
such a small population, to take such an
industrial census?
Mr. SPEAKER: I think it would be
better to put down another question.
TRANSFERRED OR SUPERSEDED
VOLUNTARY SCHOOLS IN

2. Mr. DAVISON asked the Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministry of
Education whether he can state the number of voluntary schools in Northern Ireland, the number of persons, managers of
such schools, who are recognised as such
by virtue of any office, and the nature of
the offices by virtue of which they are so
recognised.
The following question also stood on
the Order Paper:.
R
Committee.
Supply-

HOUSE OF COMMONS
3. Mr. BEATTIE: To ask the Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministry of Education whether he can state the number of
schools in Northern Ireland transferred
or superseded under the provisions of the
Education Act (Northern Ireland), 1923;
the number of persons formerly managers
of such schools who were recognised as
such managers by virtue of some office,
and the nature of the offices by virtue
of which they were so recognised.
The PARLIAMENTARY SECRE-
TARY OF THE MINISTRY OF
EDUCATION (Mr. Robb): I propose to
reply to both the hon. and learned
Member's questions together.
Up to the present, of our public elementary schools, 455 have been transferred, 102 have been closed, and 1,444
remain as voluntary schools although, of
those, a considerable number is in process of transfer.
In the case of schools under patrons
(whether individuals, trustees, boards or
committees) the nominee of the patron is
almost always recognised as manager, and
the question of his office does not enter
into the matter.
In the case of schools neither under
patrons nor under committees set up under Section 15 of the Act, in recognising
a manager the Ministry has regard to his
office, and, in such cases, where the office
of the preceding manager was, for example, that of clergyman, factory manager or estate agent, the successor in that
office is usually recognised as manager.
To supply the further particulars asked
for in the question would involve a very
large expenditure of official time and
would seriously interfere with the current
work of the Ministry. In the circumstances, therefore, perhaps the hon. and
learned Member would be so good as not
to press for it.

Motion made and Question proposed:

granted to His Majesty to complete the

year ending 31st March, 1931, in respect
of the Salaries and Expenses of the Ministry of Finance (15 and 16 Geo. V., c. 3,
s. 4 (N.I.), including the cost of administration of Revenue Services, Valuation,
Loan
Registration,
Public
Services,

Guarantee Acts (N.I.), 1922 to 1929,
Land Law Acts, collection of Land Purchase Annuities and Tithe Rent charges,
Intoxicating Liquor Acts (N.I.), 1923,

and Sundry Agency Services (10 and 11

a grant in aid."-(Note-£40,000 has
been passed on account).
THE FINANCIAL SECRETARY
OF THE MINISTRY OF FINANCE
(Mr. Barbour): I think it is hardly necessary for me in moving this Estimate to
recall in detail to the minds of hon. Members the many-sided nature of the duties
which are performed by the various blocks
of staff grouped under the head of the
Ministry of Finance. I had occasion to
refer to these last week when replying to
the debate on the Vote for Public Works
and Buildings. I would remind you in
this connection that this staff covers more
than the administration of our own Northern Ireland domestic services, in that in
drainage schemes as are the councils' rein Northern Ireland of various British
Government Departments which find it
more economical to make agency arrangements of this kind. The cost is accordingly offset by substantial credits under
Appropriations-in-Aid. I shall refer
later on to the more important of these
Agency Services. A consolidated report
covering the entire activities of the Ministry of Finance is now in an advanced stage
of preparation and will be published in
the course of the next few months. Had
this report been available at the present
time, it would probably have been
sufficient merely to move the Estimate
without detailed comment.
Looking at the Estimate as a whole, it
will be seen that the total number of staff
provided for (including the staff of the
Registrar-General's Department and the
staff engaged on the administration of
Ulster Savings Certificates-Subheads Pl
and L)-remains the same as for last year.
Changes are, however, shown in the staffs
Supply-
Committee.
7 MAY 1930
of several of the branches comprised within the Estimate. The most important
change occurs in the section relating to the
Valuation Division (page 17), where,
owing to the completion of the special
work thrown on this branch in connection
with the apportionment of the Valuation
of Agricultural, Industrial and Freight
Transport property throughout the Province for the purpose of the Derating
Scheme, it has been possible to dispense
with the temporary technical and typing
staff engaged for that work, for which a
provision of £4,475 was required in last
year's Estimates. For the same reason
the number of established clerks in this
division is reduced by two. I should,
however, explain that the Derating
Scheme will necessitate more complicated
seasonal work in the ordinary annual revision of valuation, and, consequently, it
has been necessary to make increased provision for temporary clerical assistance
under the "Miscellaneous" section of
Subhead A.
A slight reduction also occurs in the
provision for the salaries of the Works
Division. Criticism has on SO many
occasions been directed against the alleged
extensive staffs which have to be employed
on the work of this division that I feel
that I have no option but to point out
once more the nature and volume of its
activities, both as an agent department
and in connection with schemes initiated
by our own Government. Under the
latter head, hon. Members have already
considered the extensive and varied activities which are comprised in the Public
Works and Buildings Estimate, and which
were discussed last week, but that Estimate does not give the full story of what
is involved, inasmuch as the expenditure
on the Police Barrack Reconstruction
Scheme, being a charge on the Consolidated Fund, does not find a place in it.
I would, therefore, mention that up to the
end of March last about a quarter of the
work (some fifty barracks) of building and
reconstructing police barracks has been
completed, or is in hands, and the remainder of the work will proceed over the
next five years.
Furthermore, that Estimate does not
refer to the important agency work which
is performed by this Government on behalf of the Imperial Government, namely,
the agency work entrusted to it by his
Majesty's Office of Works, London, in connection with the provision and upkeep of
buildings occupied by Imperial and Reserved Departments, including Post
Offices, Telephone Exchanges, Inland Revenue Offices and Customs and Excise
Offices, as well as the buildings occupied
by the Supreme Court of Northern Ireland, the Land Purchase Commission, the
Probate Registry and the Registry of
Deeds. The Works staff is also engaged
in the planning and maintenance of cottages for ex-Service men, acting in this respect as the Agent of the Irish Sailors'
and Soldiers' Land Trust.
Before passing on, reference might also
be made to the considerable amount of
work involved in connection with the erection by education authorities of new
schools, and the reconstruction of existing schools, the proposals for which,
though prepared by the education
authorities, have to be approved by the
Ministry of Education, who obtain any
necessary technical advice from the officers
of the Ministry of Finance. An increasing
volume of work is being undertaken by
the Architects' branch acting in the direct
capacity of architects to numerous regional education committees, and evidence
of the increase in this particular branch of
work is indicated by a receipt of £1,900
provided for Appropriations-in-Aid as
against a sum of £485 for last year. Moreover, some county councils have indicated
their intention of utilising the services of
our engineers for the preparation of such
drainage schemes as are the councils' responsibility. I might also mention the
work carried out by our engineers on behalf of county councils in connection with
harbour works.
If the programme of work on the Barrack Reconstruction Scheme and the Bann
Drainage Scheme proceeds as anticipated,
expenditure at the rate of over £250,000
a year on these two schemes alone is expected during the next few years, and it
should not be difficult for hon. Members
to appreciate the vast amount of work of
a technical nature involved in these major
schemes and in the other works to which
brief reference has been made.
The increase in the provision for the
Establishment Division (page 15) is
mainly due to an arrangement recently
made between the Ministry and the
British Government Departments occupying accommodation in the Belfast Custom
House, under which the Ministry has
made itself responsible for the provision of
messenger and cleaning staff for that
building, subject to repayment by the De-
Supply-
Committee
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Barbour]
partments concerned. This repayment is
provided for in Subhead R of the Estimate.
The Accounts Division of the Ministry
shows an increase of one clerk in consequence of the greater volume of work
falling on the Land Purchase Collection
Branch as a result of the operation of the
Land Act of 1925. Hon. Members may
be interested to know that for the financial year just ended, the cost of the staff
engaged on this particular work was approximately equivalent to one-half of one
per cent. only of the total annuities collected in the year, which amounted to over
£805,000.
Turning now to the branch within the
Accounts Division which deals with Ulster
Savings Certificates, mention may be made
of the fact that the total number of Certificates sold in the year ending 31st March
last was 745,589, representing a cash investment of approximately £466,000.
The cost of the staff engaged on this work
was equivalent to only d per Certificate
issued, so that if we add the other expenses incidental to the issue of the Certificates, the total cost for each Certificate
issued is still well below 1d.
In the Legal Division, the increase of
one in the number of the staff is only an
apparent increase. The assistant solicitor to the Ministry, who is included in the
Estimate, is at present on loan to the Land
Purchase Commission, and the amount of
the salary paid to him by the Ministry is
recovered from that Department as an appropriation in aid of the Vote under Subhead R.
It will be seen that the provision for
the office of the Registrar-General and
Statistician shows an increase of one in
the clerical staff. This addition has been
made in connection with special work, the
necessity for which I will explain. Recently, a test comparison was made between the ages as entered in the death
registers and the ages at death of old-age
pensioners as determined from the evidence of age furnished in connection with
the claims for old age pensions. As a
result of this comparison, it is estimated
that some 25 per cent. of the 18,000 death
entries in Northern Ireland each year contain ages at death which are under-stated
by five years or more. It is also evident
that some 250 deaths per annum which
occur outside Belfast escape registration.
A test has also been made of birth
registration in comparison with the notifications of births furnished by midwives:
and doctors to the Medical Officer of
Health for Belfast. From this test it
appears that a number of births escape
registration, and it has also been found
that in some cases where an infant has
died shortly after birth, the death also
escapes registration. These matters indicate that something is needed to tighten
up the registration system and steps are
being taken to correct the position as far
as possible. Needless to say, no Government machinery can prove effective unless
supported by the good-will of the public
and its willingness to obey the law.
Re-registration under the provisions of
the Legitimacy Act, 1928, is working
smoothly and preparations are in hand for
the re-registrations which will arise under
the Adoption of Children Act, which
comes into force on 1st July next.
Miscellaneous actuarial matters continue to be dealt with in growing volume.
Although the publication of census reports arising out of the 1926 census was
completed during the past year, it has not
been possible to bring the preparation of
the promised review of vital statistics and
preparation of a mortality table for
Northern Ireland to a conclusion. In part,
this delay has been due to the disturbance
caused by the discoveries to which I have
referred just now as to the unreliability
of our death registration, and in part due
to the pressure of other matters.
Under Sub-head J. on page 20, which
provides for the expenses of the Statute
Law Committee, provision is made for the
completion of the work relating to the
printing of the index to the statutes
affecting Northern Ireland. It was anticipated when the Estimates for 1929-30
were being prepared that this work would
have progressed rapidly enough to enable
the bulk of the printing expenditure to
be met in that year, but this has not been
found possible. The Statute Law Committee have urged that the preparation of
an Index to the Statutory Rules and
Orders applicable to Northern Ireland is
a work of immediate necessity, and it is
hoped to put the work in hands by not
later than the coming Autumn. A token
figure of £100 is included in this Subhead for the purpose. This work, like
that for the index to the Statutes, is a
difficult and complex undertaking, and
can only be performed by persons of legal
experience.

Since Mr. Snowden introduced his Budget in the Imperial Parlaiment our income
tax is up to 4s 6d in the £ on a flat rate.
The income tax of our competitors twoand-a-half miles from my town is 3s in the
£, a distinct benefit to the manufacturers
and traders on the other side of the border of fifty per cent. Now here is a power
the very Act of 1920 itself has given the
right hon. Gentleman who is Minister of
Finance to bring something into this
House by way of a Bill. If he had been
employed on this for the last nine years
he would have been better employed than
on some of the Bills we have been wasting
our time passing here. I am reading
from the Government of Ireland Act,
Section 25:
(1) The Parliament of Northern
Ireland shall have power to grant relief
from income tax and super tax or
either of these taxes to individuals
resident and domiciled in Northern
Ireland and such relief may be given
either generally to all such individuals
or to individuals whose total income is
less than such amount as may be determined by the Act granting the relief.
(3) Such relief as aforesaid shall be
granted by way of repayment of any
part or the whole of the income tax
or super tax paid by the individuals to
whom the relief is granted, and the
Act granting the relief may provide
for the amounts so repayable being repaid in like manner as other repayments under the Income Tax Acts.
(4) The making of such repayments
shall rest with the Government of
Northern Ireland, and the repayments
shall be made out of the Consolidated
Fund of Northern Ireland.

Question proposed:
That a sum not exceeding £3,056 be
granted to His Majesty to complete the sum
necessary to defray the charge which will
come in course of payment during the year
ending 31st March, 1931, to defray the
salaries and expenses of the Public Record
Office, Northern Ireland (13 and 14 Geo.
V. (N.I.), c. 20), and the cost of the administration of the Ancient Monuments
Act (16 and 17 Geo. V. (N.I.), c. 12).
(Note £1,000
voted
has been
account.)
on
Mr. BARBOUR: It will be observed
that the total of this Estimate is £4,056
which represents a decrease on last year of
£43. Although the amount involved is
comparatively small, at the same time I
think it is an Estimate of more than usual
interest, if not to this House, to the members of the general public. The chief item
of note which arises in connection with the
Record Office Estimate is the provision for
the publication of a selection from the
Letters of William Drennan, the wellknown Ulster poet and United Irishman
(Sub-head D3). It will be within the recollection of Members that an appeal was
made to the public for subscriptions to
secure the Government against excessive
loss should it undertake this publication.
I am pleased to say that this appeal was
successful and subscriptions and promises of subscriptions to the extent
of over £120 were received. It is hoped
that the publication which will be of great
interest both for national and local history
may appear before the close of the present
year.
Under the head of Ancient Monuments
it is anticipated that the chief expense will
be incurred in the continuance of the ex-
Supply-
Committee
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Barbour]
ploratory work at the keep of Carrickfergus Castle (Sub-head C3). So far three
garde-robes have been revealed, also a long
stairway in the thickness of the southern
wall and much ancient carved stonework
in windows and doors, which had been
filled in and plastered over. On one window a number of names, in many cases
with dates appended between 1760 and
1792, were found. These appeared to be
those of Carrickfergus men who perhaps
garrisoned the Castle in time of war when
the regular troops were absent. The
souterrain or underground chamber below
Dunluce Castle has been completely.
cleared, and on the evidence of the fragments of pottery which it contained is
believed to date from about the 5th
Century B.C.
An increased provision is made under
the head of Travelling Expenses for the
staff of the branch (Sub-head B), and the
Members of the Ancient Monuments
Advisory Committee (Sub-head H). This
is due to the progress now being made by
that body in the preparation of a
schedule of Ancient Monuments throughout the Province suitable for protection
under section 5 of the Ancient Monuments Act of 1926. Members will understand that, before a monument can be
thus scheduled, a trustworthy account of
its present appearance must be obtained,
otherwise we might find ourselves committed to protect a monument, which was
no longer in existence or had been reduced to insignificance. In some cases
these reports cannot be obtained without
a considerable amount of locomotion. I
am glad to say that complete lists of suitable monuments have now been framed
for Counties Antrim and Down and the
work is in progress in the other four
Counties.
I am pleased to be able to anticipate
the receipt of a substantial sum from the
fees for admission to certain monuments
(Sub-head J). This will help to defray
the heavy cost of maintenance and caretaking.
The sales of the special guides to the
more important monuments published
last year have been promising. The first
edition of the Carrickfergus Castle guide
was soon exhausted, and a second edition,
embodying the latest discoveries, has
been issued. I beg to move.
Mr. HEALY: This is one small Estimate to which I, at all events, will not

make a suggestion to the Minister of

marked the page in this, and sent it down

he came to me in great delight and said:
"Do you know this is part of the history
of the Order of the Dominicans which has
been missing for years." He is taking
steps to get into touch with the office here.
It appears that in the bad old penal days
the then head man of the Order and his
assistant were going round disguised as
tramps, and in a house he visited he was
arrested and given up to the Government,
and these papers were all taken from him.
They were never found by the Order
through all the centuries.
Mr. POLLOCK: Where did he come
from?
Mr. COLLINS: Somewhere in the
North. There is another very interesting
edition of that work which came from the
Public Record Office. I think it was last
year's. You got the Hillsborough letters
there. They are full of the greatest
interest to any student of Irish history,
because you will see the plan laid there
in these letters how the then Marquess of
Downshire was deceived, and how it led
to the destruction of the old Irish
Volunteers of 1787 and the establishment
of the Fencibles. It is full of the greatest
possible interest to any Irishman, no
matter on what side, to see how when the
Marquess discovered the thing he was surprised and voted against the Union.
We will leave the documents. I just
want to call attention of the right hon.
Gentleman to an ancient monument in
my constituency, the castle of Greencastle.
Irish Nationalists have not so large an
interest in it because it was one of the
early castles used by the English occupation.
Mr. POLLOCK: It is a Norman
castle.

but its great antiquity is its value from
the tourist point of view. The last time

housed in it. I think if it were cleared
out and some arrangements made with
Mr. McElroy, the gentleman who owns
it he is a public-spirited gentleman-it
would be of great value from the point
of view of tourists. If it was laid out as
Conway Castle is, there would be as much
in fees got for entry as would nearly pay
the cost. I think it is a thing that
should be given attention.
Mr. POLLOCK: We will see to it.
Mr. COLLINS: I am delighted to be

like to refer to the gentleman from whom

suppose he is responsible in a great
measure for my being in this House at
all-I think letters of his should be
published in some handy way, and I for
one would rejoice.

Mr. BARBOUR: Hon. Members will
find this Vote on page 39 of the Estimates.
They will see that the gross Vote for
1930-31 amounts to £28,870 and the receipts Appropriated-in-Aid to £26,472,
leaving a net Vote of £2,398 as compared
with a net Vote of £2,990 for the year
1929-30, which shows a decrease in the
net Vote of £592.
This decrease is reflected in Subheads
A and B of the Vote, and is due, firstly,
to a reduction in the provision for the cost
of the printing, etc., of the "Belfast
Gazette," owing to an anticipated decrease
in the number of the Land Purchase
Commission notices to be inserted, and,
secondly, to a decrease in the provision
for printing, etc., of official publications
of the Government of Northern Ireland.
It will be observed from the details of
Subhead A that out of a Vote of £2,300,
required to cover the cost of the production of the "Gazette," a sum of £1,800 is
directly attributable to the statutory
notices issued by the Land Purchase Commission. The reduction in expenditure
under Subheads A and B is brought about
by the fact that the publications relating
to the census in 1926 have now all been
issued, and that the provision included in
the corresponding Vote in 1929-30 for the
cost of the publication of the register of
non-pedigree dairy cattle does not recur
on this occasion.
An increased provision in Subhead D
for the cost of printing and binding for
public departments is required to cover
the cost of the printing, etc., of a brochure
illustrating the development of the
poultry industry in Northern Ireland, and
of other literature in connection with the
official marketing exhibit at the world's
poultry congress which will be held in
London in July next. This brochure will
be distributed gratis from the stall to
persons who are likely to be interested.
Some additional expenditure is also being
incurred in connection with the printing
of Ulster Savings Certificates. These increases in the expenditure under this subhead, as will be seen, are more than offset
by the reductions in Subheads A and B.
It will be of interest to hon. Members
to know that the Vote on this occasion
covers the cost of the publication of the
second volume of the Constitution of Northern Ireland, which has been prepared by
the Parliamentary draftsman, and of the
first chronological table and index to the
Statutes of Northern Ireland. I beg to
move.

TARY OF THE MINISTRY OF
LABOUR (Mr. Gordon): At the outset I would like to emphasise the wide
range of administration for which we in
the Ministry of Labour are responsible.
Our functions are varied and increasing—
an ever-rolling stream of legislation affecting the lives and well-being of the working
people adds to the work of our Department. We have not lagged behind other
countries in humane effort but have extended social benefits, and in so doing
have taxed the resources of the country
almost to the limit.
I propose in this Estimate to give a
general survey of the work of the several
Supply-
Committee
8 MAY 1930
departments of the Ministry and show the
necessity for maintaining unimpaired its
efficiency. The employment exchanges
throughout the country continue to perform their useful work. It is through
their medium that we are able to gauge
the full extent of the ever-pressing problem of unemployment. The recent amending Unemployment Insurance Act has
greatly added to their work and I am glad
to say that, notwithstanding their increased duties, unemployment benefit has
been paid to the new claimants without
unnecessary delay. I have taken the opportunity during the past number of
months of visiting every Exchange under
our administration in order to come into
personal contact with the officials and gain
a knowledge of their methods in dealing
with claims to benefit and their attitude
towards those who are compelled through
unemployment to attend at the employment exchanges. Without a single exception, I found our officials took a broad and
charitable view and acted in a most
humane and courteous manner towards
those claiming benefit. I was impressed
with the ability of our officials in discharging their duties.
There are, approximately, 258,400 persons insured in Northern Ireland against
unemployment, and of this number there
are about 65,000 employed in the linen.
trade, over 25,000 in the shipbuilding industry and allied trades and about 22,000
in the building trades. In the distributive trades there are 33,000 persons employed and in the tailoring and dress industry over 24,000-this latter number
includes the shirt and collar industry
which flourishes in Londonderry. Unemployment in the whole of the insured
trades averaged 15.6 per cent. over the
financial year 1929-30. In the linen trade
alone the average over the year was 14.5
per cent., but I regret to say at the
moment the figures are slightly higher
than at any period during the past twelve
months.
The average unemployment over the
past financial year in the shipbuilding and
engineering trades was 18 per cent., but
in February of this year it fell from 21.6
per cent. to 13.3 per cent., which was the
lowest recorded percentage in these trades
since January, 1922, when unemployment
in those trades stood at 29.6 per cent.
Employment in the building trade was
much better than the previous year,
though unemployment in this section
averaged 21.8 per cent. over the past
twelve months. I am giving these figures
to the Committee merely to show the extent of the problem and the comprehensive
work dealt with by the officials in our
Exchanges.
Unemployment is caused by world factors.
A country like ours, manufacturing for export is affected by every slackening of trade in any part of the world.
Whatever the causes of unemployment
may be the position can rightly be described as one in which the supply of
labour exceeds the demand. Hon. Members will remember the recent amending
Unemployment Insurance Act which came
into operation on 13th March last. This
Act removed the "genuinely seeking
work" condition and, as was anticipated,
the effect of the new condition is to increase the number entitled to benefit of
persons who had little or no employment
in the previous two years.
Considerable criticism has been levelled
in the past at Exchange officials for
turning down claims to benefit. In fact
in this very House I have heard them referred to as heartless in dealing with
claimants. That charge, I think, was
unfair and unwarranted and cannot be
levelled in the future. The new conditions make it possible for the Exchange
officials to grant benefit but they cannot
turn down or refuse a claim. They must
refer it to the Court of Referees.
I am not going to say much regarding
the Courts of Referees. I venture to say
that other Members of the Committee
will make reference to them when I have
concluded my speech, but I will say that
these Courts are presided over by impartial chairmen who have exceedingly
difficult duties to discharge, and who act
in a fair and impartial manner towards
all claimants. If a person is not satisfied with the decision of the Court he
always has the right to have his case reconsidered, provided he can submit fresh
evidence which would be material to his
case. The Amending Act has increased
considerably the work of the Courts, but
we expect in a short time that this work
will be reduced.
I would like to pay a tribute to the
employers' representatives and to the
workers' representatives who form the
Courts, for the great public spirit they
have shown and for the voluntary service
they have rendered to the Department in
the discharge of a duty that is subject to

HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Gordon]
criticism and seldom receives the approval
it deserves.
We are continuing our schemes for the
relief of unemployment, and are only too
glad to undertake our share in any
scheme that will provide work for the
unemployed, provided that scheme conforms to the conditions laid down by the
Government. I am aware that relief
schemes only touch the fringe of the
problem, but while we, as a Department,
help in schemes of a temporary character,
the Government also assists in schemes
of a more permanent character which enlarge the opportunities for work by helping industry to carry on under the Loans
Guarantee Act. I feel sure that each
section of the House will join with me in
hoping that the trade of the country will
soon recover its former position of prosperity and that those men and women
who have been struggling heroically
against evil times will soon become employed.
Now I come to the increase asked for.
Hon. Members will observe on page 93
an increase of £6,257. £3,015 is due to
an increase in our staff at Employment
Exchanges due to increased work arising
out of the full operation of the recent
legislation and the rise in the insured
population. £3,242 is due to normal
salary increments and cost of living
bonus. The Committee is aware that the
Health Insurance Scheme is operated
through the Approved Societies, although
the Ministry of Labour is the responsible
authority.
The state of the Health Insurance Fund
is giving us cause for anxiety. It would
be difficult to determine the cause of increased claims for sickness benefit. The
absence of out-door relief is a contributing
factor towards sending large numbers on
the Health Insurance Fund. This
tendency has aggravated the already
serious situation in which approved
societies find themselves in consequence
of the impaired health of that portion of
the population that has been
affected by unemployment.
most
The expenditure of the approved
societies on sickness benefit is growing.
The cost of benefits and administration
has shown an increase of £12,063 as compared with the previous financial year.
The health of the worker becomes
affected through long continued idleness.
His vitality is lowered and his very
poverty compels him to seek recourse to
the Health Insurance Fund. There may
be other factors but it is sufficient for our
purpose to show the necessity for taking
steps of an energetic character towards
improving the administration, and, we
hope, reducing the growing expenditure.
We are negotiating with the approved
societies and with the medical profession
with a view to preventing improper
claims and obtaining better co-ordination.
in the administration amongst approved
societies.
The result of an examination conducted
by the official medical referee showed that
a great number of persons in receipt of
benefit receive no medical treatment, or,
at any rate, no adequate treatment.
Many of these people are a charge on
societies for long periods. We hope that
the introduction of medical benefit will
result in an improvement in the health
of the insured population.
We are asking for £500 more than the
previous year. This amount is due to
one officer engaged on preliminary work
in connection with medical benefit, and
also to the usual increments in the
salaries of officers in this section of the
Department.

Jur inspectors and officials are
tremely anxious to be of more direct assistance to industry apart from the
statutory duties delegated to them by Parliament. It is gratifying to note that
employers recognise the necessity for protecting the human element in industry by
cleansing the vitiated atmosphere, providing safeguards, improving their lighting,
ventilation and temperature. Accidents are
often caused by the carelessness or negligence of a fellow workman or by want of
instruction. Investigation in the United
Kingdom during the war led to the conclusion that the majority of industrial
accidents are unavoidable. It may not be
possible to prevent accidents in industrial
concerns, but it is possible to improve the
conditions under which persons are employed by using protective measures that
will reduce the human waste in industry.

for Belfast, and 10 King's National Roll

In 1922 we had 105 firms enrolled on
the King's National Roll, employing 1,339
disabled ex-Service men. On the 31st
March, 1930, we had 1,000 firms enrolled
employing 4,854 disabled ex-Service men.
There are also 34 local authorities enrolled.
I am sorry to say at the moment there
are 1,692 disabled ex-Service men still unemployed. I know that many of our
Local Employment Committees have canvassed employers on their behalf and every
effort is being put forth to have these men
absorbed in employment. Those firms enrolled on the King's National Roll are
always willing when opportunity permits
to offer employment to these men.
We have provided a juvenile employment centre in Belfast at a cost of £10,350,
and adapted and equipped it at a cost of
£3,500. This juvenile employment exchange is also an instruction centre for
unemployed boys and girls.
The young
people claiming benefit are required to attend for 15 hours' instruction each week.
This gives those boys and girls, and young
men and young women, wider opportunities for practical instruction in domestic
science and woodworking. The courses
also include such subjects as arithmetic,
English and physical exercises. The
present average daily attendance is about
200 boys and 100 girls. The object of
these classes is rather to maintain-or
probably, I should say, enhance their opportunity of obtaining employment, and
while they are there maintain their
employability.
The need for combining approved
courses of instruction with the Juvenile
Employment Exchange Service has also
been recognised in Great Britain (where,
however, these services are undertaken by
the local education authority). The
Belfast Juvenile Advisory Committee
made representation to the Local Education Authority to secure the setting up
of a Juvenile Employment Centre, but
without success. The Government came
to the support of the Committee by
establishing a centre under the Ministry
of Labour. The staff has been carefully
selected, with the co-operation of the
Ministry of Education, and 25 per cent.
of the running costs will be derived from
the Ministry of Education Vote, 37 per
cent. being appropriated from the Unemployment Insurance Fund.
This newly organised system is a new
advance in dealing with those of the unemployed who have reached the adolescent stage. It is a measure upon which
the Chairman and Juvenile Committee
were agreed that something should be
done to safeguard the young people,
which would be fruitful of good. Moral
delinquency is a frequent effect of Unemployment. Unemployment breeds
social unrest. It creates a dislike for
work and stimulates the desire to drift.

Richhill Centre, which was acquired by
the Department in September. 1926, is
designed to give a course in simple
agricultural instruction to single men who
desire to emigrate to one of the Colonies
under the Empire Settlement Scheme.
It has, in the past, been the subject
of much criticism, and this is my reason
for dealing with Richhill at the conclusion of my speech. Training centres
of a similar nature have been established
across the water and have had the
approval of successive Governments
The nature of the training is as
follows: First, general agricultural
operations (particularly ploughing):
secondly, milking; thirdly, handling and
care of horses and live stock; and fourthly,
tree cutting, fencing, ditching, and
general handicraft. The normal course
of instruction extends to three months,
and in some cases to four months, and we
have accommodation for 100 trainees
Training is confined to single men between the ages of 16 and 29, and applicants must be of good physique and good
character. No one is pressed to take up
a
But
course of training. Applicants are
brought to the centre free and taken to
their destination in Canada free of all
charge. Similar financial provision for
travelling to Australia is not made.
each trainee in the centre receives 5s per
week, and while training 1s is deducted
and returned in a lump sum to the trainee
on satisfactory completion of the course,
on his disembarkation in Canada, and in
the case of Australian trainees when they
arrive in London. A free issue of clothing is given to trainees, which can be retained on completion of the course of
training. Progress reports are sent to
our Department by the Canadian Government Department of Emigration and
Colonisation of trainees from Richhill
who come under the supervision of
the Canadian Government Land Settlement Branch Officers. These reports
indicate that the training given at

Mr. BEATTIE: I regret very much

ia our midst. It was very interesting to

In the main I must say my regrets are

Lieut.-Colonel GORDON : Ask Mr.

Mr. BEATTIE: I think the Conservative Government, who claim to hold the

We have had the number of the unemployed given at 52,000. If my memory
serves me right it was when this Estimate
was presented in 1923 that the Prime
Minister made that notorious declaration
of his that no matter what Mr. Baldwin
would do in England, he, as Prime Minister of Ulster, would solve the unemployment problem here. I think that at that
period there were thirty-eight thousand
some odd hundreds unemployed, but today we have some 52,000 registering at
the employment exchanges and there are
many more thousands who are not registering as they are outside unemployment
insurance altogether. There is a very
large army of persons who are not insured
within the meaning of the Act, and still
we are sitting here in an artificial position
Supply-
Committee

declaring ourselves solvent throughout the

If industry under the system which has
prevailed for a generation or
more has
failed to provide for those people the essentials of life it is time the Government
took action in regard to the concerns responsible for that position in industry. I
claim that the factors responsible for
bringing industry into its present state
should be tackled in a manner that would
surprise the gentlemen who have the power
either of strangling industry or making t
prosperous. You may think that a revolutionary idea, but let me tell you that
money lies at your command if you desire
to take an opportunity offered.
I will give you an illustration. To-day
lying in the banks are thousands upon
thousands of pounds in unclaimed
balances. I maintain the Government
should have some power over the banks
in regard to going to them and demanding
that a return should be made of these unclaimed balances. Failing that the Government should set up a Commission to
inquire into the condition of the unclaimed
balances and where the interest derived
from this money goes. If that is done 1
am certain that industry can be relieved
to a certain extent. This is money the
banks are not entitled to hold, and yet
they are holding it and taking the interest
accruing on it.
I regret very much that industry is not
surviving. I see in the Press that one of
our oldest firms is now going west. The
900 persons it was capable of employing
are being thrown on the streets without
the Government making any effort to find
appropriate employment for them.
I do
not think it can be argued that any suitable arrangements have been made by the
Government to try to hold industry together, and to try to keep in employment
all those whom industry should absorb,
giving them a decent standard of life. I Ι
do not think the Government have made

Every man takes the thing nearest to
his heart, and seeing I come personally in
contact with the unemployment situation
and the administration of the Unemployment Fund I feel that I must bring forward many questions, but before giving
my views I propose to read some letters
I have received in regard to the administration. These letters are from country
districts. The people in the country areas
find that the conditions of administration
as far as unemployment insurance is concerned constitute a most outrageous attack upon the Measure passed in Great
Britain for the purpose of alleviating the
distress amongst unemployed persons.
They feel that the conditions entitling
them to consideration under that Act are
being violated, but that would be a matter
for inquiry.
I have myself found in the City of
Belfast that the principle embodied in the
Act is being tampered with to such an
extent that portion of the Act of 1928
has been brought in in lieu of the "not
genuinely seeking work" condition. That
portion of the 1928 Act throws upon the
man the onus and responsibility of proving
that he is seeking normally insurable employment as a means of livelihood. That
is a very difficult thing to do. I do not
know whether you understand it or not,
but I will give an illustration of the hardship caused by that condition.
The Derry shipyard was a prosperous
concern for a number of years. It attracted tradesmen of all classes and shipbuilding and engineering workers to the
city. These men were there for from
twenty to twenty-five years and they
reared their families in that particular district. Their families have all found employment in Derry. In the year 1924
or 1925 the shipyard in Derry was closed
down. That dislocated all the craftsmen
and all the skilled and unskilled labour
connected with the shipyard. Those men
have been out of employment for long and
have only been able to gather up little
scraps of work entitling them to about sixteen stamps.
They were disheartened by being turned
down on the "not genuinely seeking work"
condition and so they omitted, although
some of them were living perhaps within
half a mile of the Exchange, to there
go
and register each week. For the omission
in regard to signing the register they are
now declared not normally insured persons
within the meaning of the Act and are not
receiving benefit in accordance with the
wish and desire of the people who put that
Act upon the Statute Book. The men
cannot move from the district, yet there is
Supply-
Committee
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Beattie]
no work for them in it. They have to
endeavour to take up other classes of employment but they cannot find it because
the youth of Derry have come forward.
and age cannot get work while youth is in
competition.
The greatest menace to the employed
worker to-day is the number of unemployed standing at the gate. There is a
menace hanging over every man in employment to-day because he knows that if
he turns a wrong step out he goes and in
comes a younger man. And once he is
out, if he is getting on in years, he finds
it a most difficult problem to get into employment again. The position in Derry
was created not by the people concerned
but by the system under which I myself
was compelled to live and under which I
am compelled to live now. If I had my
way it would be abolished to-morrow, as
I believe the State should give security
to those workers in Derry to such an extent that they would have an income sufficient to support them. All I ask is that
they be restored to the Unemployment Insurance Fund as insured persons. It is a
just case, which would not arise in Eng
land owing to the number of shipbuilding
centres there. The men in Derry need not
ccme to Belfast because there are too many
unemployed insured workers here. There
is no chance for them in Belfast, which is
the only centre they have outside Derry.
The other point I want to make is in
regard to the Blanesburgh Committee. I
think the intention of that Committee
should be followed closely. They used the
words "normally insurable," and I will
tell you what I took this as meaning. For
instance, take a man who has been working twenty years at a trade. He is a
married man with a family. That man's
normal occupation is his trade. If depression sets in in his trade and he is out
for a period of five or six years, and if
he has not abandoned the idea of following
his trade he has a right to be classified
as an insured person within the meaning
of the Act. No man is going to throw
up the rights he gained in his boyhood
days when he got an apprenticeship to a
trade. He spent five to seven years serving his time, and because he is out of the
trade for five years he is to be classified
as "not normally insurable," although he
has wrought at no other class of work.
The only thing he has done when he was
disallowed benefit by the Exchange was
to go on the highways and byways looking
for work and failed to recognise the labour
exchange as a place where he was
likely to find employment and therefore
did not register. Because of that he is
disallowed benefit.
I claim that the employment exchange never did function as an employment-finding centre for the unemployed
workers of Northern Ireland. The
difference between Northern Ireland and
Great Britain is that up to 1926 no provision was made in Northern Ireland for
the registration cf unemployed persons
who are not receiving benefit at the various
local exchanges. Owing to the cramped
conditions, in Belfast at any rate, no register for unemployed people receiving no
benefit was retained. An anomaly exists
there, and a grave injustice is being inflicted to-day and should be removed. I
will now read this letter I received from
Larne. I do not know which Member
represents Larne, but this letter is from
Cairns, at Cushendall, and says:
Excuse me for introducing myself, but
for the sake of fair play I felt it my

Office of the Ministry. I have signed
on 24/3/30, and after completing my
fifth form I received no money, but instead got a notice to attend a court of
referees on the 30th April in Larne. I
am sending you the result of this court
together with my record of insurable
employment. If you consider I have a
proper number of stamps under the new
Act kindly let me know by return.
There was about 30 paid off within the
last two weeks on the same grounds and
as you will see we have not even leave
to appeal.
This man has sent me his record of work,
but I will make no comment on it at the
moment. I think the least that should
have been done in his case was to allow
the right of appeal. A very serious position arises here. Here is a man living in
the country, and has so many miles to
travel each day for employment. When
that man is disallowed at the Labour Exchange surely it is not expected that he
should travel to the local exchange to sign
the register when he is not receiving unemployment benefit. The exchange has
never proved a satisfactory place for the
finding of work for the unemployed.
believe that the new Amending Act will

I feel that the Estimate itself should
not be burdened with so many charges
while the Unemployment Insurance Fund
is over three and a half millions in debt.
There are eight courts of referees sitting
per day in the City of Belfast. I do not
know the number outside, but each of
these courts costs money. I claim that is
an injustice to the Fund itself. It has
got to pay a certain amount each year
for these courts which could be presided
over by competent men who are willing
and anxious to give voluntary service as
they did prior to the appointment of legal
gentlemen in these positions. I do not
think it is fair for the legal profession to
come in when they have no interest in
the Fund. The only interest I see they
have is in getting the fees they receive for
the courts they attend. Two members of
each court attend free. They have equal
responsibilities, and for the life of me I
cannot see why the third man is paid.
If the three members of a court have equal
responsibilities there is something wrong
if they are not equally paid, but because
the chairman is a B.L., he gets his two
and a half guineas for each sitting while
the other two men who are the employers'
and employees' representatives receive
nothing. That is not a fair crack of the
whip to those two individuals who are
giving their services free on behalf of the
Fund and are trying to assist in the administration of the Act.
I have acted as chairman of these courts
for years and I can say that I gave as
satisfactory service as any of the legal
gentlemen who are now acting. It does
not require legal knowledge to say whether
a man is normally insurable or whether
he intends following normally insurable
employment in the future. Those are the
only two conditions to be decided by the
man who is in the chair and his two
colleagues. Between £50 and £60 is paid
every month to certain members of these
courts. If we put this money to the reduction of our debt to the Imperial Exchequer in regard to the Unemployment
Insurance Fund we would be doing a
greater service to Northern Ireland than
in paying these legal gentlemen. Keep
your legal chairmen by all means, but
ask them to give a little service to Ulster
for the services Ulster has given to them.
Some of these men claim to be loyal.
Their loyalty should be tested by asking
them to give their services free.
The Parliamentary Secretary mentioned.
many things which I do not intend to

think that is disgraceful. You stand for

she is entitled to a pension. There are
many cases like that. They are being unfairly dealt with, because the Ministry
has laid down the law that self-employment
outside a certain period disqualifies--
Mr. ANDREWS: Parliament has.

Mr. BEATTIE: Perhaps I should say

There are many cases like that in Northern Ireland. The Government should

If on this occasion they gave a lead to the

Another point I want to mention is in

Mr. GORDON: Are you referring to
the non-contributory?
Mr. BEATTIE: Certainly. It is the
only one to which that applies. Take the

he
goes out and earns that pound a week
you are disqualifying him. You ask him

is bad policy. If you are going to have a

decency. If you raise the standard of

doing another gracious act for the old

lead, perhaps, to the Imperial people on

With regard to blind persons' pensions,
I claim that Northern Ireland should give
a lead in that too. Each and all of us
are agreed that blind persons carry one
of the greatest afflictions that this world
can impose upon anyone. If you think
seriously of the position of blind persons,

period for a blind person to be left as a
responsibility upon his parents or upon his
friends, that is provided he does not get
a training in his early youth to assist him.
to provide for and to maintain himself.
There is another gracious act which the
Government car. do by reducing the age
for blind persons' pensions, and when

given another great lead to that Socialist
body across the water which seems to be so
distasteful to many hon. Members on the

Socialism then it is Socialism with which
I am in full agreement and with which I
know many hon. Members on this side of

The next thing to which I would like to
draw the attention of the Minister is the

national health insurance scheme. I am
not satisfied that the medical men who
come under this heading give satisfactory

have challenged the decisions of the

have been reversed in the cases to which I
refer. I claim that if a medical referee
is appointed for the benefit of the approved societies and of applicants his duty
is to see if a person is competent to carry
on work of any kind. It may not be due
to the certified disease, but if he is satisfied
in his own mind that some other complication has set in I say he is in duty bound
to decide that the person concerned in the
application is not competent to carry on
his work in accordance with the conditions
laid down either by the society or the company. I have found that in a large percentage of the cases in which the medical
referee has said that the applicants are fit
for work his decisions have been over-ruled
when they come to arbitration or are referred to other medical men. I presume
that you claim that he is a neutral man
placed there for the purpose of assisting
in what you would call differences of
opinion, that is when the society thinks an
applicant is fit for work and the applicant
thinks he is not fit. The referee is the

I for my part have never been a worshipper of any economic system. With

genuine prosperity. But I will take care

What is the condition here? When in

in 1923, 42,169 persons were recorded as

Andrews): I feel that it is necessary that

general industrial position in Northern
Ireland so far as it is possible to do so.
My answer, put very briefly, is that the
Government, since it came into being in
1922, has done everything humanly possible in every direction to help our people
in every way that it was possible for them
to do. The policy of the Ministry of
Labour is to administer those great Acts
of Parliament which are entrusted to our
care by Parliament as sympathetically as
the provisions of those Acts will permit
us.
The hon. Member for Central has stated
that Ulster is going down, and down, and
down, week by week, but the only evidence
he has really given of that is the fact that
the unemployment figures of to-day show
that the position has worsened to the extent of about 10,000 since 1923. Now,
as a matter of fact, these figures in my
opinion do not show that the position has
worsened because, as the hon. Member
will himself know, in 1923 unemployment
benefit was paid very sparingly. There
were long gaps, it was paid at a lower rate
than now, and the inducements for the
people to sign at the Exchanges were very
much less than they are to-day. Therefore the figure to-day is far more approximate to the exact number of people
unemployed than the figure of 1923
was. Besides, in 1923 we had
5,000 Specials " fully employed,
and in addition to that there were
at least a similar number of North
of Ireland men employed in the Free State
Army. These men have been disbanded
since, and that has produced a larger
supply of labour to be absorbed back into
industry.

Mr. BEATTIE: I think the word

recent

The PRIME MINISTER: Perhaps I
might be allowed to say that the Report
Stage of the Estimates taken to-day will
be on the Paper for next Thursday,
when those hon. Members who had not
the privilege of speaking to-day will have
ample opportunity. I would just like to
say, with regard to that, that it is somewhat difficult for Ministers and Parliamentary Secretaries to know exactly
what the Opposition want. If they are
very brief in their opening statements

then, on the other hand, when, as I
