that
Mr. DEVLIN: I just want to say
I dissent altogether from the view expressed by the Prime Minister that the
position is as he has stated it in either
case. As a matter of fact the Parliamentary Secretary (Mr. Gordon) to-day
made a very long, elaborate and interesting statement-
The PRIME MINISTER: Hear, hear.
Mr. DEVLIN- -but he should have
delivered it at Warrenpoint and not in
the House of Commons.
The PRIME MINISTER: I happen to
have been doing that for him at Warrenpoint.
Mr. DEVLIN: With all respect to
the Prime Minister I would suggest that
when, while Parliament is sitting, he has
a statement of that character to make he
should make it in the House of Commons
and not at a seaside resort. It shows
great disrespect for the House of Commons that, on a question of policy dealing with the great educational proposals
submitted by the Government to this
House, the Prime Minister should go
down to a watering place and, on a sunny
day and under happy circumstances, tell
a story and recite a tale that should have
been told here in the Parliament that
is dealing with the Measure at the
moment. The right hon. Gentleman,
his party, and his Ministers are in the
habit of doing what in my judgment is
an outrage upon our Parliamentary institutions, namely, that when declaring
their policy, a change of policy, or when
doing Parliamentary somersaults, instead of performing in the House here
they go elsewhere to do it
As I have said, the Parliamentary
Secretary's speech to-day was all right
if he had got it printed and handed
round for all of us to read. It was an
excellent statement. Of course, I like to
hear him as well, because he can read a
written statement, which most Ministers
and many Members of Parliament cannot
do.
But what we wanted here to-day was
what he did not give us, namely something concrete on the unemployment
question, just as the Prime Minister gave
something concrets on the education question. When you have nothing to tell us
you send your Under Secretaries to tell
it to us. When you have something to
tell us you go to Warrenpoint to tell it.
That is not my conception of how Parliamentary business should be done. I think
it is putting an indignity on Parliament
and shows a complete lack of that appreciation of this Parliament which the
Noble Lord the Prime Minister seems to
display to a greater extent than I do. The
Prime Minister professes to have a great
admiration for this Parliament.
I myself frankly confess that I have not a
great admiration for this Parliament. I
would have an admiration for this Parliament, as I would for any other body, if
it settled down and did what it could do,
namely sit round the table like a small.
respectable body of ordinary, intelligent
men and try to provide new plans and to
originate new ideas for the development
of the Six Counties and the betterment
of our people. Take, for instance, a
respectable body like the Harbour Commissioners. (Hon. Members: Hear.
hear.) It is also, I believe, an intelligent
body. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
You need not applaud. This Parliament
is not respectable, and I do not think it
is very intelligent-I mean in its procedure.
Mr. SPEAKER: I must ask the hon.
Gentleman not to make observations to
the effect that this Parliament is not respectable. I am sure that on consideration the hon. Gentleman will withdraw
the observation.
Mr. DEVLIN: Certainly I will withdraw. I meant in the sense in which the
Harbour Commissioners are respectable.
(Laughter.) If ever I should make a
single criticism of this Parliament then,
according to the Prime Minister, I commit an outrage against Northern Ireland
and against the glory of our Parliamentary institutions. I come here when 1
can to take part in the business-I do
not know what the Attorney-General
(Mr. Babington) said.
The PRIME MINISTER: He was
giving a legal opinion.
Mr. DEVLIN: Then that would be
unbiassed. I thought it was a political
opinion. You claim to have a profound
admiration for this institution and think
it wonderful, and yet you do not come
into the House even when you are in the
building.
The PRIME MINISTER indicated
dissent.

The
Mr. DEVLIN: No, you do not.
Minister of Labour (Mr. Andrews) during the important discussion to-day was
left sitting practically alone, while all of
his colleagues were in the smokeroom, in
the tea-room, or elsewhere in the less attractive parts of the building. The
Prime Minister was at Warrenpoint
making a speech upon the Education Bill,
which we will be called upon to consider
next Tuesday, instead of placing it before
us here. I also remember the Minister
of Finance (Mr. Pollock) making a long
speech adumbrating a policy at some
public meeting-some ward meeting-in
the city here, although Parliament met a
few days afterwards. This is not a Parliament. It is a convenience. You just
come here when you have nothing else to
do. It is a sort of intellectual dissipation. I have to go to two Parliaments,
and I endeavour to go to both when I
can do service in either. I do not come
here so often as I used to because it is
lost time. What is the good of coming
here? Some day or other a new set of
men will arise and boycott this Parliament, because it soon will not be worth
coming to if you go on handling the
affairs of Northern Ireland as you are
now. Therefore, when the Prime Minister rises here and lectures us
on the
way we should carry on our business and
improve our methods-
The PRIME MINISTER: I am sure
the hon. Member does not wish to misrepresent me. I did not for one moment
lecture the hon. Member or his colleagues
in any way. I only pointed out the difficulty the Government were in and how
we had to consider whether we should
make exhaustive statements in submitting our Estimates to the Committee or
remain in our seats, wait till the Opposition had made their criticism, and then
answer it. On the whole we thought the
Committee would prefer that each Minister or Under Secretary should make his
statement first. If hon. Members prefer
the other way we are perfectly willing to
fall in with their views.
Mr. DEVLIN: At the beginning of
the Session I pointed out to the Prime
Minister that the first thing about which
we ought to be told in this House was
what had been done in regard to unemployment and trade. I was then told by
the Minister of Labour (Mr. Andrews)
that I would find that out at the proper
time.
Mr. ANDREWS indicated dissent.
Mr. DEVLIN: Yes. He said I would
be told that when his Estimates were
brought before the House.
Mr. ANDREWS: On a point of Order,
the hon. Gentleman will recollect that I
said that if he would put down a Notice of
Motion on the matter I was quite prepared to discuss it at any time.
Mr. DEVLIN: It was not my business
to put down a Notice of Motion, but it
was yours to come forward frankly and
tell the House of matters that vitally concern the Six Counties, that is, if you had
anything to tell. As the Prime Minister
was not present I may tell him that I
took exception to this speech of the Under
Secretary to-day because he did not tell
us anything, but only recited the activities of the various Departments of the
Ministry of Labour. He did not tell us
the one thing we wanted to know, namely
what was being done in regard to unemployment.
Mr. ANDREWS: I told you.
Mr. DEVLIN: No. You did not. You
did not rise until the last minute.

Tuesday, 13th May, 1930.

Mr. SPEAKER in the Chair.
Oral Answers to Questions.
TELEPHONE SERVICE IN RURAL
DISTRICTS.
1. Mr. CRAWFORD (for Captain
Chichester-Clark) asked the Minister of
Commerce whether he is aware that the
telephone service in many of the rural dis
tricts is grossly unsatisfactory; that lines
are frequently out of repair, and that delays in making repairs are often of long
duration; and whether he will make representation to the Imperial Government to
have the service improved, and, in view of
the fact that country lines are out of order
for considerable periods, to have the subscription rates reduced.
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Pollock): I am taking this question for
my right hon. Friend.
The records do not support the suggestion that the service is unsatisfactory or
is subject to abnormal interruption, but if
the hon. and gallant Member will furnish
details of any particular instances he has
in mind they will be investigated.
The telephone rates in Northern Ireland
are assessed in precisely the same manner
as in Great Britain.
I shall be glad to hand particulars to
my hon. Friend if he desires any further
information.

ROSETTA P.E.S.-TEACHERS'
QUALIFICATIONS.
3. Mr. NIXON asked the Minister of
Education whether any of the female
teachers who have completed their training in Stranmillis Training College are
qualified to teach an infant class in
Rosetta Public Elementary School, and,
if so, why the Local or District Committee
sent forward to the Belfast Education
Committee only two names out of a total
Oral Answers
Oral Answers
13 MAY 1930
of 16 applicants, and gave as their reason
that those two were the only qualified
candidates.
Mr. ROBB: The great majority of
women teachers trained at Stranmillis
Training College are qualified to teach an
infants' class in Rosetta or in any other
public elementary school, but, inasmuch
as a course of training does not represent
the maximum teaching qualification, many
teachers endeavour to secure additional
qualifications such as a university degree
or diploma, or the diploma of some other
institution.
The Belfast Education Committee frequently asks for teachers with special
qualifications such as a degree or diploma,
or with a qualification to teach French,
mathematics or science. In cases where
teachers for infants' classes are required
the Committee. I understand, asks for applications from candidates with special
kindergarten qualifications
The advertisement of the vacancy, to
to which, I presume, the hon. Member
refers, stated that candidates for appointment must be trained teachers with
special kindergarten qualifications. Only
two of the applicants had the qualification
specified in the advertisement and this
was duly notified to the Belfast Education Committee by the Rosetta District
School Committee.
Mr. NIXON: Will the Parliamentary
Secretary say that in future all the
teachers leaving Stranmillis Training College will be qualified to teach the infant
class in any school?
Mr. ROBB: They are so qualified at
present.
AMOUNT OF
TEACHERS'
PENSIONS.
4. Mr. NIXON asked the Minister of
Finance whether he can state the amount
of money paid during the year ended the
31st March, 1930, in pensions to retired.
secondary, technical, agricultural, industrial, and workhouse teachers respectively,
the amount so paid to retired junior
assistant mistresses and to retired lay
assistant teachers in convent schools, and
the number of recipients in each category
on the 31st March, 1930.
Mr. POLLOCK : The figures are as
follow:-
Number of secondary teachers' pensions,
28; amount paid in the year ended 31st
March, 1930, £5,350; technical teachers.
1, amount paid, £19; junior assistant
mistresses 37, amount paid £1,253; lay
assistant teachers 1, amount paid £73.
No agricultural teachers were pensioned
in the period.
The amount paid to secondary teachers
during the period in question is unduly
high, as it includes a considerable amount
of arrears of pension consequent on the
improved pension terms granted by a
recent Amending Order of the Governor
in Council.
Teachers who retire from industrial
schools and workhouses are not pensionable under the Teachers' Superannuation
Acts.
MUNICIPAL
ELECTIONS-INTRO-
DUCTION OF BILL.
5. Mr. NIXON asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether he can state when
the Bill to alter the date of municipal
elections to a more suitable season will be
introduced.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): The question of the
synchronisation of the dates of all Local
Government elections is receiving consideration in connection with the preparation of the Bill on Local Government reform. It is hoped it will be possible to
introduce the Measure next year.

TAKING.

Home Affairs whether he can state the
total amount of capital charges, loans,
etc., on the Belfast Tramway undertaking,
and whether he approves of increasing
the amount by £210,327 on re-conditioning trams and other additions and improvements which it is held should be
charged to the Revenue Account.
Sir DAWSON BATES. For detailed
information on the subject I must refer
the hon. Member to the published accounts
of the Belfast Tramway undertaking, of
which no doubt as a member of the Corporation he has received a copy.
I may say, however, that from the
accounts published for the year ended the
31st March, 1929, it would appear that
the amount of outstanding loars was
£1,896,560. As against this amount
there was a sinking fund of £1,053,577.

CENSORSHIP OF LETTERS AND
TELEGRAMS.
7. Mr. HEALY asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether he can state if the
censorship of letters, telegrams and telephones is being continued in the postal
service in Northern Ireland by officials of
his department, and the reasons therefor.
Sir DAWSON BATES: Correspondence for delivery to, or emanating from,
persons in Northern Ireland suspected of
being engaged in seditious activities is still
subjected to censorship in the interests of
public safety.
Mr. HEALY: How does the right hon.
Gentleman know whether a closed letter
emanates from a certain class or people?
Is the right hon. Gentleman aware that
this intolerable practice of reading private
correspondence is becoming very obnoxious, particularly to the legal and professional friends of the right hon. Gentleman who fear their correspondence may
become a commonplace and their secrets
known?
Sir DAWSON BATES: No law-abiding citizen need be the slightest bit afraid
of the course the Government are taking.
Mr. COLLINS: I am a law-abiding
citizen and I do not want my professional
correspondence opened. I want the Minister of Home Affairs to understand that
I have duties to my clients.
Sir DAWSON BATES: I am absolutely
certain the police do not take the slightest
interest in my hon. Friend's correspondence.
Mr. HEALY: Will the right hon.
Gentleman answer the question I put to
him? How does he know in advance, before a letter is opened, whether it is from
a person of seditious proclivities or not?
Let him alone, he is able to answer his own
questions, Prime Minister. Will he also tell
us how many Peeping Toms he has in the
Post Office and how many secret spies are listening to telephone conversations and what
they cost, because that is an important
matter?
Sir DAWSON BATES: My hon.
Friend appreciates that we cannot tell
these little secrets. (Laughter).
Mr. DEVLIN: Does not the right hon.
Gentleman think it a very vicious principle and abhorrent to all lovers of liberty
in this land that this system should be
carried on in the Post Office?
Sir DAWSON BATES: No.
Mr. DEVLIN: This is not a Northern
Ireland service, it is an Imperial service,
and if it is an Imperial service how does
it come the right hon. Gentleman has the
right to go into the Post Office and slit
open people's correspondence?
Mr. HEALY: Answer.
REBUILDING OF BALLAGH
BRIDGE.
8. Mr. HEALY asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether he can state if he
intends to rebuild Ballagh Bridge on the
road between Armagh and Emyvale,
which was partly blown up by Specials in
1922.
Sir DAWSON BATES: The Tyrone
County Council have had a number of
damaged bridges to repair and have
naturally taken them in order of importance.
The repair of Ballagh Bridge has not
been regarded as a matter of urgency, but
when the County Council undertake its
repair the Government will, in accordance
with the undertaking already given to the
County Council, be prepared to recoup the
cost.
It is understood that its repair will be
undertaken at the earliest opportunity.
Mr. HEALY: Can the right hon.
Gentleman give us any indication as to
when it will be opportune to repair a
bridge that has been damaged since 1922?
Sir DAWSON BATES: I have already
explained to my hon. Friend it is the
primary duty of the County Council to
repair those bridges. We have undertaken, as a Government, to recoup the
County Council the expenses of doing so.
The County Council inform me they will
undertake the work of repair in due course.
They also tell me there is no particular
urgency for the repairs.
Oral Answers.

Mr. HEALY: That is an extraordinary
reply.
Mr. STEWART: Seeing the County
Council has taken no steps will the right

Sir DAWSON BATES: The County
Council propose to take it in the ordinary
course. They will ultimately repair it.

in Tyrone are not very keen to facilitate

IMPORTATION OF PARROTS.
15. Mr. NIXON asked the Minister of
Agriculture whether he has taken any
steps to prohibit the importation of parrots into Northern Ireland, and, if so,
whether he will state the grounds on
which such steps were taken.
Sir DAWSON BATES: I have been
asked to reply. The Ministry of Home
Affairs has made an order prohibiting the
importation of parrots. Similar orders
have been made in Great Britain and the
Irish Free State. The order was made
in the interests of public health to prevent the introduction of the disease
known as psittacosis which has broken
out in Great Britain and other countries.
This disease is of a very deadly character,
and has been traced to newly imported
parrots.

OUTBREAKS OF SHEEP SCAB.
16. Lt.-Colonel GORDON asked the
Minister of Agriculture to state if any
improvement has taken place in the number of confirmed outbreaks of sheep scab
since 1928, when the number was 87 for
a sheep population of 624,084.
The MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE
(Sir Edward Archdale): I am satisfied
that there is an improvement in the
sheep scab position in 1929 as compared
with 1928. This is evidenced by the facts
that while in 1928, with a sheep population of 624,084, there were 87 confirmed
outbreaks; in 1929, with a sheep population of 654,589, there were only 63 such
outbreaks.
Mr. COLLINS: Arising out of that
answer can the Minister of Agriculture
inform us if all these legs of mutton from
New Zealand that we see advertised on
our hoardings by the Empire Marketing
Board have been free from sheep scab?
Sir EDWARD ARCHDALE: I do
not think the legs take sheep scab.

CLAUSE 1 (Additional members of
education committees).
(1) The Minister of Education shall
have power to appoint, as members of an
education committee for the purposes
of the Education Act (Northern Ireland), 1923 (in this Act refered to as
"the principal Act"), persons who, in
his opinion, are representative of the
transferors by whom any schools in the
education area of such committee have
been transferred to the education
authority, and such appointments
shall be made after consultation with
the transferors (to such extent as may
seem to the said Minister practicable
and expedient) and with the education
authority concerned. In determining
the number of representative persons
to be so appointed as members of an
education committee, the said Minister
shall have regard to the number of
schools transferred as aforesaid, and
such members shall be additional to
the members appointed under subsection (2) or sub-section (4) of section
two of the principal Act, but shall not
in any case exceed in number onefourth of the total number of members
of the committee (including the members appointed by the said Minister),
and the said sub-sections shall have
effect as amended by this section.

CLAUSE 2 (Amendment of the principal Act as to Committees for management of schools and their powers).
(1) The following section shall be substituted for section three of the principal
Act as amended by the Education Act
(Northern Ireland), 1925:-
3.-(1) The education authority
shall, as respects every public elementary school within their education
area which is a provided school or a
transferred school (as hereinafter in
this Act defined), make provision for
the local management of the school by
means of a school management committee to be appointed by the education authority; but so that several
such schools may be grouped under
one school management committee, if
the education authority so desire and
the Ministry approves.
(2) A school management committee appointed under the last preceding
sub-section shall be so constituted
that, so far as is practicable, not less
than one-half of the members to be
appointed thereto shall be representative of the following persons:
(a) the transferors of the transferred schools under the local

The purpose of my Amendment is simply
to alter the guiding principle of this
Clause or rather to state what I think
ought to be the guiding principle without
doing any drastic injury to the Clause itself. I think it is most desirable in the
interests of education that when schools
are transferred to the local authority and
when school committees are appointed in
respect of those transferred or provided
schools, as many such schools as possible
should be governed by one single committee, because this Bill which has passed
its Second Reading gives the school committees enormous powers.
It has very
largely divested the powers formerly possessed by the education authorities and
proposes to transfer those powers, including the power of selecting teachers, to the
local authorities. The purpose of this
Amendment is to ensure that as far as
possible when schools are transferred they
shall be grouped together under one single
committee.
I think it would be a very disastrous
thing if for every transferred school and
for every provided school there was a
single school committee. That would be
a reversion back to the old system which
prevailed for over one hundred years and
finally died a temporary death in 1923.
Furthermore, I can see one very fundamental objection to this Clause as it
stands, and it is this. At the present
time-

This is, I must admit, a somewhat drastic Amendment, and I confess I have very

this Bill school management committees

have maintained the prestige of the education authorities by ensuring that the
education authority should have the

this Amendment.

The other Amendment I have on the

It has been pointed out, I think even to
the Minister of Education, that if this
Clause is carried we might have a case
where a man who had so mismanaged a
school that it had to be closed and the
children catered for in a provided school
must legally become represented on the
committee of the provided school, so that

is possible, although it is not probable, but
under some circumstances such a man
might have the right of appointing half
the committee, supposing there was only
one provided school with a single committee manager. In order to meet that objection I intend to move the insertion of
the words "and provided that the Ministry
are satisfied that such public elementary
school was not superseded on account of
inefficient management." I think this
will only come into operation in perhaps
one per cent. of all the cases, but I think
it is wise that we should have some safeguard of this kind.
Mr. ROBB: To take the hon. Member's
last Amendment first, the position is
this. If a school is inefficiently managed
the Ministry has the duty of doing
one of two things, either to close the school
or to remove the inefficient manager.
That is the clear duty of the Ministry.
Consequently if, up to the provision of a
new school, the school is allowed to continue in existence the Ministry has either
failed in its duty or the manager is not
inefficient. So long as the Ministry recognise the manager as the manager of the
school and allows the school to continue
there is a prima facie case that the school
is not inefficiently managed.
Therefore, to introduce an Amendment
in the terms the hon. Member has
suggested would seem to the Ministry to
give an opportunity for endless friction
where possibly some unpopular manager
might have a case made against him by an
education authority that he was not
entitled to any of its privileges, because
his school had been conducted in an
inefficient manner. If the school is being
inefficiently conducted it is the duty of the
Ministry to close the school, and the introduction of this Amendment would
only give rise to suspicion and friction
and endless trouble to meet a case which
the hon. Member himself suggested might
only arise in one per cent. of all the cases.
This does not seem a good way to do it
even if the evil were so great as to call
for a remedy.

That is not our intention at all. Our intention is that the local people shall have

Mr. ROBB: The Government cannot

the principle upon which this Bill is based
is that the local people shall have a voice

My hon. Friend who sits on my right on
these Benches (Professor Johnstone) has
said that if you can take cver a teacher
from a school that is superseded, why can
you not take over a teacher from another
school in which the attendance has declined? It is not the same thing. The
teacher in the superseded school is going
over to the provided school with the
children that he has been teaching, and
the presumption is that, as he has been
teaching the children there, he is agreeable
to the parents, to the manager of the
school, and to those in authority generally.
That is an entirely different thing from
saying that the education authority shall
be entitled to put into the school in a
particular case a teacher in regard to
whom the school management committee
have not been consulted. Take the city
of Belfast, for instance. Let us suppose
there is a vacancy in a school at Cregagh,
and a teacher at Ballysillan is about to
lose his job because the numbers attending
his school are dwindling. It might quite
well be that the people of Cregagh would
not like the teacher from Ballysillan.

whose appointment they had nothing

This is a proposal to insert the words on
the Paper instead of the original Subsection 2 of Section 16 of the Act of
1923, and it is a little bit complicated.
There are three points embodied in the new
Sub-clause. First, the contributions of
an education authority are made a first
charge on the premises of the new school,
subject, however, to any prior charge
arising out of a loan for the same building
having already been made by the Commis-
Education Bill-

sioners of Public Works or the Ministry of
Finance. This is intended to simplify the
procedure for making these contributions.
That is the first point. The original
Section says the amount should be a
charge, but it did not say anything about
the priority in which it was to rank.
We think it should rank from the
date on which the sums were paid,
subject only to any prior charge existing
in favour of the Ministry of Finance or
the Office of Public Works in respect of a
loan on the same premises.
The new Sub-clause provides that in
case of default in the maintaining of the
school the education authority may
recover the full amount, or such portion
as may have been agreed of their contribution with interest as from date of default. In the existing Act the corresponding provision, which it is proposed to
replace by this Sub-section, renders the
trustees liable to repay the enhanced value
of the premises which have been made the
subject of a contribution. The new procedure is preferred on account of its simplicity, and also because it is in accordance
with the arrangement which was adopted
in the case of grants to vested schools under
the Commissioners of National Education
and which was found to work satisfactorily.

the
The purpose of this Amendment is to
facilitate the matter of school attendance.
I find it necessary to refer hon. Members
to Section 32 of the principal Act, which
my Amendment proposes to amend by
substituting what you, Mr. Chairman,
have just read out. Section 32 of the
Education Act, 1923, deals with the power
of education authorities to make school
'attendance orders. The effect of that
Section is that there is a considerable
delay, as hon. Members will see when I
refer them to the Section, in enforcing
the attendance of children at school and
in carrying out the machinery of the
law. Section 32 says:
Education Bill-
Committee
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. McNeill]
If it appears to the education authority that any parent, who is required by
or under this Act to cause his child to
attend school, has neglected or failed.
to perform his duty in that respect, the
education authority shall have power,
after due warning to the parent, to
summon him to appear before them
with or without the child, and to require
from him information and explanation
as to his neglect or failure of duty.
The first thing the Section laid down was
that the education authority would have
power to summon the parent to appear
before them, that is before their
school attendance committee. That
means, I am instructed, a delay of
one month. The school attendance committee meets at most once a month, and
the school attendance committee ask the
parent to appear before them upon the
complaint of the school attendance officer.
You get a delay in the first instance of
one month, which my Amendment proposes to get rid of. Furthermore, Section
32 adds:
If the parent, or some person on his
behalf, either does not appear, or appears and does not satisfy the education
authority that he has not neglected or
failed in his duty, the education authority may make an order in writing to
the effect that the child shall attend
some school willing to receive him and
named in the school attendance order,
being either such school as the parent
may select, or if he does not select a
school then such school as the education
authority think expedient, and the child
shall attend that school in such regular
manner as is specified in the school
attendance order.
The old Section provides that the school
attendance order shall only be issued by
the school attendance committee if the
parent neglects to appear before them.
To complete the Section:
The education authority shall cause
a copy of the school attendance order to
be served upon the parent by registered
letter, or in such manner as may be
prescribed,
et cetera.
The purpose of my Amendment is to
expedite the law. Hon. Members will see
in what way I propose to do it. My
Amendment is .
If any parent who is required under
this Act to cause his child to attend
school has neglected or failed to perform his duty in this respect, it shall
be the duty of a school attendance
officer to serve, in writing, a "school
attendance order ".
In the very first instance without bringing
the parent before the school attendance
committee it shall be the duty—the summary duty-of the school attendance
officeron
the parent to the effect that the
child shall attend some school giving
efficient instruction.
There we have what I am told will
practically save two months. The Amendment goes on:
And if the parent fails to comply with
the order, it shall be the duty of the
school attendance officer to summon the
parent to appear before the next meeting of the school attendance committee.
If the parent does not attend, or if the
reason given for non-compliance with
the order is not satisfactory, the school
attendance committee may issue a summons against the parent, and bring him
or her before the Court of Summary
Jurisdiction.
The effect of that Amendment would
mean that defaulting parents and recalcitrant guardians of children would come
before a court of summary jurisdiction
within a very much shorter process of
time than previously under Section 32.
That is the purpose of this Amendment.
Mr. COLLINS: I would like to
support this Amendment. I think it is
an excellent thing. I would not have
supported it if the case had not come before the school attendance committee
before there is a prosecution. I can well

Member's mind. The school attendance

month. The school officer would report
that A and B are not going to school.
They would authorise him to send out a
summons, and then the thing would have
to be reported at another meeting, and an

strongly in favour of this Amendment,
and the Government should give it consideration. It is not depriving the
school attendance committee of the power
to order a prosecution, but it shortens

NEW CLAUSE (School attendance.
outside Education area).
Where children are residing in one
education area and attending school in
another area, it shall be the duty of
the education authority of the area in
which they reside to see that such
children attend school regularly, and
they shall cause their school attendance
officer to visit such school or schools
even though they are outside their
education area, and take the names of
any absent or irregularly attending
children, and to take all the necessary
steps to cause such children to attend
regularly. (Mr. Miller).

not see that this Amendment will go any

water).
For the purposes of section eightyone of, and the Fifth Schedule to, the
principal Act, the expression "land"
includes water, and any interest in or
right to or over water.

That was a most unfair Act to the minority because, according to it, we were not
entitled to any grants whatever for the
building of our schools and their equipment. For six years we have borne the
brunt, the burden and the heat of the day

people might have the necessary educational advantages through efficient schools.
Not one farthing has been subscribed or
contributed by the State towards the building of those schools.
We bore that affliction with patience,
and with silence almost, and that wrong

urgency, where the Treasury-bear this

Mr. POLLOCK : In reference to the
Second Reading of this small Measure my
right hon. Friend circulated a White
paper explaining its proposals, and I
take it for granted, therefore, that the
House will not expect me to enter in
great detail into the features of the
Measure which is very simple in its
character. Shortly, the object of the
Measure is to increase from £1,000,000
to £1,750,000 the amount which may be
outstanding at any time in respect of the
advances made by the
made by the Ministry of
Finance to the Unemployment Insurance
Fund under certain Acts. At present
the advance made is £956,000, and as I
say the object of the Measure is to increase the amount or give the Ministry of
Finance authority to increase the amount
on
loan to the Insurance Fund to
£1,750,000. The conditions which
obtained in Great Britain in respect of
this matter will be recalled. It was
necessary for Parliament to authorise an
advance to the Unemployment Insurance
Fund there from forty millions to fifty
millions, and, of course, this was reflected
upon our conditions here having regard
to the fact that parity exists between the
two Funds.
Indeed under the provisions of the
Re-insurance Agreement between Great
Britain and ourselves, which was embodied
in the Unemployment Insurance Agreement Act, 1926, and continued in force
by the Act of 1929, the Unemployment
Funds of the two countries are kept in
parity, and the increase in the deficit in
one country is necessarily seen in the deficit existing in the other country. It
has been found, therefore, having regard
to the simple facts I have mentioned,
that it is possibly necessary we may have
to increase our loans to the Unemployment Insurance Fund to some considerable extent. We expect and hope that
when unemployment in Great Britain
decreases the amount will also decrease.
At present there is a considerable
obligation on us to provide funds in order
that the two Funds may be kept in
parity.

Mr. ANDREWS: No wonder.
Mr. BEATTIE: No wonder you laugh,
because you have never yet decided to

brigade. I am sure when you read the
history of the Drennans you will find
that they did not belong to the party to
which you now belong. Therefore, I forgive you because you
do not know to what
party you belong.
And now to get back to the Bill, why is
this borrowing power required? It is required because of the failure of the present
system of society to maintain a proper
standard of life for the people. In other
words, the system under which we are
compelled to live has absolutely failed, and
no greater example of that failure can be
shown than in the Six Counties. The
great captains of industry, men who bring
their super abilities to bear on the
management of industry, cannot from
their lofty positions bring pressure to bear
upon the economic forces that are now
driving 60,000 of our people on to the
streets. They cannot bring pressure to
bear and say "Long enough have you
strangled industry. No longer are we
going to allow you to do so." Until the
Government in this House manage the
banks industry is never going to get its
head above water.
It is very easy, perhaps, for me to say
you should manage the banks, but it is
just as simple as nationalising the banks.
What right have the banking concerns to
close down industries that are providing a
livelihood for the workers. No right at
all. When they interfere with the livelihood of the worker they interfere with the
liberty of the citizen, and liberty must be
protected. You claim that the Private
Property Act protects private property,
and you claim to use force if necessary to
protect it. Why do you not claim to use
force to protect the life of the Six Counties. Industry is closing down all over
the area, and no hope is being held out
whereby the workers who are displaced can
take their labour into another industry.
To-day rationalisation of industry is
driving thousands and thousands of craftsment out of positions. Some people may
say that Thomas agrees with that. That
is quite true, but every member of the
Labour party holds his own view as far
as the ideal of rationalisation is concerned.
I am not so mad in my day and generation
as to oppose the introduction of machinery. I know it will come whether I like
it or not. But I also feel that there is an
obligation on me, in respect of the element
that has been displaced by the introduction of new machinery and the elimination
of the human element, to provide openings
for that element so that it may have a
reasonable standard of life. Until the
whole system under which we are compelled to live is changed I expect the right
hon. Gentleman (Mr. Andrews) to come
here every year to ask for an extension of
his borrowing powers under the Unemployment Insurance Acts.
Mr. GORDON: I hope not.
Mr. BEATTIE: You know as well as
I do that the system demands that the
unemployed shall be at the beck and call
of the employing classes. You could not
exist without the unemployment situation.
It is an impossibility for the capitalist
system to exist without the unemployment
situation. Therefore, if you wish to
abolish unemployment you will have to
abolish that system.

Mr. POLLOCK : As hon. Members
will note from the fact that the
greater portion of the Bill is italicised the
Labourers Cottages Bill, the Second
Reading of which I now propose to move,
is almost wholly a financial Measure.
The financial proposals fall into two parts,
firstly the continuance of the financial
arrangements which have operated since
1st April, 1927, in respect of labourers'
cottages contructed by rural district
councils, and, secondly, arrangements
consequential on the possible taking over
by this Government of the burden of
financing those Labourers' Cottages
Schemes which were in operation prior to
1st April, 1927, the loans for which have
hitherto been found by the Land Purchase Commission, a subsidy being given
by this House towards the loan charges.
I shall develop these two points by taking the House back a little way.
The Labourers Cottages Loans Act
(Northern Ireland), 1927, brought to an
end, save for schemes then in train, the
old arrangements under which the construction of labourers' cottages was
financed by means of loans made to rural
district councils by the Land Purchase
Commission from the Land Purchase
Fund, a grant of 36 per cent. of the loan
charges being made annually from the
Northern Ireland Exchequer. Instead,
in the case of new schemes, the money
was to be lent from the Northern Ireland
Government Loans Fund, and to make
up for the less advantageous borrowing
terms the annual Government subsidy was
increased to 40 per cent. of the loan
charges.
The Government subsidy to which I
have last referred, that is to say, the subsidy payable under the 1927 Act, was only
provided for a temporary period, namely,
in respect of schemes lodged with the
Ministry of Home Affairs before 31st
March, 1930. That date having now
passed the Government have decided to
ask the House by means of this Measure
to extend the period of the subsidy. As
to the necessity for this extension I think
that there can be no doubt, and from the
information also that I have we reckon
that at least 696 cottages are now called
for by these authorities.
Mr. HEALY: Can you tell us the
localities or counties in which they are
going to be erected?
Mr. POLLOCK: My right hon. Friend
who is responsible for the administration
of these Acts will be able to give any details with regard to the areas which favour
the continuance of the production of these
houses. The Bill, therefore, proposes the
continuance of the arrangements which
have just lapsed for a further period of
five years, that is to say, from now until
1935. The provisions of the 1927 Act,
which limit the expenditure towards
which Government contributes to a sum
of £350 per cottage, will continue to
apply.
I turn now to the second financial point
in the Bill. When steps were about to be
taken, at the close of March, to introduce
a Bill dealing with the extension of the
period of the subsidy, a suggestion was
received from the Home Office in London
that the Government of Northern Ireland
should take over the financing of those
schemes which, having been submitted to
the Ministry of Home Affairs prior to 1st
April, 1927, fell to be financed by advances from the Land Purchase Fund.
Only a small number of these schemes
remain unfinished, but in order to pro-

Mr. ELLIOTT: I rise to support
this Bill, and I am rather sorry to see
hon. Members opposite complain
bitterly about the houses erected all over
Northern Ireland, not only for the
labourers but for those who are unable to
supply houses for themselves.
Speaking
for County Tyrone, which has been
brought into the picture by scme Members who do not represent the County, I
think the record of County Tyrone as far
as providing houses for agricultural
labourers and artisans is concerned, will
compare favourably with that of any
other county in Northern Ireland. In
the two rural districts which I know
something about, Dungannon and Cookstown, both these councils have taken full
advantage of the Government's generous
contribution, and they have provided a
great number of labourers cottages which
are beautiful houses, well built, and let
in most cases at about 2s a week. In
Cookstown rural district some short time
ago newer cottages were let at 2s 6d a
week, and one of the Councillors brought
forward a motion that the rents should
be reduced to an average of 2s per
week.
I am glad to say that that was
done, and many of our agricultural
labourers in the Cookstown rural district
and South Tyrone are now living in comfortable houses which would never have
been built had it not been for the
generous way the Government met the
rural district councils and provided the
money.
Subsidy houses have also been attacked
by hon. Members opposite. I am quite
prepared to admit that there are subsidy
built houses which are let to tenants at
a rent which is higher than it should be.
At the same time, there are two sides to
every story, and I know that in County
Tyrone there are a great number of very
comfortable subsidy houses which are let
to artisans and agricultural labourers at
rents of 3s and 3s 6d a week. I have not
yet heard any hon. Member have the
audacity to get up in this House and say
that these houses in County Tyrone were
jerrybuilt or built of material that was
not all right. If hon. Members opposite
will only come to County Tyrone I shall
be very glad to show them what is being
done there by private enterprise to provide houses for the people at an economic
rent. There are some hon. Members in
this House who are always decrying what
other people have done, and always
blaming the Government for not giving
a grant of 100 per cent. when they
give 50 per cent., but I have never
yet heard or seen of anything practical that these same hon.
Members have done to try to ease the housing
shortage. I believe that an ounce of
practice is worth a great deal more than
this camouflaged nonsense that we hear so
much about.
I would like to see hon. Members opposite trying to do something practical
in their own areas
to provide suitable
houses at a economic rent for those who
are unable to build them for themselves.

Mr. HEALY Yesterday I put down.
a question to the Minister of Home
Affairs dealing with the opening of letters
in the postal service in Northern Ireland,
and the reply of the right hon. Gentleman was a confession that that practice
was in operation but that it was only
adopted in the cases of people whose
loyalty was suspected. "Necessity knows
no law," and that this thing should continue after Judges of Assize, and indeed
members of the Government have declared so frequently in recent times that
everything is peaceful in the Six Counties
is quite incomprehensible. I asked the
right hon. Gentleman yesterday to give
me some indication of the number of
people he had in the telegraph_department and the number of Peeping Toms he
had at the telephones listening to conversations that might be going on all over
the place, and he said that he could not
reveal these little secrets. It must be
obvious that the postal telegraph staff at
least know the number of these officials of
the Ministry of Home Affairs who are
stuck in post offices all over the Six
Counties.
The right hon. Gentleman tried to convince the House that only the letters of
suspected persons were opened. How in
the name of commonsense can the Minister of Home Affairs make it clear that
he can tell by looking at a letter whether
the writer is a suspect person or not?
There may be some of his colleagues in
the legal profession whose letters are
opened, and some of his clerks may be
digesting as a sort of interesting tit-bit.
some secret passing between a client and
a lawyer in Belfast. I think it is an exceedingly undesirable practice that the
whole community should be laid under
tribute because the Minister of Home
Affairs or someone in his Department
thinks that a seditious document is passing between one party and another.
Does the right hon. Gentleman not remember the time when he was in insurrection himself? It does not require a
great effort of memory to recall it. Did
he use the post office for arranging the
wonderful coup at Larne? I venture to
say he did not. And when the Mayflower landed at Bangor with guns I am
sure the information was not conveyed
Does he think
through the post office.
that anybody conspiring in these days is
any less wise or shrewd than he was when
he was laying the foundations of his
reputation and his fortune?
When these letters are opened they are
not merely, as was done in war time,
marked as having been opened, and sealed,
and censored. There is a meaner trick
than that adopted towards them. Someone comes along with an implement or
pencil, and he pulls the letter open in
whatever way he can. He seals it up
again, in the meantime having photographed it. That is a contemptible
practice, because any private letter passing between two people in the Six
Counties is liable to fall into the hands of
the emissaries or spies of the right hon.
Gentleman.
If it were merely a question of preserving the peace of the Six Counties,
particularly with that Secret Service Fund
-very ample for the purpose-with 3,000
R.U.C. men on duty all over the territory,
and on top of that 14,071 "B" men, he
has ample resources at his command to
see and ascertain what is going on without
putting into the Post Office service, which
is not a Northern Ireland service, a
number of spies. If there be people in the
Six Counties who feel so indignant that
they must revert to what he would describe
as seditious practices, probably it is caused
by the ruthlessness with which he endeavours to down every opinion that is at
variance with his own. You had a recent
case of that in Dungannon, where some
boys marching into town, and merely
wearing rosettes of a particular kind, were
interrogated by the police, brought to the
There
barracks, and put under arrest.
was no attempt there at holding a public
meeting. There was no thought of breaking the peace, but simply because they
were wearing a colour that acted upon
the sergeant of police like a red rag to
a bull, he must needs drag them to the
police barracks.
You had the same thing
repeated in the Belfast Cemetery a few
Sundays ago.
The people in every community, even
the Six-County area, have surely the
right to express their political or national
opinions, if they have such opinions.
They ought to be as free to express them
as I am free to express them in this
House. If the right hon. Gentleman
thinks, by means of this petty
tyranny, he will closure that opinion
he is making a tremendous mistake.
Up to
time when the Minister of Home Affairs put his agents
into the Post Office in Belfast there
was nothing ever heard of letters missing,
letters stolen, or important despatches

I want to know from the right hon.

whoever they are and whatever they do?
I want to know that. In my opinion any

That question, if he has no reply to make
to it, will have to be tested elsewhere and
we will be forced to ask and to find out
whether the Imperial Government and the
Imperial Post Office authorities, who
alone control the Post Office, should permit any individual, however exalted his
position may be, in another State to come
in and tamper with the rights of the
Post-master General and of the Post Office.
That is point number one.
My second point is that I see no reason
whatever, even if he had a legal right,
for the pursuance of this policy by the
right hon. Gentleman. It is all very well
for him to say "Oh, we are only looking
for seditious literature or for illegal documents." How can he find seditious
literature and how can he engage in a
policy of exploration for sedition unless

will shake, and ought to shake, public
confidence in the Post Office and in the

out-I did not know of it myself till it was
raised by my hon. Friend (Mr. Healy)—
to the public that the correspondence of
men in Northern Ireland is not safe from
-I will not say the spying but from the

else. Who these people are I do not know.
The right hon. Gentleman (Sir Dawson
Bates) was invited to tell us who they are
but he has not done so.
In the third place, what are we to think

Hear, hear)--and where we have an Empire Week organisation---(Hon. Members:

sees is a policeman armed with a revolver,

I think it casts a very serious reflection
on this community, and certainly will

After all, supposing the right hon.

I suppose I under-value the capacity of

In regard to the Richhill Training Centre
there have been many criticisms in this
House. I am not going to stand here and
say that everything in the garden is beautiful, but I will say and I think the House
will bear me out-that I appreciate all the
work which the Department does in the

who has no ambition to go abroad but who

Canada. I have had experience in that
line myself, and I say he will do better
every time if he goes out with the right
idea, in the proper spirit, and takes the
work that is offered to him.
I was something like fifteen or seventeen
years in Canada and went through a lot

The PRIME MINISTER: I rise at the

mine some
years ago, that before I
was done I hoped to solve the unemployment question in Ulster. Well, I may

people for being able to solve their own

I would point out to the hon. Member
that from then until now I have done

and manufactured articles. We have
started an association, thanks to the kindness of some of our leading citizens, called
the Ulster Industries Development Association, for the very purpose of accomplishing the end which I had in mind
when I made that speech.

to restart the yard on sound, economic

I said, and I think I was quite correct in

a short time the yard would be restarted.
That prognostication came true. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear).
I should like to point out that the Government here--my right hon. Friend, the

Act, as it is called in Great Britain, being

yards are built at the present moment.
That was a strong action to take, and one

The PRIME MINISTER: I did not
take the figures down right. In 1921 the
number was 100,000; to-day it is 54,000;
so that at any rate from the time that the
Northern Parliament and Government
were established we have been able to
bring down the number of unemployed
very nearly to half of what it was then.
As everyone in the House realises, at the
present moment the figures are
doubtedly inflated, for the reason that has
been so ably stated by my right hon.
Friend, the Minister of Labour, and the
Parliamentary Secretary of the Ministry
of Labour. No one denies the fact that
many people were led into putting in
claims for unemployment benefit without
very much hope of securing it. In the
meantime, until those cases have been
disposed of, the figures are somewhat inflated. I think that is as accurate a statement as I can make in regard to the
situation at the moment.
My hon. and gallant Friend, the Member for St. Anne's (Major McCormick),
touched on the subject of Richhill, and
I have to say that so far as I am concerned I am satisfied, and more than satisfied, with the duties that are performed
at that preliminary training establishment. It was by no means established
for the purpose of inviting the youth of
Ulster to leave their native country. That
has been made clear over and over again.
What are the real facts of the case? Prior
to the establishment of Richhill, the boys
who left Ulster and arrived in Canada,
Australia, New Zealand, South Africa, or
any of our Dominions, found themselves
in a very much worse position than those
who were leaving Great Britain. They
became the hewers of wood and the
drawers of water out in those Dominions,
instead of being able to plunge in and take
the same advantage of the training at
home as their brothers across the Channel.
I say that was a grave injustice to our
Ulster people, because if we had not taken.
some steps to give them this preliminary
training before their going out it was very
difficult for them to recover lost ground
and to take the prominent position which,
I am glad to say, many of them hold at
the present moment. I confirm to the
fullest extent the hon. and gallant Member's experience with regard to those boys
who have gone out from Richhill.
One
of the last visits paid to me when I was
in New Zealand was by a boy who immediately said to me, "I am from Richhill."
I inquired how he was getting on,
and I got a most satisfactory report not
only regarding his progress in New Zealand, but also in regard to quite a number
of others who had sailed with him to that
far-distant Dominion. There is no compulsion on anyone to attend Richhill;
none whatever. A boy can go on board
ship and go to the furthest of our
Dominions without going near Richhill at
all, but, if he is a wise boy, he will take
advantage of the training that is given
there before he goes out into the world,
not knowing the initial essentials of what
is expected from young emigrants. Then
the hon. Member for Foyle (Mr. McCarroll)-I think perhaps it slipped out of
him said that this showed aiding and
abetting of emigration. It is a very
wrong impression to go outside. I do not
think myself that the boys and girls who
go abroad to our Dominions should be in
any way discouraged if they cannot find
honest work to do at home. I have seen
fathers at home here in humble circumstances on a small farm of a few acres,
and in New Zealand I have met their sons
and those sons have had sometimes one
and sometimes two holdings of considerable extent, and some of them are county
councillors even within the last few years,
showing great progress and showing that
the Ulster boy if he sets his hand to work
out there can do a great deal in a comparatively short time. Is it not far
better for them to be populating the
Dominions with stout Ulster blood rather
than loafing about the streets looking for

-wherever it may be the hon. Member

dealing with them.
The machinery is the Act of Parliament
passed by this House. That Act of Parliament follows closely the lines of Acts
of Parliament governing unemployment
in Great Britain, and we cannot move further along sympathetic lines without
breaking the agreement which enables us
to live pari passu with those out of employment in Great Britain. To do that
would be one of the most foolish acts, because the right hon. Gentleman has

of the Exchequer in Great Britain-not
any individual, but the Chancellor of the
Exchequer for the time being-that so far
as the administration of our Unemployment Insurance Acts is concerned we will
strictly carry out the law in accordance
with the same principles laid down on the
other side. So my hon. Friend will
realise that no matter how hard the case
may be the right hon. Gentleman can
only deal with it within the strict letter of
the law.

Sir WILSON HUNGERFORD: I do
not intend to take up much of the time
of the House, but I should like to say a
few words with special reference to the
Richhill Training Centre. I am
vinced of the necessity of this school in
order to prepare many of our young men
for the work that awaits them in Canada.
I had an opportunity of visiting that great
Dominion last year, and of meeting boys
from the North of Ireland who, I am glad
to say, are making good there. We discussed the question of the Richhill Training Centre, and one of them said to me,
"I only wish that that school had been in
existence before I came out. When I arrived here, the first thing they did was
to throw down a set of harness, and to
ask me to pick out the breeching, and I
had not the faintest idea of what they
were talking about." A course of training is necessary before they go out to the
Dominion.
At the same time I am inclined to think
that the young man who saves up the £10
necessary for his fare has a greater incentive to make good than the lad who,
feeling that anything is better than hanging around, tries his luck in Canada without any expense to himself. Those who
are trained at Richhill at the expense of
the Government are taken out to Canada
and carefully looked after until they are
handed over to the Canadian authorities,
who send them to the different farms.
Whether they all take kindly to the job
is another question. No doubt some of
them settle down, but the majority try to
make their way into the towns, which is
a great mistake. However, so long as
Great Britain provides facilities for young
men who are desirous of learning a little
about farm life, I hope this Government
will continue the existing arrangements in
Northern Ireland.
Last year certain statements were
made in this House regarding the Richhill trainees who went to Canada, and it

15 MAY 1930
Mr. HEALY: I rise to protest against
this large Vote in the present condition
of the rural areas. It is well known that
there are some thousands of decrees issued
for the non-payment of land annuities in
most of the counties with which I am
familiar, and yet at a time like this we
find on this Estimate a sum for the headquarters of the Special Constabulary of
not less than £76,878. We have six
County Commandants, who get from £450
to £500, and yet, notwithstanding that
their employment is part time, they must
also get a very generous locomotion allowance. The bonus for the men at £2 per
annum is, I take it, not for the discharge
of police duties at all, but for political
services rendered, and to that I take the
strongest possible objection. You have
here a body of 14,071 men, and you are
not paying those men for police service at
all, because if you were the sum of £2
per year would not adequately cover it.
You are paying them for rendering
political service, and that is a disgrace to
any Government at a time like the present.
You are paying them for doing registration work, for acting as touts, and for
various other purposes-not State service,
but purely and simply political service,
and to that I take the strongest possible
exception.
Another item to which I take objection
is a sum of £800,000 for the provision of
police barracks for the R.U.C. It is far
too large a sum of the taxpayers' money
to waste, because many of the existing
police barracks are quite adequate and
quite serviceable, and having served their
purpose for a great number of years they
are certainly adequate to the needs of the
present day. In Fermanagh it is proposed to erect twenty-one barracks, and
in a little county like Fermanagh that is
about ten too many, making the most
liberal allowance I possibly can for the
proper discharge of police duties. I must,
in the short time at my disposal, deal with
the question of the Royal Ulster Constabulary itself. I find there are no fewer than
64 well paid officials engaged at headquarters, and notwithstanding that the
Inspector-General is receiving the very
generous salary of £1,750 he must needs
have the State pay his rent. That I regard as a scandal. Any professional
man in this or in any other area with a
salary of approximately £2,000 a year
for discharging duties that are merely
nominal ought to be very well able to pay
his own rent.
The same applies to the Deputy Inspector-General and the Six-County
Inspectors. The Deputy Inspector-General
receives £100 a year as rent allowance,
and £1,200 by way of salary. Surely
there can be found many efficient police
officers at a salary of £1,200 minus a rent
allowance of £100. I know you established a bad precedent, because, in the
case of the Prime Minister, you pay for
various things connected with his establishment. In the case of Belfast and
Derry District Inspectors are given a rent
allowance of £80, and those in the country
are granted £60. These rent allowances
are absolutely unnecessary, and if they
were put to a free vote of the taxpayers
to-morrow they would, in every case, vote
for no rent allowance. These police
officers are generously paid, and there
ought to be no trimmings of this kind to
their salaries and allowances. Yet I find
that the Deputy Inspector-General and
the County Inspectors are allowed £160
a year for locomotion, and the District
Inspectors are allowed £120. I do not
know whether they incur these sums or
not, but whether they do or not, I think
these allowances are bordering on generosity. As well as that there is an allowance for 1,216 bicycles at £3 a year each.
I do not know whether the police force
maintains as large a number of pedal
bicycles as that.
I see that, notwithstanding the large
item for secret service, you have in the
Vote a sum for detective work. 65 officials
-I suppose they are policemen-receive
£18 4s Od. If they are full-time officers
surely it is not necessary to give them
special fees for detective work that is part
of their ordinary duties, I should imagine.
But not only must you provide these
policemen with a free residence and locomotion allowance, but you must provide
them with plain clothes.
Sir DAWSON BATES: They cannot
go out without them.
Mr. HEALY: They have the same
means of providing their own clothing as
anyone else has, and they are in a much
better position to provide clothes than
are the people who are unemployed. You
are very generous to some people and very
niggardly to others. To these detectives
there is a plain clothes allowance of 7/-
a week, and to 103 sergeants and constables an allowance of 5/- a week. I
regard that as a scandal at a time when

National Health Insurance Bill.
