Mr. ANDREWS: It has always been
the policy of this Government-and I am
entitled to add the policy of this Parliament--that, in connection with our great
social services, we should always ensure
that they should be on a basis of equality
with similar services in Great Britain.
There is general agreement amongst us
that that is the only policy which this
Government could have adopted with fairness to our industrial classes. And I
think we are also all agreed that in times
of adversity it is necessary that our working classes should be helped, whether their
adversity arises from sickness, from old
age, from unemployment, or from bereavement.
The only exception to this general policy
of similarity has been in connection with
health insurance. When this Government came into existence and took over its
powers in 1922 we found that the Imperial Measure, which had been passed in
1911, was only applied to Ireland in a
mutilated form. I mean by that that
those provisions dealing with the prevention and cure of disease, or, in other words,
medical benefits, were not applicable to
this island home of ours. It is to right
that wrong, which was done to our insured
persons almost twenty years ago, that the
Government are introducing this Measure
to-day. It would be fruitless for me to
attempt to place the responsibility or the
blame for what occurred so many years
ago. As regards the past legislators need
not worry themselves too much. What is
important is that in the present we should
do what we feel to be best for the people
that are to live in the days that lie ahead.
To-day I feel that it is necessary that
I should explain quite frankly to the
House the reasons which have influenced
the Government to believe that they are
doing the right thing in introducing this
Measure to-day. There are several
reasons, but I would like to say, in the
first place, that this matter has given the
Government much anxious thought. We
have viewed the position from every point
of view and from a great many angles.
But what influenced us most, if I may say
so, was the fact that admittedly the death
rate in Northern Ireland-the general
death rate is higher than in England and
Wales by 3 per 1,000. At first sight that
might not seem a great difference, but
when I say that the total general death
rate in Great Britain is only 12 per 1,000
per annum hon. Members will see that
three is a considerable percentage.
in addition to that, we hear almost every
day in this House, and very often from
public platforms, about the 40,000 people
in Northern Ireland who are, unfortunately, unemployed.
Mr. NIXON: 50,000.
But
Mr. ANDREWS: On the average approximately 40,000 of our people are unemployed because they can find no work
to do. But it is rather a strange fact
that we scarcely ever hear anything about
the approximately 20,000 persons who, on
the average, are unemployed because they
are certified to be sick and unable to work.
Now when we take these two facts into
account in the first place the death rate
and then our sickness rate-I think it will
be agreed that the Government would not
have been justified in remaining inactive
in connection with this matter. It has, I
know, been said by some people that our
climate is a contributory cause to our high
sickness rate. Personally I do not think
it is. It is true that in the South of England, during the greater part of the year,
they are blest with a better climate than
Health Insurance Bill—
Second Reading
20 MAY 1930
we enjoy here, but I feel that the climate
in the North of England and in Wales is
no better than in Northern Ireland, and
that the climate in Scotland in many
parts of it at any rate, is more trying.
Therefore, the cause of these regrettable
facts that I have mentioned is not to be
found in connection with our climate.
It is true that factory life is somewhat
trying, but here again I feel that we are
not behind Great Britain. As regards
ventilation, sanitary arrangements, et
cetera, our factories here are quite equal
to the factories across the water.
I would
like to acknowledge the fact that during
the last eight or ten years our employers,
notwithstanding the industrial depression
through which we have been passing, have
spent vast sums in installing dust removing plant and in other ways making
our factories healthier than they ever were
before.
Again, the Government have considered
the opinions of those who are most capable
of advising us in connection with this
matter. I am entitled to say that every
practitioner in Northern Ireland-or most
of them is in favour of the introduction
of medical benefits. All the doctors' organisations have spoken in favour of the
proposal. Again, I am entitled to say
that many distinguished doctors have expressed their views on this matter in no
uncertain way. I would like to read one
extract from the Report of the Chief
Tuberculosis Officer of this city. I refer
to his Report of 1928 when he wrote:
I am still of the opinion expressed in
my last annual Report that the extension of medical benefits to insured persons in Northern Ireland on the same
terms and conditions as at present
prevail in Great Britain would be of
enormous value to the community.
Again I would remind the House that
there was set up in Great Britain a Royal
Commission in 1924. That Commission
was appointed to investigate the problem
of health insurance generally and in particular medical benefit. Referring to
medical benefit in their report they use
these words:
We can say confidently that medical
benefit has proved in practice a successful and most invaluable factor in advancement of the health of the nation.
Therefore, I feel that even were I to
advance no other argument than what I
have done and also these opinions which
I have read I have done sufficient to urge
that this Measure should to-day receive
a Second Reading with the unanimous
approval of the House. But there are
other reasons. I would like to remind
hon. Members that our approved societies
are divided into what I may call two
classes, those which are international in
character and which operate both here and
throughout the United Kingdom, and those
which are called national or purely local.
These approved societies, which are very
capable of forming an opinion worth giving in connection with this problem as
they have been so closely associated with
it for almost twenty years, are unanimous
in their desire that medical benefits
should be introduced.
All the international societies, which
are the ones that act both here and across
the Channel, have told us quite clearly
that unless the conditions are changed in
Northern Ireland they will not be able
to continue to operate here, which in my
opinion would be a serious disadvantage
to our insured persons in Northern Ireland, because it is true to say that more
than half of our insured persons are members of these international societies. Besides, our local societies are also equally
feeling the strain of our excessive sickness
rate. Apart altogether from the human
side of the problem to which I am sure
hon. Members will attach considerable
importance, the drain upon the sickness
funds of the approved societies in Northern Ireland has been much greater in
recent years than across the Channel. In
England and Wales the drain has been
per head of insured persons per annum
£1 1s 6d; in Scotland £1 Os 1d, and in
Northern Ireland £1 14s Od. The result
of that upon our societies' funds both
national and international has given me
very considerable anxiety for several
years, and it is also giving the approved
societies great anxiety.
It is correct to say that the international societies each year are sending
over here £170,000 which is obtained from
their British members in order that the
same statutory benefit and additional benefits shall be given to their
members here as are given to their
members in Great Britain. It is natural
that the international societies, therefore, should take a serious view of the
position and threaten to do what I have
described as being most serious, namely,
cease to operate here in Northern Ireland, because I would like the House to
appreciate fully that our health insurance
1359 Health Insurance Bill-

HOUSE OF COMMONS
Second Reading.
[Mr. Andrews]
scheme to our great advantage is very
closely linked up with the British scheme.
We are actual members of the Joint
Committee, and in addition to that we
are party to what is called the Central
Fund, which is available to help weak.
societies whether they are situated in
Great Britain or in Northern Ireland.
But there is a third reason, which I
feel I ought to tell the House, why this
Measure should become law without unnecessary delay. At the Peace Treaty at
Versailles, as hon. Members know, a great
many things beyond what the war was
waged about were actually settled, and it
was decided to establish an international
labour organisation which sits at Geneva
from time to time. Upon that organisation was placed the responsibility of dealing with social problems not in one
country alone but in all the countries
which were associated with the organisation. One of the first efforts that was
made-and the British representatives
took a leading part in this-was to have
the social standards raised all
Europe to the level of the social standards
in Great Britain, which as hon. Members
know always leads the way in these
matters.
over
Well, as I have said, Great Britain
took a leading part in this, and the first
matter which came under the consideration of that organisation was health
insurance. Two conventions were passed
to the effect that the health insurance
schemes of those countries which were
parties to these conventions should all be
brought up to the same level. Medical
benefits were included in the health insurance scheme. These conventions have
been ratified by no fewer than fifteen
countries already, including France, Germany, Belgium, Austria, Hungary, etc.,
but the strange and regrettable thing is
that Great Britain has been unable to
ratify these conventions because very
much to our advantage we are represented at Geneva at these conferences by
the British representatives. The United
Kingdom is looked upon as one unit and
the British representatives speak for us.
Therefore, they cannot ratify these conventions for the United Kingdom until we
no longer block the way. I am sure it is
not the wish of any hon. Member in this
House that it should be said with truth
that Northern Ireland blocks the way to
progress throughout the whole of the Continent of Europe. We have had, therefore, a demand from successive British
Governments that we should agree to establish medical benefits here.
I know quite well that objections have
been raised to the introduction of this
Measure in certain quarters, not since the
Bill saw the light of day, but previously.
I was approached by certain people from
time to time with the view expressed that
this Bill was unnecessary in Northern
Ireland. Well, as I have said, I do not
feel that it is unnecessary. I have given
the opinion of those who I feel are best
capable to express an opinion, namely,
our medical men and the approved
societies. In addition to that our trade
unionists in Northern Ireland, without
exception, are in favour of the establishment of medical benefits here. The
Ulster Labour Unionist Association,
which contains representatives of all the
trade unions in Northern Ireland, have
unanimously expressed their approval of
the Measure. Last but not least the
delegates assembled in Belfast representing our local employment committees
unanimously some months ago expressed
the view that medical benefits should be
applied here without further delay.
The chief criticism that has reached my
ears has been directed along the line that
we ought not to deal with this problem by
itself and that we should wait until the
whole question of the poor law commission's
report was considered and dealt with.
That is not the view of the Government,
because we feel, and I think feel rightly,
that matters such as this, if the best is
to be done to act in accordance with what
is done in Great Britain, must be removed
from the field, and when that is done I
feel satisfied that the bigger problem will
be more easily dealt with. It has also
been urged that there would be overlapping between our poor-law system, the
dispensary system in particular, and the
medical benefit scheme of things, but I
am glad to say that there will be no overlapping of this character. An arrangement has been made with our dispensary
doctors, to which I will refer later, which
will ensure that no doctor will be paid
twice for attending the same patient,
which I understand overlapping really
means in practice.
I am glad to say also that the fears
of some people that this will mean an
increase to the rates is quite groundless.
It will not be an increase to the rates in
any way except possibly to a very small
1361 Health Insurance Bill-

20 MAY 1930
Second Reading
extent in Londonderry borough as they
have not yet established a tuberculosis
committee. I hope, however, they will
do so without further delay. It has been
urged by some people I know that this
Measure should go beyond the scheme of
things in Great Britain and that not only
should we provide for insured persons but
that we should also provide for their dependants.
Hon. Members know quite
well that financial and other considerations will not permit of our going beyond
the British scheme. Our effort is to get
into a position of equality with Great
Britain and not simply to get out of
equality by going from one direction.
into another. People have said to me,
"After all, why should the breadwinner
have the benefit of service of this kind.
and his wife and children not enjoy it?"
There is an answer to that. When the
breadwinner is himself the patient the
home very often is unfortunately plunged
into something equivalent to poverty, but
on the other hand when the breadwinner
is well and able to earn, if he does not
wish to apply to the dispensary system for
medical aid for his dependants, he is certainly, it must be admitted, in a better
position to pay for a doctor for them than
he would be if he himself were ill and
unable to work.
It has also been pointed out to me
that the contributions might be a burden
upon some. Now, I do not take that
view. All the additional contributions
required to bring this scheme into operation will be 1d from the worker, 1d from
the employer for each worker he employs,
and the statutory grant. No worker in
Northern Ireland, and no workers' organisation or trades' union has objected to pay
this additional contribution, and I think,
therefore, that we are entitled to feel today that in giving support to this Measure
we have behind us the vast volume of
working class opinion in Northern Ireland. I also want to say that no employers' organisation has objected to this
additional penny, nor have employers
done so generally. I think that is to
the credit of the employers, if I may say
so, especially when we remember, and we
cannot forget, the difficult industrial
times through which they are passing.
Some months ago I know--I want to
face every difficulty in connection with
this matter and to be perfectly frankthere was a feeling amongst farmers that
this additional contribution should not
be imposed upon them. I have met many
organisations representing farmers, and I
have met a great many individual farmers, but I have never yet met a farmer
who when the whole matter was explained
to him and he understood the correct
position maintained his objection. That
is also to the credit of our farming community who, I believe, are just as anxious
to help their workers as any other section
of the people in Northern Ireland.
The position as regards our agricultural
workers is simply this: There is a feeling
that they enjoy better health than our industrial workers. The returns of the
approved societies do not show that. It
is true that the farm labourer escapes
certain diseases from which the industrial
worker suffers, but, on the other hand,
owing to the exposed life which he leads.
he is subject to asthma, bronchitis,
rheumatism, and other complaints of the
kind to an even greater extent than the
industrial worker. Therefore the sickness
experience between town and country, in
my opinion, does not differ to any appreciable extent.
It has been urged, I know, that agricultural workers should be excluded from
the benefits of this Act. That is quite
unthinkable for many reasons. In the
first place, it would not enable us to conform to the Geneva Conventions which I
have already mentioned if we were to exclude farm workers, and, in the second
place, it would be an injustice to the farm
workers if they were not brought within
this great beneficent scheme. Further,
in my opinion, it would create insuperable
administration difficulties which, personally, I would not like to face.
May I consider for a moment the elements which are necessary for any medical
service of the kind? In the first place,
I think there will be general agreement
amongst us that the doctors should be
available as quickly as possible after the
patient becomes sick and with as little red
tape as possible; in the second place, that
the scheme should be free from the taint
of charity (Hon. Members: Hear, hear)
-and in the third place, that the workers
should pay something for their doctor not
when they are ill and cannot afford to do
so but when they are working and earning
wages and consequently in a better position to pay.
Then, again, I think there should be
a free choice of doctor. We will all
agree, I am quite sure, that a patient cannot be very well and effectively treated by
a doctor unless both doctor and patient
Health Insurance Bill-
Second Reading
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Andrews]
feel that the patient has confidence in the
doctor. One of the objections that have
been urged against our dispensary system
is that there is not a free choice of doctor
and that very often patients have to pass
doctors whom they would like to consult
simply because they cannot afford to
go to anyone but the dispensary doctor.
I do not want it to be taken that I am
saying a word detrimental to the dispensary doctor. Quite the contrary. In my
view they have been performing their responsible duties faithfully and well and
in the public interest, but the dispensary
doctor would be the first to admit that
he is called upon to discharge his duties
very often under unfavourable circumstances.
May I say that one of the difficulties
in connection with the establishment of
medical benefits in Northern Ireland has
been that we have here a dispensary system which they do not possess in Great
Britain? To prevent the overlapping to
which I have already referred it was
necessary that an arrangement should be
made with the dispensary doctors. We
have had many conferences with these
doctors, and I am entitled to say to-day
that I feel that with great public spirit
they have accommodated themselves to
what is to be the new order of things, and
in the public interest they have asked
and have received nothing but what, in
my opinion, is fair and reasonable.
I may say that we have also arranged
satisfactorily with the general practitioners. The arrangements which have
been come to are that our general practitioners will receive the 9s capitation
grant the same as the practitioners receive in Great Britain, less 2d which is to
form a reserve fund for a purpose to which
I will refer later on. With our dispensary doctors it has been arranged that
they will retain their dispensary salaries
but that in consideration of their doing
so they will accept a capitation grant 1s 6d
less for each of the insured persons they
agree to treat.
I would like to tell the House now how
it is proposed that the scheme shall work.
Every insured person will receive a medical card and on that card he will fill up
the name of the doctor whom he chooses
to attend him in case of sickness. That
insured person will be added to the
doctor's list or, as it is called in England,
the doctor's panel. When the insured
person gets ill it will be the duty of the
doctor to examine him, to advise him, to
give him a medical certificate if he is unable to work, and a prescription for medicine if he requires it. Medical appliances
will also be prescribed, if necessary, by
the insurance doctor. These prescriptions
will be taken by the patient, or by a friend
of the patient, to a chemist in the area,
whom, again, he will be free to choose.
There the prescription will be filled up
with the very best medicines available regardless of cost and free of charge to the
insured person.
Now, I would like to say a word or two
as regards the administration of the
scheme, which I think is very simple. In
the first place, the Ministry of Labour
will be responsible for the general administration. Our aim will be to discharge this duty with efficiency and
economy, and we will have the advice of
a Medical Benefit Council, as it is to be
called. That Council will be composed of
four sections of the community, if I may
put it that way. One-fourth will be medical
practitioners and chemists, one-fourth will
be insured workers, one-fourth will represent employers, and one-fourth will be
nominated by the Minister of Labour for
the time being. In addition to that in
different areas all over Northern Ireland
local committees will be appointed. There
will also be committees of doctors and
committees of chemists.
At this stage I would like to point out
to hon. Members that they will see in the
Bill provision is made for the establishment of a general visiting scheme in order
to
ensure equality of administration
throughout the whole of Northern Ireland. I think a scheme of this kind is
required. I am glad to be able to tell
the House that the approved societies at
the present time are investigating this
problem. They admit that all is not well
in connection with this matter and they
are working out a scheme-I hope they
will be able to do so-which will make this
provision in the Act inoperative.
But
should the approved societies fail to arrive
at an agreement amongst themselves then
it will be the duty of the Ministry of
Labour under the provision to devise and
establish a scheme of the kind. I have
said that I think a scheme of the kind
is necessary to ensure equality of administration. I think that must be obvious to
anybody. At the present time some of
our societies have quite efficient schemes.
Other societies have schemes that are

moderately satisfactory; while again there
are other societies which have no scheme
of the kind at all. Well, obviously that

Hon. Members who have studied the

is simply because the work they have been

to-day, if I may, to pay a tribute to those

many years have served on these committees, and have done much valuable work
through their membership of those committees in the public interest.
Now I come to the financial arrangements which I have already referred to
and they are really very simple. The
worker will give a penny per week when
working. The employer will give a penny
for each worker whom he employes. In
addition to that the State will add oneseventh of the benefits paid and the cost
of administration in the case of men and
one-fifth in the case of women; and any
further sum which may be required in
order to finance the scheme will be provided by the approved societies. I have
said that the approved societies are favourable to the scheme. Well, they are backing their opinion to the extent of £27,000
per annum, because, if the scheme does
not work out as we all hope and pray that
it will and if the sickness rate is not reduced as we believe it will, the cost to the
approved societies of the scheme will be
£27,000 per annum. Again the Government is backing its view to the extent of
an Exchequer grant of £13,500. I admit
that considering the importance of the
scheme that is not a sum which should
alarm anyone.
And now I come to the Bill itself, and
I feel that it is not necessary for me to
deal with the various Clauses at any great
length, because in the general statement
which I have made I have really dealt with
a great many of its most important provisions, and, further, an explanatory
memorandum has been issued to hon.
Members which I think very clearly and
simply explains the various provisions of
this Measure. But in the first place I
may say that Clause 1 provides for the
establishment of medical benefits in
Northern Ireland, and it defines medical
benefits to mean medical treatment and
attendance including the provision of
proper and sufficient medicines and appliances.
Clause 2 deals with the contributions to
which I have already referred, and provides that these contributions will be payable from the 7th of July next. Clause 3
deals with voluntary contributors, and
provides that disabled ex-Servicemen will
receive medical benefits even though they
are not insured persons. I am sure that
every Member of this House will approve
of that provision.
Clause 4 sets out the arrangements
which have been made with the medical
profession to which I have already referred. I may say that all doctors in
Northern Ireland will be entitled to participate in the scheme. This Clause also
sets out the arrangements under which
the chemists will supply the necessary
drugs as prescribed by the doctors.
Clause 5 deals with the constitution and
powers of the medical council, to which I
also have referred. Clause 6 deals with
the local committees which I have mentioned. Clause 7 deals with the arrangements which have been made with the
dispensary doctors for the purpose of
avoiding overlapping and which I have
explained to the House at considerable
length.
Clause 9 deals with sick visiting scheme
to which also I have referred, and
Clause 10 provides that the cost of medical
benefits to the approved societies shall not
exceed the sum of 13s per head of insured
persons per annum. Clause 12 provides
for altered arrangements in connection
with the treatment of tuberculosis in
future, and domiciliary treatment will be
given by the insurance practitioners who,
when necessary, will meet the tuberculosis
medical officers for the county or county
borough as the case may be. Sanatorium
treatment will continue to be arranged for
by the county tuberculosis committee and
the necessary financial adjustment with
the local authorities is set out in Clause 13.
It means, when you take together the
work which these committees are being relieved of and the payments which the
Exchequer is going to make to the local
authorities to enable them to meet the liabilities which will be left upon them,
that there will be no additional charge
upon the rates.
Clause 14 provides that insurance committees will cease to exist because the
necessity for them no longer remains, and
Clause 15 provides for alternative employment being given to the secretaries of these

insurance committees, or if alternative

Clause 16 sets out that this Bill will become operative from the benefit side not
later than 5th of January next. But I

little flexibility we ask for in case unforeseen administrative difficulties might arise
which would necessitate the postponement

Now may I just say in conclusion a very
few words. I have tried to seek out today those points on which we are obviously
in agreement. One other I would like to
refer to. You will all agree with me when
I say that the health of our people is our
chief national asset, and this Bill is introduced for the purpose of improving the
health of the industrial insured workers in
Northern Ireland. May I point out that
this is not a great experiment which the
Government is asking the House to embark
upon. It is a well known road. Medical
benefits have been in operation in Great
Britain for almost 20 years. The scheme
of things there has been improved from
time to time. The minds of the greatest
men England can produce for the work of
the kind, from Sir Walter Kinnear downwards, have been engaged upon this
scheme, and we are in a position to-day
of being able to take advantage of all that
research work which has been done. Now
may I thank Members on both sides of the
House very sincerely for the very patient
and kind hearing which they have given
me. No Minister in introducing
Measure of this kind has ever been, I
think in any Parliament, given a fairer
opportunity of expressing his views than
I have had to-day.

with its provisions and its effect.
Speaking as a business man, I wish to
say that no business man in this country
wants to lay any further burdens on industry. Industry, as we all know, is
struggling against adversity, and the
effect of placing more burdens upon it
might have the effect of the straw
on
the camel's back. Still, I do not think
these medical benefits will on the whole
place a burden upon industry. I think
we will get the benefit of better health on
the part of the working people. In any
case I should much prefer to ease the
burden in another direction than to ease
it by withholding medical benefits from

pleasure indeed in assuring the Minister

this Bill.
Mr. BEATTIE: I rise heartily to support the introduction of this Measure,
even at this late hour of 1930. May I
say that I have been earnestly hoping for
the breaking of the day when medical
benefits would be extended to Ireland?
That day has now arrived, and I rejoice
that the insured population of Northern
Ireland are now to receive the consideration that by right they should have received in the year 1912. I have been
reading over what you might call ancient
Parliamentary history-the debates on
National Health Insurance in 1912-and
in the light of experience I certainly deplore the failure to introduce medical
benefits in Ireland at that time. In 1912
the standard of health in Ireland was
higher than that in England, Scotland.
and Wales; the sickness ratio was also
lower; the vitality of the people in this
country was greater. But, after eighteen
years absence of medical benefits, Ireland
is well below the standard of England,
Scotland and Wales, as the masses of the
people owing to their impoverished condition could not afford to pay doctors in
times of illness.
If any Member of this House requires.
conversion on the subject of the necessity
of medical benefits in this country, I shall
rely not on my own words but on a statement made in 1912 in the Imperial House
of Commons. These words were spoken
by a member of a party that, with its
100 per cent. strength, could have done
wonderful work in the way of getting
medical benefits for Ireland. He said:
The health conditions, however, are
not uniform. They are not the same
throughout Great Britain and Ireland.
If Ireland be taken as a whole it will be
found that the rate of sickness there is
lower than in Great Britain. The
simple reason is that whereas the overwhelming majority of the people of
Great Britain lives in towns and urban
centres, a similar overwhelming

majority, if not a larger majority

1,800 voluntary

should like to congratulate the Minister on

certain that it will be only the beginning

this is only the first of other Measures

am sure he is aware of the fact-
Mr. HEALY: New Zealand.
Mr. GORDON-is that questions
affecting the working people of the country
are discussed at Geneva. Hours of
labour, conditions of employment, the
wages paid in different countries, these

form of resolutions, such as, for instance,

benefits we can now say that the whole
social services of Northern Ireland are

I am not going to quote them if you rule

to tell the Prime Minister that he ought
in justice to deal with the 33 per cent.
of Catholics in the Six Counties as fairly
as the Free State have dealt with the
9 per. cent. of Protestants across the Border. If I were allowed to quote from the
Bishop of Limerick and from another
eminent divinę it would be to the effect
that they have received every consideration and fair play from the Free State
Government in the matter of education
and in the provision of their schools. That
is all I am going to say about that point.
The practical effect of what is contained
in this Bill will be that people who cannot for conscience sake transfer their
schools will be obliged to pay 50 per cent.
of the construction, 50 per cent. for cleaning and upkeep, and the whole of the repairs. That is in effect putting the Penal
Act, supposed to have been repealed in the
time of O'Connell, into practice in 1930.
I do not think that is a generous gesture
of the Prime Minister towards the
minority, and I do not suppose that in
doing that he is representing the views of
the mass of the Protestant people in the
Six Counties. I think he has a mandate,
if he will only open his eyes to perceive
it, to deal justly with this question from
our standpoint. Surely it can be held.
that whether we are taxpayers or ratepayers we are contributing our share to
the general taxation of the country,
whether national or local and that we
should be treated as other classes of the
community are treated.
There has not been a single reason given
by the Parliamentary Secretary or the
Prime Minister or by anybody on the
Government benches as to why we ought
to be penalised since our schools fulfil every
condition that the schools of any other
denomination fulfil in this country today. We are prepared to submit to any
test, to any examination, to any formula
that you are pleased to apply. We want
neither privilege nor preference, and
therefore I think it will be a stigma upon
this Government and upon this House and
upon the legislation you are enacting that
your children in the future will find very
difficult to explain away if you allow it
to go forth that you are penalising a large
body of the people for a matter that is
purely one of conscience.

the Protestant community to have its

expect us to bow down and to say that you
have treated us with the generosity that
a powerful Government like yours could
well afford towards a minority such as
ours, when you have the example that
has been given in the Free State of the
extraordinary liberality with which your
people-only 8 per cent of the population
are being treated there.
Captain DIXON: All that is left of
them.
Mr. McCARROLL: They are not
hurrying away so far as I know.
Mr. GRANT: No, they have all gone.
Mr. McCARROLL: Their Minister of
Finance is one of your own party, a good
Ulster Presbyterian. There is no great rush
of Protestants from the Free State; in my
opinion they are emigrating more rapidly
from the Six Counties. We are penalised
to the extent of 50 per cent., and while
that position remains the grievance will
remain. We are not an insatiable people,
and we are not, as the Prime Minister
said the other day, a party that could not
be satisfied. When religion ceases to be a
barrier in any walk of life, when I-or
anyone belonging to me or to anyone on
this side of the House-am entitled to the
same consideration as anyone from your
side of the House, when religion ceases
to be a barrier to preferment in any
position in commerce or in public life or
anywhere else, then you will have made
some advance towards appeasement, and
some advance towards the time when we
will regard your attitude as generous.

HOUSE OF COMMONS
Mr. MURPHY: I rise to support the
Third Reading of this Bill, and to congratulate the Government on the Bill and
particularly the Parliamentary Secretary
(Mr. Robb) on the manner in which this
Measure has been piloted through Committee. A number of my constituents
have taken the liveliest interest in this
Bill, and in the discussions and debates
that preceded its introduction. They have
taken the liveliest interest in the Bill in
all its stages, and it is only right that I,
on their behalf, should acknowledge the
efforts made by the Government to see
that conflicting interests should be as far
as possible reconciled, and that certain
defects that had manifested themselves in
the Act of 1923 should be remedied. On
their behalf I thank the Government, and
I acknowledge that in this Bill the Government have redeemed to the letter all the
pledges that were given at the time this
Bill was introduced.
That would conclude my remarks were it
not for the fact that, like other hon. Members in this House, I have listened, I think
I may say, to every word that has fallen
in all the stages of discussion of this Bill
from the time that its Second Reading
was moved and throughout the Committee
stage. In all its stages we on this side of
the House have listened to speeches identical almost in language at all stages from
the Nationalist Members on the other side
of the House-violent protests uttered
against this Bill. I for one have never
understood the meaning, or at least I have
never appreciated the reality, of those protests.
This Bill was introduced to remedy certain defects in the Act of 1923, and in
all the stages of the Bill we have heard
protests not against this Bill, but against
the policy of the Act of 1923, which has
been on the Statute Book for seven years.
Assuming that those protests have any
relevancy to the matter that has been discussed by this House in Committee and
in the other stages, is there any substance
or is there any reality in those protests?
Despite the speeches we have heard from
the Nationalist side, I for one do not believe in the reality. I do not believe in
the reality for this reason. It is idle for
hon. Members on the other side of the
House to say, "We cannot take advantage
of the benefits that other sections of this
community have got under the Act of
1923, and that they get under this Bill."
We know that some of them are taking
advantage of those benefits, and it is idle
for hon. Members to say what they have
been saying when some of their coreligionists are taking advantage of those
benefits.
Mr. McCARROLL: Some of yours are
not.
Mr. MURPHY: I quite agree.
Mr. CONNELLAN: Why not?
Mr. MURPHY: If they choose to remain outside this Bill they do not come
into this House and through their representatives in this House, or outside the
House, refer to this Bill as one of the
penal laws. We on this side of the House
are tired of that extravagant language,
and when we see that four-and-two committees have already been set up we are
not much impressed by the only two
answers I have heard to the question why
have four-and-two committees been set up
for certain Roman Catholic schools?
Mr. McALEER: As the last resort.
Mr. MURPHY: I think that is a third
answer. I have heard from the Member
for South Fermanagh (Mr. Healy) that
one swallow does not make a summer; but
when we see swallows appearing in every
one of the Six Counties we may assume
that at all events summer is not very far
off.
When I hear an hon. Member say
that that is due to pressure of circumstances, and that it only occurs in the
poorer areas, I rub my eyes and ask myself, "Is Bangor one of the poorer areas?”
It may be in the opinion of my hon.
Friends, but again that argument does
not appeal very much to us on this side
of the House.
We have heard four-and-two committees
denounced by hon. Members on the other
side of the House; but even on that subject they speak with two voices. It is
said that the four-and-two committees are
mere camouflage, that there is nothing of
democratic control in four-and-two committees. The hon. Member for the Central Division of Belfast (Mr. Devlin) in
one of his speeches on this Bill made that
point, and made it very forcibly. May I
ask hon. Members, if that argument put
forward by their Leader, the hon. Member
for Central Division of Belfast (Mr. Devlin), is sound, why do not the people they
represent adopt the principle which has
been adopted in other places in the Six
Counties and try the four-and-two com-
Education Bill-

mittees? If they are camouflage, it does
not affect them. If they do not introduce
any element of popular or democratic
control, how does it in any way worsen
their position? Does it in any way reduce
their grip upon their schools? Does it reduce their control? If it is mere
camouflage, obviously not. It seems to
some of us on this side that when hon.
Members, even at this eleventh hour, are
getting up and delivering the speeches to
which we have been listening those
speeches cannot represent, and do not represent, the real feelings of the Members.
I speak with all respect in regard to those
who have delivered those speeches.
We heard when the Prime Minister introduced this amending Clause a storm of
protest. What did that storm of protest
amount to? The Prime Minister has
stated again and again that he considers,
and all we on these benches consider, that
the 1923 Act and this Bill as it stood before this Amendment were perfectly just
to the Nationalists. But assuming that
the Nationalists had any occasion for these
protests the Prime Minister, who had been
just, and the Government, who had been
just, determined to be generous and introduced this Amendment providing 50
per cent.-an unexpected boon for the
gentiemen opposite. Was it treated with
any sign of gratitude? I am glad to say
it was, contrary to some of the speeches
that have been delivered. I am sorry that
one hon. Member, the hon. Member for
Foyle (Mr. McCarroll), has receded from
that position that he at all events took
up from the generous move on the part
of the Prime Minister.
We on this side of the House all remember the speeches delivered on the
Money Resolution in connection with this
Bill, and in those speeches I find that the
hon. Member for Foyle endorsed an appeal. What was the appeal? This penal
Act, one of the penal Acts that have been
introduced, was to be remedied. How?
The Prime Minister having given 50 per
cent. was to get rid of all these difficulties
if he gave 75 per cent. All these violent
protests depended on the difference between 50 per cent. and 75 per cent. for the
grant. The hon. Member for Foyle,
dealing with the 50 per cent. grant, for
which we now hear no word of generosity
-certainly not very much appeared in
the speeches to-day-when referring to
this concession on the part of the Prime
Minister, said:
In a few words I should like to endorse the appeal that has been made for
a larger grant. I do not think it is
necessary to labour the question. The
concession that the Prime Minister has
made, the comparative generosity of
which is recognised by us, shows that
the four-and-two committees are going.
-(Official Report, 13th May, 1930,
vol. 12, col. 1165).
I am sorry that in his speech to-day the
hon. Member for Foyle has not remembered that aspect of the question. It is
an aspect that certainly appeals to us.
We back-benchers consider that the Prime
Minister has been generous. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear). We are glad to hear
that his generosity was recognised, to a
limited extent at least, by one of the
Nationalist Members opposite, and we are
sorry that on the Third Reading there is
no sign of that recognition here to-day.
Mr. LEEKE: The preceding speaker
is a colleague of mine and I honestly
thought he would uphold a reputation
worthy of his profession, and would adopt
a
critical attitude, at least, when the
Government was wrong. But instead of
that he is the most obsequious follower of
the Government. He says, and the hon.
Member for Antrim (Mr. Minford) says
also, that we on this side do not labour
under any grievance. I can tell them the
grievance under which we labour. It is
plain not only to the Six Counties but to
the world that the Catholics are penalised
in Ulster. We must accept the 50 per
cent. grant for the building if we are to
have our children taught according to the
conscientious beliefs of their parents.
That is the position, and if we want 100
per cent. we must accept Protestant
doctrine and Protestant teaching for our
children. (Hon. Members: No, no).
That is what you ask us to do in effect.
Is it fair? The Prime Minister took very
careful steps before introducing the Bill.
He consulted the Orange lodges and he
consulted the heads of the Protestant
Churches. He found out their views and
he framed the Bill to meet their conscientious wishes. He will not deny that. He
has no excuse this time. He also got the
views of the Catholic leaders. They were
laid before the Parliamentary Secretary
before the Bill was introduced, but instead of their wishes being acceded to they
were turned down and penalised by 50 per
cent. of the building fund grant. Is that
fair? Can anybody stand up here to-day
and say that is fair? I say "No."

Strandtown Unionist Club. I would like
to ask the Minister of Home Affairs has
the Strandtown Unionist Club a permit to
hold these two presentation rifles, a
souvenir of the gun-running expedition in
Ulster. If they have not a permit why
do you not take action immediately?
Sir DAWSON BATES: Perhaps it
might shorten discussion of this matter if
I told my hon. Friend that the rifles which
I presented were my own personal property, but they were not rifles in the ordinary sense because they were unfit for use.
My hon. Friend surely knows enough
about the Firearms Act to know that it
only applies to a serviceable weapon.

Mr. BEATTIE: I do not object to you

Hear, hear)-which saved Ulster from the

You
can give them all away as far as I am
concerned, but give them away in a state
not fit for service. I ask the Minister of

ammunition.
With regard to lighting sets in barracks,
it has now come out clearly that the
production of electric light by selfproducing sets is very expensive. The
Minister of Finance challenged me time
after time in this House and claimed that
economy had been affected by the installation of those plants, but now he is coming on to the market to sell those plants
because of the cost of production and is
reverting to the town supply. He is now
trying to dispose of plants for which he
paid upwards of £350-another heavy loss
to the taxpayers of Ulster. I would ask
the Minister of Finance to consider sometimes the position he occupies as the
protector of the people's money and not
to be so generous on occasions such as when
he is buying lighting sets, or furniture, or
old buildings, and least of all when he is
buying land. The market price when you
are selling land may be £1 per acre, but
when you are buying it you have to pay
upwards of £300 an acre. I ask the Minister to be more careful in future when
buying land, property, or anything of that
kind.
The last thing on which I want to speak
is the question of widows' and orphans'
pensions. I feel that a great injustice is
being done to many widows in Northern
Ireland owing to trade depression and circumstances over which they had no con-
Appropriation Bill-

trol when their husbands were living. I
have asked repeatedly that some compassionate consideration should be given.
The Act of Parliament is wide enougn and
the scope of it broad enough to meet the

Act of Parliament through which a coach
and four could not be driven. A little
bit of elasticity would enable provision to
be made for some widows and orphans who
have been denied the pension, and would
bring some comfort to their homes which
they do not enjoy at the present moment.
I will give you particulars of one case,
and then I will sit down. It is the case
of a man who worked in the shipyard until
1924. Owing to depression in the shipbuilding industry he became self-employed
for a period of two years. At the end of
two years he died, and left his widow with
four little babies. Because he had been
self-employed for two years his widow and
children have been denied the pension.
There is the case of a man who
was insured from 1912 until 1924. I
believe that the pension could be paid
to his widow and four children quite
legally under the Act. I ask the Government to give sympathetic consideration to
borderline cases such as the one I have indicated. If they do that they will be
rendering a great service to the widows
and orphans of Northern Ireland.

Mr. MINFORD: I am delighted to see
the Act extended, but I am sorry to say
that the terms on which the money will be
given to local authorities could not be
taken advantage of. Under the 1906
Act cottages were built and let prior to
1914 at a rent of 1s 9d a week. Under the
present Bill we have to borrow money at
5 per cent., and on £350 this would work
out at £18 5s 4d a year. If you then add
rent collection, repairs and insurance it
amounts to £21 3s 4d. If we are now to
go on building cottages and let them to
rural labourers at 2s 6d a week, which
amounts to £6 10s 0d, and the Government
pays £7 14s 2d, that leaves a balance of
£6 19s 2d to be borne by the rates. I
think it is a most inopportune time to ask
householders to pay higher rates than they
are paying. I suggest to the Government
that if they gave the rural councils the
same terms as under the 1906 Act it would
result in doing away with the want of
housing accommodation in the
the rural
districts.
In the Antrim rural district 177 cottages
were erected prior to 1914, and they were
let at 1s 9d per week with no additional
cost to the ratepayers. They built 50
houses sometime in 1924 which are let at
3s a week. This was done by money
which was obtained at 31 per cent. It is
impossible to ask our workers to pay a
rent of 5s 6d for their houses. We know
that the agricultural industry was never in
a more depressed condition, and I do not
see how a worker is able to bear the burdenof 5s 6d a week for rent. I suggest that
workers who do not come under the same
conditions as industrial workers should get
a concession from the Government. If the
Government cannot see their way to give
the loan at 3 per cent. they should give
a higher grant than 40 per cent. of the
cost.
As one who represents a rural part of
Antrim district I would like to see this
scheme put in force and carried through,
and houses let at an economic rent, but I
cannot see how we can take advantage of
this scheme if we are to saddle the rural
workers with a rent of 5s 6d. It is impossible to pay that sum at the present
moment. I would ask the Government to
devise some scheme whereby it would be
possible to wipe out all bad and defective
buildings. I believe I am right in saying
that if 150 houses were built in the Antrim
rural area it would mean an additional 9d
in the £ on the ratepayers in that area,
and that would not be met in any friendly
spirit. People have been clamouring for
better houses, and their only recompense is
that they are going to get houses at treble
the amount which they can pay.
I would ask that the 51 per cent. should
be reduced to 3 per cent. Give us the
same terms as under the 1906 Act, and I
believe inside five years there would be
sufficient houses built to house the rural
workers. The time has come when we
must give some inducement for people to
settle in the rural areas. The outlook for
agriculture is dark, and unless we do that
the country will be left desolate. We
cannot shut our eyes to the fact that we
have in the rural areas houses which are a
disgrace to the twentieth century. I
would like to see the Ministry taking steps
to find out how many houses would be required to be built inside the next five
years, and have all these old houses cleared
and better ones built. Nothing makes a
man more happy than to have a house in
which there is accommodation for his
family. There are houses with only a

existing terms under the Labourers'
Cottages Acts. It does not. It simply
continues for a further period of five
years the Act passed in 1927, and on
precisely the same terms.
I am sure my
hon. Friend will agree with me that the
Government are doing much to try to
improve the conditions of labourers. As
a matter of fact the Government bear no
less a cost than 40 per cent. of the total
cost of each labourer's cottage. Approximately each rural council pay 30 per
cent., leaving only 30 per cent. to be
borne by the tenant. As regards new
houses this works out in rent on an
average at 2s 9d a week which, I think, is
a very reasonable figure. When the first
Labourers' Cottages Act was passed it
was never intended that the Government
should bear the entire cost. It was intended that the ratepayers in the country
districts should bear a certain proportion
of the cost 30 that the tenant could get
the house at a reasonable figure.
That was at a time when money was
cheap and it was possible to let houses
at Is and 1s 6d a week, but I do not
think anyone will question the fact that
a rent of 2s 6d or 2s 9d a week is
reasonable. So far as regards the rural
councils taking advantage of the Acts, I
may say that there are no fewer than
696 cottages involved in different schemes
which are at the present time before the
Ministry. I hope that figure will be
doubled. I would suggest to my hon.
Friend that he should use his influence
with the rural district councils to put
forward further schemes where they have
not done so. In Antrim no fewer than
50 are being put; Ballymena, 193; Ballymoney, 113; Downpatrick, 300; Londonderry, 50, and Lurgan, 40. There is no
reason why other schemes should not be
put forward. I think those are the main
points.
Mr. MINFORD: I think perhaps hon.
Members would bear me out that under
the present Bill it is impossible to build
houses to be let at 2s 9d a week. The
cost of a house in Antrim is £350. The
interest on that works out at 51 per cent.,
at £18 5s 4d, and with rent, collection,
repairs, and insurance added the amount
is £21 3s 4d. If we let the house at
2s 6d a week, which would bring in
£6 10s Od a year, and we got £7 14s 2d
from the Government, that would leave
£6 19s 2d to be borne by the ratepayers.
My contention is that the Minister is
mistaken, and it is impossible to let
houses at the figure he names.

whether the same privileges will be permitted in the case of teachers and pupils
who may wish to get a holiday by greeting
and cheering for other politicians.
The PARLIAMENTARY SECRE-
TARY OF THE MINISTRY OF EDU.
CATION (Mr. Robb): I have seen the
Press report referred to. The Ministry
has power under the Statutory Regulations
to accede to requests for the closing of
public elementary schools on special occasions and the visit to the locality of a
person holding high office in the State has
been deemed a special occasion. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear).
Mr. NIXON: Would the Parliamentary Secretary kindly answer the latter
part of the question?

hear).

question?

Railway and Canal Traffic (Amendment) Bill.
Considered in Committee.

CLAUSE 1 (Amendment of s. 45 of 51
& 52 Vict., c. 25, as to abandonment of
unnecessary canals).
Section forty-five of the Railway and
Canal Traffic Act, 1888 (in this Act referred to as "the principal enactment')
shall, in its application to the abandonment of unnecessary canals in Northern
Ireland, have effect subject to the
following Amendments:-
(a) A warrant of abandonment
shall not be granted unless the proprietors of the canal have given
security, to such amount and in such
manner as the Ministry of Commerce
may require, for the making of compensation to all persons who may be
determined under this Act to be entitled to compensation by reason of
the abandonment of the canal;

thereof (whether in connection with

forfeiture or reverter or other

Mr. DAVISON: I beg to move on

All along the course of the canal the
company is liable to keep certain works in

owners who are mostly farmers. Sometimes a canal alters the drainage system
and the company has had to provide works
to keep up the drainage of the lands. If
this canal is abandoned these drains will
have to be maintained by the farmers
themselves and they will be resasonably entitled to compensation for the
consequences of
any order releasing

under Clause 5 in every respect. It is
also framed in the very widest terms so
as
to enable the Lagan Navigation

justice ought to be done to all parties.

To ask the Attorney-General what

Practices Acts by threatening the poor
that if they do not vote for certain
candidates at Parliamentary
and
Municipal elections they will get none

To that the Minister of Home Affairs
(Sir Dawson Bates) replied in writing,
or rather replied verbally; this is his
written answer from which I am reading:
I have been asked by my right hon.
Friend to answer this question. There
is no information on record as to any
such offences as those referred to in the
hon. Member's question.
Now I challenge directly the accuracy of
that statement, and with your permission,
Mr. Speaker, I mean to prove here and
now that there is a record of that. I hold
in my hand a record of it. The record
is Hansard of the 20th March, 1930,
columns 328 and 329. It was I, myself, who
brought it under notice here, so that it
was inaccurate for the Minister to say
that it was not brought under notice or
that there is no record of it.
There are a lot of good charitable
people in this city who subscribe a lot
of money to what is called a coal fund.
Last May a public man told people in
Urney Street, Langford Street, and
other streets if they did not vote in a
certain way they would get no coal at
Christmas. That, I hold, is corruption.
In case I am overstating the case it
is very easy for the Attorney-General
to send detectives to Urney Street and
find out if this is true. Last Christmas, before the January election, there
was a man retiring, and he went to a
political meeting and sat down and
proceeded to collect names
of poor
people who might want a bag of
coal. Last November a candidate and
another man-there is evidence of this,
too-sat down in his office and got scores
and scores of people to put down their
names for coal, and one question invariably was: "Who will you vote for
Prime Minister's Ulster Tour 1512
Adjournment-

on Tuesday?" That is the worst class
of corruption. I do not like to make
a statement that is wrong, or to take
advantage of my position to make

1. Mr. ELLIOTT asked the Minister
of Commerce whether, in the event of
the failure of the Government's proposal
to purchase the shareholders' interest in

is the intention of the Government to

the guaranteeing baronies to enable them
to meet the guaranteed interest on the
Company's capital share.
The MINISTER OF COMMERCE
(Mr. Barbour): The whole question of the
future of the Clogher Valley Railway
Company is under consideration. The
hon. Member will appreciate, therefore,
that it would be premature for me to
make any pronouncement at this stage.
LOUGH NEAGH TOURIST
AMENITIES.
2. Mr. ELLIOTT asked the Minister
of Finance whether, in view of the importance of improving the amenities of Lough
Neagh from the tourist standpoint, he
would make available the services of a
Government engineer to advise the Lough
Neagh Development Committee in the
efforts they are making to devise a scheme
of road improvement around the Lough.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): I have been asked
to reply.
I can assure the hon. Member that the
Engineering Inspector of the Ministry
will be prepared to give his advice and
assistance in connection with any scheme
which may be put forward in this connection, but I would remind the hon. Member, who is himself a member of one of the
county councils, that such schemes must
emanate from the road authorities concerned.
Mr. HEALY: Is this the first time a
public body has been willing to accept
advice from the Government although
they are generally willing to give advice?

when tendered by passengers for their
fares.
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Pollock): I understand that the question raised by the hon. Member has in
recent months been considered by the
Tramways Committee of the Belfast Corporation, and quite apart from the fact
that Free State coinage is not legal
tender in Northern Ireland, it is obvious
that the presence of any appreciable.
amount of silver or copper belonging to
another currency in the day's takings of
the tramways must inevitably cause cash
inconveniences in the Tramway Office.
Moreover, although I am aware that the
banks for the convenience of their customers accept occasional deposits in Free
State currency, it would be most unreasonable to expect that the Corporation's

4. Mr. McALEER asked the Minister

Dog Tax, and the heavy work and

Sir DAWSON BATES: The hon.
Member is not, perhaps, aware that the
receipts from dog licences form part of the
basis upon which the salary of a Petty
Sessions Clerk is calculated, and that,
moreover, an allowance of 10/- per each
100 licences issued is paid to the various
clerks to provide for assistance during the
dog licensing season.
I am not prepared to accept the suggestion of the hon. Member as to the inadequacy of Petty Sessions Clerks' salaries,
and I see no grounds for the payment
of an additional commission on dog
licence duty as proposed.
The answer to the second part of the
question is in the negative.

of Home Affairs grant that commission on

Sir DAWSON BATES: No, I do not
think that would be practicable. I believe the Petty Sessions Clerks would be
worse off as the result of my hon. Friend's
suggestion.

THE BUDGET.
Considered in Committee.
[Mr. MOLES in the Chair.]
Financial Statement, 1930-31.
Mr. POLLOCK: This is the ninth
annual statement which I have been privileged to submit to Parliament, so that
in this year of 1930 we are now approaching the end of the first decade of
our national life as an autonomous Province. During that period. we had
undoubtedly a great deal of leeway to
make up to remedy the long continued
absence of popular interest and local control. Whether the results of our labours
will be found to be commensurate with
the expenditure of money and effort involved time alone will show, but we can
at any rate claim that the standards of
our physical, social and educational life
have been raised far beyond anything to
which previous generations were accustomed.
The workman has not only secured free
education for his children, but he is also
insured against ill-health, unemployment,
accidents, old age, blindness, and, in
addition, provision is made for his widow.
and orphans. It can be definitely
affirmed that no comparable advantages
are found in any country in the world.
For the moment, however, I am only
concerned with these reflections in so far
as they affect in their operations the financial aspects of our provincial problems,
which it is my duty to submit to the
Committee to-day, and to which in more
prosaic language I will now apply myself.
The accounts for the financial year which
closed on the 31st March last have been
in the hands of Members of the Committee
for some little time. Notwithstanding
this, it is desirable that I should now
make a brief survey of the operations of
the year and compare the actual realised
results with the Estimates which I presented to the House some twelve months
ago.

[Mr. Pollock]
EXPENDITURE, 1929-30.
CONSOLIDATED FUND SERVICES.
I will deal firstly with the Expenditure
of 1929-30, and if hon. Members will refer
to the White Paper in their hands, they
will find on page 4 a table setting out
in some detail the comparison between
exchequer issues and the estimates of expenditure for the year.
The Committee is aware that under the
terms of the Unemployment Insurance
Agreement which was made between this
Government and the British Government,
and which a short time ago received the
force of law, the Government of Northern
Ireland assumed full responsibility for the
redemption of what is commonly called
the old debt of the Unemployment Insurance Fund, amounting to £3,424,000.
The arrangement made and which was
carried out required the debt to be
31st
written down to £3,000,000 on
March, 1929, and that in each succeeding
year there should be written off a further
£100,000. In order to provide for this
depreciation of the assets covering the
Exchequer advances, I have for the past
few years made an equivalent allocation
to reserve. I was unable to make provision for this allocation in the Estimates
last year, but I was fully determined to
make every effort to effect such savings
in expenditure that I would be enabled to
transfer the £100,000 from the Exchequer
at the end of the year. I am glad to say
that I have been successful, and the expenditure under the head of sinking funds
is thus exactly £100,000 greater than the
Estimate.
The condition of our sinking fund
should give satisfaction. During last
year £93,000 was allocated to the sinking
fund established to preserve in perpetuity
the revenues comprised in the Land Purchase Annuities presented to our Government as a free gift under the terms of
the Government of Ireland Act, 1920.
At the close of the financial year this
particular sinking fund possessed a cash
value of £921,000. £83,000 was transferred last year to the sinking fund
established to provide against the interest
due on Ulster Savings Certificates. This
fund possessed a cash value of £469,000
on the 31st March.
No allocation was made during the year
to the Church Temporalities Sinking
Fund, which stands at a total of
£116,000, as it appeared, on investigation, that none was required. By the
operation of the Land Purchase Acts,
these tithe rent and other charges are
constantly being redeemed, and the proceeds are invested in the ordinary way.
The other items which appear under
the head of Consolidated Fund Services
do not call for comment, although it will
be noted that the issues to the Road Fund
amounted to some £27,000 in excess of the
Estimate of £440,000. This item is, of
course, the counterpart of the receipts
from motor taxation.
I come to the supply services of last
year. The estimated requirements of the
Government for ordinary supply services
were proved by the experience of the year
to have been, on the whole, accurate.
The chief discreprancy occurs in the Estimates for the Ministry of Labour, where
the actual requirements proved to be
almost £200,000 below the total anticipated. The explanation of this is to be
found in the working of the Unemployment Insurance Fund (Equalisation)
Agreement with Great Britain. Under
that Agreement, the condition of our
Unemployment Fund is to be kept in
parity with the British Fund by grants
from our Exchequer, a proportion of
which is ultimately borne by the British
Exchequer. Accordingly, hon. Members
will see that if unemployment in Great
Britain is very light while it may, perhaps, be heavy here, the sum required
to equalise the two Funds will be correspondingly great. The Estimates were
based on the assumption that during the
year unemployment in Northern Ireland
would be much greater than in Great
Britain. Unfortunately, however, unemployment in Britain has steadily increased
during the past twelve months, and so
the net effect has been to reduce very
considerably the demands which
made upon the Exchequer for the
equalisation of the two Funds.
were
I trust that I have succeeded in making.
myself clear on this rather intricate point,
but the chief thing I wish to impress
upon the Committee is that the saving in
the Ministry of Labour Vote is due almost
entirely to fortuitous circumstances and
has no bearing whatever on the ordinary
administration of Services here. Therefore, in spite of the grim determination
to save, we should have been £200,000
to the bad but for circumstances outside
our control.

I come to the expenditure on the reserved services, that is the services carried
out by the Imperial authority. There are

Nevertheless, it may be of interest to observe that the total expenditure on these
services amounted to £1,808,000, or just

The final balance sheet for last year

Lastly, there is the provisional contribution to Imperial Services. This was

REVENUE, 1929-30.
I come to the revenue last year to meet
the expenditure which I have just dealt
with. I still direct myself to last year.
Last year, the transferred taxes, that
is to say, taxes for whose imposition and
collection we here are responsible, yielded
a total revenue of £1,534,000, against an
Estimate of £1,445,000, an increase of
£89,000 over the Estimate. To a small
extent this is attributable to the increased receipts from motor vehicle duties,
which yielded in all £467,000 against an
Estimate of £440,000.
The yield of stamp duties was disappointing, as, although I budgeted last
year for £275,000, I received only
£227,000, that is to say, practically
£50,000 below the Estimate. I do not,
however, have to look very far for an
explanation, as it will be fresh in the
memory of every Member of the Committee that toward the end of last year
a serious financial crisis arose in America,
and certain fradulent stock operations in
The
London also accentuated its effects.
result, of course, was practically to paralyze business on the Stock Exchange, and
the revenue receipts from the stamping of
transfers and other documents suffered
materially.
The failure of stamp duties to come up
to expectations was, however, more than
neutralised by the yield of the death
duties, the receipts from which amounted
to £104,000 in excess of the Estimate of
£600,000. The ordinary excise licence.
duties and entertainment duty yielded in
all £136,000, which is just slightly over
the Estimate of £130,000. Of this total,
entertainment duty receipts amounted to
£65,000. Including motor vehicle duty,
the total yield of the transferred taxes
amounted to £1,534,000.
In regard to the reserved revenue
assessed and collected by the Imperial
authority, a return of which we give at
the end of each year, I am more than
gratified at the response of these reserved
taxes, because I consider that the receipts from taxes, such as the duties of
customs and excise and the income tax,
provide a very fair indication of the
condition of trade and commerce in the
Province. Customs and excise duties
yielded in all £3,970,000, that is to say,
approximately £100,000 above the Estimate. I will not enter fully into the
detailed examination of customs and excise receipts, but it will be found interesting to look for a moment simply at a
comparison between the yield last year
and the Estimates for the same period.

EXPENDITURE, 1930-31.
was
I have now completed my survey of the
outcome of our financial arrangements for
the past year, which, in the main, cannot
be regarded as altogether unsatisfactory.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear). I will
now turn my attention to a more important
feature of my statement, namely, our
financial position for the year into which
we are now entering. I have not up to
the present touched upon the effect on
our
finances of the major legislative
changes of the past twelve months, as their
effect is not fully felt until the present
year, but when I come to consider our
estimated expenditure for 1930-31. T am
at once faced by the unprecedented expansion in our ordinary Supply Services.
Hon. Members will recollect that the
expenditure on Supply Services last year
amounted in all to £7,356,000. The estimate for the present year is more than a
million and a half above that figure,
reaching a total of no less than £8.881.000.
Only a very small, indeed almost only
a fractional, part of this expansion can he
The Budget-
Committee
27 MAY 1930
attributed to any growth in the ordinary
administrative services of government. It
will be seen that agricultural services and
commercial services remain practically unchanged. Education accounts for only a
slight increase. We have, of course, made
provision for special engineering and
architectural services in connection with
the Stormont Buildings and the prosecution of the Bann Drainage Scheme.
But in the main, we find that this huge
increase is accounted for by social or local
commitments into which we have entered
as a result of our legislation.
Looking back over the history of social
services it is impossible to fail to be struck
by their remarkable growth within the last
few years.
Taking our own Province as
an example, social and local services in
1922-23-the first year of our separate
existence amounted to slightly less than
£2,000,000. In the present year they
account for over £4,000,000, that is to
say, nearly half the total expenditure of
the State on social services. This takes
no account of Education, which, although
not ordinarily included amongst so-called
social services, possesses a great deal in
common with them, viz., expenditure of
money for the poorer classes in the community. If it is added, this proportion
rises to almost three-quarters. But, returning to the purely social services, it is
obvious that the whole trend of legislation
during the past eight years has been not
only in the direction of the introduction
of new services, but in the expansion of
the old, so as to make it continuously
easier for people to obtain assistance from
the State.
I do not know whether hon. Members
ever read the Ulster Year Book issued
from my Ministry. If they do, they will
have noted an interesting sidelight in the
development of social services, and the
corresponding reduction of the Imperial
contribution on looking at the pictorial
representations to be found in the 1929
edition and comparing it with the same
picture in the 1926 volume. The illustration in the next edition will be even
more startling.
It is only a matter of months since most
drastic changes were made in the law relating to Widows', Orphans' and Old Age
Contributory Pensions, and also to Unemployment Insurance. In consequence of
the modified conditions laid down in the
former code, the cost to the Exchequer
has increased from £140,000 last year to
£315,000 in the present year, although
this increase is partly due to an underestimate of the cost of the 1925 Act.
More recently still, this Parliament passed
a Bill which extended the period of transitional benefit in Unemployment Insurance and which, moreover, in order to
relieve the burden on the Unemployment
Insurance Fund, transferred the cost of
transitional benefit from the fund to the
Exchequer. This cost us £120,000 for
last year; this year I have had to provide
an additional £400,000 to meet that
charge, and so the Budget estimate for
Unemployment Insurance has increased to
almost a million and a half, but against
this liability we expect to receive Great
Britain's contribution of approximately
£500,000 to the equalisation payment.
Local services also have added to my
responsibilities. This is the first year in
which we feel the full effects of the derating scheme. We have now to make
provision for a complete twelve months'
expenditure, and so we find that the
estimate under the head of Grants to
Local Authorities has increased from its
old figure of something under half-amillion to over £1,400,000.
Of this sum no less than £1,112,000 is
represented by derating grants, and this
leads me to say that this question of the
effect of derating on the finances, not
only of the Exchequer but of local authorities also, is one which is giving me great
concern.

that derating has been established and

REVENUE, 1930-31.
I will now proceed at once to deal with
the question of Revenue for the present
year, 1930-31.
1. Reserved Taxes:
I have received from the British Government the Treasury Estimates for the
yield of Reserved Taxes. The changes
recently made by the Imperial Chancellor
in regard to the standard rate of Income
Tax and the rates of Sur-tax are estimated
to produce an increased revenue in Northern Ireland of £225,000 this year, so
that the estimated receipts from Income
and Sur-tax amount to £3,195,000.
Before leaving this item, I should like to
allay fears which have been expressed to
me on many occasions by Income Tax
payers who feel that the fact of the
standard rate of tax in the Free State
being 1/6 below the standard rate of tax
operating in Northern Ireland is bound
to militate very considerably against the
interests of our Province.
This difference certainly does exist in
the standard rate in favour of residents
in the Free State, but it must be borne
in mind that the rates of allowances for
earned income, for children and so on
are more generous here than in the
neighbouring area. I am advised, on
good authority, that the tax payable by
a married man with an earned income
not exceeding £1,000 is lower in Northern
Ireland than in the Free State. To cite
an example, a married man with three
children and having an earned income of
£500 a year would pay
£3 3s 4d tax here;
in the Free State he would pay £10 2s 6d.
I do not need to enlarge on this, for it
illustrates the simple fact that the ordinary middle-class people, who comprise the
great bulk of our population, are better
off here that they would be in the Free
State. I think this great advantage of
the British connection should be fully
understood and appreciated. (Hon:
Members: Hear, hear).

3. Transferred Taxes:
I now, therefore, reach the stage when
I must consider the estimated yield of
these taxes, and I must place before the
House my proposals in regard to various
changes which I consider it necessary to
make. I feel that it is important that
we should introduce here the changes in
the rates of Estate Duties made by the
Chancellor in his Budget at Westminster.
Apart altogether from Revenue considerations, which, of course, are uppermost in my mind to-day, it is undoubtedly
the case that the majority of Estates
passing in Ulster include some British
assets, and the obtaining of Probate is,
therefore, very much simplified when the
general conditions in Northern Ireland
are the same as in Great Britain. But,
moreover, I am advised that a decision
not to make the changes which are proposed across the water would have a
curious and unwelcome reaction, since,
owing to the working of the law under
which estates are aggregated for Death
Duty purposes, it would cause a loss in
the Revenue we might expect to receive
on the existing basis of taxation.
Accordingly, I propose that the rates.
of duty payable in respect of estates exceeding a net principal value of £120,000
should be increased by amounts rising
from 1 per cent. in the cases of estates
exceeding £120,000 but not exceeding
£140,000 to 10 per cent. in the case of
estates having a net value of over
£2,000,000.
