In my Budget statement last year, I
announced the setting up of an Inter-
Departmental Committee to examine the
question of motor taxation. The actual
terms of reference were:-
To examine the position of the Road
Fund, and, having regard to the future.
commitments of that fund, to make
recommendations for such changes in
the taxation of motor vehicles as may
appear desirable, on the understanding
that the revenue of the Road Fund
must be sufficient to meet its expenditure without any grants from the Exchequer.
I must stress the importance of this.
When speaking on this subject a year ago,
I said-
Whatever may be done in regard to
motor taxation, the Road Fund must
be self-supporting.
Comparisons with Britain are interesting,
but have no practical value, since we must
face the simple truth that we have got to
make our own arrangements for the maintenance of an efficient system of roads in
Northern Ireland. I cannot do better
than quote the Committees observations
on the futility of comparisons. They
say:-
The investigations which we had
made on behalf of the Ulster Motor
Trade Association made it obvious that
the state of the Road Fund would not
admit of the introduction of the British
rates. We are, in any event, under no
illusions in the matter. No real comparison of British and Northern Irish
conditions is possible. Neither the expenditure nor the revenue side of the
Road Fund in Northern Ireland is com.
parable with that for Great Britain.
Motor taxation receipts in 1927-28
amounted to 6s 6d per head of the popu
lation in Northern Ireland, as con.
trasted with 12s 6d in Great Britain.
Northern Ireland, therefore, has not
the same field to draw on. There are
very few high-powered luxury cars in
Northern Ireland, the cheaper car
being the more popular.
The mileage of roads in Northern
Ireland per head of the population is
much greater than in Great Britain,
which means that with less receipts proportionately more roads require upkeep.
Furthermore, certain roads in Northern
Ireland are expensive to maintain, as
they pass through long stretches of
bog.
That summarises the argument in
respect of the necessity for living here in
our own house, looking after our own
affairs in regard to the maintenance of
roads, and depending entirely on our own
resources. I received the report of the
Committee a short time ago, and I have
decided with the full approval of my right
hon. Friend, who administers this fund,
and also of the Cabinet, to accept in full
its proposals in regard to the question of
motor taxation. I may say, in passing,
that I very much regret that the two important Northern Ireland Associations
declined to avail themselves of the Committee's invitation to give evidence on the
subject, but notwithstanding the absence
of any assistance from these bodies, the
Committee has made a most thorough and
impartial investigation of the whole problem, and its report will, I am sure, become a standard work of reference. I
hope it will be in the hands of hon.
Members this afternoon.
During its investigations, the Committee obtained from local authorities as near
an estimate as could, in the circumstances,
be given of the future expenditure likely
to be required on roads during the next
five years, and concluded that the Road
Fund must anticipate having to bear
annual charges of about £507,000 during
that time. Further, with the disappearance of the Road Fund reserve, it will be
necessary to ensure that the ordinary
annual income of the fund shall be fully
adequate to meet the demands made upon
it. It is expected that on the present
basis of taxation the receipts will average
about £440,000 a year, and thus there
is a debit of something over £60,000 per
annum to be provided for.
The Budget-
Committee.
27 MAY 1930
Briefly, I propose to ask Parliament for
the necessary powers to make the following changes, which I may say initially I
do not think will be very burdensome on
any interest.
(1) As from the 1st January next, the
margin of 5 cwt. at present allowed in the
scales of taxation of commercial goods
vehicles will be abolished, and the taxation
will revert to the ordinary ton basis. The
circumstances of the change from the ton
basis to that of 25 cwts. will be remembered. It has been found very embarrassing from that day to this. I propose,
however, that there shall be intermediate
points in the scale in respect of vehicles
between 1 and 3 tons, with corresponding
intermediate rates of duty, and I have
no doubt that this adjustment will be very
welcome to a large class of small vanowners.
I also propose to amend the existing law
in regard to the definition of goods vehicles,
so that all vehicles weighing more than
8 cwts. and used for the conveyance of
goods shall be taxed as commercial goods
vehicles and not on the ordinary horsepower basis that obtained in the past.
(2) I propose to make an amendment in
the rates of duty chargeable on motor
hackneys, including, of course, buses. I
am fully satisfied that the present rate of
taxation does not secure the payment of a
fair contribution representing the wear
and tear caused by buses to the roads.
Accordingly, in future, hackney carriages
seating more than eight people will be
taxed at the flat rate of £2 10s per seat.
I submit to the Committee that this is
a more logical and scientific basis of taxation. While producing an increased
revenue, it will, in many cases, afford
relief to the man whose bus comes midway
between two points on the old scale, and
so remove what I feel is an unfortunate
anomaly.
A further concession I am making is in
regard to the ordinary taxicabs. The tax
at present is £12. I propose to reduce it
to £10.
There is also a considerable class of
small hackney-cab, which has accommodation for seven or eight people. At
present they are taxed at £28. Under
my proposals this will be reduced to £20.
The present rates of duty paid in respect of road locomotives and tractors is
a matter which, in the opinion of the
Committee, requires revision. It is true
that these vehicles do not travel at great
speeds, but
but their
their great weight undoubtedly puts a severe strain on roads,
and I am in full agreement with the view
that an increased scale is called for. Details of the changes I propose will be
given in the White Paper.
As regards motor cycles, I propose to
vary the scale now in force so that cycles
not exceding 224 lbs. in weight will pay
a duty of £2, while cycles exceeding that
weight will pay £3. That £2 was
originally £2 10s.
I am not inclined at present to contemplate any increase in the rate of taxation of ordinary private cars, because,
in comparison with the other scales, it provides for a fair apportionment of the cost
of maintaining the road system, and also
because of the reactions an increase would
have on cross-channel tourist traffic. I
am sure hon. Members will agree that it
is right the Government should not contemplate any change in the taxation of
private motor cars.
But at the same time, it is only reasonable that the private driver should contribute something towards the additional
revenue required, and so I propose to increase the fee for the grant of a driver's
licence from 5s to 10s. This change will
only apply to the drivers of private cars
and motor cycles, and I am confident that
it will not impose any hardship.
Mr. O'NEILL: It will be very
popular.
Mr. POLLOCK : The total effect of
these various changes will be to augment
the income of the Road Fund by £43,000
in a full year, and I anticipate receiving
an additional £25,000 from this source
during this year, making a total of
£495,000. Hon. Members will notice
that this still leaves a small adverse
balance between the outgoings and income
of the Road Fund, but I am confident
that, in consultation with my right hon.
Friend, we will be able to take administrative action which will successfully
bridge the gap.
A reduction in the percentage grants for
third-class roads is, as suggested by the
Committee, one possible line of approach.
But this is one of the matters which will
require consideration in conjunction with
the other questions I intend referring to
the new body which will investigate the
bearing of derating on our general financial system.

I am, however, at this important

Britain, greatly concerned with the moral
to be drawn from these results.
As between our Revenue and Expenditure, the financial position of the State
has now reached the verge of danger
point, and I feel it my duty to impress
upon this House, and, so far as my words
can carry, warn the Local Authorities
and the ratepayers of the Province that,
in respect of State assistance, the limit
has been reached, and that they must rely
on their own resources for any further
expenditure they contemplate. The only
alternative is heavy additional taxation.
I hope and trust it will not be my lot to
have to revert to such an expedient.

The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): I have been asked to

An engineer was appointed by the

Mr. HEALY: I desire, in the first
place, to congratulate the Minister of
Finance upon the exceedingly lucid
statement of the financial position he
gave the Committee yesterday. Most of
us have read it in the local papers to-day
with mingled feelings.
The Minister started out yesterday to
investigate the financial field. He began
with his head in the sunshine on the
hill tops; he ended in the shadows of the
valley. He began by telling us of all the
blessings and social services we have enjoyed. We were insuring against unemployment, ill-health, accidents, old age
and blindness. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear). He even suggested that our widows
and orphans, being so liberally provided
for, their losses were likely to be of a mere
sentimental character in the future. We
have, in fact, everything, save money.
We have everything save trade. I wondered, as I listened to his litany of our
well being what the rising crowd of the
unemployed would say when they read
the papers to-day. I wondered too what
the farmers would think when they heard
how well the land annuities had produced. I know the great efforts that
many of them have made in order to pay
these annuities even with borrowed
money.
The Minister, taking the most optimistic view he could, closed his balance sheet
with £3,000 to the good. It is a small
sum, relatively, but he is entitled, I think,
to get what comfort he can out of it. I
noticed the faces on some of the Government back benches as the right hon.
Gentleman began his statement yesterday.
They were wreathed in rosy smiles as they
learned of the decreasing revenue from intoxicating drinks. When he came to the
danger point and the words of warning to
local authorities the smiles departed and
it was a gloomy assembly that beheld him
hang out his "danger signal" at the end.
I think the most optimistic in this House
must admit that the red light is hoisted on
the Government Building at last.
What a transformation! It seems only
yesterday that the Prime Minister, like a
re-incarnation from the Arabian Nights,
was going around the country distributing
bridges and roads from Derry to Fermanagh, draining the Bann and setting
the almost derelict shipyards of Belfast
into activity with 10 million pounds-

proper way to go about the matter would

Mr. HEALY: I was saying that the
Prime Minister had gone about the
country and with very liberal prodigality
had been scattering gifts of bridges and
roads from Derry to Fermanagh, and not
only that but that he had been setting
the Belfast shipyards, now partially derelict, into activity again by grants from
the Loans Guarantee Funds of ten million
pounds.
Mr. POLLOCK: Not grants.
Mr. HEALY: Guarantees for which
the whole Six Counties are held in pawn.
Indeed, the mission of the Prime Minister
has generally been in flinging slogans of
optimism along the roadsides with all the
Ways and Means-
Report Stage
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Healy]
prodigality of a fatherly figure in a
Christmas pantomime. From "I shall
solve the unemployment problem" of 1923,
to "I will come to the aid of agriculture"
at Omagh in 1930, nobody can claim that
his pessimism has worked the sad change
in our finances. I am afraid the Minister
of Home Affairs has banned the gramophone at an inopportune moment. There
never was a time when the Government
needed a hopeful slogan more for Unionist tea meetings. Where can it be found?
I am sure the Ministers will not be able
to rise to the occasion in future with the
warning of the Chancellor in their ears
and that £3,000 surplus before their
eyes!
I shall never believe in financial experts again. In 1920 the genuis of the
Imperial Exchequer believed that Northern Ireland could pay an Imperial contribution of almost eight million a year.
That anyone in Belfast could for a moment
toy with such a figure shows that something is lacking here, too. From that
hour to this it has been vanishing from
the scene. In 1930 it is spoken of as
£150,000, although when the figures are
finally made up by the Joint Exchequer
Board I doubt not we shall find even that
figure gone.
The Financial Secretary to
the Treasury in 1924 was credited with
saying that he dreaded the sight of the
Northern officials in the rooms at Whitehall; they were always wanting money!
I must congratulate the Minister of
Finance upon having no sentimental feelings about the relationship. He told
them plainly he could not pay, that the
1920 bargain could not be kept.
Mr. POLLOCK : It was no bargain.
Mr. HEALY: I hope the next Government in the Free State will not be slow
to profit by his example.
Mr. GORDON: They have done very
well.
Mr. HEALY: You have not kept to
the strict letter of the bond; why should
any party in the Free State be foolish
enough to do so? I trust we shall soon
see the whole Irish question under review
again, and that the injustices done Northern Nationalists will be remedied. The
Opposition do not take any pleasure in
recalling that they warned you many
times in the past as to the danger of the
step-by-step policy. You never seemed
to see the inconsistency of your position,
being, like Paul, all things to all people.
Mr. GORDON: Wrong quotation.
Mr. HEALY: The hon. Gentleman
has had some experience of that policy in
his own time. If I do not mistake I
heard the hon. Gentleman say he carried
the Red flag in the backyard.
Mr. GRANT: It is the right place to
keep it.
Mr. HEALY: If it is there it will
remain there for some time. You never
seem to see the inconsistency of your
position. To the Tories you are Tories,
to the Socialists you are Socialists. Whatever they decreed yesterday you decree tomorrow. If Birmingham wanted something, Fermanagh must have it, too.
This Government ought, in decency, to
save printing and talk, procure a rubber
stamp and across every British Measure
print: "This Act now applies to Northern
Ireland." Our talk upon such Measures
in this House has about as much relation
to reality as the figures of the Minister
of Finance have to the £11,000,000 Budget
statement you heard him discuss yesterday. Neither he nor this House controls
those figures. We cannot call the tune
and we do not pay the fiddler.
actual expenditure controlled by us is
relatively small-one-twentieth-an English county council's budget would exceed
it many times. We like to give ourselves
airs in this Parliament, talking grandiloquently of large sums, over the spending
or collection of which we have no earthly
control. We are the true "Playboys of
the Western World."
The
I wanted at this stage to recall to the
Prime Minister, if he had been here, a
statement he made in this House on the
12th of May, 1927. He contemplated the
disappearance of the Imperial contribution even then and professed himself unwilling to release Great Britain from the
possibility of giving us a subsidy to enable us to carry on. The Prime Minister
said
The Act of 1923 provides that they
would be paying us a contribution instead of our paying them a contribution, and, consequently, if we were to
offer the British Government to-day
to take away altogether the contribution and to say: "We will not ask
you in future if you let us off in the
present," why, I think, the Chancellor
of the Exchequer would jump at it at
once.-(Official Report, Vol. VIII,
12th May, 1927; cols. 1386, 1387).
Ways and Means-
Report Stage
28 MAY 1930
I think that is a plain indication that we
will pay no more, and further that we

£1,081,000. Yesterday we were told by

Of spirits.

There was one wise remark made yesterday by the Minister in the course of
his speech, and I think it epitomises practically all I wish to say in the way of
pointing a moral. He referred to the
report of the Inter-Departmental Committee on the question of motor taxation.
I took the following excerpt from the
Report:
We are, in any event, under no illusions in the matter. No real comparison of British and Northern Irish
conditions is possible.
I say that is quite applicable to every
phase and every feature of your activities.
No real comparison of British and
Northern Irish conditions is possible. But
still you insist upon having that equality
which is not equality at all, upon having
that parity which always acts against
yourselves, and upon glorying in what you
call your British connection but which is
not a connection at all but a subjection.
Mr. ANDREWS: Do not say anything
against a neighbouring State. Be consistent.
Mr. CONNELLAN: Australia, Canada,
India, and South Africa are as much part
of the British Empire as you are, and in
this connection I may tell
you something
that perhaps you have not heard before.
When the noble Lord, the Prime Minister,
was on his tour through Australia some
time ago he made use of a word in describing this organisation of States which
did not please the Australians and to
which exception was taken. He referred
to the "Empire" when they preferred the
word "Commonwealth," and he referred
to "Colonies" when they would have preferred that he should have used the word
"States." In any event, I was saying
that Australia, Canada, and South Africa
are as much part of the British Empire as
you or the Free State are, but all these
places are able to manage their Own
affairs. Their association with the
Commonwealth of nations known as the
British Empire is a connection. Yours is
the only one in all that area where the
association is a subjection. You sent out
your soldiers to South Africa-how many
years ago?-to defeat the claims of the
people there for a certain form of Government. And your soldiers are out serving
in India and in Egypt at the present time.
What will you find in a couple of years?
You will find that India's claims will be
allowed, that they will be a self-governing
Dominion. Egypt is on the verge of obtaining self-government. South Africa
has already obtained it. The only people
who are denied it are the people who went
out from here to try to prevent those other
people getting what they wanted. Is it
not a wonderful lesson?
This step-by-step policy is bad and is
bound to end in disaster. You cannot
carry it on for ever. The only parallel
to the step-by-step policy that I know of
is this: There was an old man travelling
from Lisburn to Belfast one day with a
donkey. He went into the station, and
was going to bring the donkey into the
train when the guard says "You cannot
put that donkey in there." "Well, where
can I put it?" he asked. "You can put
it at the back," said the guard, meaning
the guard's van. The old man, not understanding what the guard's van was, went
to the end of the train and tied the
donkey to the two buffers of the hindmost
carriage. As the train sped along the
lines a few miles out the old man said to
himself: "Well, whoever sees Ned now
he is stepping it out." That is exactly
what you are doing by this step-by-step
policy. I am afraid of what the result
will be unless the whole thing is overhauled. If the whole situation is not
surveyed in a proper light you will find
that this stepping out will do you infinite
harm.

those services, and in which I hope to
them, extended in the near future.
It has been stated during this debate
that we are up against competition from
other countries, but I hope the time will
never come when we will have to return
to sweated labour to compete with it.
With regard to the proposed new motor
taxes, I have not much sympathy with
the motor car drivers, because men who
own motor cars can afford the extra 5s,
but I do think the proposed scale for
buses will interfere with the working
classes who use those vehicles very largely
in going to and from the country.
The new scale is bound to involve the
bus services in additional expenditure, and
will affect the man who has to pay his
weekly bus fare out of his wages. I think
that the working people very largely use
the bus services both for health purposes
and for going to and from their work.
The bus services bring people into the city
to make purchases, and thus provide additional revenue for the business people of
Belfast. Any interference with those services would be very much against the interests of the working people. It will
also have a tendency to drive the people
back to the railways, which in many cases
are not nearly so convenient. I hope that
the right hon. Gentleman will see his way
clear to reconsider that proposed increase
on buses, so far as it applies to the working
class people.
I listened with interest to the hon.
Member for the University (Rev. Professor
Corkey) who was congratulating himself
on the reduction in the amount of revenue
derived from spirit duties. At a time
when our financial position is becoming
weaker, I can give the Minister of Finance
a tip as to where he can obtain some extra
revenue. This reduction in the revenue,
I think, is very largely due to the number of people who leave the Six Counties
and go into the Free State in order to get
refreshments. That revenue would be
very useful here for the social services if
for nothing else, and would make a great
improvement in the financial position of
the Six Counties.
I would not congratulate the Six
Counties so very much on the falling off
in the revenue from spirits, due to the
hasty legislation passed here some time
ago imposing additional restrictions on
the licensed trade. I quite agree
with
the hon, and gallant Member for the Dock
Division of Belfast (Major Blakiston-
Houston). I think he spoke very sensibly. I think the noble Lord, the Prime
Minister, did promise that he would give
the Intoxicating Liquor Act a reasonable
trial, and that he would amend it in such
a way as to enable people to get refreshments at a reasonable time.
I know that
there are large numbers of people who
during the week-end leave the Six Coun
ties in order to get refreshments in the
Free State, and that large numbers of
people would come into the Six Counties
on Sundays if they could get reasonable
refreshments when they want them.
Ways and Means-
Report Stage
28 MAY 1930
I am a member of the trade-I do not
deny that and I am as much opposed
to drunkenness as any Member of this
House. I regret that any man should
take more drink than he can afford to
buy. (Laughter.) That has occurred.
Men have taken more drink than they
can afford to buy. As a member of the
licensed trade I am sorry to say that I
have seen men taking more drink than
they could afford to buy. But I should
like to see them able to get reasonable
refreshment and in that way increase the
revenue of the Six Counties to a large
extent.
I think that is all I need say. The
income-tax has been referred to but I
need not enter upon that subject. Power
to reduce the income-tax is in the hands
of the Government of the Six Counties,
and it would be a great advantage to
merchants if the Government would reduce that tax to the same level as that of
the Free State. We all know that factories are being erected by Ulster firms
in the Free State. Gallaher's have gone
to the Free State, and other firms have
gone, too.
That is all taking away
revenue from Northern Ireland, and we
are bound to feel that. I think that
matter should be considered seriously. If
we could get as much increased revenue
from the liquor as would compensate the
Government for making a rebate on the
income-tax I think it would be a good
thing for the Six Counties.
Mr. MINFORD: I congratulate the
Minister of Finance on his presentation
of the Budget, and I was delighted to
hear him congratulate the farmers upon
their prompt payment of their annuities.
I was disappointed, however, when I
found that he was going to penalise the
farmers who use motor lorries. Farmers
in general use motor lorries of 1 ton 4
cwt. or 1 ton 5 cwt., and instead of paying a tax of £16 they will now have to
pay £24.
The farmers use their motor
lorries two or three days a week, and
this addition of £8 on the tax will have
a very serious effect. This question is
very prominently in the minds of the
farmers of Northern Ireland. I should
like to support the hon. and gallant
Member for East Down (Lieut.-Colonel
Gordon) in what he said regarding this
increase of the tax on motor lorries.
We all know that the farming industry
is not in a healthy condition, and I think
it is not fair to ask the farmers to pay
this additional tax of £8 on their motor
lorries. I agree with the taxing of the
big lorries, because the men who are using
the roads should pay for them, but the
farmers as a rule use their lorries only
two or three times a week. I raise no
objection to the increase in the driver's
licence. I think it is only right that
the owner of a motor car should pay the
extra 5s. I was delighted to hear the
Prime Minister say that no reduction
would ever be made in the social or educational services.
I was amazed to hear the hon. and
learned Member for the University (Mr.
McNeill) suggest that we in Northern
Ireland should ever attempt to bring the
social and educational services down to
a scale lower than that which prevails
in Great Britain. I have hopes that even
at this late hour the Minister of Finance
will reconsider this increase of the tax
on motor lorries from £16 to £24. If
he could leave that tax as it was he would
be conferring a great boon on the agricultural community. I should say that
the farming community are very grateful to him and the Government for the
derating scheme. They appreciate it
very much; it came at a most opportune
time. But the increase tax on motor
lorries will mean increased freight on
produce.
I cannot agree with what my hon.
Friend the Member for Bann Side (Mr.
Young) said. If he knew the convenience
it is to the farming community to have.
their produce taken from their doors and
feeding stuffs brought out to them he
would not have made the statement he
did. As one who comes in contact with
farmers more than any other Member of
this House, I believe it will be a long time
before you will get the agricultural community asking that the big motor lorries
should be scrapped. With these few
remarks I say again that I hope the
Minister will yield to the request made by
the hon. and gallant Member for East
Down (Lieut.-Colonel Gordon) in regard
to the proposed increased taxation of the
25-cwt. lorries which are so largely used
by farmers.
Mr. CRAWFORD: I would like to
congratulate the Minister of Finance on
his Budget statement. I have had the
privilege of hearing every Budget introduced into this House by the right hon.
Gentleman, and certainly his statement.

HOUSE OF COMMONS

yesterday was as clear and lucid as any

I would like especially to direct the

Mr. POLLOCK: That was the trouble

Mr. POLLOCK: The hon. Member is

Mr. POLLOCK: No.

I see that Supply Services are costing

the County Council.

throw out the suggestion so that something may be done to alter the way in

mense advantage by asking for tenders

first. If you increase the private driver's

the point raised by my hon. Friend, we
do not intend to interfere with the drivers
of private vehicles who come over from

Sir
DAWSON BATES: My hon.
Friend, of course, will appreciate the fact

Sir DAWSON BATES: My hon.

it out in the place where he resides.
When an English visitor is coming over

Oral Answers to Questions.
CENSORSHIP
OF GRAMOPHONE
RECORDS AND FILMS.
1. Mr. HEALY asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether he can state the
titles of the objectionable gramophone records mentioned in a recent Special Order,
and his reasons for taking special powers
to deal with them.
The PARLIAMENTARY SECRE-
TARY OF THE MINISTRY OF HOME
AFFAIRS (Mr. Hanna): I have been
asked to answer this question.
Special powers, by Regulation under
the Civil Authorities (Special Powers)
Act (Northern Ireland), 1922, have been
taken to prevent the introduction of objectionable gramophone records or cinematograph films into Northern Ireland.
No Order has yet been made under
this Regulation in respect of any particular gramophone record.
Mr. HEALY: Arising out of the
answer, will the Parliamentary Secretary
kindly tell us what he is trying to get at
in this matter? Does he want to ban
gramophone records or films dealing with
the Soviet or the Republicans? In view
of the fact that this city is full of books
of a more or less immoral character does
the Government not think they are simply
shying at straws and jumping over camels
and beginning at the wrong end?
Mr. HANNA: It is the intention of
the Government to prevent the introduction into this country of any films or
gramophone records that would be subversive of law and order or that would
interfere with religion or morality. We
hope to deal effectively with any person or
persons who may attempt to have them
introduced into Northern Ireland.
Mr. HEALY: I asked a question to
which you have not replied.
Do you
intend doing anything with regard to the
flood of immoral literature scattered
throughout the city?
Mr. SPEAKER: The hon. Member
had better put down a question on that
subject. It is a different subject from
gramophone records.
Mr. HEALY: He is afraid of that
subject.
UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE-
EMPLOYEES OF ROCKPORT
HOUSE SECONDARY SCHOOL.
2. Mr. BEATTIE asked the Minister
of Labour whether he can state the reasons
why the employees of Rockport House
Secondary School, Craigavad, are not
covered under the Unemployment Insurance Act; and whether he is aware that
this school is a profit-making establishment, and that being so, will he have the
employees placed under the Act.
The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.
Andrews): It has been held by the High
Court in England that a school such as
Rockport House School, Craigavad, being
primarily an educational establishment, is
not a trade or business carried on for the
purposes of gain within the meaning of the
Unemployment Insurance Acts. Accordingly, those persons employed by that
school on domestic and analogous duties
are regarded as not insurable under the
Unemployment Insurance Statutes.

The section of the Act of Parliament
dealing with the offence of personation
where it is discovered at the time of the
offering of the vote set up machinery for
dealing with the offence so discovered, and
did not purport to interfere with the
ordinary law in the case where the commission of the offence had been discovered
after the voter had left the polling booth.
This is to secure the operation of the law
in relation to offences discovered after the
voter had left the polling booth by the same
machinery as in the case that we have now
provided for in the new Act of Parliament, that is to say, that the investigation should be made by a resident magistrate. The House having adopted that
principle before, I take it they will have

or expensive cars from which to receive
revenue. Therefore, we cannot walk
step-by-step in that regard with Great
Britain. If you go on walking step-bystep where will you land the Six Counties!
You will admit we are not in a position
to make any further Imperial contributions. I admit it is only £150,000 this
year, and perhaps the Minister of Finance
will admit we are not in a position to pay
that.
Mr. POLLOCK : We are.
Mr. O'NEILL. Last year we were
able to pay £600,000, and now that has
been reduced by a further half million.
If that is our position to-day what will
it be five years hence? Some alteration must be made. We cannot possibly
go on as we have been doing, although it
was stated in the House by the Prime
Minister that we have paid our way and
are not in debt. You must admit that
our Unemployment Fund is something
like £4,000,000 in debt. That is due.
Then we have also pledged our credit to
the extent of £10,000,000 in guaranteeing
loans. Those are things we are responsible
for, and I hope we shall not have to pay.
We are £4,000,000 in debt on the Unemployment Fund.
Mr. POLLOCK:
Three millions.
Mr. O'NEILL: It is over £3,000,000,
it is between £3,000,000 and £4,000,000.
Therefore, I think I am doing the right
thing in warning the Government and the
Minister of Finance who, I am sure, is
quite well aware of our financial position,
that they will have to handle the thing
very carefully if we are to survive at all.

tween revenue and expenditure in 1922

so year by year this went on by the increasing of expenditure, and in some cases

provided that if it appears to the satisfaction of Mr. Speaker, after consultation with the Government, that the

shall meet at any earlier time during the
Summer adjournment, Mr. Speaker may
give notice that he is so satisfied, and

duly adjourned to that date."-(The

Lieut.-Colonel GORDON: I beg to
move in page 5, line 33, to leave out

In bringing forward this Amendment.
I have no wish to cut across the finances
of this Bill, and I have no wish in any
way to upset the Minister's calculations
in regard to the revenue he expects to get
from this increase of the tax from £16
to £24. I would like to say to the Committee that as regards these figures one has
had no time to go into the whole question
with the officials of the county council of
the county part of which I have the
honour to represent. My points in support of the reduction from £24 to £20
are these: I think I am right in saying it
is the policy of the Government to try to
keep the heavy traffic limited as much as
possible and to encourage light traffic.
Then another point which incidentally
comes in that the more light lorries you
have on the roads the more employment
you are giving.
The farmer now as regards fast trotting traffic has had practically to take his
horses off the roads as they are slippy.
A good many farmers for the purpose of
going to market have invested in this
light lorry which at the present is taxed,
if it is between 1 ton and 30 cwt., at
£16. The farmers and the farming
interest have gone in for these lorries,
knowing what the tax stands at now.
This Schedule proposes a jump of 50 per
cent. The farmer was recently called in
this House a "Weary Willie," or a
"Weeping Willie." I think that sort
of thing is deeply resented. I stand here
and say that I do not see why the farmer's horse and also his lorry should have
to go off the road.
As regards the finance part, that is as
regards the Road Fund, if you take off
these light lorries by putting on a heavy
tax it is clear to me the Road Fund will
suffer by the total reduction of the
lorries, and in the end there will be no
gain to the Exchequer. In fact, it might
mean a loss. In this opinion I am supported by the officials of the county
council. I ask the Minister to consider
my request. I am not asking for the
total abolition of this tax on these light
lorries, I am asking that a lorry between
one ton and 30 cwt. be rated at £20.
That will be an increase of 25 per cent.
instead of 50 per cent. It is & fair rise.
I have no wish that the farming community should forget its liabilities. I
raised these points on the Finance
Resolution, but between Wednesday and
to-day I have had very little or no time
to go into detail, but on the general
principle I ask the Minister, in fact, I
ask the Cabinet, to consider this matter
very seriously indeed.

Oral Answer to Question.
EJECTMENT DECREES IN BELFAST
The following questions stood on the
Paper in the name of Mr. BEATTIE:-
1. To ask the Minister of Home
Affairs whether he can state the number
of cases where proceedings have been
taken in the Recorder's Court, Belfast, for
ejectment for arrears of rent in the case
of dwelling-houses during the past three
years, and the number of such cases; what
number of the decrees for ejectment have
been granted, and in how many cases
were these decrees executed.
2. To ask the Minister of Home Affairs
whether he can state the number of cases
where proceedings have been taken in the
Petty Sessions Court, Belfast, for ejectment for arrears of rent in the case of
dwelling-houses during the past three
years, and the number of such cases; what
are the number of decrees for ejectment
that have been granted, and in how many
cases were these decrees executed.
Mr. SPEAKER: Does the right hon.
Gentleman wish to answer the questions
on the Paper? He has the option of
doing so if he thinks it is in the public.
interest.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): The answer to the
first question is:
During the years 1927, 1928 and 1929,
respectively, the number of ejectment
cases entered for hearing in the Recorder's
Court, Belfast, was 508, 470, and 416;
the number of decrees granted was 313,
317, and 276; and the number of cases
in which decrees were executed was 62,
41 and 42.
The answer to the second question is:
During the years 1927, 1928 and 1929,
respectively, the number of cases in which
ejectment summonses were taken out was
4,272, 4,920, and 4,355; the number of
decrees granted was 352, 415, and 427,
and the number of cases in which decrees
were executed was 20, 29, and 28.

CHAIRS FOR PARLIAMENT
BUILDINGS.
Motion made, and Question proposed:
That this House do now adjourn."-
(Mr. Robb.)
Mr. GRANT: There is a matter to
which I would like to draw the attention
of the Minister of Finance. In the local
Press during the last few days it has been
reported that a cargo of chairs has been
landed at the Belfast quays for Parliament
House. I understand that these chairs
are labelled "Made in Germany." I will
be told, I am sure, by the right hon.
Gentleman that we have nothing to do
with the provision of these chairs, and
that it is a matter for the Imperial Parliament. I think we have something to
say as to whether we will sit on the chairs
or not. We can refuse to do so.
At the present time all over Northern
Ireland there is a great campaign going
on for pushing Ulster goods and buying
British goods. No one is taking a
deeper interest in this matter than the
Prime Minister, who was in Banbridge
recently opening a campaign there, and
who will be in Lisburn to-morrow. In the
middle of this campaign for buying British
goods we are to have a cargo of German
chairs dumped into Belfast for the Parliament Buildings. There is great indignation throughout the city about this. I
hope the Minister of Finance will be able
to assure the House to-day that no matter
what action the Imperial Parliament take
in this matter our Government will see
that these chairs are never put into
Parliament House.
Mr. SPEAKER: The hon. Member
can only ask this Government to make
representations to the Imperial Government who are entirely responsible for the
seating accommodation of the new Houses
of Parliament. This Government have no
responsibility for it whatsoever. The
hon. Member can ask for representations
to be made; he can go no further.
Mr. GRANT: I am not particular what
the right hon. Gentleman does so long as
these chairs do not go into Parliament
Buildings.
Chairs for Parliament 1686
Adjournment-
5 JUNE 1930
Mr. SPEAKER: Yes, but I am particular. I want the hon. Gentleman to
take the course of asking the Government
to make representations to the Imperial
Government and thereby put himself in
order. Otherwise he is out of order.
Mr. GRANT: In my opening remarks
I drew the right hon. Gentleman's attention to the matter, and asked him if he
knew anything about it. If he does not
know anything about it I want him to see
that something will be done. There is
much unemployment in our midst to-day,
and these chairs can be made in Northern
Ireland. If they cannot be made here
they can be made in Great Britain. The
Minister of Unemployment in Great
Britain is out of work because he could not
find employment for himself. He is not
on the dole, but he has got another
job. It is an insult to the people here
to be sending this stuff over. I would
appeal to the right hon. Gentleman to
make representations to the Imperial
Parliament to take these chairs away from
here.
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Pollock): If my hon. Friend is sure of
his facts he has certainly good grounds for
calling the attention of the Minister to
the alleged arrival of these chairs. As a
matter of fact neither I nor my Ministry,
the Department which has charge of this
matter, have any knowledge of any such
arrival. I am aware we have no responsibility even if they were in existence, but
all I can say is to assure my hon. Friend
that an investigation will be made in regard to the matter, and the necessary
representations will be made. It is a long
time yet, let me remind my hon. Friend,
before the necessity for the provision of
these chairs arises. It will be more than
a year, possibly more. I hardly think it
likely that the British Department is in a
hurry to provide this material to which
the hon. Member refers.
Mr. GRANT: I would like to make it
clear that I have not seen the chairs myself, but with the permission of the House
I will read an extract from a local newspaper:
Over 500 cane chairs had been sent
from Hamburg to Stormont Castle, said
Councillor Agnew.
I do not agree with Stormont Castle, but
I understand these chairs have been sent
over for our Parliament Buildings. This
is the "Irish News" of Tuesday last.
(Hon. Members: Oh!) This statement
was made at the monthly meeting of the
Belfast Corporation, and nobody challenged it. If that is true I think we
ought to see that this matter is made
right.
Mr. POLLOCK: It will be investigated.
Question put, and agreed to.

DEATH OF MR. W. T. MILLER, M.P.
The PRIME MINISTER (Viscount
Craigavon): With the leave of the House,
I think it would be the desire of everyone present here if I were to express the
very deep sense of grief which pervades
this assembly at the death yesterday of
the Member for North Tyrone (Mr.
Miller). We have been spared during
the time of this Parliament from very
many ravages in our ranks. It is seldom
the
that we have to deplore the death of one
of our Members, and I am sure we were
all shocked-I certainly was yesterday
when the news came through of
tragic and sudden death of our late
friend Mr. Miller. I feel this House
would like to assure his widow, his son,
and his other relatives that we all deeply
feel the loss of a Member who, in the first
instance, represented Tyrone and Fermanagh, and subsequently the Northern
Division of County Tyrone. It is unnecessary for us to move a Resolution.
I think the same feelings will actuate hon.
Members opposite, that do us here, that
we have lost in Mr. Miller a friend and
a colleague.
Mr. McALEER: I would like to
associate myself with the regret so ably
expressed by the Prime Minister. Mr.
Miller and I were associated on public
boards for over twenty years. During
those years we were very bitterly opposed
to each other in the political arena, but
notwithstanding that in his social life he
was a perfect gentleman. He was good,
he was kind, he was hospitable to all, and
whenever a good turn could be done to
any of his constituents, or friends, or
neighbours, whether of different creed or
politics, he was always ready and anxious
to do that good turn. (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear).
ORDERS OF THE DAY.
Marketing of Fruit Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.
Motion made, and Question proposed:
"That the Bill be now read a Second
time."
The MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE
(Sir Edward Archdale): As the House is
aware, legislation has been promoted in
recent years with the object of ensuring
that certain of our agricultural exports
reached the British market in satisfactory
condition. Parliament has already given
its consent to Measures dealing with eggs,
potatoes and dairy produce. As a result
of the Marketing of Eggs Act our eggs
now fetch higher prices in Great Britain
than the eggs of any of our highly
efficient foreign competitors. It
can
safely be said that without this legislation Northern Ireland eggs would by now
have largely disappeared from the British
market. In normal seasons the Marketing of Potatoes Act should place our
potatoes in a secure position in cross-
Channel markets at prices remunerative
to our farmers. Unfortunately, last
year surplus production in these islands
led to a slump in the potato trade.
However, notwithstanding a glutted
market, 50,000 tons of our potatoes were
exported last season to Great Britainwithout grading as provided by the Act
this would not have been possible. The
Dairy Produce Act has not yet come into
operation, but equally beneficial results
are anticipated from that Measure.
With regard to fruit-the subject now
under consideration-it may be observed
that for the past two years public bodies
and trade representatives have been impressing upon the Ministry the need for
such legislation if the fruit industry of
Northern Ireland is to be preserved from
extinction. For various reasons, however,
consideration of this question by Parliament has had to be postponed until now.

It is true that the area under fruit in
Northern Ireland is small. Nevertheless
our exports of fruit, mainly apples, to
Great Britain and the Irish Free State
were in 1929 valued at approximately
£100,000. This export trade could however, be considerably expanded if the
fruit were properly graded and packed.
That would mean more money for the
growers, and it might reasonably be expected that if such better financial results
were forthcoming commercial fruit growing would be taken up seriously by many
farmers who now regard fruit culture as
of little or no economic importance..
Experiments conducted by the Ministry.
and county horticultural staffs from 1922
onwards have demonstrated that by improved methods of cultivation satisfactory
crops of apples can be grown almost every
year, not one year in two or three, as
formerly. It is satisfactory to note that
the better methods advocated by the
Ministry as a result of the experiments
referred to have now been taken up with
successful results by progressive growers.
It will be the business of our horticultural education service to see that the
improved processes of cultivation.
brought to the notice of all growers and
on this work the staffs concerned are now
concentrating. However, if our growers
are to receive maximum profits efficient
production must
must be accompanied by
efficient marketing and that means, in
the first place, grading.
are
It has become more and more clear that,
with present marketing methods, Northern Ireland fruit is being driven off even
the home market by the overseas product. A glance round the fruit shops in
Belfast or any other of our cities and
towns will illustrate this, because, invariably, the fruit that is properly graded
and that fetches the best price is imported.
Broadly speaking, the present Bill falls
into two divisions. The first is fruit for
export. It is proposed that all merchants
who export fruit shall be licensed and
shall grade their fruit up to certain
standards. The Bill, of course, only refers to fruit produced in Northern Ireland. Licensed merchants will pay an
annual fee of £1.
Permits, free of charge. will be given
to growers to export fruit grown by them.
In such cases grading will be required.
It is provided, however, that permits may
(a) To fruit not grown in Northern
Ireland but which is merely conveyed
across Northern Ireland for export;
(b) To fruit consigned to the Irish
Free State, except to such extent as
may be found necessary and practicable.
This is following the system established
by the Marketing of Potatoes Act
which has worked well;
(c) To sinal consignments.
I now come to trade within Northern
Ireland. In view of the discussions reported in the Press there would appear
in certain quarters to be a misapprehension regarding the manner in which the
fruit trade within Northern Ireland will
be affected by this Measure. In order
to remove any doubt which may prevail
on this point, it is desired to emphasize
that so far as the home trade is concerned
the compulsory provisions of the Bill will
not apply except in one respect, and that
is that steps will be taken to prevent what
is known as topping." At present,
owing to this nefarious practice, the man
who grades his fruit and packs it honestly
does not get his proper reward for the
simple reason that the buyers have to
regulate their prices generally to cover
losses due to "topping"
Clause 13 provides that fruit sold or
exposed for sale in a container shall be
packed in such a manner that any fruit
exposed to view fairly represents in size,
maturity, condition and variety the entire
contents of the container. The same
Clause provides that types of containers
may be prescribed for particular classes
of fruit. The remainder of the provisions
of the Measure that apply to the home
trade are purely voluntary and are on
the lines of the National Mark system in
force in Great Britain. Briefly, persons
who grade their fruit for the home
market up to certain standards will be
authorised to use a grade designation
mark which will be a guarantee of quality.
Persons who do not wish to grade their
fruit will be quite as free as they are at
present to market their produce in Northern Ireland without being subject to
any regulations, except that as already.
stated the practice of topping" must
be stopped. That, in a nutshell, is the

Major
I should
first like to place before the House and
before the Government the feeling that
this Bill has aroused in County Armagh,

hand, there is a very large body of public
opinion against any Measure of this sort.
Among that body of men are very large
growers of apples, men who are sending
their produce to the English and Scotch
markets where they are securing the
highest prices. These men maintain
that they could not secure the trade in
these markets and get the high prices
they are receiving except the fruit
supplied was in a satisfactory condition.
According to them there is no necessity
for this Bill which is likely to increase
their overhead charges. I would like to
have a little information from the Minister, as to whether there is any foundation for that. These men feel that in
order to get the same prices they are
getting for their produce and keep the
markets they now have, they will be compelled owing to inspection and other
matters to increase their overhead
charges.
This is one of the principal fears at the
back of the opposition to this Bill. We
have all seen in the Press quite a lot against
the Measure. There are some arguments which I cannot find are borne
out by reading the Bill, and there are
some arguments in which there is something. It has been stated in the Press

likely to increase overhead charges without a corresponding advantage in the
prices for the apples put on the market.
I would like the Minister to enlighten the
House to some extent on that point.
It has also been pointed out in connection with the grading of apples for
the English markets that it will place
our growers here at a disadvantage. If

Sir ROBERT LYNN: I beg to move
to leave out the word "now" in order to
insert at the end of the Question upon
this day six months." I move the rejection of the Bill for a few cogent reasons.
First, it is Socialistic and coercive, and
secondly it is not going to benefit either
the producer or the consumer. In fact
it is a Bill, if carried in its present form,
that runs a good chance of ruining a very
important and very flourishing industry
in Northern Ireland. I have read the Bill
through several times, and I wondered.
what could have been the cause for the
Ministry of Agriculture introducing a
Bill of this coercive kind. Can it be that
they want to share with the Ministry of
Home Affairs a few of the laurels taken
from the crown of Karl Marx? I see no
other reason for the introduction of this
Bill
We are in a rather ridiculous position.
here because on this side of the House we
spend most of our time denouncing Social-
Marketing of Fruit Bill-
Second Reading
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Sir Robert Lynn]
ism outside and of late we have started
to carry through Socialistic legislation.
Indeed we are in a peculiar position, in
that we have a Government in Great
Britain that calls itself Socialist and pursues a Conservative policy, whereas we
have here a Government that calls itself
Conservative and pursues a Socialistic
policy. It is about time that we ended
that. I have read the Bill as carefully as
I could, I have looked for any helpful suggestion, and I am bound to say that I
have found none, nothing that is going to
improve the fruit growing industry in
the Province. I cannot help thinking that
the author of the Bill must have read the
Athanasian Creed because the Bill seems
to be one of pains and penalties all
through.
My hon. and gallant Friend who has
just spoken says there is not much in the
Bill except the powers it gives to officials.
That is just what we object to, because it
is going to give officials enormous powers
to which we say they have no right. There
is no safeguard in the Bill for a grower
anywhere. He may take every reasonable
precaution and yet find himself in gaol.
The police and the officials of the Department may come along and open his
package and take fruit out of it, and there
is no compensation, no help for the unfortunate grower. The idea that the grower
should have to submit to the things that
are prescribed-in fact the word "proscribed would be much better than prescribed--is to my mind highly ridiculous.
Those engaged in this industry will be
at the mercy of officials through their
right to go in and inspect and see how they
carry on their business. They have to go
and get permits from officials and police.
These permits may be revoked without
any reason whatever given. A policeman
or official may hold up these perishable
goods on mere suspicion. Then, by the
time the unfortunate grower discovers
that his fruit is lost he can get no redress
whatever against the Government. The
Ministry have given themselves the widest
possible powers in this Bill.
The Minister of Agriculture mentioned
something about an advisory committee.
I would like to know who are the members
of the advisory committee. Are they
growers or do they know anything bevond
the sale of fruit? I agree with my hon.
and gallant Friend that it would be much
better and much wiser to continue to engage in education rather than to indulge
in these coercive measures. The Minister
of Agriculture referred to the prohibition
put on with regard to cattle and with regard to eggs. I have met a good many
intelligent and progressive farmers who
do not share the opinions of the Ministry
of Agriculture regarding the effect of
these prohibitions. In fact they say instead of helping they are injuring agriculture.
Another thing the Minister of Agricul
ture referred to. He described his intention

topping. But it strikes me that an
attempt has been made to work up a campaign on this rather flimsy case. If at
the present time there is an unscrupulous

found on the top row surely the ordinary
common law is sufficiently strong to deal
with such people. Besides this is a moral
question and you cannot really reform the
morals of the immoral very easily by Act
of Parliament
I do think that a good deal of harm has

think the feeling in the country is that it

of ours people do not get this sort of thing

you have got voluntary boards, and the

We have had far too much of this

Once started one never
knows where it is going to end. Only

in which he urged the setting up in this

The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
Under the Acts
(Sir Dawson Bates):
constituting the old Royal Irish Constabulary a Fund was established known
as a Reward Fund into which was paid:
(1) Disciplinary fines imposed on members of the Force; (2) Fines awarded at
petty sessions in certain cases to Police
prosecutors; (3) Part of the fees paid in
connection with the stamping of Weights
and Measures. The proceeds of this
Fund were used for the purpose of rewarding or benefiting members of the
Police Force.
It will be appreciated by hon. Members that at the time this Fund was
originally established, the conditions of
service of policemen were nothing like
what they are at present. In the old
days a policeman received something like
15/- a week, whereas now the most junior
policeman in our Force receives 10/- a
day and allowances, and therefore this
Fund met a much-needed want at that
time. Under the Constabulary Act,
1922, the principle was continued, but
the amount that became necessary to pay
out was very much less. The result was
that large accumulations took place in
this Fund.

ORDERS OF THE DAY.
Agricultural Produce (Meat Regulation)
Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.
Motion made, and Question proposed:
"That the Bill be now read a Second
time."
The MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE
(Sir Edward Archdale): The object of
the Bill is to secure that only sound meat
is sent from Northern Ireland to Great
Britain. By meat is meant beef, mutton,
pork, bacon and hams and edible offals
such as heads and feet. Great Britain is
for all practical purposes our only export market for meat products. So far
as beef and mutton are concerned the
exports are negligible, but might very
possibly be capable of profitable development under a system which
would guarantee soundness.
Pork
is, however, very important. In
the year 1929 we exported 360,000 cwt.
of pork, bacon and hams. In addition
there is a valuable export trade in edible
offals, such as pigs' heads, feet, etc. The
total value of our dead meat exports in
the year mentioned was about 2 million
pounds sterling. That trade is now in
jeopardy, and it is to preserve it that the
present Bill is brought forward.
Frankly, consignments of unsound meat
from this country have reached Great
Britain and been condemned by the
public health authorities there. These
authorities have asked us to give a
guarantee that all meat exported from
Northern Ireland to Great Britain
1737 Meat Regulation Bill-

8 OCTOBER 1930
Second Reading
has been inspected by a Government
veterinary officer and passed as sound and
free from disease. They have reminded
us that such a system of inspection is in
force in other countries, such as the
Argentine, Denmark and Holland. We
know that the Irish Free State have introduced such legislation, and their Act
has been in force as from the 1st
September.
We are, therefore, now left in a very
isolated position, and we have been told
that unless we are prepared to fall into
line steps will be taken to exclude Northern Ireland meat and meat products
from cross-Channel markets. We have
consulted our legal authorities and, unfortunately, there is no doubt whatever
that the Department of Health for Scotland and the appropriate authorities in
England have ample power without reference to Parliament, and in spite of the
fact that Northern Ireland is part of the
United Kingdom, to exclude dead meat
from British markets unless the guarantees demanded are forthcoming.
It should be borne in mind, too, in considering this matter, that if once the
market is lost our utmost efforts would
not suffice to recover the position. The
policy of "wait and see" in this matter
would, we are convinced, be fatal. It is,
therefore, up to us to do at once what is
required by our British customers. We
are now at the parting of the ways. If
we are to preserve, not to say expand, this
trade-worth 21 million pounds sterling
per annum-we must give our British
customers the protection they demand.
If, knowing these facts, we fail to bring.
forward this legislation we should be guilty
of a gross dereliction of duty for which
there would be no conceivable excuse.
After careful consideration, and with
the approval of the North of Ireland
Bacon Curers' Association, which I understand represents about 60 curers, and also
of our Pig Advisory Committee, on which
the producing interest is fully represented,
we are of opinion that the best way
to proceed so as to interfere as little as
possible with existing pork marketing
conditions in Northern Ireland is to provide systems of inspection as follows:-
No fresh pork, beef or mutton is to be
exported unless the animal has been inspected before and after slaughter and
killed on registered premises. All exporters of such fresh meat will require
to be licensed. A licence will be given
only where the exporter has suitable
premises of his own for the slaughtering
of animals, or has satisfied the Ministry
that he can make arrangements to have
the use of such premises.
Now as to slaughtering premises, let it
be clearly understood
understood that nothing
elaborate will be required. Where public
abattoirs are not available we shall be
prepared to register any premises where
the conditions are reasonable and, further,
there is no fee for the registration of premises. Inquiries made at the chief centres
from which fresh meat is exported indicate
that there will be no difficulty in meeting
these requirements. There are, we know,
a few farmers who at present slaughter
pigs on their farms for export as tresh
pork. It may be that in some cases it will
be necessary to require such pigs to be
brought to convenient abattoirs, because
owing to the small number dealt with inspection at the farms at time of slaughter
might be uneconomic, or the farm premises might not be quite suitable for the
purpose. Our policy will be, however, to
disturb existing trade practice as little as
possible, and if in a few cases there is
slight inconvenience we would ask those
concerned to remember, as already
pointed out, that the whole trade in meat
products is at stake.
All bacon factories will have to be
licensed, and pork carcases will be inspected on arrival at the curing establishments. This arrangement is necessary to
meet the special conditions of the Northern Ireland pork trade.
With regard to the finance of the
Measure, it is proposed to charge annual
fees for licences and, in addition, a small
fee for each carase inspected. The money
realised in this connection will be applied
towards the cost of the inspection system
which it is proposed should be substantially self-supporting.
Following the system adopted under
the Marketing of Potatoes Act, it is proposed that trade with the Free State
shall be regulated in such manner as experience may determine to be most practicable and economical. It is intended
for one thing that domestic supplies.
crossing the border and any pork that may
be going to Free State markets shall not
be interfered with. It will be observed
that it is not proposed to interfere with
the existing powers of public health
authorities to make any regulations they
Meat Regulation Bill-
Second Reading
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Sir Edward Archdale]
taken.
ham.
may think necessary to ensure the soundness of meat for home consumption. The
Bill provides that before registering any
slaughtering premises the local authority
concerned will be consulted. Further, it
is intended to confer with the public
health authorities, so that overlapping of
inspection systems may be avoided.
It is sometimes said that we suffer from
an excess of zeal for legislation of this
character. That charge, however, cannot
be laid against us in the present instance.
As has been demonstrated, we are really
left with no option in the matter.
I am
aware that opposition is threatened to
this Bill, but I would say to those who are
opposed, think carefully, think wisely, before voting against this Measure. The
Bill is not one of our choosing, we have
no option, all we are trying to do is to
give the minimum guarantees that will
satisfy the British authorities. In doing
so we have endeavoured to interfere as
little as possible with existing trade practices. If the Measure is rejected you will
not only deal a blow at our dead meat
trade from which it may never recover,
but you will place Northern Ireland in
the position of being the only country in
the world which has refused to guarantee
its meat as free from disease and there
will be created throughout the length and
breadth of Great Britain a feeling that
our stock is so unsound that we are afraid
to tackle the problem. Needless to say
such an impression would not only ruin.
the dead meat trade but would seriously
imperil our live stock industry as a whole.
Our competitors would not fail in their propaganda to make full use of our unfortunate position. I have, therefore, very
much pleasure in bringing this Bill before
the House in the full hope that any opposition will be met by small changes on
the Committee stage. I beg to move.

There are some things in connection
with the Bill which, I think, must be
altered. For instance, there is the case
of the farmer who brings his pork to the
market. There you give the buyer the
option of charging him 1s. per carcase.
have no doubt that in most instances that
will be done. That charge is made on
the assumption that something may be
wrong with the carcase and is supposed
to defray the expenses in connection with
this examination. I have no doubt that
where there is nothing wrong with the carcase the pork buyer will make this charge
and the farmer who markets the pork will
have to pay. With the present state of
most articles he does market the farmer
can ill afford to have any additional
charges put upon him.
One other thing in connection with this
Bill that seems to me to be very strange
is that a policeman who may think that
a carcase of meat or of pork may not be
fit for human consumption can call in a
magistrate and have the carcase destroyed.
I would have thought in a case of that
sort the judge should be some professional
man and not a magistrate. There are
many instances of your refusing to give
magistrates jurisdiction in cases of far less.
importance than this. In a case where
you are giving power to condemn an
article belonging to a farmer, such as a
carcase of pork or meat, I thought you
would have gone for a professional man, a
veterinary surgeon or the medical officer
of health, or some other person who is
competent to decide whether a carcase was
fit for human consumption
or not.
That is a defect I see in this Bill, and
one that should be remedied before it
passes through this House.
Another item in the Bill which the Minister tried to explain, but has not made
very clear, is that these diseased or unfit carcases of pork may be exported to the Free
State. There is no inspection of any
meat that is to be exported there. I
quite understand that the Minister stated
that that was only intended for people
who market their pork there, the farmers
from the district, but there is nothing to
prevent an exporter from exporting pork
to the Free State. You have no power
to prevent the importation of such pork
except whatever powers you have under
the various Acts in force at the present
time.
These are some of the defects in this
Bill and they should be remedied before
the Bill finally passes from this House.
There is no doubt that few Members will
take exception to any Bill that will improve the marketing of these things and
probably also improve the price to the
producer, but the House has not been
satisfied with regard to many of the Bills
designed in a similar way, such as those
in regard to potatoes and fish and even in
regard to eggs, of which the Minister
boasted so much in connection with this
and other Bills.
It is feared also that there will be
additional expense by the way of new inspectors being appointed. I have mentioned one instance already of additional
expense being put on the farmer, who if

is not in a position to pay those charges,
and if this Bill is to be a success the
fewer inspectors and the less interference
on the part of the Ministry there is the
better, both from the point of view of
the Government and of those to whom
the Bill will apply. When the Committee stage of the Bill comes on we will
be in a better position to judge as to its
real merits.

reasons.
There is another aspect of this Bill to
be considered. This, I consider, is the
important part because it affects my area.
In the smaller towns there are many small
curers who kill and cure from two to four

going to kill this trade. I will give the
First there is the £10 licence.
A small man cannot afford to pay a

Again there are farmers who in past

Another point is that, with so many inspections and licences under this Bill, it
is obvious that a very large number of

Now, having pointed out what I may call

to try to overcome the objections which I

no matter on what side of the House we

there is no greater instance of it than
Denmark, to which country reference has
been made several times during the
debate. Denmark has now captured the
greater part of the bacon trade in Great
Britain, and it has done that under these
hampering restrictions which have been
so much criticised in this debate.
The export trade of Denmark is under
the most rigid system of inspection and
licence, as the hon. and gallant Member
for South Derry (Captain Chichester-
Clark) has stated, and it is under those
very hampering restrictions that Denmark.
has produced bacon and has captured the
trade of Great Britain. That country
produces and sells to Great Britain a far
greater proportionate amount of bacon
than does Northern Ireland, which is part
of the United Kingdom. Therefore it
seems to be only reasonable that we should
try a similar system to that which has
This
proved so successful in Denmark.
Bill is an attempt to do that. I do not
care whether it is done under State control or some system of voluntary submission to the saine control. The effect is the
same, and the actual conditions under
which bacon is produced are the same, but
those restrictions have not only not
hampered the Danish trade but they have
increased it. I believe this Bill, when it
becomes law, will have the same effect
upon our trade in Northern Ireland.
Mr. HEALY: Several suggestions
have been made to the Minister of Agriculture this afternoon, and I would like
to remind him of a suggestion made to
him from this side of the House during
last Session which, I think, will have a
greater bearing on the pork industry of
Northern Ireland than the combined
effect of all the regulations contained in
this Bill. I asked him to get the Northern Ireland pork curers to publish at
least a week in advance the prices they
are going to pay for pork, because at this
moment the producer does not know on
Saturday night what price he is going to
be paid for his pork on Monday morning. In England the prices are quoted
for a considerable period in advance, I
believe, as long as a fortnight. If this
suggestion is carried out the pork raiser
will then be in this position-that he will
know before he kills his pork what price.
he will receive for it in the market.
The extraordinary fluctuation that
sometimes takes place from 55/- to 70/-,
makes one wonder what is the economic
factor that determines these sudden
fluctuations, because whether they get
55/- or 70/- the consumer during the
whole period, practically speaking, is
paying the same price. Therefore the
curers must certainly be reaping an undue advantage at some point. If they
can buy pork at 70/- and sell it at a
profit it surely stands to reason that they
must be making an undue profit when
they pay only 55/- for it. The Minister
has a splendid opportunity now, when he
is legislating, to compel the pork buyers.
to give their price at least a week in
advance, and that will enable the farmer
who has pork to sell to determine
whether he will kill his pork next week
or keep it for a higher market in the
future.

PRICES OF PORK IN NORTHERN
IRELAND MARKETS.
1. Mr. STEWART asked the Minister
of Agriculture whether he is aware of the
fluctuating prices of pork in the markets
of Northern Ireland and consequent loss
to the farmers concerned; and whether he
will introduce legislation fixing a rate for
a definite period in order to stabilise this
important industry?
The MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE
(Sir Edward Archdale): I am aware that
fluctuations in the price of pork may at
times cause serious inconvenience to farmers in the marketing of their pork. It
must be remembered, however, that prices
fluctuate upwards as well as downwards,
and it would be quite impossible for the
Government to attempt to regulate the
price. The great bulk of our bacon and
ham production is exported to Great
Britain, and is in competition with imports from Denmark and other countries.
The factors causing fluctuations in pork
prices do not simply arise locally but are
also due to conditions in foreign countries
from which bacon and hams are exported
to Great Britain. An increase in imports
of bacon and hams when demand is poor
inevitably results in lower prices. The
best safeguard against fluctuating prices
is the dissemination of more information
regarding market prices and supplies to
the farming community, and my Ministry
is doing all in its power to improve the
service of market information for farmers
in Northern Ireland.
Mr. HEALY: Arising out of that
answer, will the Minister say whether he
or his Department made representations
to the principal pork buyers in Northern
Ireland some time ago at the suggestion
of the Fermanagh Pig Curing Association, and whether the pork buyers turned
down the suggestion that they should
publish their prices a week in advance?
ARCHDALE:
The

any improvement.
