ORDERS OF THE DAY.
Electricity (Interim Supply) Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.
The MINISTER OF COMMERCE
(Mr. Barbour): The short Measure which
I have the honour to submit for the approval of the House to-day, although
limited in scope, marks the opening
stage of a scheme of comprehensive development which will, I believe, have farreaching effects in increasing not only the
future prosperity of our industries but
also the
as
the everyday amenities of the
Province at large. And so I feel that
the House may expect me to touch upon
the history of the development of electricity in recent times in these Islands,
for it is true to say that the Bill now
before hon. Members, providing
it does the first stage of a much more
comprehensive scheme, largely owes its
conception to the expert knowledge on
matters relating to the generation and
transmission of electrical power which has
resulted from years of pioneer effort elsewhere. It was in the nature of things
that the densely populated and highly
industrialised areas of Great Britain
should be the arena in which this youthful industry should fight out its early
battles.
In examining the history of electricity
development in the United Kingdom,
with, of course, especial reference to Northern Ireland, it is necessary in the first
place to have regard to the investigations
undertaken by an expert Committee,
known as the "Williamson" Committee,
which reported in 1918, and of which Sir
Archibald Williamson (now Lord Forres)
was chairman. Prior to 1918 electricity
was generated and distributed mainly by
statutory undertakers working under the
Electric Lighting Acts of 1882 and 1888
-Acts which were framed at a time when
electricity was used principally for lighting and its application for power purposes was almost unknown. The rapid
advance in the use of electricity for power
purposes necessitated a further Act in
1909, which gave somewhat wider facilities to electrical undertakers designed to
meet the new conditions; but the march
of events soon made it clear that the
whole field of existing legislation was too
limited in scope.
a
To the Williamson Committee was entrusted the task of considering and reporting what steps should be taken,
whether by legislation or otherwise, to
ensure an adequate and economical supply
of electrical power for all classes of consumers in the United Kingdom, particularly industries depending upon
cheap supply of power for their development. The Committee came to the
conclusion that the proper expansion of
the electrical supply industry was being
restricted by the fact that electrical areas
were too parochial, and that the existing
organisation had encouraged the growth
of small uneconomical stations with
higher fuel and general charges than
would have been the case with larger
areas,
the concentration of plant in
larger units, and more economically
Furthermore,
placed power stations.
owing to
absence of any attempt to standardise
the
pressures and
frequencies, co-operation between neighbouring authorities
difficult and
expensive.
was
It is only right to say, however, the
position that had so arisen and the slow
progress that had been made up to that
time could by no means be attributed
entirely to the defects of existing legislation. Manufacturers and many of the
great railway companies had been slow
to take a public supply of power purely
through a mistaken but understandable
eluctance to be dependent on others for
Electricity Supply Bill-
Second Reading
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Barbour]
anything they could do themselves. This
is a point of view, which, I think, is now
receding, and there is a growing realisation of the fact that in electricity supply
there must be closer co-operation and less
isolation, if there is to be that rapid progress and increase in comsumption which
must precede the general cheapening of
supply which is the ultimate goal of our
endeavour. In many localities, too, progress was undoubtedly retarded by the
fact that an efficient gas supply was available. Here, also, I should say that it is
becoming a matter of common acceptance
that there is a place in the economic unit
for both of these great sources of energy,
each with functions of advantage to the
public interest.
a
Two great facts emerged from the exhaustive inquiry conducted by the
Williamson Committee-firstly the recognition of the importance of cheap
electrical power as
factor in the
industrial progress of the country, and,
secondly, the necessity for the concentration of larger generating units in larger
and fewer power stations, with the resultant conservation of coal and reduced
costs of industrial power. As a result of
that Committee's recommendations
had the Electricity (Supply) Act of
1919 which, perhaps, unfortunately,
underwent considerable modification in
its passage through Parliament.
we
It is hardly necessary for me in introducing this preliminary Measure to
deal in detail with the original proposals
of the 1919 Bill and of those sections of
the Act as they finally emerged upon the
Statute Book, and as they now apply in
Northern Ireland.
Since that date, the Imperial Government has found it necessary to conduct
a further expert inquiry into electricity
development, and amending legislation in
1922 and also in 1926 has been passed
at Westminster. The findings of the
Weir Committee of 1925 are not quite
applicable to conditions in Northern Ireland, nor are the provisions of the
Statutes of 1922 and 1926.
In examining the problem in Northern.
Ireland we have to bear in mind that,
out of a total population of 1 millions,
roughly one-third is located within the
Borough of Belfast. What exactly this
means in electricity development you will
appreciate when I mention that, during
the calendar year 1929, the total
consumption of electricity supplied by
authorised undertakers throughout Northern Ireland was 71 million units, of
which Belfast sold 653 millions, or, if we
leave out of account the amount of
current consumed by the tramway undertaking, approximately 51 million units
represented the normal consumption of
the community. While speaking of these
figures it is of interest to contrast the
sales by stations in the hands of local
authorities with those controlled by
private enterprise. The latter account
for only 1.8 per cent. of the total sales
within our area, or about 25 per cent. of
the total sales in districts outside Belfast.
In Great Britain the problem which
faced the Government was the linking up
of large industrial load centres. Here,
if we leave out of account Belfast with a
population of 415,151, and Londonderry
with a population of 45,159, there are no
such centres, our next largest towns being
Bangor with a population of 13,311, and
practically no industrial load, Lurgan
with a population of 12,500, Lisburn with
The
12,406, and Newry with 12,226.
problem, therefore, which we have to
face is how we can provide for provincial industrial centres and country
districts a cheap and reliable supply of
electricity.
As the field of development available
in Northern Ireland had failed to attract
private enterprise in so far as a comprehensive scheme was concerned, I called
in a year ago Mr. J. M. Kennedy, one
of the greatest electrical authorities in
these Islands, a consultant who was not
only very closely associated with the Weir
Committee but who is now engaged in
the actual carrying into effect of the
schemes contemplated in the 1926 Act.
Mr. Kennedy's reports have been available to the public for some time, and hon.
Members will recollect that what Mr.
Kennedy suggests is that the Government
should set up a non-profit earning
authority which will purchase from the
Belfast undertaking supplies of energy
at cost, and will thereafter transmit such
energy over publicly owned lines to the
various provincial centres. From the
calculations produced it is clear that the
energy so delivered can be made available in bulk in the various centres at a
cost less than the cost of local generation.
Moreover, with local generation little
benefit can accrue to the factory whose
consumption of power is substantial since
it is obvious that in such circumstances
1777 Electricity Supply Bill-

14 OCTOBER 1930
Second Reading
the manufacturer would normally find it
preferable to instal his own plant.
Northern Ireland may roughly be
divided into three sections for the purposes of electricity development. One of
these is covered by the first Report by
Mr. Kennedy and may be referred to as
the South-Eastern area. Another is the
area of supply of the Antrim Electricity
Supply Company, to which this Parliament gave certain powers by an Act
passed in the year 1928. A third is the
North-Western area lying between Londonderry and Enniskillen, sparsely
populated, but with a number of country
towns and small industrial centres dotted
throughout the area.
For the moment we propose to deal only
with the South-Eastern area. The
Measure providing for a comprehensive
scheme of development will, I hope, be
laid before Members at the beginning of
the Spring Session, but in the meantime
there is certain preliminary work which,
as the hon. and gallant Member for
Clifton (Major Hall-Thompson) pointed
out the other day, should be undertaken
if we are not to hold up development.
Hon. Members are already aware that
a main transmission line now connects
Belfast with Holywood and Bangor, while
another connects Belfast with Lisburn.
By means of Government assistance, the
latter line was provided of such capacity
as to enable it to form the first link of a
main line joining up the various industrial centres in what we might term the
Lagan Valley. At the present time this
line is being extended from Lisburn to
Lurgan, and in this connection I should
like to pay a tribute to the public-spirited
action of the Chairman of the Electricity
Committee of the Belfast Corporation, the
hon. Member for Woodvale (Mr. Nixon)
-(Hon. Members: Hear, hear)—and of
the Chairman of the Lurgan Urban
District Council. These gentlemen have
taken the long view and collaborated in
carrying through this extension of the
Belfast-Lisburn line rather than consider
the step, less troublesome but less progressive, of extending the generating
station at Lurgan. There are other
stations in the South-Eastern area where
additional generating plant will shortly
be required, and hon. Members will
readily appreciate how undesirable it is
that public funds should be expended
upon further generating plant which at
no distant date may have to be scrapped.
Although the Measure
before the
House to-day is merely an enabling Bill,
hon. Members will, no doubt, desire to
know now what are the Government's intentions in regard to the gradual electrification of the Province. I have already
mentioned the fact that the Antrim
Electricity Supply Company's area is
being left out of consideration for the
time being. In this connection I am informed that there is on foot at the
moment a scheme for a comprehensive
system of distribution throughout the
Company's entire area, the full details
of which are likely to be made available
to the public at an early date.
The North-Western area, taken as a
whole, is one which will tax the ingenuity
of the Board to develop on comprehensive
and at the same time economic lines. For
the moment, therefore, we are limiting
our discussions to a scheme for the South-
Eastern area.
In this area, which lies to the south of
a line drawn from Belfast to Dungannon,
we have six statutory undertakings owned
by local authorities, namely, Lurgan,
Armagh, Newry, Bangor, Holywood and
Rostrevor; five statutory undertakings
owned by companies, namely, Lisburn,
Dunmurry, Portadown, Markethill and
Warrenpoint. In addition to these we
have several non-statutory undertakings,
of which those at Dromore, Banbridge,
Kilkeel, Newcastle, Castlewellan and
Ballynahinch lie in the direct route of
the main transmission lines proposed by
Mr. Kennedy.
The total generating plant installed in
the various centres possessing statutory
undertakings in the South-Eastern area
is 1357.5 k.w., but this figure includes
a substantial proportion of standby plant.
Through the courtesy of the nonstatutory concerns I have certain information as to their stations, but while
existing legislation confers on my Ministry powers of obtaining very full information from the statutory concerns, no
such powers exist in the case of the nonstatutory concerns. To remedy this, you
will observe it is proposed to take additional powers in the present Measure. As
the information regarding non-statutory
undertakers has been given to me under
pledge of secrecy, I regret I am precluded
from laying such data before the House.
In a number of centres the system of
supply is by direct current, and the
generating costs and overhead charges of
a small station render it impracticable

to
for such an undertaking to supply cheap

standardise frequency, there is not

must bear in mind the fact that the

are limited in scope and that there is no
likelihood, so long as generation remains in the hands of scattered units, of
any marked development of the supply
of electricity. Moreover, the nonstatutory undertaker is under no public
obligation or control in such important
matters as the giving of a supply to any
specific premises, of the maintenance of
such supply when it has once been given.
He is not even obliged to keep the
voltage constant and he can charge what
he likes, or what he can get.
We owe it to the people of the outlying districts to remedy this state of
affairs, and in the major Measure, of
which the present Bill is the forerunner,
we propose to empower the Board to
acquire local distribution undertakings.
In so doing it will be necessary to ensure
that equitable compensation is paid.
A point which has been put to me is
whether the area of Northern Ireland,
if it were all under the Board, would not
be somewhat unwieldy for one concern to
manage. My answer to that is that if
we consider some of the undertakings in
Great Britain, for example, the Newcastle-upon-Tyne Electric Supply Company and its associated undertakings with
installed generating plant of a capacity
of 285,300 kilowatts, or the Yorkshire
Power Company with generating plant
of 89,000 k.w. capacity, or the Clyde
Valley Electrical Power Company with
total installed plant of 103,750 k.w., and
then contrast these figures with Mr.
Kennedy's estimate of the maximum demand by the South-Eastern area on the
power station, namely, 613 k.w. in 1931-
32 rising to 10,773 k.w. in 1941-42, we
begin to see the problem in its proper
perspective.
In introducing the short Measure, of

present Bill so that hon. Members may
be able to envisage the development.
scheme we have in mind. The present

supplies in readiness for the more detailed

I should explain that it is not the intention of the Government to retain the development of the scheme in its own
hands. Hon. Members are, no doubt,
already familiar with my foreword to
Mr. Kennedy's Report on the South-
Eastern area, wherein I mentioned that

Accordingly, the lines, which it is now

If hon. Members will turn to Sub-

I have no doubt that the question will

Lurgan, Portadown, to Armagh, and

and a further main line from Belfast

see at present these are the

as we can

become a national necessity, and, therefore, I think the Government of Northern

Considered in Committee under Standing Order No. 65.
[Mr. MOLES in the Chair].
Motion made and Question proposed:
"That it is expedient to amend the provisions of the Exchequer and Financial
Provisions Act (Northern Ireland), 1923,
with respect to the Reserve Fund and the
Capital Fund established under that Act,
and to provide for the application of certain moneys issued to the said Reserve
Fund." (Governor's recommendation
signified).-(Mr. Pollock).
Mr. POLLOCK: The Resolution which
I now submit to the Committee is the
forerunner of a small but comparatively
important Measure, technical in character
and somewhat involved. Having regard
to that I have prepared a short White
Paper, which I assume is now in the hands
of hon. Members, and which will give
them more detailed information than
could be supplied in dealing with a Resolution such as I am moving at the
moment. It will be remembered that in
the year 1925 the deficit in our Unemployment Fund reached a very alarming
and portentous figure. That figure
amounted to more than £3,000,000, and
it was quite obvious at that time that a
small area such as ours could not maintain a sound insurance fund of any kind
indeed, on normal lines with contributions
and benefits on the same scale as those in
the larger area of Great Britain.
It was at that time that the negotiations
with the British Government were commenced which ultimately led to the reinsurance arrangement. This agreement
is now embodied in Acts of both Parliaments and has recently been established
as a permanent feature of our relations
with Great Britain.
The agreement, however, required us
to assume responsibility for the amortisation of the old unemployment insurance
debt of, in round figures, £3,000,000,
representing advances which had been
made to the Fund from the Exchequer.
In order to make this good to the Exchequer, I decided to allocate from our
revenues for this purpose the sum of
£100,000 per annum by way of special
payments to Reserve. But on account
of complications which arose with the
Joint Exchequer Board, this arrangement has become impracticable, and I
accordingly propose that instead the free
capital resources of the Government, representing funds of one and a quarter
milions, should be allowed to accumulate
until this debt to the Exchequer has been
cleared off. I expect that this will be
achieved about the year 1952.
The net effect of this operation is to
consolidate the position of the Exchequer
in relation to the Unemployment Insurance Fund and to make full provision for
discharging the debt liability taken over
by the Exchequer under the terms of the
agreement.
Had it not been for this agreement,
the debt of our Unemployment Insurance
Financial Provisions (Money)- HOUSE OF COMMONS
Committee
[Mr. Pollock]
Fund, which is to-day 4 millions, would
have stood at the appalling figure of
£10,000,000. I need hardly say that this
is unthinkable, and it would have been
necessary either to increase the contributions from the different contributors
or reduce the benefits, neither of which
would have been an acceptable course.
This is a bald, but I hope clear explanation of the purpose of the Bill which is
to be presented.

MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT.
Motion made, and Question proposed:
"That this House do now adjourn."-
(Captain Dixon).
Mr. O'NEILL: I endeavoured by way
of a question to elicit from the Minister
of Home Affairs why he refused to prosecute some persons in Banbridge who
were reported to him by the police for
rowdy conduct and undue interference
with the ordinary and lawful rights of the
people. In the same question I also
gave him an opportunity of explaining
the difference between his action in this
case in Banbridge and one of a similar
kind that occurred in Derry, where he
employed the Attorney-General to prosecute. The facts of the case so far as
they relate to Banbridge are these.
On the 7th September, a Sunday, a
sports meeting had been organised just
outside the town. These sports were
organised by the people with the assistance of their respected parish priest, and
in order to attract the crowd, a wellknown band from Newry, St. Joseph's,
was invited to attend. This band is
particularly well known in this country
and, indeed, in England. It has performed at many functions organised by
different sections of the people throughout the country. This band accepted the
invitation, a thing that it was perfectly
entitled to do, and a laudable undertaking, for which it deserves credit.
When the band arrived in Banbridge and
formed up to march out to the field, it
was surrounded by a mob, and the members were told by the ringleaders of that
mob that they would not be allowed to
play. Notwithstanding this threat, the
band proceeded to play on the way out
to the field.
Just when they started they were
surrounded by this mob or rabble. Stones
and other missiles were thrown at them,
while the most vile and violent language
was used by the crowd composed of both
men and women. This continued, I
understand, for some hours while the
police were there and they were either
powerless or did not want to interfere.
It will be admitted, I think, by all, that
no provocation whatever was given for
this conduct on the part of the crowd,
nor do I think that in any instance anyone
retaliated. I understand the matter
was reported to the higher authorities,
and I assume that to mean the Minister
of Home Affairs in the first instance.
Why that should have been reported
there I do not know.
Evidently the procedure was different
from that which obtained in the more
minor case in Derry, where the individuals
who caused the disturbance were taken
in the ordinary course before the magistrates at the Petty Sessions. But in
this instance the matter was reported to
the Minister of Home Affairs, and after
deliberation he decided that no prosecution should take place. I should like to
know from the Minister of Home Affairs
why no prosecution took place in connection with the Banbridge matter? Does he
not think members of the Catholic faith
have the same right to the public road or
thoroughfare as the members of his own
party? Evidently he does not. That to
me would be pursuing a policy that has
been in existence in Ireland for many
years. It has not been altered here in the
North since you took charge, and I
have no doubt it would not have been
altered in the South if your former
friends still had their way there.
I know we have no power to remedy
this thing. We can only expose it, and
to expose it on all occasions I am prepared
as far as I am personally concerned. I
do not see how the Prime Minister or any
other Minister can on the platform, or
in the Press, make statements that the
Catholic people of Northern Ireland are
treated just the same as the other members of the community. That is not
Sunday Sports Meeting-- HOUSE OF COMMONS

In order to show, I suppose, their civil

HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Crawford]
I would like no one for a moment to
imagine I am antagonistic to the
Government. I am not going to make
any complaint regarding any official of
this House or in connection with the
Civil Service. I will not say that the
sum of £200 allowed as expenses to
Members of this House is too much at
the present time, and I will not say it
is too little. I am not going to enter
into that. I am not going to make any
suggestion that the officials are too
numerous, although there are suggestions of that sort.
I believe this is a time of unusual
and marked depression, and in the
whole of Northern Ireland every industry you can think of is very deeply
affected. It is well known to everyone
in this House that income tax was increased very considerably last year. It
is well known that dividends are decreasing at a very rapid rate. I was
speaking to a person last week who lives
entirely on dividends coming from investments made during a long and
arduous life. and on a careful valuation
they have decreased 60 per cent. in the
Jast. two years. Therefore, there is
absolutely no question about this being
a time of depression.
That refers to the people who are
living, and then we think of the heavy
death duties. It is clear to any thinking person that there is scarcely any
opportunity for expanding business or
investing money. Shipbuilding is in a
very bad way, and even when new ships
are ordered-and I am thankful to say
some have been ordered through the
loans initiated and carried out by the
right hon. Gentleman, the Minister of
Finance--when they are being built
the use of new machinery results in
fewer men being employed than in the
past, consequently a greater number
of people are unemployed. Then many
ships are lying idle in different parts of
the world in various harbours. They
cannot get cargoes to enable them to go
backwards and forwards through the
world.
I come to the linen industry. A great
many factories are closed and the remainder are on short time. The
spinning mills are nearly all closed. I
am thankful to say one to keep longest
at work is in Ballymena, but even at
present it is on short time. Foreign
competition with longer hours and
lower wages has made it possible for the
Americans to buy in other countries
goods which they used to buy here. I
heard recently of a large buyer who
came from America to buy handkerchiefs. He used to be a buyer who
could keep one factory employed all the
time, but on his recent visit to Ireland
he did not buy one dozen articles. These
are things we have to take into consideration. The manufacturers cannot
get orders. I know people who are
willing to take orders even at a price
that would not pay them in order to
keep their employees going, but they
cannot get orders.
Unemployment is increasing. In this
week's paper you will see there were 1,994
added to last week's number, and that
the total is now 70,443 in Northern Ireland. Foundries and iron works are in
a bad state. A good many are closed
entirely. In a recent issue of the paper
I saw that great iron works, in Merthyr I
think, which employed nearly 3,000
persons were about to close down. Then,
agriculture is one of the things in a bad
state.

Remember that the salaries of

the world were on an increased basis of
remuneration, a bonus system was adopted
conformable to the particular additions
to the cost of living figures as they were
published. Those figures were adjusted
half-yearly.
Now I find on examination that when
our Parliament was established those
figures were at the peak, and, therefore,
the bonuses of our civil servants were
based upon the peak. Since that time.
there have been progressive reductions,

bonus addition of 46 per cent that is
the addition which accrues at present to
the salary of a civil servant-in substitution for the 117 per cent. which was
operative at the time when the bonus
system was adopted. In other words, a

ORDERS OF THE DAY.
(By
Third Parties (Rights Against Insurers)
Bill.
Order for Second reading read.
Motion made, and Question proposed:
"That the Bill be now read a Second
time."
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): This is in no sense
a controversial Measure, and I do not
think it will be necessary for me to detain
the House by explaining it at any great
length. It is, of course, outside the scope
of the major Bill, that is the Motor
Traffic Bill, the Second Reading of which
I hope to take on Tuesday.
The object of this Bill is to deal with
the position of a person who is insured.
against third party risks, and after incurring a liability to
a third person
becomes bankrupt or dies insolvent, or in
the
case of a company, goes into
liquidation or has a receiver appointed.
Perhaps the simplest way in which I can
make the position clear to the House and
convince hon. Members of the necessity of
this Bill is to give them the concrete facts
of a case which came before the Courts in
England not very long ago.
A company which owned motor cars was
insured against third party risks. One
of the drivers of that company had the
misfortune to knock down a pedestrian.
An action was raised, the pedestrian saying it was the fault of the motor car
driver, and the motor car driver saying
it was the fault of the pedestrian.
due course the action was heard, and the
pedestrian was awarded somewhere about
£500 damages. The action, of course.
was brought against the insured person
but was, as is commonly the case, defended in fact by the insurance company.
In
Judgment was entered for £500 but,
before execution could be levied or the
money paid, the owner of the motor car
who had been found to blame went into
compulsory liquidation. The insurance
company, in order to discharge their
liability, which they were perfectly willing
to do, had to pay the money-not to the
injured pedestrian, but to the liquidator
of the company, and it then became part
of the general assets of the company in
the hands of the liquidator.
It was,
along with the other assets, distributed
amongst the creditors of the company pro
rata, and the unfortunate pedestrian
merely received a dividend on his judgment.
Unlucky as the pedestrian was in the
case I have quoted, his position was fortunate compared with what it would have
been if the judgment had been obtained by him after the bankruptcy had
taken place instead of before, as actually
did happen, because in this case he would
have had no right even to get a dividend
and the money which he was awarded
would have had to be utilised in priority
to his claim altogether, in order to satisfy
the creditors in existence at the time of
the bankruptcy.
1 am sure that hon. Members will agree
that it is impossible to defend this state.
of the law, and, accordingly, we propose
to remedy it by this Bill, which, put
very briefly, provides that where a person
who is insured against third party risks
incurs a liability to a third party and
then becomes bankrupt, the injured third
party shall be entitled to step into the
shoes of the bankrupt and have all his
rights against the insurance company. A
similar ruling will apply where a company
in similar circumstances is wound up or
where a receiver is appointed.
The principle is not by any means a
new one, because a similar rule was ap-
1841 Third Parties Bill-

15 OCTOBER 1930
Second Reading
plied in the case of Workmen's Compensation where an employer becomes
bankrupt, by Section 7 of the Workmen's
Compensation Act passed by this Parliament in 1927. I beg to move.

speak more particularly of the vicinity of

the motor car has not even been traced.

There was a
point I want to make.
Constable Attwell. He had considerable

Ministry of Home Affairs,
Northern Ireland,
Belfast,
22nd October, 1930.
Sir, In reply to your letter of the
30th ult., inquiring as to why a pension has not been granted to the children of the late Constable John Attwell.
I am directed by the Minister of Home
Affairs to inform you that children of
deceased members of the force are not
entitled to payment of allowances un-

CLAUSE 3 (Registration of premises
for slaughter and crating).
There shall be kept by the Ministry
of Agriculture a register of premises (in
this Act referred to as "registered premises') to be used for the slaughter of
animals in connection with the sending
of meat from Northern Ireland to Great
Britain, the Irish Free State or the Isle
of Man by any person holding a fresh
meat licence, and the following provisions shall apply with respect to the
registration of such premises:-
(a) The premises may be registered for
the slaughter of animals of any class
or classes, and the Ministry of Agriculture shall before registering any
premises be satisfied that the
premises and the equipment thereof are
suitable for the slaughter of animals
of the class or classes to be dealt with
therein, and for the preparation for
sale of the meat of such animals;
(b) The Ministry of Agriculture may
refuse to register any premises unless
satisfied that not less than a prescribed number of animals will be
dealt with annually on such premises,
and may cancel the registration of
any premises where the number of
animals dealt with in any year has
fallen below the prescribed number;
Mr. CRAWFORD: I beg to move in
page 3, line 6, after "slaughter" ("the
slaughter of animals") insert "by the
most humane method."
This Clause deals with the registration
of premises for slaughter and crating, and

CLAUSE 4 (Restriction on carrying on
business of curing bacon and hams)—
(1) A person shall not carry on the
business of curing bacon and hams unless he holds a licence for that purpose
under this section, and any person who
carries on or attempts to carry on the
said business in contravention of the
provisions of this section shall be guilty
of an offence under this Act.
(2) Subject to the provisions of this
Act, the Ministry of Agriculture shall
have power to grant, revoke and suspend
licences authorising the persons named
therein to carry on the business of curing bacon and hams.
(3) The Ministry of Agriculture
shall, on application being made in the
prescribed manner, and on payment of
the fee specified in this section, grant
to any person, upon such conditions as
may be prescribed, a licence for the purpose aforesaid :
Provided that the said Ministry may
revoke or suspend a licence if satisfied

The ATTORNEY-GENERAL: May I
point out the scope of Clause 14? A
member of the Constabulary or authorised
officer is given power to detain in custody
any consignment of meat which is sent,
or suspected of being sent, out of the
country in contravention of any provision.
of the Bill. The officer does not inspect
the meat. That merely refers in practice
to the detention of meat in cases where a
person who has no licence for the export
of this particular commodity or who has
not had that meat inspected. All this
meat will be marked with the name of the
consignor, and it will be immediately
known whether he is a person who is
licensed or not. It will also be marked
with the mark of the inspector, showing
that it has been inspected, and when it
comes through on rail or on the boat the
inspectors there who are looking for meat
which is being sent contrary to the regulations, will know at once whether it has
complied with the regulations. It is plain.
that if it does not comply with the regulations it must be immediately stopped
in transit.
It might be that it had not been inspected, or there might be a mistake
through the consignor not putting his
name on it, but that would be his fault,
and in practice I do not think it will be
found by the exporters that this will in
any way interfere with their trade.
As
a matter of fact, similar provisions have
been passed by this House both in the
Marketing of Potatoes Act and in the
Fisheries Act of 1928, and up to the
present, although from time to time consingments have been stopped under those
Acts, no real difficulty has been experienced by the trade. I think when the
Committee understand the facts under
which the officers will be entitled to stop
this meat from going across the water
they will see there is really no necessity
for any appeal.

Mr. BLACK: I beg to move in page
14, line 7, after "slaughter houses" ("in
relation to slaughter houses") insert
"and the licensing thereof."
The three Amendments standing in my
name are merely drafting Amendments.
Under this Bill there is being established
a register of premises to be used for the
slaughter of animals for export. As the
Committee are aware urban authorities
have extensive powers for the licensing of
of slaughter houses not only where meat
is slaughtered for export but slaughtered
for use in the country itself. This Bill
does not touch slaughter houses where
meat is being slaughtered for use in the
country. Moreover, in regard to the registration provided by this Bill, all that the
Ministry is concerned with is the
slaughter house itself, the nature of the
house, and the conditions under which
work is carried on. In issuing licenses
the local authorities are concerned with
something further. They are concerned
with the general health of the locality,
and make regulations that slaughter
houses should not be within so many feet
of the dwelling house, and that there is
no store accommodation over the slaughter
house. It is obvious that when you have
registration under this Bill the existing
powers of the urban authorities will have
to be preserved. It was clearly designed
by this sub-section (2) that the licensing
power of the local authorities should
remain in force. The Amendments I
propose are merely drafting Amendments
to make that necessary provision clear.
We are really adding nothing to the intention of the Bill. It is to make clearer
the intention which was conveyed by subsection 2 of the Clause.
Sir EDWARD ARCHDALE: I agree
to the Amendment.

Her name is Isabella McMurray. At

the Shankill Road. About seven or
eight years ago she adopted a little boy
and what I would call an adoption deed
was drawn up and stamped. No other
steps were taken, and she is in receipt
of a widow's pension, and if she got the
adoption order in respect of this little boy
then he would be recognised as her boy
and he also would get the pension. She
called at the Ministry of Pensions and
she informed me she was there very
courteously received, and it was explained

the court she would get the pension in
respect of the little boy. She went to a
solicitor and he asked her for £4 which
she was unable to pay. She came to me,

and the clerk introduced her to Mr.
Toppin, R.M., who very courteously explained to her that adoption orders were
made in the county court. I got a copy
of the Act myself and saw that that was

the Crown and Peace and sent it over
with her.
Sir,-Isabella McMurray, 8 James

hon. Member for Woodvale showed me

Of course it is difficult for people who

because until such time as the rules are

be made to the court.
As to the suggestion that has been

or whatever form of application will be
prescribed under this Adoption of Children

with responsible duties, and if any person

HOUSE OF COMMONS.

Thursday, 16th October, 1930.
The House met at Three of the Clock,
Mr. SPEAKER in the Chair.
Oral Answers to Questions.
IMPORTED RUSSIAN OATS.
1. Mr. ELLIOTT asked the Minister
of Agriculture whether he is aware of the
fact that a cargo of oats was recently
discharged at the Port of Belfast from
Soviet Russia; whether all necessary
precautions are being taken by his Department to ensure that these oats come
from non-infected areas in Russia;
whether he can guarantee that no foot
and mouth disease has been known to
exist where these oats were grown; and
whether he is satisfied that a properly
constituted and efficient Ministry is acting in Russia to issue to his Ministry
declarations regarding this very
very important matter.
The following Questions also appeared
on the Order Paper in the name of Mr.
Elliott:-
2. To ask the Minister of Agriculture
whether his Ministry is taking steps to
trace the various consignments of Soviet
oats now being despatched all over the
Six County area, so that in the event of
an epidemic arising he will be able to
localise it.
3. To ask the Minister of Agriculture
whether the description given to these
oats ("Baltic Oats") is not a misleading
one, and what steps he is taking to see
that these oats are sold and described to
the purchasers in such manner so as to
ensure they will know exactly what they
are purchasing, and the risks they are
running by using them for feeding
purposes.
The MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE
(Sir Edward Archdale): It will be convenient if I answer this and the two
following questions by the hon. Member
together.
1,350 tons of Russian oats were landed
in Belfast last week consigned to four
Belfast firms. Samples of the oats have
been drawn by the Ministry's Inspectors
and examined. The grain is thin and
husky and of much poorer feeding
quality than home produced oats. It
contains weed seed impurities, but not in
excessive amounts. The Ministry has no
means of ascertaining the district or
districts in Russia in which the grain
was grown.
With regard to the question of animal
diseases, it is desirable to bear in mind
that a very substantial proportion of the
imports of maize into the United Kingdom comes from countries where foot and
mouth disease is prevalent. There has never
been any evidence to suggest that such
importations of oats and maize render
the country liable to outbreaks of foot
and mouth disease. Consequently, the
Imperial Authorities have no import restrictions on the importation of cereals
into the United Kingdom. In view of
these facts no useful purpose would be
served by taking steps suggested in the
second question.
""
With regard to the hon. Member's
third question, the description "Baltic
Oats leaves no doubt in the mind of
the purchaser that the oats are of
foreign origin. The Ministry is watching the position carefully and is satisfied
that although the Russian oats are of
poorer feeding quality than home produced
oats, there are at present no grounds
upon which such importations could be
restricted.
Lieut.-Col. GORDON: Will the Minister inform the House who the unpatriotic
firms or gentlemen are who are handling
these oats?
Mr. BEATTIE: I would like to ask
the Minister whether it is a fact that full
diplomatic and trade relations have been
restored between the British Government
and Soviet Russia?
Mr. SPEAKER: That does not arise
out of the answer.
Mr. BEATTIE: It does so far
trading relations with Russia are
cerned.

The PARLIAMENTARY SECRE-

CATION (Mr. Robb): The cases referred

KING'S SCHOLARS AND
APPOINTMENTS.
10. Mr. NIXON asked the Parliamentary Secretary of the Ministry of
Education whether he can state the number of King's Scholars who completed
their course of training in the three recognised training colleges respectively on the
30th June, 1928, and passed their final
examinations, and yet have failed to
obtain permanent appointments; how
many who completed their course of training on the 30th June, 1929, are still
permanently unemployed; how many
vacancies in Northern Ireland since the
30th June, 1928, were filled up by appointing teachers from outside Northern
Ireland, and what steps, if any, the
Ministry proposes to take to ensure that
there will not be trained more teachers
than are neccssary for Northern Ireland.
Mr. ROBB: Disregarding 8 students
who entered for third and fourth year
courses of training, and one to whom permission to postpone taking up employment was granted, the number of students
who finished their course of training in
1928 and who have not yet secured permanent posts is 19.
Apart from 14 students who entered
upon a third-year course of training and
2 who have decided to take up secondary
teaching and are, in consequence, refunding the cost of their training, 53 students
who finished their course of training in
1929 have not yet secured permanent
posts.
Since 30th June, 1928, 43 teachers from
outside Northern Ireland have been appointed.
Examination of the statistics on various
dates during the year shows that about
75 trained teachers are constantly
required to fill temporary vacancies
arising in the schools. The Committee
for the Training of Teachers, with the approval of the Ministry, reduced the
number admitted to training in 1929 and
made a further reduction in 1930, but
the effect of these reductions has not yet
been felt. The question of the supply of
teachers is being kept under close observation, as the Ministry has no desire to
train teachers who cannot obtain permanent employment within a reasonable time
of the completion of their training.

contemplated making provision for the

whether to implement the promise of the

the Minister of Finance proposes to grant

retired since these sums began to be paid
in Great Britain.
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Pollock): I presume the hon. Member is
referring to the Education (Ireland) Bill
introduced into the British House of Commons in November, 1919, and re-introduced with some variations in the year
1920. Neither Bill received a Second
Reading.

Oral Answers
16 OCTOBER 1930
Both Bills made specific provision for
the preparation of a superannuation
scheme for teachers, but left the particulars to be introduced into the scheme to
be prescribed by the proposed Department
of Education and the Treasury.
As regards the inclusion of the payment
of a lump sum on retirement in addition
to pension, the Bills only gave a permissive power to introduce such a provision
and did not make it mandatory.
think, therefore, that the hon. Member
can base any argument upon the provisions of these Bills.
I do not
With regard to the second part of the
question. At the time of the introduction of these Bills, the School Teachers'
(Superannuation) Act, 1918, applicable to
Great Britain but not to Ireland, was
already in operation. That Act made a
mandatory provision for the payment of a
lump sum allowance in addition to pension, but, as I have stated, such a mandatory provision was not introduced in the
abortive Irish Bills of 1919 and 1920.
It follows, therefore, that the abortive
Bills of 1919 and 1920 do not provide the
precedent which the hon. Member seeks
to import into them.
In any event, I do not consider that the
payment of such pensions or lump sum
allowances falls within the category of
social services. Our expenditure in Northern Ireland in a matter of this kind
must be governed by our financial resources, and, in view of the additional
expenditure which would fall on the Exchequer, if the hon. Member's suggestion
were carried out, I cannot contemplate
such provision.

SHANKILL ROAD POLICE
BARRACKS.
18. Mr. NIXON asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether there is any objection to the Medical Officer of Health for
the City of Belfast inspecting and reporting on the sanitary and general hygienic
condition of Shankill Road Royal Ulster
Constabulary Barracks, or any other
police barracks in the jurisdiction of the
said Medical Officer.
Sir DAWSON BATES: Police Barracks are exempt from the provisions of
the Public Health (Ireland) Acts by
Section 32 of the Public Health (Ireland)
Act, 1878, and, therefore, are not subect to inspection by the Medical Officer of
health of the local authority.
As these buildings are vested in the
Ministry of Home Affairs, which is the
ultimate health authority, and it is the
luty of the Ministry's Medical Inspectors
to report on the state of these barracks,
there would be no object in having them
inspected by the Medical Officers of the
local authority.
At the same time, the Ministry's Inspectors are always ready to consult with
the Medical Officers of Health on any

barracks which may affect the sanitary

was fully satisfied as to its sanitary and

No one inside this House or outside it
can justify the statement that the Cabinet
have been overworked. The Prime
Minister has tried to justify the expense
of the Government on the ground that
the high salaries were fixed in order
to encourage the best businessmen in
Northern Ireland to come forward and
take office. I will give him credit, until
we hear otherwise, for getting seven of
the best super-men in Northern Ireland
in his Cabinet, because they have the
highest salaries of any Government for
the amount of the duties appertaining to
their offices. That being so, this Motion
calls for a return for the money expended
on the Cabinet. It wants something
practical, something immediate; it wants
all Ulster to be taken out of the chaos
and disorder and disastrous times she is
passing through at present. That is the
reason for a Motion of this description
standing in my name.
Resolved: "That this House, at its
rising this day, do adjourn until Tuesday
next." (Mr. Gordon).
ORDERS OF THE DAY.
UNEMPLOYMENT.
Mr. BEATTIE: I beg to move:
"That this House views with alarm the
appalling condition of employment in
Northern Ireland, and regrets that no
attempt has been made by the Government to grapple with an economic and
industrial situation which has caused the
gravest concern to the community, and
calls upon the Government to state what
steps they have taken in the last six
months, and what proposals, if any, they
intend to submit to this House to solve
the unemployment problem in Northern
Ireland."
I am sure that the House will be deeply
interested in the statement by the Prime
Minister likely to follow this Motion. Not
only Members of this House but trade
and industry outside are most anxious
that something of a definite kind should
be set forward by the Prime Minister.
The wording of this Motion, I think, is
so concise that it can be easily understood. We may have repeated to us the
history of what the Government have
done for unemployment and trade and
industry since they came into power in
Northern Ireland. I do not want that.
We on this side have found many faults
with the repetition of that from the Government side. The Motion calls definitely on the Government to come
forward with their proposals and to give
an account of what they have done for
the past six months.
The Unionist party in front of me are
to-day blaming the Socialist Government
in Great Britain for being responsible
for the great depression in trade and the
large volume of unemployment. The
generous hand of the Socialist Government is at the present moment feeding
the Unionists of Ulster, and while they
accept that generosity and are bounty
fed they go out on the hustings every
night and denounce the Socialists as being
responsible for this desperate evil in our
midst. I am not going to denounce the
Unionist party as being responsible
although they were in power, and I am
not going to denounce this Government
as being responsible although they have
been in super-power for the past ten
years.
No handicaps or hampering of any description ever came from this side of the
House. We offered useful suggestions
which were rejected on many occasions.
Therefore, I am only going to quote from
the leaders. I want to know what voice
the Unionist party of Ulster speaks
through. Is it the Baldwinian voice, or
the Churchillian voice, or the voice of the
Senate the day before yesterday. Baldwin
is laying at the door of the Socialist Govcrnment the responsibility for the great
unemployment evil in England. He has
said that very tactfully, but he has said
it as an electioneering plea, so that the
people will not perhaps see the good
work of the Labour party while in office.
Churchill makes no bones about his
statements. He admitted in the Imperial

We come now to the linen industry.
Is there anyone going to tell me that Protection is going to save this industry?
It is a most ridiculous thing that while
we can do anything as regards exports
we have no power at all under the sun
to interfere with imports. You are now
asking the Labour Government to give
you the Protection you require. I would
ask the Prime Minister did he ask his
party when they were in power in Britain
to do that? Surely if Protection is good
to-day when Labour is in power, it should
have been good in 1925, 1926, and 1927
when the Unionist party were in power
with an overwhelming majority at their
command. The linen trade has only recently come into a depressed state. The
linen trade has been depressed since 1921.
That being so Labour has not been in office
since 1921, but the hustings now
echoing with the sound of Protection
for the linen industry. All the Protection in the world will not save the linen
industry.
are
I am going to quote a case that happened three weeks ago. Protection means
protection of price, that is, to get a better
price for the article. A Member on the
other side of the House and I were together the other week, and he had
forgotten his pocket handkerchief. He
went into a shop in this city and paid
eighteen pence for one. Will the Government say if they had Protection what it
would do for that price of 18d. Is it
going to make a greater demand for linen
in the Home market and in the British
market? If people have not got the purchasing power to buy, will Protection or
anything else make them buy? I say no.
Protection is no use if it does not protect
the price for the manufacturer. Therefore
Protection of linen is ridiculous to suggest
for the present price as I saw it in Belfast.
I advise the Government-and this
thought has sprung from General Crozier.
General Crozier played many important
parts in Ulster.
Mr. HEALY: The Prime Minister will
want no introduction to him.
Mr. BEATTIE: No. You may court
the British market of 45 millions of
people. You may court that market as
much as you like. But you are like the
lady who lives in the suburbs. There is a
shop opposite her selling an article she
wants. But she takes a tram at 2d and
goes into town and buys it.
She spends
2d on the tram and buys the article at
the very same price as she would have got
it at next door to her, and at the finish
she is 4d out of pocket. It is the same
with the Government here to-day. You
have an area of 26 counties and over
3,000,000 of a population who would be
more eager and more anxious to support
Irish linen than the British household,
but you are like that lady. You will go
across the seas to court the 45 millions and

You have got to put these old shibboleths away.

I have no hesitation in saying that this.
Government, through my right hon.
Friend, has done more to assist education
during the past few years than any other
Government I know of in the world. A
great deal of statistics can be produced.
Mention was made of development schemes,

full how extensive these development
schemes have been. There was £54,000
granted for the purpose of accelerating
agricultural development in various directions. The grant was spread over four
years and was devoted to County Agricultural Education Schemes, to Grantsin-Aid of Milk Recording Associations and
the Improvement of Breeding of Mountain
Sheep. These schemes proved to be so
beneficial that the Government decided to
provide further money to continue the
schemes after the grant was exhausted.
In the year 1927, moreover, the sum of
£40,000 additional to the above was set
aside to establish a fund for the purpose
of improving live stock by the extension
of the premium schemes in respect of
bulls, boars and rams. Last year a poultry
development scheme, estimated to cost
£24,000 over a period of ten years, was
commenced. This provides for the establishment of additional poultry stations
with a view to speeding up development
of this very important branch of the agricultural industry. Besides these grants,
the annual grants to county authorities
have been increased by about £7,500.
Provision has also been made for the
extension of scientific research into agricultural problems and for University
education in agriculture. When the
Northern Government was established
practically no institutions existed in Northern Ireland for such purposes, but it
can now be said that Northern Ireland
possesses research stations equal to those
to be found in any country. In the
Faculty of Agriculture of Queen's University, which has been provided and is
maintained from public funds, means are
afforded for the training of students in
the higher branches of agricultural education. Such work has been of the utmost value in stimulating the production
of the right type of article.
The Ministry of Agriculture has also
given consideration to the improvement of
marketing of all agricultural produce.
The Marketing of Eggs Act, 1924-1928;
the Marketing of Potatoes Act, 1929; the
Marketing of Dairy Produce Act, 1929;
the Meat Bill and the Fruit Bill, now
under consideration; all these measures
have had for their object the improving
of the quality of agricultural commodities
exported so as to enable Northern Ireland
produce to obtain the highest prices in
cross-Channel markets. (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear.) We have insisted on proper
testing, grading and packing, and to-day,
with the exception of English National
Mark eggs, Northern Ireland eggs are
commanding the highest prices on the
British markets. I only quote that-and
I will also give the figures to emphasise it
-in order to show to the House, and I
hope through the House to individual
constituencies, the really sound value
there is in the careful marketing of our
goods and the grading of them, and to
express the hope that with the co-operation
of all classes with the Government, who
only look upon themselves as the centre
of a co-operative movement by the whole
of Ulster, we will be able to claim our
rightful position in British markets and
markets across the sea.
What are the facts and what have we
done? Every credit should be meted out,
I think, to those who initiated legislation

English National Mark eggs is 24s 6d to
25s Od; Northern Ireland, 22s 6d to
23s Od; Irish Free State, 16s 0d; Danish,
14s 9d to 15s Od; and Belgian, 14s 9d
to 15s 6d. Therefore, by care, by cooperation amongst all those engaged in
the industry, thank goodness Northern
Ireland is only second to Great Britain
in this industry which means so much to
the farming community to-day. Leans
have also been made for fencing, purchase
of farm machinery, &c. As regards and
improvements, a scheme was commenced

way we can to carry them through the

claimed to move, "That the Question be
now put."
Question, "That the Question be now
put," put and agreed to.
Question put: "That this House views
with alarm the appalling condition of employment in Northern Ireland, and regrets that no attempt has been made by
the Government to grapple with an
economic and industrial situation which
has caused the gravest concern to the community, and calls upon the Government
to state what steps they have taken in
the last six months, and what proposals,
if any, they intend to submit to this
House to solve the unemployment problem in Northern Ireland."
The House divided: Ayes, 6; Noes. 23.

ORDERS OF THE DAY.
Motor Vehicles and Road Traffic Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.
Sir DAWSON BATES: This Bill
might be described as another step
in the Measures which the Government have taken, and are taking,
with the object of making the
roads safer for both motorists and
pedestrians, and when I say that, I think
I am entitled to claim that the Measures
which this House have passed up to the
present dealing with this important
matter have had most satisfactory results
in reducing the number of accidents to
motorists and pedestrians arising from the
use of motor cars.
When I introduced the Motor Traffic
Bill at the beginning of this year, I
explained to the House the difficulty I
had in giving effect in that Bill to the
principle of Third Party Insurance, and
this Bill is the fulfilment of the undertaking which I gave to the House at that
time to introduce a Bill dealing with the
matter. The Bill is divided into three
parts. The third part is of formal
character, and it is unnecessary to deal
with that.
As regards the first part of the Bill,
it deals with three important matters
which, however, I do not think, present
any feature of difficulty. There has been
in existence for a number of years an informal arrangement between the Govern
ment of Northern Ireland and the
Imperial Government whereby licences to
drive which are issued in Great Britain
were valid in Northern Ireland, and in the
same way licences issued in Northern
Ireland are valid in Great Britain.
I need not point out to this House the
value of having reciprocity, more
especially having regard to the Tourist
Traffic, and it is extremely desirable that
these
continue.
arrangements should
The informal arrangement which has
hitherto existed was based on the understanding between the two Governments

With regard to Clause II, this point
was inserted after consultation and at
the request of the Postmaster-General.
I think hon. Members will appreciate
how necessary it is to increase the facilities for postal service, and the Postmaster-General, with a view of providing
additional facilities is using the bus services to a very much larger extent than
hitherto. Up to the present the amounts
paid by the Postmaster-General are a
matter for agreement between the two
parties, but it is open at the present time
to any bus owner to decline to carry the
mails, except at an extortionate price.
We therefore propose by this Clause to
impose an obligation on every bus owner
running a regular service to carry whatever mails may be desired of him by the
Postmaster-General to or
or from places
along his route. At the same time we
must not lose sight of the primary purpose of these vehicles, for the carrying
of passengers, and, accordingly, we propose to limit the obligation of the bus
owner to such mails as can be carried
without inconvenience to the passengers.
Railways and tramways are subject to
a similar obligation, and we propose to
follow a corresponding procedure laid
down for fixing the payments in the case
of the payments to railways and tramways for carrying out a similar service.
The parties may in the future fix the
price by agreement, but if they cannot
agree between themselves the price will
be fixed by the Tribunal which has been
set up under the Act passed by this House
last year.
I think hon. Members will agree that
this is a very necessary Clause, and that
the Postmaster-General should be facilitated in every possible way in his desire
to provide better postal facilities, more
especially in dealing with districts which
are only served by buses.
Clause III deals with automatic signals. This enables local authorities to
incur expenditure in the provision_and
maintenance of automatic signals. Hon.
Members will agree with me that it is
eminently desirable that local authorities should have this power. Most hon.
Members are aware that an experimental
series of signals have been set up in Belfast. The experiment, I may say, has
proved an unqualified success, and it is
proposed to set up 12 further sets in the
City of Belfast. I am convinced that
these signals will do much to make the
streets safer for traffic of all kinds, and
they will, I think, ultimately lead to
considerable economies being effected in
the direction of traffic control. I look
forward to further extensions in this
direction. Some doubts, however, have
been expressed as to whether local authorities had power to incur any expenditure
in this direction, and this Clause is designed to remove all doubts on the matter.
We are now coming to Part II of the

urged in this House, and also in another

view on the point, because at that time

that Act, I would remind hon. Members,

The number of public service vehicles to

have
to deal with no fewer than 35,000 vehicles,

regards Great Britain the number of

Therefore, to my mind, it would have

land until a similar scheme was inaugurated in Great Britain. This scheme has
now been adopted in Great Britain, and

I am correct in saying that the insurance

I further learn that certain insurance

It
has happened, again and again, that
where drivers have been guilty of gross
negligence and have caused serious injury
to a third party, sometimes crippling
them for life, or depriving dependants of
their breadwinner, it has been found
utterly useless even to attempt to recover
damages because the driver, or the owner
of the car, is a person of no substance. A
great hardship has been caused to many
people by this state of affairs, and I submit that if a person enjoys the privilege
of driving a car upon the public road, it
is not unreasonable to ask that he should
put himself in a position to meet all legal
claims that might arise as a result of his
negligence in exercising such a privilege.
It is only too true that the people who
do not insure at the present are the
people who have nothing to lose, and this
Bill is designed to rope in such persons.
In broad outline, the scheme contained.
in the Bill is that every person using a
motor car on the public highway shall
carry a certificate to the effect that in
respect of the user of the car that he is
either covered by a policy of insurance,
or that he is covered by an authorised
surety against third-party risks.
The policy of insurance must be issued
by a company which is an authorised insurer, that is a company which has made
certain cash deposits in the Supreme
Court for Great Britain or Northern Ireland as required by the Assurance Companies Act in Northern Ireland, as
amended by this Bill.
The certificate of security to which I
have referred is an alternative to the
certificate of insurance, and consists of
an undertaking given by an authorised
insurer or by some body of persons which
carry on in the United Kingdom the
business of giving securities, and which
has lodged a sum of not less than £15,000
in the Supreme Court in Great Britain
or Northern Ireland. The undertaking
must be a guarantee to make good any
default of the person guaranteed in the
discharge of any legal liabilities to third
parties arising out of the use of a motor
car in the public highway up to a limit
of £25,000 in the case of a public service
vehicle, and the sum of £5,000 in the
case of any other class of vehicle.
There is a further provision in Clause
4 to which I would draw the attention
of the House which exempts certain local
authorities from the operation of the Bill.
The local authorities exempted are those
who would be in a position to meet any
claims that might be made against them
without imposing any undue hardship on
the ratepayers, and as they have unlimited rating powers, security for the
insured person is unlimited. There is a
further exemption which we propose to
give, and that is any person, or group of
persons, who lodges a sum of £15,000 in
the Supreme Court in Northern Ireland
or Great Britain as security that he will
be able to meet any claims which may be
made against him even though he may
not be insured. The particular value of

So far as we have had experience with
insurance companies in connection with
the insurance of public service vehicles
we have never found them either unreasonable or inclined to refuse an insurance unless there is very solid ground
for their action.
There are some limitations set out in
the proviso to the first Sub-clause of
Clause 5, with regard to the exception
to the liability which must be covered
by insurance. First, the compulsory
insurance provisions of this Bill do not
apply to the employees of the owner who
sustained damage from injuries arising
out of, or in the course of, their employment. The reason for this will, I
think, at once occur to every hon. Member in the House. It is that the Workmen's Compensation Code covers this
case already very fully.
Hon. Members may have observed in
the newspapers from time to time reports
of cases where persons who have been
given a friendly ride by owners of motor
cars have brought actions against the
owners when they have sustained injuries whilst being so driven, and these
actions have in many cases been successful. We do not, however, think that it
is at all necessary that we should compel
the owner to insure against such risks.
If, for instance, an hon. Member of this
House accepts a ride in the car of another Member, he does so at his own
risk, and if he is injured during the
course of that ride, we must leave it to
the hon. Members concerned without
compulsory insurance.
In the third place we do not require
the owner of a vehicle to insure against
any liability arising in connection with
the use of a motor vehicle on the road
out of a contract. Perhaps I can make
the point clear to the House most easily
by giving an imaginary concrete case.
The owner of an omnibus is liable to his
passengers at common law for any injury
they may receive through the negligence.
of the owner, his servants, or agents.
This liability does not depend on any
contract.
But suppose that the owner of
one of the omnibus undertakings in order
to induce passengers to prefer his service
to that of a competitor were to agree that
he would indemnify any passenger against
the result of an accident, whether the
accident was due to the negligence of the
driver or not. If an accident then
occurs which is not due to negligence,
the owner becomes liable to the passenger
injured, not at common law, but by
reason of a special contract which has
been made between them.
If it were not for the limitation in
paragraph 3 of the proviso to which I
have referred the owner would be liable
to penalties under the Bill if he failed
to insure against this liability arising out
of his contract. I think it will be obvious
to hon. Members that we could not justify
compulsory insurance in respect of such
liabilities.
I would direct the attention of hon.
Members to the terms of Clause 7 of the
Bill which will make a somewhat important change in the law. It is the almost

Hon. Members will realise that this

Any person who is fit to get a licence to

It is perfectly ridiculous that people

The physical test is far more important
than that. Any man who can stand the

A body of men living in an isolated part

plan of building a hall for themselves for
social purposes.
They live where there

Here we have a case where a number of
men-I believe they belong to the Ancient
Order of Hibernians-I do not belong to
the Order at all-made up their minds
they would have this hall, as has been suggested by the hon. Member for the Central
Division (Mr. Devlin), for social purposes
in this country district, and a lot of men
said they would not allow them to have
the hall. Following the advice, or
sheltering under the statement, of the
Attorney-General, they went out at two
o'clock in the morning. The burning of
this hall was not an unpremeditated thing
as I understand-I am relying purely on
the "Belfast Telegraph" for my information-they brought crowbars and razed
the hall to the ground, that is, the concrete. Petrol was sprinkled on hay and
any timber they succeeded in getting at
was burned. The information, I understand, was got from the two policemen,
who were members of the Royal Ulster
Constabulary.
The question for the Government is,
can these two men be believed, these two
reliable constables who were on duty?
Let us assume they can. They have told
us one hundred men at least were there
with rifles and that those men tied them

these two constables state they fired into
the hundred and that the hundred fired

South Armagh (Mr. Connellan) has well
described it as equalling the Battle of
Scarva. It is a most extraordinary

hit or graze any of the hundred, but the
fact, according to the newspaper, is that
they could not. Then they were tied up
and this work was carried out and the
hundred men disappeared into empty air.
We cannot be fooled. The Government may think they can fool us, but they
cannot fool us. They brought in the

The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Pollock): This Bill has been in the hands
of hon. Members for the last week or
eight days. Concurrently with its distribution I also had circulated a White
Paper which explains in very full detail
all the particulars of this Measure. This
simplifies my work to-day, because I do
not think the House will expect me to
recapitulate all the details which appear
in this White Paper. To put it shortly,
it will be within the knowledge of the
House that the Unemployment Insurance Fund had at an early period in
our story here in Ulster accumulated a
deficit of something over £3,000,000. As
it was quite impossible for the Province
to continue to bear such a continued
accumulation as was represented by this
sum a re-insurance agreement was entered
into with the Imperial Authorities
whereby an immediate writing off of a sum
of four hundred odd thousand pounds,
the odd figures in the amount, was completed and the amount reduced to an even
figure of £3,000,000.
The nature of that arrangement is also
within the knowledge of the House. In
effect our Government undertook to extinguish the £3,000,000 to which I have
referred by an annual sum of £100,000.
It was contemplated that in 30 years that
amount would disappear. It will also be
within the recollection of the House, at
least some of the Members who give their
attention to financial matters will recall,
that for three years in succession I charged
the sum of £100,000 by way of expenditure against our revenue, that figure representing the amount required to carry
out the bargain with the Imperial
Authorities, but when we submitted our
accounts to the Joint Exchequer Board
they declined to admit that this was a
charge that was proper against our contribution, and, therefore, we had to discover some other means by which we
could in effect carry out the arrangement
we entered into in regard to the extinction
of the debt.
The British Government undertook at
that time to pay a very substantial part
of the interest on this £3,000,000, so that
the burden was not actually so heavy as
would appear on the face of it. This Bill
provides the method by which the result
that I have referred to can be accomplished, and the White Paper which has
been circulated gives the House the information that the cash value of the
capital fund and of the reserve fund which
has been accumulated amounts to
£1,275,000. It is contemplated by this
Measure that the investment of that
money will provide a yearly sum which
based upon a 4 per cent. return will extinguish the liability in a period of something less than 22 years. Of course, if the
interest is calculated upon a higher rate,
say 5 per cent., such as we have been

APPOINTMENT OF ASSISTANT
PRINCIPALS.
1. Mr. HEALY asked the Minister of
Finance whether any arrangements have
been made with the Imperial Civil Service Commissioners for the appointment
of British competitors to the grade of
Assistant Principal in the Northern Ireland Service; and whether he does not
think these officials should be recruited
for the Northern Service by local examination.
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Pollock): An arrangement has been in
force for some years under which the
British Civil Service Commissioners have
allowed Northern Ireland to utilise, for
the recruitment of assistant principals
for our administrative Departments, the
examination which they hold annually
for the Home, Indian, Colonial and Consular Services. In view of the fact that
only occasional recruitment to this grade
is required in Northern Ireland (on the
average one candidate per annum), the
use of the British examination, which is,
of course, open to Northern Ireland candidates, is considered to be the most
effective and economical means of recruitment.
As regards the latter part of the hon.
Member's question, I presume I interpret
him rightly as suggesting that the
assistant principal grade be filled in
future by a special local examination confined to junior officers already in our
service. I am unable to assent to such a
suggestion. Recruitment to assistant
principal posts, must, in
my view,
normally continue to be made from outside the Service by competitive examination amongst candidates of University
Honours standard. However, vacancies
may, in exceptional circumstances, be
filled by the promotion of suitable officers
serving in one of the junior grades, as
has been done in the past.
Mr. HEALY: Does the right hor
Gentleman not think that is an insult to
the efficient Junior Civil Servants he has
got at present?

TEACHERS PREMATURELY
RETIRED.
a conse-
3. Mr. BEATTIE asked the Minister
of Finance whether he is aware that a
number of teachers have been obliged to
retire prematurely on account of mental
and physical maladies, and as
quence are inadequately pensioned and
necessarily very embarrassed; and whether
he will consider the propriety of formulating a statutory order which would
enable him to increase the pensions of
such teachers by adding years to their
services, as has been done in the case of
Model School Teachers.
Mr. POLLOCK: In reply to the hon.
Member, a certain number of teachers
retire prematurely each year on medical
grounds, but I do not agree that the
amounts of pension granted are necessarily
inadequate, having regard to the greatly
increased salaries on which the amounts
of pension are now based.
The award of additional years to
certain Model School Teachers was made
by the Civil Service Committee under
the powers conferred upon them by the
Government of Ireland Act, 1920, by
reason of the transfer of Model Schools
from Government to Local Authorities.
There is no power to award additional
years, for the purpose of pension, to the
actual service of any other class of
teacher, nor do I consider that the circumstances warrant the introduction of
a Statutory Order to that end.

PENSIONS OF MODEL SCHOOL
TEACHERS.
4. Mr. BEATTIE asked the Minister
of Finance whether he can state the
number of the teachers employed in
Model Schools who retired since the
Government of Northern Ireland assumed
responsibility for education; the number
of years added to the service of each;
the pensions to which each would have
been entitled had no years been added to
the service; the number of years of
service each actually had without the
added years, and the actual pension
allocated to each.
Mr. POLLOCK : The hon. Member
evidently refers to Model School Teachers
who were serving as such on the 1st
February, 1922, and who were awarded
compensation by the Civil Service Committee as a result of the transfer of the
schools in which they were serving to
Local Education Authorities. All the
teachers who received such compensation
continued their service under the various
Local Education Authorities, and, with
the exception of five, are all still serving.
The number who received compensation
was 70.
The number of added years varied
according to the age and length of
service of the teacher, the maximum
number being 11 years and 10 months.
It is not possible to say in the majority
of cases what pensions these teachers
would have been entitled to if they had
not been granted added years,
as the
award of pension depends on a teacher
continuing to serve a requisite number of
years and is based on average salary
payable at the end of the term of service,
and these teachers had not served for the
number of years necessary to qualify for
pension.
It would not be possible, without considerable labour, to set out the number
of added years and the actual amount in
the case of each compensation award,
but it may be stated generally that each
teacher obtained an additional oneeightieth of average salary for each added
year, subject to a maximum of 40/80ths.

EDUCATION COMMITTEES.

The PARLIAMENTARY SECRE-
THE
TARY OF
MINISTRY OF
EDUCATION (Mr. Robb): Free books
are supplied to necessitous pupils by the
Belfast and Londonderry Education
Committees and by the North Antrim,
Londonderry and Limavady, Magherafelt, Clogher, Strabane and Castlederg,
and Omagh Regional Education Committees.
The following Committees also have
made provision in their financial schemes
for the supply of books to necessitous
children should the occasion arise-Antrim, Larne, Lisburn and Belfast, Fermanagh, Coleraine, Cookstown and
Dungannon.
Free mid-day meals are supplied to
necessitous pupils in the City of Belfast
and about sixty pupils in Lisburn Free
School are supplied daily with bread and
milk, as was customary prior to the
transfer of the school.
