RIFLES IN NORTHERN IRELAND.
8. Mr. HEALY asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether he has seen the
report of a London trial, at which a man
named William R. Horend, giving a
Newry address, sued the National Provincial Bank in respect of rifles inscribed
"For God and Ulster" purchased in Belfast and shipped to China; if he can
state whether these were Government
property, and the price received; or
whether the approval of the Home Office
was sought before the removal of the
rifles from the Belfast arsenal.
Sir DAWSON BATES: I have seen
newspaper reports of the trial referred
to by the hon. Member, but I may point
out that he is in error in suggesting that
arms have been purchased in Belfast and
shipped to China. The latter part of the
question does not, therefore, arise.
I think it desirable, however, in view
of the sinister implication underlying the
hon. Member's question, to explain to the
House that while applications for the
purchase of surplus arms, etc., in the custody of the Police Authorities are made
from time to time by various parties, before any such proposal is entertained the
most searching inquiries are instituted to
test the bona fides of the transaction.
All arrangements in regard to the disposal of such stores are carried out in
accordance with most stringent regulations laid down for the purpose by the
Imperial Authorities in co-operation with
my Ministry involving full disclosure of
the parties concerned, the country of destination, and finally, the issue by the
Board of Trade of the necessary licence
for export.
I can, therefore, give the House the
assurance that no such transaction as that
suggested by the hon. Member has taken
place or could possibly take place.
Mr. HEALY: Will the right hon.
Gentleman tell us whether he or any
member of his Department had any
negotiations with this gentleman, Mr.
Horend, from Newry, and also whether
he was aware at the time that these rifles
were intended to be shipped over to South
America or China?
Sir DAWSON BATES: The gentleman referred to did try to get rifles, but
he did not get them.
Mr. HEALY: Did you at the time
make any inquiry as to where these rifles
were intended for, and whether the
possible effect was not to kill Christian
missionaries in China?
Sir DAWSON BATES: If my hon.
Friend had really taken the trouble
to listen to my answer he would
have seen the steps my office took to avoid
any such possibility as my hon. Friend
refers to. May I add again that no rifles
were purchased or sent out.
Mr. HEALY: Owing to the unsatisfactory reply given I purpose to raise this.
matter, with your permission, on the adjournment.
Mr. DEVLIN: Can the right hon.
Gentleman explain the invitation sent to
contractors to tender for rifles, ammunition and revolvers in the possession of the
Government, and say whether these contractors have so tendered?

:

MEDICAL BENEFIT SYSTEM.
10. Mr. BEATTIE asked the Minister
of Labour whether he can state if it is a
fact that when a prescription is given to
a panel patient by a doctor a chemist
has a right to refuse to include in the
prescription one of the prescribed ingredients owing to cost, and thereby
deprive the patient of the best treatment.
Mr. ANDREWS: The answer is in the
negative. The chemist's term of service
require him to supply, with reasonable
promptness, any drug or prescribed
appliance ordered by an insurance doctor
on an official prescription form, irrespective of its cost.
Mr. BEATTIE: Is the Minister aware
that chemists have already refused cases
owing to the cost of the prescription received, and whether in such cases the
Ministry of Labour would not pay the
surplus required?
Mr. ANDREWS: No, I am not aware
that that statement is correct. If the
hon. Member will furnish me with the
names of such chemists I will have the
matter carefully investigated.

competition to which our farmers are
being subjected at this time of intense
agricultural depression.
The MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE
(Sir Edward Archdale): The answer to
the first part of the hon. Member's
question is in the affirmative.
With regard to the apprehension which
may exist in the minds of stock-breeders
as to the danger of the introduction of
disease through the use of these imported
oats, I would refer the hon. Member to
the reply which I gave on the 16th instant
to a similar question by the hon. Member for South Tyrone. I would assure
the hon. Member that there is no reason
to suppose that there is any danger to
the health of our stock arising from such
importations.
I am
aware of the competition with
which farmers in Northern Ireland are
faced through the importation of oats
from Russia, but it is not within the
powers of the Government of Northern
Ireland to prohibit such imports.

The following report was made from the

Oral Answer to Question.
LABOURERS' COTTAGES IN
IRVINESTOWN RURAL DISTRICT.
Mr. O'NEILL (for Mr. Healy) asked
the Minister of Home Affairs whether he
has seen a report of the proceedings of
the Irvinestown Rural Council on a recent
occasion, when applications for cottages
were received from eleven labourers,
all of which were rejected without inquiry, and whether he will cause an
inquiry to be held into the needs of these
people, some of whom live in places that
are unsanitary.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): I have seen the
minutes of the proceedings of the Irvinestown Rural District Council, and it
appears that the applications for cottages
referred to in the question have not been
rejected, but are still under consideration
by the Council. The necessity for an inquiry by the Ministry does not, therefore,
arise at present, but if there is an unreasonable delay on the part of the
Council in dealing with the applications I
shall take the matter up with the Council.
I may add that the Medical Officer of
Health does not appear to think that
there is so much necessity for new houses
as for some repairs to be done to the existing houses.

riders. If we were to make the owner of

the law. We are keeping the legal

be covered by third-party insurance.

NEW CLAUSE (Taking Motor Car
without Owner's Consent or other
Authority to be an Offence).
4. (1) Every person who takes and
drives away any motor car without having either the consent of the owner
thereof or other lawful authority shall
be guilty of an offence, and shall be
liable-
(a) on summary conviction, to imprisonment for a term not exceeding
three months or to a fine not exceeding fifty pounds;
(b) on conviction on indictment, to
imprisonment for a term not exceeding twelve months or to a fine not
exceeding one hundred pounds, or to
both such imprisonment and fine;
Provided that if on summary proceedings under the section, the court,
or on proceedings under this Section on
indictment the jury, are satisfied that
the accused acted in the reasonable belief that he had lawful authority, or in
the reasonable belief that the owner
would, in the circumstances of the case,
have given his consent if he had been
asked therefor, the accused shall not be
liable to be convicted of the offence.
(2) If on the trial of any indictment
for stealing a motor car the jury are of
opinion that the accused was not guilty
of stealing the motor car, but was guilty
of an offence under this Section, the
jury may find him guilty of an offence
under this Section, and thereupon he
shall be liable to be punished accordingly.
(3) Any police constable may arrest
without a warrant any person reasonably
suspected by him of having committed
or of attempting to commit an offence
under this Section.
(4) The provisions of sub-section (2).
(3) and (4) of Section twenty-one of
the principal Act, and Section four of
the Motor Vehicles and Road Traffic
Act (Northern Ireland), 1929, shall
apply to any summary proceedings and
to any conviction by, or order of, a
court of summary jurisdiction under
this Section.
Brought up, and read a First time.
Sir DAWSON BATES: I beg to move,
"That the Clause be read a Second time.'
This Clause is proposed to meet the point
raised by the hon. Member for the University (Professor Johnstone) and some
other hon. Members on the Second Reading. It deals with the question of joy
riders who take cars out without the wishes
of the owners. I made certain inquiries
from the police in order to find out to
what extent this habit was actually in
practice. I find that there has been a very
alarming increase in offences of this kind.
I find that, while for the half year ending
the 31st December, 1929, there were only
two cases of this kind in Belfast, in the
half year ended 30th June last there were
16, and from the 1st July until 17th
Motor Vehicles Bill-
Committee
28 OCTOBER 1930
October--the present month-the figures |
have gone up to 40 cases. I think hon.
Members will agree that it is necessary to
deal with the matter.
I may point out that the difficulty in
the way of prosecution in these cases
arises from the definition of "larceny"
in the Larceny Act of 1916, which defines
larceny as "the felonious taking and
carrying away with intent at the time of
taking permanently to deprive the owner
thereof." As hon. Members will appreciate, in a great majority of these cases
where cars are taken away it is not the
intention of the person taking the car
away to deprive the owner permanently
of the car. Therefore, the only thing
that can be done in cases of this kind is
to prosecute the person who takes the car
for the larceny of petrol, oil, et cetera.
We therefore propose to provide in this
new Clause that
every person who takes and drives
away any motor car without having
either the consent of the owner thereof
or other lawful authority shall be
guilty of an offence, and shall be liable.
on summary conviction, to imprisonment for a term not exceeding three
months or to a fine not exceeding fifty
pounds on conviction on indictment, to
imprisonment for a term not exceeding
twelve months or to a fine not exceeding one hundred pounds, or to both
such imprisonment and fine;
he
But if the accused can show that he acted
in the reasonable belief that
had lawful authority, or in the
reasonable belief that the owner would,
in the circumstances of the case, have
given his consent if he had been asked
therefor, the accused shall not be liable
to be convicted of the offence.
Hon. Members, I think, will appreciate
that cases will arise where in an emergency
a person might genuinely believe that the
owner of the car would have allowed him
to use it if it had been possible to get his
permission. Where a person is indicted
for stealing a motor car it may turn out
that the jury might come to the conclusion not that the accused was guilty
of the more serious offence of stealing,
but that he had taken the car within the
meaning of this Clause without the permission of the owner and without the
reasonable belief that the owner would
allow him to use it. Under those circumstances the jury can convict on that
particular account. After all, it would
be unreasonable, if the jury would not
convict of the theft, and they could and
would convict on the other count, that
the man should get off scot free.

The CHAIRMAN: I have had a new

No person may drive or permit any

Before submitting any Amendment or
new Clause to the Committee it is my
duty to examine whether it be a competent Amendment and in particular
whether it be within the title of the Bill,
and if it be not within the title of the
Bill it is my duty, as a matter of order,
to reject the Clause or Amendment. There
are exceptional cases in which the House
by order empowers and directs the

the title of the Bill, but that is not the
position in relation to this Bill. Therefore the first matter to be decided is that

Weights and Measures (Amendment)
Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.
Motion made, and Question proposed:
"That the Bill be now read a Second
time."
The MINISTER OF COMMERCE
(Mr. Barbour): I venture to say that
while discussion on Weights and Measures
Legislation is unlikely to arouse any particular interest in the minds of the general
public, yet such legislation most closely
affects the individual and the trader in well
nigh every walk of life.
Hon. Members will observe that the
basic statutes, under which the administration of the Weights and Measures Service is carried on, were passed as long ago
as 1878 and 1904. There have, of course,
been many developments in commerce
since then and one of the main objects
of the present Measure is to bring legislation into harmony with modern business
conditions by bringing within the scope of
the Acts measuring instruments which may
not have been in existence at the time
of the earlier enactments. I refer in particular to petrol pumps, though hon.
Members will note also that instruments
for measuring superficial area or for
measurement by counting are also brought
within the definition of "measuring instruments' in the 1889 Act.
Another clause of the Bill, Clause 3,
will enable fees to be charged for the comparison and verification of a local
standard. This work falls to be undertaken quinquennially.
Under existing law every petty sessions
district must keep a local sub-standard
and scales for use by Inspectors of Weights
and Measures. Under the present system of local administration, this is no
longer required, and it is desirable to
bring the law into conformity with practice. Accordingly Clause 4 of the Bill
provides that such local sub-standards and
scales shall be kept only in such places as
the Ministry of Commerce may direct.
Clause 5 embodies an amendment cf
existing law designed to relieve boroughs,
such as Bangor and Coleraine, from the
obligation to provide sets of local standards
and scale beams for use within the borough.
I think it will be generally agreed that
the requirements as to the provision of
local standards would be reasonably met
by limiting the obligation to keep such
standards to the six county councils and
the two County Boroughs of Belfast and
Londonderry.
I may add that there is to my mind
really nothing in the Bill of a controver
sial nature, and I hope the House will give
it a Second Reading. I beg to move.
Mr. COLLINS: The only thing I
noticed in this Bill is that it is like all
other Bills, it does not make much change
in anything, but there is a standard of
fees that the public will have to pay.
May I appeal to the Minister to make
these fees as small as possible having regard to the hard times the traders in
Ulster are going through at the present
time?
Mr. NIXON: I notice a few things in
this Bill. The first thing is that like
other Bills it is legislation by reference.
It refers to four different Acts-the Acts
of 1878, 1889, 1904, and 1919. Subsection 2 of Clause 3 is, I fear, going to
throw an
additional burden on shopkeepers. I will read it:-
Any power conferred by the Weights
and Measures Acts, 1878 to 1904, or
by this Act, on the Ministry of Commerce or on inspectors of weights and
measures to charge fees in respect of the
testing, examination, comparison or
verification of any weighing or measur
ing apparatus shall include and be
deemed always to have included power
to charge fees in respect of the matters
aforesaid whether or not the apparatus
is found correct or is stamped.
I wish to draw particular attention to
the last line, "whether or not the apparatus is found correct or is stamped."
I may say that I hold a Weights and
Measures certificate from the Board of
Trade, and there is a good deal more in
the subject of weights and measures than
is generally thought. A practice—and a
very useful practice it is too--has grown
up in the country districts of Northern
Ireland under which traders bring in
their scales and weights to be inspected
2169 Weights and Measures Bill -
Tithe Rentcharge Bill 2170
28 OCTOBER 1930
and tested. Of course, they must have
been stamped or they would not be in use.
If on inspection they were found to be
correct no fee could lawfully be charged.
The best way 1 can put forward my
point is by an illustration.
If a shopkeeper brought me twenty weights to be
tested and I tested them by the local substandard and found fifteen of them correct I could not legally charge him for
those fifteen weights, but only for the five
that were incorrect and that would have
to be adjusted and then re-stamped.
Under this sub-section I take it that all
weights and scales that are tested will
have to pay a fee to be fixed by the Ministry of Commerce whether they are
correct or incorrect. I may say that
weights and measures-weights particularly-that are used for dry goods, tea
and the like, do not require to be adjusted very often. On the other hand,
butchers' weights require a lot of watching because they become incorrect very
soon. I would like the Minister of Commerce to give attention to this point. I
know it is not the object of the Minister
to put any more difficulties in the way of
traders, because a lot of them find it
sufficiently hard to exist at the present
time, but I would like the Minister to
consult some person who would be in a
position to give him information on this
point.
As the law stood in my time there was
no authority to charge a fee on weights
and measures that were tested and found
to be correct, and I am quite sure the
law has not been changed since then. The
Ministry will have considerable power as
to the fixing of the fees to be charged for
the inspection and verification of weights
and measures, and I hope the present
fees will not be increased. I know that
at the present time there are a lot of
weighing machines in this city-I refer
to small counter weighing machines-that
are in perfect order but do not actually
weigh correctly owing to the way they
are used. I refer to the small machines
on handcarts. No matter how perfect
a machine is, before it can give correct
results it must be on a level surface.
When a machine is used on a handcart
it will not give correct results, and
machines are to be seen being used in that
manner in this city every day. I just
mention that in passing in the hope that
it will receive attention in the future. I
am glad the Bill is going to be extended
to deal with petrol pumps, because I have
often wondered if they measured correctly. I do not know whether they have
been subjected to any inspection up to
the present. The Minister signifies they
have not, and I think it is time they were
tested and inspected just like any other
weighing or measuring instrument.
Question put, and agreed to.
Bill accordingly read a Second Time
and committed to a Committee of the
whole House for to-morrow.
Tithe Rentcharge and Variable Rents
Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.
one-
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Pollock): This Bill, which I now have the
duty of submitting to the House for
Second Reading, is known as the Tithe
Rentcharges and Variable Rents Bill. As
probably most of the Members of the
House know, the system of the payment
Under
of tithes is a very ancient one.
the Mosaic dispensation an obligation was
thrown on all people, as a moral and religious obligation, to contribute
tenth of the produce of the soil towards
the establishment and continuance of their
religious institutions. This moral obligation afterwards acquired the full force of
custom, and custom, as we know, is very
often as strong a feature of obligation as
the law itself. Later on ecclesiastical law
took its place. It was of a very definite
character and really took the place of
Statute law in respect of its observance
by the people. Finally the system became part of the jurisprudence not only
of this country but of almost all the
Christian countries of Europe.
Coming to our own country, which
naturally is the matter that concerns us
at the present moment, it was found in
the early part of the last century that the
conditions obtaining regarding the imposition of tithes which largely involved
payment in kind of the produce itselfwere unsatisfactory, and consequently in
the year 1838, an Act was passed under
which the Tithe Rentcharge was liable to
be increased or diminished by the Courts
of Quarter Sessions in accordance with the
rise and fall in the price of corn as
published in the Dublin Gazette. By the
Trish Church Act of 1869, as we know,
the Church in Ireland was disestablished.
Tithe Rentcharge Bill-
Second Reading
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Pollock]
Under this Act, the ownership of Tithes
belonging to the Church was transferred
to the Church Commissioners, and later
on, by subsequent legislation, to the Government. During this period, that is to
say, from 1870 forward, the Tithes still
continued to be paid on a system proportion to the value of produce, and these
values, as I have said, when adjusted annually, were published in the Dublin
Gazette.
In the year 1898, however, exception
was taken to the unsatisfactory method of
publishing the prices of corn, and in that
year, the Court of Appeal decided that
the Court of Quarter Sessions had no jurisdiction to vary Tithe Rentcharges. To
meet this difficulty, the legislature passed
an Act in 1900, which set up a new canon
of variation for terms of fifteen years to
correspond with the average percentage
of variation of fair rents in each county.
This scheme was embodied in the wellknown Irish Land Act of 1903, known as
the "Wyndham Act."
In the last period of fifteen years,
commencing in 1915, there were very few
fair rents fixed, owing to war and other
disturbed conditions. Furthermore, by
Section 23 of the Northern Ireland Act
of 1925, the system of
of fixing fair
rents by means of a Judicial Tribunal
was abolished. In order to meet this
difficulty, it is proposed to deal with this
by legislation in the Measure which I am
now submitting, in the manner set out in
Clause 1 of the Bill. If hon. Members
will refer to that Clause they will see
that if the valuation of rentals, based
upon what was regarded as a fair rent,
had continued to be assessed by the Land
Commissioners, it is estimated that the
probable reduction would have amounted
to eight per cent., and, therefore, as will
be seen from the first Clause of the Bill,
provision is made to dispose of them
based upon this principle.
In the case of private persons receiving
Tithe Rentcharges, Sub-section (2) of the
Clause enables these holders to agree to
the eight per cent. reduction, but if
agreement cannot be reached between the
two parties, the Clause leaves them in
the position of having recourse to the
original Tithe Rentcharge Act of 1900.
The point is dealt with in this way, because it is doubtful whether a public
general Bill of Parliament should impose
a direct alteration in any sum payable
by one private individual to another.
That deals with the first Clause of the
Bill. The second Clause is concerned
simply with the power of disposal by the
Ministry of Finance of tithe rent charges
which are vested in them and form part
of the Irish Church Temporalities Fund.
The proceeds of the sales of these tithes
are handed over to the Exchequer and
merged in this fund, and little by little
we expect the whole system of tithe rent
charges will disappear altogether as a
source of revenue. I beg to move.
Mr. O'NEILL: I do not know whether
I am doing my duty or not in not moving the rejection of this Bill, because I
think that but for Clause 2 of the Bill

I think I am right in stating that Clause

Northern Ireland.

the Ministry of Finance may sell any

amount of the tithes. Automatically that
passed to the Exchequer. That was done.
automatically. And so all the talk the
hon. Member indulged in in regard to the
utilisation of funds has no bearing whatever on this particular case. The amount
is very trifling. As I say, they are only

To introduce the question of the Unemployment Insurance liability into this
question is outside the argument altogether, and has no bearing on it in any
shape or form. That is all I can say in
relation to the picture the hon. Member
has drawn of the liability forced upon

It has no bearing whatever on this particular case. It is simply a question of

very simple method which we are introducing by this small Measure.

and farmers. But, as I say, they never

:-

CENSORSHIP OF FILMS.
4. Mr. CONNELLAN asked the Prime
Minister whether the Government proposed to introduce legislation for the
enforcement of a more stringent censorship of cinematograph productions and
pictorial advertisements relating thereto;
for the grading of pictures in adult only
and juvenile groups; and whether the
Government propose to introduce legislation to deal with objectionable literary
publications.
Sir DAWSON BATES:
This matter
has been kept carefully under supervision
by the Government of Northern Ireland
for some years. A censorship of films
which appears to be in every way adequate
is exercised by the British Board of Film
Censors, whose certificate embodies a
classification, stating whether the film in
question is suitable for universal exhibition or for adult audiences only. Local
authorities have power to refuse a licence
to any place of entertainment at which
films are exhibited which have not been
passed by the British Board of Censors.
There is also power under the existing
law to deal with pictorial advertisements
or literary publications of an indecent or
objectionable character.
In view of these facts the introduction
of fresh legislation does not appear to be
called for.
Mr. CONNELLAN: Might I ask the
Minister if he is satisfied that the present
conditions are sufficient to meet the great
demand there is for a more rigorous
censorship of plans and publications.

CLASS IV. No. 3.
UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE.
Question proposed: That a supplementary sum not exceeding £261,000 be
granted to His Majesty for the service of
the year ending 31st March, 1931, to defray the contribution to the Unemployment Fund, under the Unemployment
Insurance Acts, 1920 to 1930, and the
Equalisation Payment to the Northern
Ireland Unemployment Fund, under the
Unemployment Insurance (Agreement)
Acts (Northern Ireland), 1926 and 1929.
The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.
Andrews): If I wished to pursue the line
of least resistance to-day I probably would
make a very short direct explanatory
statement as regards the estimate itself.
But considering that I am asking hon.
Members to vote a very large sum,
namely, £261,000, and also that I am
aware of the fact that there is a great
deal of loose thinking and many misunderstandings and some misrepresentations in reference to the payment of
unemployment benefit, it has occurred to
me that I ought to take advantage of this
opportunity to make a full and perfectly
frank statement in connection with the
matter. But before doing so I would like
your ruling as to whether it would be
permissible under the circumstances which I
have tried to describe.
The CHAIRMAN: The matter has
been so frequently explained to the House
that I think there will be little doubt.
The debate at large upon the general
question of unemployment must arise
upon the principal estimate and that,
upon the ground that the sum set down.
Supply-
Supplementary Estimates
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[The Chairman]
for the salary of the Minister is supposed
to cover all the activities of the Ministry
and therefore are subject to criticism at
that stage.
In this estimate there is no
sum relating to the salary of the Minister
and the discussion upon this particular
Vote must take cognisance of and be circumscribed by that fact.
Upon the other hand the question
raised is clearly one of very great magnitude and I propose to deal with it therefore and afford Members the exercise of
rights upon the generous scale that I have
hitherto permitted, subject always to this
condition: If I reach the opinion at some
stage that the discussion has then passed
beyond the reasonable limits of this Resolution, I will expect hon. Members, in
virtue of the liberty I have afforded, to
return to what is, after all, the main
question. It must be remembered that
what is here asked in this Resolution is a
sum to defray the contribution to the Unemployment Fund under the Unemployment Insurance Acts, and second, in
relation to the Insurance Agreement Act.
Now I apprehend that hon. Members will
desire to co-operate with me in affording
what might perhaps be regarded from the
strict point of view a somewhat generous
indulgence, and I know they will respond.
I think that will make the position clear.
Mr. DEVLIN: In order that there
may be no misunderstanding in this matter, do I understand you to rule that it
is not within the province of hon. Members to discuss the general question of
unemployment? Because that would be
most extraordinary.
The CHAIRMAN: No. It would be a
most ordinary ruling, and it would be
most extraordinary if it were otherwise.
I think I have made it perfectly clear
that the one occasion on which there can
be practically unfettered discussion on the
general question is when the main
Estimate is before the Committee. I
have so frequently dealt with the decision
of May upon that point that it must be
within the memories of all hon. Members.
Discussion on a supplementary Estimate,
in the strict interpretation of the rule,
must be restricted to the subject matter
of the Estimate. But I am now indicating to the Committee that I do not propose to confine them so rigidly as that,
and when the hon. Gentleman (Mr.
Devlin) comes to speak presently, as I
have no doubt he will, he will find that I
am not unwilling to be generous in my indulgence, always assuming, of course,
that the Committee will co-operate with
me in keeping the discussion within
reasonable limits.
Mr. ANDREWS: I am very much
obliged for your ruling and will en
deavour to conform strictly to the limits
which you have laid down. In dealing
with this matter I want to say at the
very beginning that I do not intend to
say one word of a political or party
character, because I have always held,
and have frequently stated in this House.
that there is so much tragedy associated
with unemployment that it ought to be
lifted above party controversy and placed
upon the higher plane of public service.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear).
I feel that it is desirable that we should,
in the first instance, endeavour to see how
far we are in agreement. I take it that we
are all agreed that in a Christian country
such as this people must not be allowed
to starve. It follows from that that when
it is impossible to obtain work for those
who are available for work, and who are
willing to work, it is necessary that
they should obtain from somewhere the
necessaries of life. Now, as far as I
know, there are only two ways in which
that can be done. One is that the responsibility-the entire responsibilityshould be placed upon the guardians and
that the financial burden should be
thrown upon the rates. There are very
few people who agree with that view, because it is generally recognised that what
the guardians give, either in the form of
indoor or outdoor relief, although, unfortunately, necessary in quite a number
of instances, is demoralising, because it is
nothing more or less, obviously, than a dole.
The other way is to pay unemployment
benefit, which is much less objectionable,
because it is unfair to describe it as a
dole, in view of the fact that the workers
pay contributions when in employment.
I would like to point out at this stage
that no one has suggested a better plan
of dealing with the matter than through
the medium of unemployment benefit
when work cannot be obtained for those
who are anxious to get work. I think
that those who in such a sweeping way
condemn this scheme ought to be able to
recommend a better one.
I was speaking a few days ago to two
American gentlemen. They pointed out

As a
Now, of course, we all know that the
best method of dealing with the problem
is to secure work for everybody. I am
not going to criticise Mr. Thomas.
matter of fact I sympathised with him.
greatly for a fellow feeling makes us
wondrous kind-when he was Minister of
Employment. A very short time after he
took over his duties he said that he wished
the Government to be judged by their
success in dealing with the unemployment.
problem, but later on, when he had become-I say it with all respect-a wiser
and a somewhat sorrier man, he stated
what I have often stated in this House
and on public platforms, namely, that,
as far as I can see, there is no way of
solving the unemployment problem,
speaking quite frankly, except by getting
more work for our people through our
obtaining more customers for the commodities which we produce not only at
home but throughout the world.
But coming back to the payment of
unemployment benefit, I would like to
point out that it is criticised from two
sides, very often at the same time. On
the one hand it is held that it is too
generously given. It is said that it is
demoralising. I have already dealt with
that aspect of the case. It is stated
openly that it prevents people from
taking low wages which they might
otherwise be willing to accept, and,
further, people go on to say that under
our recent legislation practically everybody that comes along can get unemployment benefit. In answer to that I am in
a position to say that, except to some
extent in domestic service, and at very
busy times of the year in certain districts
on certain farms, there is practically no
vacancy in Northern Ireland which is
not filled. You may change the personnel of the unemployed by putting
pressure upon certain persons, if need be,
to accept work, but you do not alter the
number of unemployed unless you can
produce more work, and that is the Alpha
and the Omega of the whole problem. As
regards everybody that comes along
getting benefit-I may now be giving an
argument to some of my opponents, but
I do not mind that; I am going to make
this statement perfectly frankly-some
people are not aware of the fact that
18,000 claims have been turned down by
the courts since our recent Act was passed.
These claims have been turned down for
various reasons, most of them due to the
fact that it was held that the claimants
were not normally in insurable employment.
Now the attack from the other side is
that it is not given generously enough,
that people are turned down unfairly and
that this not normally insurable condition
is quite unjust. I do not think so, and
for this reason: You must remember
what the Unemployment Fund is. It is
an insurance scheme, and it is a contributory scheme. Obviously it would be
unjust to give from a fund to which the
many contribute benefit to those who do
not contribute. The people who contribute would have a great grievance if
benefit were given equally freely to those
who do not contribute at all, or who,
at any rate, have not contributed for a
great many years. The whole thing would
become impossible from an administrative
point of view.
I would further reply to the criticism
against my Department and against myself,
that the legislation and administration here.
are exactly the same as in Great Britain,
just as if this Parliament did not exist
and as if the matter were dealt with from

than their fellow-country men in Great

I have never said that I approve of every
provision in our Unemployment Insurance
Acts. Quite the contrary is my view.
When I introduced the last Unemployment Insurance Act in this House I
pointed out quite clearly that I felt that
the pendulum was swinging too far and
that I dreaded the recoil in the interests
of our working people. I dread that recoil more to-day, because, if you read the
history of matters of this kind, you will
always see that if there is a step too far
in one direction there is a step back, perhaps, too far in another direction.
I know quite well that one form of
criticism that is directed at the present
time against the administration of the
Fund from one section of our community
is that certain persons-I am only citing
this as an example-can work two or three
days in the week earning £2 or £3
per day, and then draw unemployment benefit for the other three
four days. I do not justify that, but it
is so in Great Britain and so, putting first
things first always, it must be so here.
or
course, the
Another form of criticism is of quite a
different character. I am going to give
two examples from my own experience of
the last few days in order to show what I
mean. It is ill-informed criticism. In
the first place, I met a friend who said
"You know this scheme of yours of giving
the dole broadcast is perfectly preposterous. I offered a young man of fourteen years of age 10s a week and he would
not take it because he preferred to
be on the dole." Of
obvious
answer to that is that a
young man of 14
years of age is
not an insured person. He does not become insured until he is 16 years of age,
and therefore it was unthinkable that he
refused to accept employment at 10s a
week because he looked forward to getting the dole two or three years afterwards. That is one form of ill-informed
criticism that I am up against almost
every day.
Another example is this. There is, I
dare say, a difference of opinion upon
cases of this kind. I was told of a man
who had refused £1 a week and said he
preferred to remain on unemployment
benefit. I inquired into the case. What
did I find to be the position? The man
had a wife and four children, and was,
therefore, entitled to 34s a week unemployment benefit. What about the
£1? I found that he was paying
7s a week in rent, rates approximately
is a week, his insurance contributions
approximately another shilling a week, a
total of 9s a week, leaving only 11s a
week for the man, if he had accepted
work, to support his wife and four children and himself. Obviously no man can
be expected to keep his wife and children
and himself in respectability on 11s a
week. Under those circumstances, therefore, I maintain it was not that the
amount of unemployment benefit was too
much, but that the wages offered were too
low.
I observed, with satisfaction, yesterday
evening in the evening paper that in His
Majesty's Gracious Speech the Imperial
Government stated that they were
preparing to set up a Commission
to inquire into unemployment insurance legislation and its alleged maladministration. I venture to hope
very sincerely that those who will form
that Commission will approach the problem from a non-party and non-electioneering point of view. I hope that they
will be earnest, thoughtful, practical men,
whose one endeavour will be to do the
right thing at the right time. Such a task
is indeed a difficult one for any body of
men to be asked to perform; but I say
that if, when they have investigated the
problem, they can remove from the scheme
of things certain just criticisms which can
be brought against it, directed from both
sides, they will have done a great service
to our country and a great service to our
working people in particular.

nation. A nation is respected; a country

that it is not the practice to allude to
hon. Members by their names but by the
constituencies for which they sit.
Mr. STEWART: I would make a suggestion which I made here a year and a
half ago with regard to the revival of
existing industries that are in a deplorable state. In the town of Cookstown,
the principal town in my constituency,
which I am sure I am right in stating is
the town which has been the most severely
hit by unemployment in the whole Northern area, industries which were very
flourishing a few years ago are now closed,
and no effort that I am aware of has been
made by the Government to assist in the
re-opening of them. In Caledon the
largest woollen industry in the Six
Counties has been closed, and no effort,
as far as I know, has been made by the
Government to subsidise it or to keep it
going. There is no reason why, if the
Government were very anxious to keep
employment going in a place like Caledon,
they could not find the money. I will be
asked where are we to get the money, but
I could find many other sources of expenditure that are less pressing than that of
giving employment. If the Government
made an honest effort to subsidise and to
create industries much of this unemployment would be wiped out. I support the
Vote most heartily.
Mr. MCALEER: In supporting this
supplementary estimate I wish to say that
the figures given for unemployment in
Northern Ireland are appalling, but even
then I believe that the figure of 70,000,
which has been given, only feebly expresses the number of people who are unemployed or who wll shortly be unemployed. There are 70,000 persons on the
official list. 18,000 have been turned
down on some technicality. There is no
mention of those in the rural districts
who are not insured, and there is no
doubt that by Christmas there will be
100,000 people unemployed in Ulster.
I say that, after seven or eight years of
administration, the Government stand
condemned by the figures that have been
quoted. In Belfast, the most populous
place in our area, containing as it does
one-third of the population of Northern
Ireland, the linen industry is in a woeful
state. The shipbuilding industry is the
same. Even during the present week
£1 shares in one concern in Belfast were
offered at 5/9. Belfast Corporation have
had loans approved to the extent of something over £9,000,000. I say the Government have not risen to the occasion and
our people are in a deplorable state.
While I think the Vote is necessary and
support it, I say that the Government
have not risen to the occasion as they
should in the interests of the workers and
insured people of Northern Ireland.
Queston put, and agreed to.
Resolution to be reported to-morrow.

and sixty-one thousand pounds be granted
out of the Consolidated Fund of Northern
Ireland." (Mr. Barbour.)
Resolution to be reported to-morrow.

and 64 Vict., c. 58, and s. 90 of 3 Edw. 7,

(1) Where any tithe rentcharge or
variable rent is payable to the Ministry
of Finance the sum payable in respect
of every gale thereof accruing due after
the twenty-second day of October,
nineteen hundred and thirty, shall be
Ideemed to be varied from the amount
at which it stood on the said day by
being reduced by eight per cent., and
shall be payable accordingly; and no
tithe rentcharge or variable rent payable to the said Ministry shall be varied
except in accordance with this subsection.
Mr. POLLOCK : I beg to move, in
Clause 1, page 1, line 8, to leave out the
words "twenty-second day of October,"
and to insert instead thereof the words
"first day of November."
The object of this Amendment is simply
to change the date. November 1st is the
ordinary gale day and by an oversight the
22nd October was inserted in the Bill.

Motion made and question proposed,

Mr. HEALY: I gave the Minister of
Home Affairs notice earlier in the evening
that I would ask him a question with regard to certain legal proceedings in London. There a witness stated that he had
been in negotiation for the purchase of
rifles with certain people unnamed in
Northern Ireland. The suggestion was
that there were stores of rifles in Belfast
probably under the control of the Government, and possibly rifles in other parts
of Ulster not under the official control of
the Government. What the public
would like to know is, whether before any
negotiations began, the right hon. Gentleman communicated with the Imperial
Authorities to ascertain whether a permit
would be available if the deal for these
rifles came off.
What we should also like to know would
be what price the enterprising gentleman.
from Newry offered per thousand for these
rifles, and what price the right hon.
Gentleman agreed to accept. We should
like the right hon. Gentleman to place
upon the Table the correspondence that
went on between himself and this Mr.
Horend, of Newry, over these weeks.
should also like to know at the time of the
negotiations whether he had any suspicion
of the destination of these implements of
war; whether Mr. Horend told him that
they were destined for a republic in South
America, or whether, indeed, he had an
inkling of the real destination which was
China.
We
In either event, the right hon. Gentleman hardly can say that he is guiltless,
because if the rifles were going to South
America they were obviously going there
to disturb the peace of the community,
and to be used against legitimate governments. And if they were going to China
the object was similar. Legitimate governments, established governments, do not
buy rifles through the medium of private
gentlemen, either in Newry or in Belfast.
They come direct, I think, to other governments. Therefore, the Minister of
Home Affairs must have been well aware
that he was entering into very suspicious
negotiations, and under very suspicious
circumstances.
What is troubling the public in this
matter particularly is that another event
of a very unfortunate character has occurred in this country owing to the presence of too many rifles. It would appear
that in a particular part of Northern
Ireland every man of the right hon.
Gentleman's party seems to have a rifle,
and that the people of an opposite way
Rifles in Ulster-
Adjournment
29 OCTOBER 1930
of thinking cannot secure a licence to hold
a gun even when it is to be used for the
legitimate purpose of scaring away crows
from their fruit trees.
There is published in to-day's papers a
statement by a man who lives in the
County Armagh. He said that he applied
to the right hon. Gentleman's officers for
a permit for a shot-gun and was refused.
In that same locality, and within a few
weeks of that application being rejected,
a certain event occurred to which I cannot refer in detail this afternoon, in
which hundreds of people carrying rifles,
service rifles, too, appeared on the scene
and committed a most deplorable and
wanton outrage.
I should like particularly in this matter
to refer to a statement made by the Prime
Minister a little while ago in this House.
It concerns the disposal and the keeping
of arms in Northern Ireland. The hon.
Member for Woodvale (Mr. Nixon) was
referring to certain demonstrations made
by "B" Specials to the Prime Minister
on the occasion of his visits to a certain
district in Belfast in 1923, and the Prime
Minister is reported in Hansard as saying
-22nd May, pages 1515-16
I have never asked for a mobilisation
of either the Royal Ulster Constabulary
or the "B" Special Constabulary when
I attended the hall to which the hon.
Member referred, and certain members
of the "B" Constabulary turned out of
their own accord without my knowledge.
It would appear, therefore, that we have
in this country an armed police force
responsible to nobody, not even to the
Government, who can turn out when and
where they please. This is an exceedingly
serious matter, and it gets to the bottom
of the matter that is exciting the people
of a particular district at the moment.
If
the Prime Minister's statement is correct
it means that this House is paying one
hundred thousand pounds a year to a
force of constabulary who owe no allegiance to this House or to anybody, who
are prepared to sally forth when they
please, and on any secret mission that they
may devise.
It also suggests that there
must be in Northern Ireland, apart from
the ordinary weapons of which the Government has cognisance, a certain number
of dumps or places of that kind. I should
like the Minister of Home Affairs to inform us whether his Department or he
is cognisant of such places or any stores of
arms of this kind.
Some time ago in the County Armagh
-I am not referring to Annahugh at the
moment-another place was levelled to the
ground at Breagh, three and a-half miles
from Annahugh. The outrage was repeated about twelve months later, and,
more singular still, it was publicly referred to as a matter of glorification from
an Orange platform at Scarva.
Mr. McBRIDE: There is no platform
at Scarva.
Mr. HEALY: I am speaking about an
Orange platform, not a railway platform.
The hon. Gentleman can think of no platform but a railway platform, but I understand that on at least one or two occasions
he himself figured prominently on a public
platform.
Mr. CONNELLAN: Not at Scarva;
they have only a battlefield at Scarva.
Mr. HEALY: Yes, there is a sham
battle at Scarva. The case I am speaking
about was a real battle. One of the devices in which all Governments and all
Ministers take refuge is denial, "We
know nothing of this." I remember the
occasions when somewhat similar outrages
were committed-the burning of Cork,
the looting at Trim and the burning of
Balbriggan. A very respected and prominent Member of the Imperial Parliament, Sir Hamar Greenwood, when
questioned said "We know nothing of
this, and we deny that any of our forces
took part in it." Exactly the same denial
was made by the right hon. Gentleman
a few days ago in this House in regard
to the Annahugh incident, but in connection with the case which I have quoted
for you, and in which Sir Hamar Greenwood denied responsibility a book has
recently been published by General
Crozier-
Sir DAWSON BATES: Do not
believe all those fellows.
Mr. HEALY: You believed them once.
You were bed-fellows for a while. According to the book he has published you
lived in such conditions at Craigavon. I
would not be surprised that sometimes
you had no bed. You cleared out the
children of the house and prepared yourselves for a seige. I am sure you would
not run away.
Mr. SPEAKER: I think it would be
better if the hon. Member addressed the
Chair.

ADOPTION OF CHILDREN ACT-
CASE OF ISABELLA MCMURRAY.
1. Mr. NIXON asked the Attorney-
General whether Isabella McMurray, of
8 James Street, is to be deprived of the
benefit of the Adoption of Children Act
by reason of the fact that she is unable
to fee a solicitor, and because no rules
have been made for the administration
of the Act, and, if so, whether the Act
is to become inoperative so far as people.
without means are concerned.
(Mr.
The ATTORNEY-GENERAL
Babington): In a statement which I
made when the hon. Member raised this
question on the Motion for the Adjournment on the 15th instant, I stated
specifically that the absence of rules did
not prevent the court from making an
order, and that until such time as the
rules were made the court is bound to
make its own rules.
In reply to a question by the hon.
Member on Thursday, 23rd instant, I informed him that the lack of funds to
employ a solicitor did not in any way bar
an applicant from obtaining the benefits
of the Act.
These two replies appear to answer the
question now put by the hon. Member,
and I am afraid that there is nothing
which I can say that would elucidate
the matter further.
Mr. NIXON: Will the Attorney-
General kindly say why a paid official
instructed the woman to get a solicitor
instead of doing what he was paid to do
himself?

The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.

I assume that my hon. Friend refers
to the Ulster Farmers' Produce Society.
to whom a loan was made some years ago
from the Government Loans Fund under
statutory powers. The loan which was
made against security, is repayable
over a period of years. There is a certain
amount of the loan repayment in arrear.
but this does not necessarily imply that
the money is lost. This matter has been
under the notice of the Public Accounts
Committee, and in the event of a loss
ultimately emerging, the matter must
automatically be brought by me to the
notice of this House as, under Statute,
the direction of Parliament is necessary

written off.

PROTECTION OF SEA FISHERIES.
3. Mr. LEEKE asked the Minister of
Commerce whether he is aware that seaplanes are being used to detect poaching
trawlers, and as this seems an effective and
economical method whether he will engage
one to protect the fisheries of Northern
Ireland.
The MINISTER OF COMMERCE
(Mr. Barbour): I understand that it is the
practice of the patrols of the Royal Air
Force to co-operate with the Imperial
Ministry of Agriculture and Fisheries in
the detection of offences committed by
foreign fishing vessels inside British territorial waters. So far as my information
goes, however, seaplanes are not employed
exclusively on fishery duties and the services rendered by them in connection with
fishery offences are performed in the course
of their normal patrolling duties.
In regard to the latter part of the question, I am unable to accept the view that
the employment of a seaplane would offer
either the most effective or the most
economical means of protecting the Northern Irish fisheries since, in the majority
of instances, a seaplane could not itself
effect an arrest and could only function
effectively in conjunction with a protection
cruiser, and also because the employment
of a seaplane and the provision of the
shore organisation necessary for its upkeep for the sole purpose of protecting
our fisheries would entail a wholly inordinate expenditure.
Mr. LEEKE: Does the right hon.
Gentleman mean to say he is going to
}
take no steps to protect the Northern
fishermen from the ravages of the English
trawlers?
Mr. BARBOUR: Not at all. In fact,
I may say that included in the report of
what I might term the Bag Net Committee, which has just been completed, a suggestion is made as to whether or not the
employment of a quick motor launch
might be suitable for this purpose, but
any method which might come within
reasonable outlay will be considered to
see if protection can be given.
Mr. NIXON: Will such protection
cover the disputed waters of Lough Foyle?

DRAINAGE SCHEME-SURVEY
OF UPPER BANN.
7. Mr. O'NEILL asked the Minister
of Finance whether a survey of the Upper
Bann, between Portadown and Lough
Neagh, was made before the present
drainage scheme was put into operation,

any part of the drainage scheme provides
for the removal of these obstructions.
Mr. POLLOCK: No detailed survey of
that part of the Upper Bann River to
which the hon. Member refers has been
made by my Ministry's engineers.
The Bann Drainage Scheme recently
prepared does not make any provision for
the carrying out of any improvement
works in the Upper Bann other than such
improvement of the outfall to Lough
Neagh as may be found to be necessary
in order that the greatest possible benefit
may be derived from the reduced level of
Lough Neagh.
I may add that there are apparently
three public bodies interested statutorily
in the maintenance of the river channel
of the Upper Bann, namely, the Lough
Neagh Drainage District Trustees, the
Upper Bann Navigation Trustees, and the
Newry Port and Harbour Trust, and I
am at present investigating the precise
responsibilities of these bodies in order
that any neglect in the proper maintenance of the channel may be rectified.

Education Committee, on 14th August

Elementary School.

August to terminate this teacher's employment on 29th November. No inquiry
has been asked for or held.
Mr. NIXON: Do you consider that the
4th August, the anniversary of the day on

Gentleman, it is difficult to discuss an
important matter of this character, and
I venture to say that if he calls at the
Ministry of Education offices, my hon.
and learned Friend (Mr. Robb) will give
him satisfaction.
Mr. ELLIOTT: Would the hon.
Gentleman tell this House where Ballycregagh is?

OPENING OF NEW PARLIAMENT
BUILDINGS.
12. Mr. HENDERSON asked the
Prime Minister whether he can state the
date of the official Opening of the New
Parliament Buildings at Stormont.
Mr. POLLOCK: I have been asked
to reply to the hon. Member. I have
considerable hesitation in attempting to
forecast, even approximately, the probable date of the official opening of the
New Parliament Buildings. 1
may,
however, state, for his information, and
that of the House generally, that, so far
as can be seen at present, the transfer
of the Departmental Staff which will be
occupying the upper floors of the building will be effected in the summer of
next year.
A considerable volume of
work will then remain to be done in the
Parliamentary portion of the building,
but this, I am given to understand, will
occupy at least a further twelve months
before its completion. This points to the
opening of the building, referred to by
the hon. Member, taking place some time
in 1932.
Mr. HENDERSON: In view of the

in Northern Ireland could the Cabinet
not take steps to have the Processional

competent to carry out that work?
Mr. POLLOCK: All these matters
that are associated with the completion of
the Processional Road have been anticipated and are being proceeded with now.
In regard to the question of furniture, the

House, and therefore I am not prepared
to give any undertaking. It will be done.
by tender. We may use our influence,

PAYMENT OF PENSION-ESTHER
MCCORMICK.
14. Mr. NIXON asked the Minister of
Labour whether the pension payable to
an afflicted orphan, Esther McCormick,
101 Sugarfield Street, was stopped because
the child was certified by a doctor as unfit
to attend school; whether he does not consider the Act unjust in respect of such
cases by penalising the afflicted; and what
steps he proposes to take to correct this
and other similar injustices which the
working of the Act has disclosed.
Mr. ANDREWS: 14 years of age is
the normal limit at which children's
allowances cease to be payable. With the
object of encouraging attendance at school
after that age, however, the pensions
Acts permit the allowance to be continued
in cases where children between 14 and
16 remain full time at school.
The child referred to by the hon. Member is over 14 and, for reasons which I
deeply regret, is not attending school and
the law, which is the same here as in
Great Britain, does not provide for the
continuance of the allowance in her case.
When the pensions Acts come to be
amended again I shall be very pleased if
it is found possible to make provision for
cases of this kind.
Mr. BEATTIE: I would like to ask
whether it is a fact that in cases of sick
children between 14 and 16 years of age
who are forbidden to go to school this
allowance which is given for educational
purposes has been denied in order to pay
for private tuition in the homes? Has
the right hon. Gentleman heard of any
such cases?
Mr. ANDREWS: I have not heard of
such cases, but if it is permissible under
the Act it will be done here.
Mr. NIXON: In view of the importance
of this case, but not as a reflection on the
Minister, I propose to raise it on the Adjournment.

HOUSE OF COMMONS
VALUATION OF LABOURERS'
COTTAGES.
16. Mr. NIXON asked the Minister
of Home Affairs whether he can state the
valuation of the labourers' cottages that
have the highest valuation, the valuation
of those that have the lowest, the valuation between those extremes, the number
of each denomination, the reason of these
disparities, and whether it is the purpose
of the Government to take steps to have a
uniform valuation inasmuch as the cotages are of equal value.
Sir DAWSON BATES: I presume the
hon. Member refers to Poor Law Valuation.
In order to obtain the information
asked for, I should have to obtain returns
from the clerks of all the rural districts
in Northern Ireland, and I do not consider the value of the information
obtained would justify me in putting them
to this trouble.
I may point out, however, that the
value of all labourers' cottages is not equal
as stated in the question. The accommodation provided, and the extent of land
attached vary, and for these and other
reasons a uniform valuation could not be
placed on these cottages.
Labourers' cottages are valued on the
same principles as other dwelling-houses,
and I do not see any good reason for a
general revaluation.
BALLYMONEY LICENSING CASE.
JAMES MCHENRY, PUBLICAN.
17. Mr. BYRNE asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether his attention has
been drawn to a police case heard at a
licensing court in Ballymoney, on Monday, October the 20th, when James
McHenry, publican, of Drumaglea, Co.
Antrim, was indicted on two counts for
breaches of the Licensing Act, on one of
which the magistrates held he was not
guilty, and on the other, owing to the
unusual methods adopted by the police,
the case was dealt with under the Probation of Offenders Act; whether the
District-Inspector had the authority and
approval of the Home Office for his action
in this case when he instructed Sergeant
D. Smith, Ballycastle, to procure and
consume intoxicating liquor in McHenry's
public-house, on Sunday, 3rd August,
contrary to the law, and generally to use
every means at his disposal to entice the
publican to a breach of the Licensing Act;
and whether the Minister will mark his
disapproval of such conduct by issuing
instructions to have this instigation to
law-breaking by the police immediately
discontinued.
Sir DAWSON BATES: As an appeal
has been lodged in this case, the matter
is sub judice, and it would not, therefore,
be proper to discuss it at the present
time.
IMPORTED STRAW FOR PACKING
PURPOSES.
18. Mr. LEEKE asked the Minister of
Agriculture whether he can state if it is a
fact that the Department of Agriculture
orders all foreign imported straw used for
packing purposes to be destroyed immediately after contents of cases are unpacked; whether the Ministry possess
these powers, and, if so, why they do not
exercise them to prohibit the importation
of foreign oats and so safeguard the home
trade.
MINISTER OF
The
AGRICUL
TURE (Sir Edward Archdale): The importation into Northern Ireland of foreign
hay or straw used as packing materials is
by order of the Ministry of Agriculture
prohibited save under licence from the
Ministry. Licences for such importations
are given only in exceptional circumstances, and are subject to such conditions
as the Ministry may in any particular
case consider necessary to preclude the
possibility of the introduction of infectious animal disease. The destruction by
fire of such packing materials is a usual
condition of a licence.
The Orders of the Ministry which affect
such importations are made in exercise of
the Ministry's statutory powers under the
Diseases of Animals Act, 1894, as
amended and adopted by subsequent
enactments.
The importation of grain does not, in
the opinion of the Ministry, involve any
risk of the importation of animal disease.
To support this opinion there is the fact
that for years regular consignments of
maize from countries in which foot-andmouth disease is prevalent have been imported into Northern Ireland, and no
case of animal disease has ever arisen
therefrom.

foreign oats by an Order under the
Diseases of Animals Acts would be an
unjustifiable misuse of the powers conferred by these Acts.

I have repeatedly been told in this

children during the day, and as long as

suitable employment she is regarded as
an insured worker and is entitled to draw
benefit. In Northern Ireland that same
lady would be disallowed benefit owing to
the fact that she remained in her own
home looking after her children. That
is one instance where Northern Ireland
is out of step with Great Britain.
Another instance is in regard to the interpretation of the term "insurable
class." Insurability as interpreted in
Northern Ireland means that a person
must have been working more than fifty
per cent. of the time he has been in the
industry in which he is engaged. Assuming a boy went into an industry in 1920,
that is ten years ago, worked for four
years out of the ten, was unemployed for
the remainder of the time, and got no work
of any other kind, he is classified as not
being in insurable employment, although
during the six years he was out of work
he was seeking insurable employment. My
contention is that a man can be ten years
out of work and still be an insurable person. A man who worked in the shipbuilding industry for thirty years up to
1922 and has been unemployed for five
years is to-day disqualified from receiving
benefit on the ground that he is not an
insured worker. If the same man had
been working for only two years at the
latter end of the five years and had thirty
contributions to his credit he would be
entitled to benefit immediately. That is
a most unfair discrimination. The letter
I am about to read is a decision that has
been given in three cases:
I believe I am correct in saying that
he understands the term "normally
employed" to mean in the first instance
employment for at least half a person's
time, but that he would not say that a
man was normally working if, in fact,
he was more than half of his time idle.
If over a long period of time a person
has been employed for less than half
of each working year it is for him to
prove there is something abnormal
about his trade or his particular circumstances which prevented him from
being at least half time employed.
These three people have been for more
time out of insurable employment than
in it.
In other words, according to this insurability interpretation, a person must
have at least six months' employment out
of every year, a most outrageous and
ridiculous condition. I will not read the

forward. I know the Minister of Labour
does not agree with that interpretation of
insurability and no honest man would do
so. Some of the mill and shipyard
workers have had no employment for
several years, but they have been twenty
or thirty years in the industry and they
have had no other class of employment.
Therefore I contend they should be
treated as insurable.

Labour knows that 90 per cent. of the
men unemployed would gladly go to any
place if they got a decent hard job. I met
one man at the corner of Church Lane
yesterday who was a human derelict. He
is not in receipt of the dole. His sister
keeps him at the present time; she lets him
sleep in her house, but he has to go out
through the day. He is only one of the
many thousands of men who receive no
unemployment benefit. If we have a
Parliament of our own, why should we
deny anyone the right to live or exist? It
would be far better and cheaper for the
Minister of Labour to pay that man unemployed benefit than to keep him in the
workhouse. It would assist the Minister
of Labour if that was done.

HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Henderson]
Sooner or later you will find that the
rising generation in Northern Ireland will
rise. (ion. Members: Hear, hear.) The
day may not be far distant, and being one
of the young men I may have to grapple
with the important question of unemployment that the Minister of Labour is grappling with when that time comes. I
am convinced that if the Cabinet do not
take action some of the young unemployed
men will rise and take the same action
that the young men took in Italy. That
will mean the displacement of the right
hon. Gentleman and a good number of
his colleagues. There is no necessity why
the Cabinet should not take up this matter immediately and try, if possible, to
revive some of the industries which are
crippled at the present time. I appeal to
them not to go gallivanting round the
country during the Recess. I know some
of them will have a good time although
the Minister of Labour may not. The
Minister of Labour, who has to shoulder
the whole of the burden of the unemployed, should invite any Member on this
side who thinks he can offer suggestions
that would help him in order to reduce
the number of unemployed on the register.
He should also invite the merchant princes
and all concerned with industry in the
Province to a round-table conference in
order to see if something could not be
done to relieve the Minister of Finance
bringing in Bills to borrow money.
The right hon. Gentleman knows you
can borrow money for a time, but you
cannot borrow all the time. Sooner or
later you will find that you will be unable
to get this money even to pay unemployment benefit. The right hon. Gentleman
should take the bull by the horns, call a
conference, and see if something could not
be done to revive industries. He will thus
be helping himself and the poor people
who have, unfortunately, to go to the
labour exchanges. We were told that if
Mr. Baldwin did not solve the unemployment problem it was going to be solved
here. The right hon. Gentleman is
actually building larger labour exchanges
to cope with the increased number of unemployed. That is a terrible state of
affairs. It shows that the Government
have failed miserably in their duty. I
will be quite frank. I did not think it
worth my while to come here and waste
time over a Cow Bill. I suggested the
introduction of Bills which, if they had
been brought in, would have given employment. That was not done.
At the very least there are 100,000 men
unemployed and the number is increasing.
The outlook is not too bright, and we want
to try to brighten it. You cannot reduce
unemployment in Northern Ireland if
you go gallivanting round the country
holding political meetings at which you
run down your friends on this side of the
House. It would answer you better if
you courted the friendship of Members on
this side in grappling with this great evil.
We have a Parliament here, and it is only
what I might term an up-to-date duplicating machine, which brings in Measures
that are passed on the other side of the
Channel It would save trouble if the
money required to run this expensive
Parliament could be utilised to increase
the unemployment benefit, and let the
affairs of the Province be administered
across the water.

Mr. LEEKE: I am sorry the Minister
of Agriculture is not here, because I wish
to raise a matter of very serious import to
the whole community of Northern Ireland, and particularly to the farming
community. I may say that I gave the
Minister the usual notice that I would
raise this matter. It is with regard to
the importation of Russian oats.
I put
down a question to the Minister of Agriculture to-day and I received an answer
which I thought was very unsatisfactory,
at any rate from the point of view of the
farmers of Northern Ireland. It will be
admitted, I think, by all people who have
any knowledge of agriculture in the Six
Counties, that 1929 was the worst year
in history. I have here the official return
of the prices for 1929 and 1930, and I
will quote the comparative prices of one
or two items. I am glad to see the Minister of Agriculture has come into the
House. Take the first item in the listoats. White oats in 1929 were 6s 8d, and
in 1930, 5s 6d. The next item is flax.
The DEPUTY-SPEAKER: Will the
hon. Member tell me which of his questions he had in view when he gave notice
to raise this matter on the adjournment?
Mr. LEEKE: Number 18. In 1929
the price of flax was 10s 63d, and in 1930
it was 5s 9d. With such a condition of
affairs as that facing the people it is an
extraordinary thing that the Ministry of
Agriculture allows the importation of
foreign oats, and for what purpose? In
order to depress the home product so that
it can be bought cheaply.
The DEPUTY-SPEAKER: Do I
understand the hon. Member to argue
that it is within the competence of this
Government or the Ministry of Agriculture to prohibit the importation of
Russian oats. The hon. Member knows
that that is not within the control of this
House.
Mr. LEEKE: In his reply to-day the
Minister of Agriculture said he had
similar powers under the Diseases of Animals Act.
The DEPUTY-SPEAKER: That is a
different matter.
Mr. LEEKE: They have already prohibited the importation of straw.
The DEPUTY-SPEAKER: The hon.
Member is rather mixing up two things.
The prohibition of the importation of
straw is a matter in which the two departments act in conjunction to prevent Foot
and Mouth disease infection. In this
particular case the facts are entirely
different. It is the proposal of the hon.
Member, as I understand it, to prohibit
the importation of foreign oats absolutely,
and not under the conditions which attached to the prohibition of the importation of straw, and other matters of the
kind. That, as the hon. Member knows,
is not a matter over which this Parliament
has control.
Mr. LEEKE: If they have power to
prohibit the importation of straw why
not of oats, if it is dangerous to the community.
The DEPUTY-SPEAKER: Now the
hon. Gentleman is shifting his ground.
What we have to ascertain is a question
of fact. Does the hon. Member definitely
argue now as a matter of fact that the
Government has power to prohibit the
importation of foreign oats.
Mr. LEEKE: I will argue that they
have power to prohibit the importation of
oats, but I want to show first why they
should use the power they have. They
can stop the importation of grain and why
not oats, because both are a danger to the
public health. The Minister admitted in
his answer to-day that his Ministry had
the power to stop the importation of straw,
and that they only admitted it under
licence.
The DEPUTY-SPEAKER: Perhaps
we had better have this quite definite to
prevent any irregularity in discussion.
Will the Minister state definitely whether
his Department has it within its power
to prohibit the importation of oats as indicated in this question, or not.
Sir EDWARD ARCHDALE: No, we
have not.
Mr. LEEKE: But in his official reply
he admitted that he had the power.

examined, and if I offered an opinion on
one side or the other it might perhaps
prejudice the work going on.
I would remind hon. Members that we
are passing through a period of great depression in industry generally, and I have
no doubt that the great depression in
agriculture in particular is having its
effect on the work of this co-operative concern just as all businesses are affected. As
to the suggestion made by hon. Members
opposite as to winding up this concern,
forcing a liquidation and such things, it
must be remembered that if the bankers
were to wind up all the concerns that depended on them for credit the whole
business community would be wound up.
Mr. NIXON: A terrible state of
affairs.
Mr. POLLOCK: Would we be justified
now, when a co-operative concern of this
character is going through a period of
phenomenal depression, in taking this
particular opportunity for closing it up,
or are we sufficiently optimistic of the
future to assume that their operations, if
continued, will be successful? As I say,
the matter is being considered and I cannot tell exactly what the outcome will be,
but I can give the House generally the
opinion of the Government on the general
question as to whether it is desirable or
not desirable that encouragement should
be given to those interested in farming
work to carry on rather than to cripple
and interefere with the work continued
by this co-operative society. I cannot say
any more on the subject at the present
time. I think it would be in the interest
of the community generally if these
attacks were not pursued with a vindictiveness out of proportion to the character
of the enterprise.
Question, "That this House do now
adjourn," put, and agreed to.

minutes after Six o'clock until

meet on Thursday, the 20th of

at its rising shall adjourn until

(4) Nothing in this Section shall

Act.
Senate Amendment:

in any part of Ireland to drive or be

Sir DAWSON BATES: I beg to move,
"That this House do agree with the
Senate in the said Amendment."
Hon. Members will recollect that the
Clause in which this Amendment has been
inserted provides that a drivers' licence
issued in England will be valid in
Northern Ireland and similarly that the
Section of the Imperial Traffic Act of
1930 provides that a Northern Ireland
licence will be valid in Great Britain.
This reciprocal arrangement is, of course,
intended to facilitate visitors going from
one country to the other, but it is
obviously desirable to ensure that residents of each area should drive under a
licence obtained in the particular area in
which they reside, and not under licences
obtained in other countries. This Amendment is designed to ensure this, and to
make the intention of the Clause perfectly
clear. I do not think this Clause requires
any other explanation. The Clause is to
promote a reciprocal arrangement between
Great Britain and Northern Ireland. At
the same time the individual who owns
a motor car should take out a licence in
the particular country he resides in.

Traffic Act? The first thing we are led

has to produce a Northern Ireland driver's
licence.
Sir DAWSON BATES: No. Perhaps
I did not explain the matter fully. While
we are prepared to recognise the licence.

Sir DAWSON BATES: I beg to move,

This Amendment does not apply to side
cars.
They can carry as many people as

Amendment will make the roads safer for
ordinary road users and for motor

The ATTORNEY-GENERAL: Perhaps I might say a word with reference
to this matter under discussion by the

as our law, and it originated in this,
that the Crown servants are engaged by
the heads of the various Departments of
the Crown, either the Postmaster-
General, the Minister of Home Affairs,
or any other Minister of the Crown.
has been decided for hundreds of years
that there is no contract of service between the head of a Department and
the individuals under him from which
the relationship of master and servant
could be construed so as to make the head
of the Department responsible for the
individual acts of his servants. In the
theory of our law they take
positions or appointments directly from
the Crown, and the rule of our jurisprudence has always been that the Crown
can do no wrong and cannot be sued in
respect of any matter, either in respect
of the Crown itself or in respect of its
servants.

Captain CHICHESTER CLARK:
What about France?
Mr. DEVLIN: We know the reason

is another matter altogether. America

America, with all its advantages, has today over six million people unemployed,
and if America had the same system of

I merely point to these things in order

brought to a healthy condition again. That

has occupied our attention here since this

It is all very good to say that the

I do not know whether the hon. Member

The truth of the matter is that, like
America, like Australia, like England
herself, like a great many other countries
throughout the world, we here in this
small unit are suffering along with them.
I repeat in this House what I said once
before outside, namely, that I believe
when the crisis is over, when the turn
in the tide does come, as it surely will
come--and we are not such awful pessimists that we do not look forward to the
turn in the tide--the Ulster people will
be found in a better position to meet
that return of good trade than any other
part of the Empire. The reason I say
that is that Ulster men and Ulster women
have greater grit and greater determination, and, in many instances, greater skill
and knowledge in the businesses in which
they are employed. Therefore, although,

Ireland.
There is no use anyone trying to get
round the fact that at the present time,
in all the working-class districts in the
City of Belfast, there are thousands and
thousands of people in a state of semistarvation, and some of them in a state of
starvation. The Minister of Labour told
us the last time Parliament met that over
18,000 applicants for unemployment benefit had been rejected, and in a great many
cases there is nothing for them. The
Minister of Labour himself admits that
the Poor-Law Guardians do not come to
the relief of the people in the way that he
would like. I know that, and the Minister
will not dispute it.
Yesterday there called at my house
from 5 p.m. to 10 p.m. sixteen people.
Some of the tales I heard would draw a
tear from a stone. There were a woman
and daughter from Northumberland
Street with 14/- a week to live on.
There was a man, with four or five of
a family, who has 15/- a week to live on,
and he has to face a court of referees on
behalf of his wife, who was knocked off.
That is the sort of tale I hear every day,
every night and every morning. If anybody comes to me whose financial position
is fairly good, he goes very quickly.
What I want to know is what the Government are going to do for those people.
There is no use in telling us of the glories
of the past; there is no use in telling us
of the glories of the future. Read the
Rev. J. W. Stutt's letter, and tell us
what you are going to do for the starving
people at the present time. That is what
we want to know.
I switch off to another subject of which
