The question of the school is another matter
altogether, and you can argue that
from two sides I quite admit.
But that is
not what I am dealing with now. The
hon. Member opposite raised the question
of unemployment, and it is my duty to
reply to that, and that is what I am going
to reply to.
In the next place, the hon. Member for
Woodvale said he was going to criticise the
administration of the Unemployment
Fund. I do not at all object to his doing
that, because I can admit he never
does so, with the information which he
possesses unfairly. But at the same time
I do not think he would have brought
forward the case which he brought forward
to-day if he had known the whole truth as
I do, and for this reason. I would point
out that my Department has never wished
to dictate, nor presumed to dictate, to any
R.M. in the discharge of his responsible.
duties. The distinguished R.M. to whom
the hon. Member referred has on himself
the responsibility of giving his decisions,
and upon him alone rests the responsibility. But I feel it was not wrong of my
Department to point out in a general
way to the distinguished R.M. that
frauds upon the Unemployment Fund
were numerous, that no right-thinking
man desired that frauds should continue, and that there was very often
great difficulty in bringing those who
committed frauds upon it to justice, owing
to the difficulties at times of procuring
evidence. All that the Department asked
was that when the sentence was being
given it would be borne in mind that such
a sentence should be given as would be a
deterrent to others to do likewise.
Mr. NIXON: That was wrong.
Mr. ANDREWS: As regards the particular case which the hon. Member
raised I would like to point out that the
matter is sub judice and that in those
circumstances--
Mr. NIXON: Would you allow me one
question. That is a most serious statement. The case was dismissed by the
court. How is it sub judice? How does
that arise?
The
Mr. ANDREWS: It is this way.
case was dismissed without prejudice,
which I think the hon. Member knows
enough about courts to know is a different
thing altogether from a person being
absolutely acquitted. He was acquitted
of that particular charge.
Mr. NIXON: I appeal to you not to
degrade yourself further by going on.
Mr. ANDREWS: As a matter of fact
I am not going to refer to this case any
further, beyond saying this, that the responsibility whether the case goes on any
further or not does not rest with me.
rests with the Crown Solicitor.

Mr. NIXON: I deny that statement.
Mr. DEPUTY-SPEAKER: That must

I am

Mr. NIXON: With all due respect if

As
a matter of fact a case is pending.

I dispute that it is engaging the attention of either the Crown Solicitor or the
Deputy Crown Solicitor, who I believe.
are Mr. Carson and Mr. Mussen.
Mr. ANDREWS: Of course, if the
hon. Member will not accept as correct
the information which I possess. I
can do nothing more. But, as I have
said, I am not going to be drawn into
an argument about the case under the
special circumstances which exist at the
moment. There is very little more to
which I need refer, except this.
No suggestion, I maintain, has been put forward
by the Opposition during the debate
to-day which would in any way go to
relieve the unemployment situation in
Northern Ireland. I can only join with
the Prime Minister in saying that, no
matter what quarter the suggestion may
come from-
Mr. NIXON: Will you take one now?
Mr. ANDREWS- -we will gladly
welcome that suggestion, and if it is possible in fact to do-
Mr. NIXON: Will you take one now?
Mr. ANDREWS: But I would point
out to hon. Members opposite that we are
as anxious as they are or more anxious,
perhaps, if the whole truth were knownto help the people of Ulster. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear.) The hon. Mem.
ber (Mr. Nixon) keeps shouting at me
will I take a suggestion from him. The
only suggestion he made to-day-
Mr. NIXON: I have another for you.
Mr. DEPUTY - SPEAKER: Order,
order. In the course of a speech these
interruptions must not be maintained
continuously.
Mr. NIXON: I was not interrupting.
He was asking for suggestions.
Mr. DEPUTY-SPEAKER: I know,
but the hon Gentleman must not be
drawn into interruptions on that basis.
Mr. ANDREWS: The only suggestion
which the hon. Member for Woodvale (Mr.
Nixon) did make to-day was that we should
have given a subsidy for flax. He said
that if we had more flax grown we would
have more flax-pullers, we would have
more scutching done, and in fact there
would be a great deal more employment
given all over Northern Ireland. The
fact of the matter is that, owing to the
state of the industry, largely due, I maintain, to the dumping of foreign goods into
Northern Ireland-(Hon. Members: Hear,
hear) there is more flax than the industry
can use. The price of flax has been driven
down to somewhere between 4/- and 7/-
per stone, and every farmer who has
grown it has lost by so doing. Further,
if we had subsidised the growing of flax,
the hon. Member has suggested,
we would have encouraged other farmers to have grown the crop, and so
other farmers, in addition to those who
are already losing money, would have lost.
substantial sums. Therefore, I feel that
I am justified in maintaining that hon.
Members opposite, during the interval
between now and the time when we meet
again, had better get together themselves
and then unitedly come forward with some
concrete, practical suggestions for the
solution of the problem.

Oral Answers to Questions.
RICHHILL FARM TRAINING
CENTRE.
1. Major HALL-THOMPSON asked
the Minister of Labour whether he can
state the number of persons trained at
the Richhill Farm Training Centre; the
number of men who sailed to the
Dominions after a course of training; and
the number of such men who have since
returned to Northern Ireland.
The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.
Andrews): Seven hundred and sixtyseven men have been trained at the Richhill Farm Training Centre, of whom 505
sailed to Canada and 176 to Australia.
According to the Department's information 98 trainees have returned to Northern
Ireland, 93 from Canada and 5 from
Australia.
HOUSING SUBSIDIES.
2. Mr. GRANT (for Mr. O'Neill)
asked the Prime Minister whether it is
the intention of the Government to introduce legislation to continue the housing subsidies after the 31st March, 1931.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): I have been asked
by my right hon. Friend, the Prime
Minister, to answer this question.
The question of the continuance of the
system of housing subsidies after the 31st
March next is receiving the earnest consideration of the Government.
The hon. Member will appreciate that
in view of the very heavy financial commitments involved, a matter of this
character cannot be decided until all the
financial considerations have been fully
considered, but I hope to be in a position
to announce the Government's policy in
the matter at an early date.
COURSING OF CAPTIVE HARES.
3. Rev. Professor CORKEY asked the
Minister of Home Affairs whether his
attention has been called to the widespread dissatisfaction with the law as it
at present stands with regard to the
coursing of live captive hares, and
whether, in view of the fact that the bait-
Oral Answers
Oral Answers
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Rev. Professor Corkey]
ing of other harmless and innocent
animals has long since been prohibited by
law, and in view of the brutality
associated with the coursing of captive
hares, he will consider the question of introducing at an early date legislation to
make this practice illegal.
Sir DAWSON BATES: My attention
has been drawn to the correspondence and
discussions which have taken place in
connection with this matter, and the hon.
Member may rest assured that the whole
subject is being and will be carefully considered by the Government.
As the law now stands, under certain
conditions the coursing and hunting of
hares and other animals are exempted
from the provisions of the Cruelty to
Animals Acts, and the question as to
whether these exemptions should be removed is one which involves consideration
not only of the coursing of hares but also
of the hunting of animals generally.
The hon. Member will, therefore,
appreciate that the question involves consideration of the whole subject matter of
coursing and hunting from every aspect,
and that it would not therefore be possible to make any definite statement in
the matter at present.
ANCIENT RELICS IN THE BANN.
4. Major McCORMICK asked the
Minister of Finance whether it is a fact
that certain antique articles of gold and
silver were found in the River Bann
through dredging operations, and what
steps have been taken to ensure the
safety of any articles of archæological
value to the State.
The PRIME MINISTER: In the
absence of my right hon. Friend at an
important meeting this morning I have
been asked to take this question.
I am informed that no antique articles
of gold and silver, or, indeed, anything
of material value have up to the present
been recovered from the River Bann in
connection with the dredging operations.
which are now in progress. Under the
terms of the Bann contract which is in
force, adequate provision has been made.
for the transfer to the Ministry of
Finance of any articles of archæological
value which may be found during the
execution of the works.
PAYMENT
OF
BENEFIT.
UNEMPLOYMENT
McCORMICK
asked the
5. Major
Minister of Labour whether it is a fact
that an insured worker leaving this
country and going to America to obtain
work and coming back again is thereby
prevented from obtaining work or benefit
for twelve months by the Labour Exchange, though his wife and family and
home remained here.
Mr. ANDREWS: The answer is in the
negative.
To qualify for unemployment benefit
such a worker has to fulfil either the first
statutory condition requiring 30 contributions in two years or the transitional
condition requiring that he should be
normally employed in insurable employment. These conditions can be fulfilled
in less than twelve months.
No obstacle is placed by my Department in the way of an insured worker
obtaining work on return from America
except in the case of relief schemes in
Belfast where a residence qualification is
in force to give a preference to those permanently resident in the city or neighbourhood.
Major McCORMICK: In connection
with this matter may I ask the Minister
of Labour does he consider it fair or
proper that a man whose domicile is here
and who endeavours to do his best by
going away to seek for work should be
penalised to that extent?
Mr. ANDREWS: I have already stated
that no obstacle is put in the way of a
worker returning from America except as
regards relief schemes. As regards relief
schemes arranged with the Corporation,
preference is given to men resident in the
City.
Major McCORMICK: I understand the
Corporation have penalised such men
under their schemes. Would the Minister
allow these men to have a chance of getting work outside the area of the Corporation of Belfast on relief schemes?
Mr. ANDREWS:
very wide question.
That opens up a
In the rural districts the interests of the country workers
have to be considered.

6. Major McCORMICK asked
Prime Minister whether he is prepared to
appoint a committee representative of all
parties of this House to inquire into and
recommend certain reductions in expenditure in all departments of the Government, including administration.
The PRIME MINISTER: I have to
remind the hon. and gallant Member that
a Select Committee, consisting of Members
from both sides of the House, quite outside the Government, after exhaustive investigation and consultation with, among
others, Lord Colwyn, Lieut.-Conimander
E. Hilton Young, D.S.O., M.P., Finan
cial Secretary, and Sir Warran Fisher,
K.C.B., Permanent Secretary to the
British Treasury, and the Hon. F. M. B.
Fisher, ex-Minister of New Zealand, presented a unanimous report fixing the remuneration of Ministers and Parliamentary Secretaries, and that as regards the
civil service my right hon. Friend the
Minister of Finance dealt fully with the
subject on October the 14th last, besides
which the whole question can be raised
when the Estimates are presented in the
spring.
I am not prepared to appoint a Committee as suggested.

25 NOVEMBER 1930
PROROGATION.
Message from the Senate.
A Mesage was delivered by the Gentleman Usher of the Black Rod, as follows:
I am
commanded to inform this
honourable House that the Proclamation of His Grace the Governor of
Northern Ireland proroguing this present Session of Parliament is to be
communicated forthwith, and, further,
I am commanded to invite this houourable House to attend in the Senate in
order to hear the said Proclamation.
The House went, and having returned.
Mr. SPEAKER: This House has this
day attended in the Senate when the following Proclamation proroguing this
present Session of Parliament was read by
the Speaker of the Senate:-
BY HIS GRACE THE GOVERNOR
OF NORTHERN IRELAND.
A PROCLAMATION
For proroguing the present Parliament of
Northern Ireland.
WHEREAS it is provided by section
eleven of the Government of Ireland Act,
1920, as modified by and in pursuance of
certain enactments amending the said
Act, that the Governor of Northern Ireland shall in His Majesty's name
summon, prorogue and dissolve the Parliament of Northern Ireland;
AND WHEREAS it is desirable that this
present Parliament of Northern Ireland
should be prorogued to the third day of
March, One Thousand Nine Hundred
and Thirty-One.
NOW I, JAMES ALBERT ED-
WARD, DUKE OF ABERCORN,
KNIGHT OF THE MOST NOBLE
ORDER OF THE GARTER, KNIGHT
OF THE MOST ILLUSTRIOUS OR-
DER OF ST. PATRICK, Governor of
Northern Ireland, by this Proclamation
do publish and declare His Majesty's
Pleasure that the said Parliament be, as
from the reading of this Proclamation in
the Parliament of Northern Ireland,
prorogued to Tuesday, the Third day
of March, One Thousand Nine Hundred
and Thirty-One.
AND I do hereby further declare His
Majesty's Royal Will and Pleasure to be
that the said Parliament shall on the said
Third day of March, One Thousand Nine
Hundred and Thirty-One, assemble and
be holden for the despatch of divers
urgent and important affairs, and the
Senators and Members of the House of
Commons of Northern Ireland are hereby
required to give their attendance accordingly.
Given at the Council Chamber, Belfast,
this 25th day of November, One Thousand
Nine Hundred and Thirty.
Signed by his own hand.
ABERCORN.
GOD SAVE THE KING.
End of the Second Session (opened

Tuesday, 11th March, 1930) of the Third
Parliament of Northern Ireland in
the Twenty-first year of the Reign of
His Majesty King George the Fifth.
